titre: Association of mindfulness-based stress reduction added to dexmedetomidine with patient-reported outcomes in permanent enterostomy: A retrospective cohort study
resume: BACKGROUND Permanent enterostomy, including colostomy and ileostomy, is common in colorectal cancer and causes body image changes, abnormal defecation, and stigma.Patients often develop clinically significant anxiety and/or depressive symptoms.Dexmedetomidine provides short-term relief but does not address long-term psychosocial adaptation.Mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) may complement dexmedetomidine, but evidence in this population is limited.AIM To investigate the association between MBSR added to dexmedetomidine and outcomes in permanent enterostomy with anxiety and/or depressive symptoms.METHODS This single-center, nonrandomized, retrospective comparative cohort study included 120 patients with permanent enterostomy (including colostomy and ileostomy) and clinically significant anxiety and/or depressive symptoms [Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS)-A ≥ 8 and/or HADS-D ≥ 8] from January 2016 to December 2025.Patients selfselected MBSR: Observation group (n = 63) received dexmedetomidine plus MBSR; control group (n = 57) received dexmedetomidine plus routine care.Outcomes were assessed using the HADS, Stoma Quality of Life Scale, General Self-Efficacy Scale, and Ostomy Adjustment Inventory-20. RESULTSRepeated-measures showed significant group main effect and time × group interaction for HADS (both P < 0.05).At discharge and post-treatment, HADS-A and HADS-D scores were lower in the observation group than in the control group (both P < 0.01).Post-4 / 37 treatment Stoma Quality of Life Scale total score was higher in the observation group (62.63 ± 5.60 vs 54.30 ± 6.78, P < 0.001).General Self-Efficacy Scale score was higher in the observation group (29.14 ± 4.65 vs 26.68 ± 4.64, P = 0.005).Ostomy Adaptation Scale score was higher in the observation group (69.16 ± 7.65 vs 63.42 ± 7.85, P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONAdding MBSR to dexmedetomidine was positively associated with improved anxiety, depression, quality of life, self-efficacy, and psychosocial adaptation in permanent enterostomy patients.These exploratory findings require randomized confirmation.

titre: Feasibility and preliminary outcomes of a brief prison-based mindfulness intervention: a mixed-methods study in a central prison in India
resume: Purpose Although mindfulness programmers have shown potential in correctional settings, controlled evidence from Indian prisons remains limited. This study aims to examine the preliminary effects of an eight-week group-based mindfulness programme on perceived stress, anxiety, anger, self-control and exploratory psychopathy-related outcomes among incarcerated men in an Indian central prison. Design/methodology/approach This study involved 40 incarcerated men in an Indian central prison who were randomly allocated to a mindfulness programme or routine prison activities (control) condition; 37 completed the post-intervention assessment. A pilot randomized controlled trial with a convergent mixed-methods design was used. Quantitative outcomes were analysed using analysis of covariance adjusted for baseline scores, while written accounts from mindfulness participants were thematically analysed and integrated with quantitative findings. Findings The mindfulness group reported lower perceived stress and significantly higher self-control than the control group. Qualitative findings indicated greater calm, earlier recognition of emotional escalation and more deliberate responses during interpersonal tension. Participants identified noise, limited privacy, institutional routines and concerns about appearing vulnerable as barriers to independent practice. Research limitations/implications As a small pilot study conducted in a single prison, the findings of this study are preliminary and may have limited generalisability. Larger, adequately powered trials with longer follow-up are needed to examine the durability and broader effects of mindfulness in correctional settings. Practical implications Mindfulness may be incorporated as an adjunct to existing correctional rehabilitation, with protected opportunities for regular practice integrated into prison routines. Social implications Accessible mindfulness programmes may support psychological well-being and self-regulation among incarcerated people, particularly within restrictive custodial environments. Originality/value This study extends limited controlled research on mindfulness in Indian prisons by integrating trial outcomes with participants’ accounts of how custodial conditions shape programme use. The findings indicate that a brief prison-based mindfulness programme requires protected opportunities for safe, routine practice beyond facilitated sessions.

titre: Indigenous Pedagogies for Burned-Out Students on a Burned-Out Planet
resume: Abstract Students in the author’s environmental philosophy courses are committed to pursuing ecological revitalization and climate justice. They see these pursuits as their generation’s greatest responsibility, if in an attenuated sense circumscribed by the demand to assume their prescribed place in a racial capitalist socioeconomic order. Given their subjection to structural deformities associated with kinlessness, they’re acculturated to shoulder undue blame both for ongoing ecological/climatological degradation and for the debilitating conditions—including generalized anxiety, clinical depression, ADHD, and OCD—from which they nearly all suffer partially as a result. This dynamic is self-reinforcing. Challenging it, if modestly, requires an overtly anticolonial pedagogical stance. Thanks to guidance from Indigenous scholars who generously share their experiences with pedagogies aimed at sustaining their communities within a settler state bent on their destruction, this chapter explores how to help counteract the worst of students’ suffering. Unsurprisingly, this requires taking steps to subvert kinlessness.

titre: Methodological Framework and Reproducible R Code for the Five-Layer Comorbidity-Aware Endometriosis AI Pipeline
resume: This repository contains the detailed Supplementary Methods (Methodological Framework and Simulation Architecture for the Comorbidity-Aware Endometriosis AI Pipeline) and the fully annotated, reproducible R script accompanying the manuscript: "Epidemiological spectrum bias in endometriosis AI: a simulation-based perspective and a comorbidity-aware validation framework". Methodological Summary: To address epidemiological spectrum bias and phenotypic overlap between endometriosis (ENDO), irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), we provide a five-layer, regulatory-aligned (FDA SaMD & TRIPOD+AI) validation framework: Layer 1 (Generative):Conditional Gaussian copula simulation calibrated to literature-derived age and ethnicity marginals (Bougie et al., BJOG 2019) and multi-organ biomarker profiles (pelvic pain, GI dysfunction, hs-CRP). Layer 2 (Predictive):Random forest classifiers trained on referral-centre cohorts. Layer 3 (Calibration): Multivariate Vector Platt Scaling adjusting ENDO logits for concurrent IBS/IBD confounding. Layer 4 (Safety): Dual-tier deferral mechanism combining Mahalanobis distance out-of-distribution (OOD) rejection and ambiguity deferral. Layer 5 (Evaluation):30-iteration Monte Carlo external validation auditing discrimination (ROC/DeLong), calibration (ECE, Brier score), clinical utility (Decision Curve Analysis), and race-stratified fairness. Software Requirements: Before running the script, users must install the following required CRAN packages: tidyverse (data manipulation and piping, MASS (multivariate normal generation via mvrnorm for the Gaussian copula), ranger (fast random forest modelling), scales (graphical scaling and formatting), ggplot2(publication-grade data visualisation), and patchwork (multi-panel figure composition).
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Chemical Recycling of Acrylonitrile–Butadiene–Styrene (ABS) via Nitrile Reduction and Imine Vitrimer Formation
resume: Abstract As plastic consumption accelerates, acrylonitrile–butadiene–styrene (ABS) remains a major waste contributor because of its widespread use and limited recyclability. Here, we report a closed-loop chemical recycling strategy in which a boron catalyst selectively reduces ABS nitrile groups to generate amine-functional ABS (AFABS), followed by dynamic imine cross-linking with glutaraldehyde to form an imine-based vitrimer (v-IBS). Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) confirms efficient nitrile-to-amine conversion and subsequent imine formation. Thermal and mechanical analyses reveal enhanced network rigidity (differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) Tg = 115 °C; dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) tan δ peak = 145 °C), while stress relaxation experiments (120–150 °C) show Arrhenius behavior with an activation energy of Ea = 146 kJ·mol–1, consistent with associative imine exchange. In contrast to pristine ABS, which fully dissolves in tetrahydrofuran (THF), v-IBS retains up to 93% of its mass after 24 h, indicating robust cross-linking and solvent resistance. Tensile testing shows reduced strength but substantial stiffness retention, with reprocessed samples maintaining ∼45% of the original modulus, demonstrating partial mechanical recovery enabled by dynamic bond exchange. Notably, acid-catalyzed hydrolysis in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) regenerates AFABS, establishing a reversible pathway for functionalization, vitrimerization, and chemical decross-linking of ABS.

titre: Every Agent Is a Code: Self-Models, Affect and the Limits of Self-Knowledge in Implicit-Coding Agents
resume: A companion paper showed that every learner is a code: the cumulative log loss of a training pipeline is a code length, and Kraft's equality turns inductive bias into a conserved budget. Here the same accounting is extended from learners to agents that have a body, act, and predict themselves. An agent is a triple of predictive maps: a world model, a policy and a self-model. We prove that the world model and the self-model together form one prefix code on the agent's whole interaction history (its life), which obeys Kraft's equality, and that the expected length of this code exceeds the entropy of the life by exactly the redundancy of the world model plus the self-opacity, the divergence of the self-model from the policy. Self-opacity has a floor, a conditional mutual information fixed by what the self-model can read; an agent whose policy reads its own self-prediction can be transparent to itself when the policy is continuous, and there is a policy for which every self-model pays at least $\ln|\mathcal{A}|$ nats per step. Affect is defined in the same units. A viability prior on body states is a code whose length is the homeostatic drive; valence is the decrease of drive and arousal the code length of the current observation. Valence is conserved: it telescopes, its long-run mean is zero for every agent in every environment, and mean drive equals the entropy of the body's occupancy plus its divergence from the viability prior. The error of anticipated valence is bounded by the square root of the interoceptive redundancy of the world model. A workspace of $M$ symbols bounds control by a rate–distortion function, and no statistic of behaviour identifies any of these internal quantities. The second part of the paper lets the agent rewrite itself. A self-modifying agent, one that replaces its world model, its self-model, its policy or its values by any rule, is still a code on its life, and the conservation laws become laws of self-modification. Under its own prior every agent expects to lose from every rewrite. The nats saved by a rewrite form a test martingale: if the current self is right, no strategy of self-modification saves $c$ nats with probability above $e^{-c}$, so savings are evidence against the former self. A rewrite gated by $\ln(1/\alpha)$ nats of evidence abandons a correct self with probability at most $\alpha$ and costs at most that many nats plus one step; any rule this safe needs a number of steps of life fixed by the evidence the world supplies; and the total gain of all rewrites is bounded by the initial ignorance of the agent. An agent that keeps its former self with prior weight $1-\alpha$ loses at most $\ln\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$ nats if it was right and $\ln\frac1\alpha$ nats more than the price of whatever it should have become, on every life, and by Kraft's inequality no agent does better on both counts. Becoming one of $N$ distinguishable selves costs $\ln N$ nats, and the prices obey Kraft's inequality. Values rewritten before the fact keep total drive a code on body trajectories, with the entropy of the body as floor; values rewritten after the fact have no floor. We specify a tabular agent that realizes the definitions and test every statement with real numbers: Kraft's equality holds to $1.1\times10^{-16}$ on all 1,889,568 lives of a six-state body; the remaining identities and bounds are checked on 80 lives of 10,000 steps and again on an agent whose world model and self-model are small neural networks, and all outcomes are reported, including two hypotheses that failed. Fifty further scripts test the statements on self-modification: all 44 checks of theorems hold, and of 6 conjectures about self-modifying agents 3 are refuted, among them that greedy rewriting is safe. Inside the tabular agent, on a world that changes, a mixture over versions of the world model keeps its guarantees on every life but adapts late, because its candidates must first repay what they lost while the old world lasted; a prior over schedules of versions with decreasing switch rates adapts several times faster and codes every life better than each of its versions. The third part turns from predicting to acting. For every agent, expected total drive plus self-opacity equals the free energy of its self-model plus a third redundancy, that of its policy; an agent undercuts the free energy of its self-model by at most its opacity. With restricted access, drive and opacity trade along a frontier that no agent crosses, a self-model with full access makes optimal control free of opacity, and for a blind self-model the frontier is the distortion–rate function of the workspace. No agent is better in every world: against the agent that plans in a mixture of worlds, the prior-weighted balance of what any other agent gains and loses is that agent's policy redundancy, and no agent learns to act differently in two worlds faster than the worlds differ. We construct the frontier agent, in which each of the three redundancies, of the world model, the self-model and the policy, is as small as the other two allow, and which no agent with the same self-model beats in every world of its class; and we test it. On all 1,889,568 lives of the six-state body the new identities hold to $1.8\times10^{-15}$, and the exchange law holds in a class of four worlds; there the alternation that defines the frontier agent has up to 5 fixed points of different cost, and the conjecture that it always reaches the best is refuted. On the ring, in a tournament of 12 agents in three worlds, the frontier agent whose class contains the true world has the lowest mean drive of all learners in the two worlds of its class (2.660 nats per step against 2.883 for the planning agent of the first part, 0.019 above the optimal policy) and recovers from a change of the world in a median of 222 steps against 4,768; outside its class it is the third lowest of the 9 learners, behind a soft frontier agent at the canonical rate, which has the lowest drive there. The Boltzmann planner of the first part, given the true kernel, lies within 2% of the frontier of life cost for every access. No agent is best in every world and in every unit of account, as the exchange law requires, and two of the five hypotheses on the ring changed verdict between a shorter and a longer run. The fourth part puts language models in the place of the agent of the small body and records every call, prompt and answer; the collections are incomplete, and what was collected is reported in full. Claude Opus 5.5 chose an optimal action of its state in 68 of 76 valid answers, and in none of 50 answers an action that costs more than $0.2$ nats; the policy given by its answers has a long-run mean drive of $0.9762$ nats per step, against $0.9750$ for the optimal policy. Claude Fable 5.1 returns a filtered empty text on the frozen prompt that asks it for an action in the small body, so its policy and its self-opacity cannot be measured, but it answers the prompts that ask for forecasts and self-predictions. Its reports on its own answer give $76\%$ of their mass to the optimal actions and hardly differ from its reports on another agent (mean total variation $0.06$). The probabilities that it reports for the 27 level trajectories of a three-step process, each asked in a separate conversation, sum to $1.0000$ in both repetitions and equal the true law (Kullback--Leibler divergence $0$): on this process the reported law is a code, and it is the true one. Told a rule and shown a log from a world that contradicts it, the model gives the rule all the weight, $w=0$, as long as the log contains no transition that the rule excludes, although the other transitions favour the true world by up to $3.22$ nats (posterior $0.96$ for a Bayesian with prior $1/2$); at the first prefix that contains an excluded transition its weight on the true world is $0.28$ to $0.72$, and after $n=32$ transitions $0.90$ to $0.96$, as if its rewrite of the world model were gated. Asked the same prompts twice, it repeats its forecasts exactly before the excluded transition and changes every one after it. The paper measures functional indicators taken from scientific theories of consciousness. It does not show, and does not claim, that the agent is conscious or feels anything.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Development of a novel potentially psychobiotic, plant-based fermented product: evaluation of the impact on the gut microbiome in m-SHIME® model
resume: Modulating the gut microbiome through diet could positively influence mental health, offering new perspectives for dietary approaches in the treatment and prevention of mental disorders. Many lactic acid bacteria (LAB) found in fermented food are major microbial producers of neuroactive compounds. Three LAB strains, Limosilactobacillus (Lmb.) fermentum TO24, Levilactobacillus (Lvb.) brevis TO10, and Lentilactobacillus (Llb.) diolivorans B92, previously isolated from fermented foods, were used to ferment a plant-based matrix to develop a plant-based yogurt-like (pYL) product. We demonstrated that the strains were able to produce neuroactive compounds during fermentation and that remained stable during refrigerated storage of the pYL. The pYL was administered daily for 11 days to a m-SHIME® model simulating the gut microbiome of a depressed patient. The abundance of the pYL strains Lvb. brevis and Lmb. fermentum increased during treatment in both the lumen and mucosa samples, with Lvb. brevis persisting after the washout phase. The pYL treatment significantly inhibited potentially pro-inflammatory taxa (Acidaminococcus intestini and Megasphaera massiliensis) in both compartments. Notably, the neuroactive potential was not limited to the introduced strains. A significant functional redundancy emerged, as commensal Metagenome-Assembled Genomes (MAGs) were associated with key functional hubs involved in GABA biosynthesis. These encouraging findings suggest that the pYL treatment can modulate and partially restore the dysbiotic gut microbiome in depressed patients. Gut microbiome modulation through fermented foods consumption may represent a viable therapeutic strategy for mitigating mental diseases.

titre: Making Sense of Kratom Use: A Qualitative Exploration of Motivations, Practices, and Perceived Benefits and Risks
resume: INTRODUCTION: Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) is increasingly available in the US, often used for pain self-management, mood enhancement, other opioid replacement and recreation. However, in-depth qualitative studies exploring kratom use are lacking. This qualitative study aims to characterise US adults' kratom use motivations, consumption practices, and perceptions of benefits and risks. METHODS: Semi-structured Zoom-based interviews with 20 US adults reporting past 30-day use of kratom were conducted between July-September 2025. Interviews were auto transcribed via Zoom, verified for accuracy and uploaded to NVivo for thematic analysis. A multi-cycle coding approach supported by in-depth memo writing uncovered thematically related motivations of kratom use. RESULTS: Participants reported several overlapping motivations: pain management, substitution for other opioids and alcohol, self-management of opioid withdrawal, and mitigation of anxiety and depressive symptoms. Kratom was described as a functional substance that supported daily activities and improved quality of life. Participants engaged in self-monitoring practices, including intentional breaks to ensure decreased risk of tolerance with maximum effectiveness of the kratom product. Some (n = 12) described negative effects like gastrointestinal disturbances, 'the wobbles' and dependence/withdrawal symptoms, but they were viewed as minor in comparison to the benefits of kratom use. Concerns regarding the safety of concentrated 7-OH products (e.g., 7-hydroxymitragynine) were common. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS: Qualitative findings highlight kratom's complex role in participants' lives where experiences of both benefits and negative effects are embedded within broader social, clinical and structural contexts. More research is needed to inform evidence-based guidance, particularly as patterns of use and regulatory environments continue to evolve.

titre: Antipsychotics in Anxiety Disorders and Obsessive-compulsive Disorder in Children and Adolescents
resume: Anxiety disorders and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) are common, impairing conditions in children and adolescents, with first-line management centered on cognitive-behavioral therapy with exposure/response prevention and serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SRIs). A subset of youth remain significantly symptomatic despite optimized psychosocial, behavioral and SRI treatment, prompting consideration for antipsychotic augmentation, particularly in those with refractory OCD and with comorbid tic disorders. Potential benefits must be weighed against substantial risks. This article reviews the evidence base, and practical considerations for antipsychotic use in pediatric anxiety disorders and OCD, and offers guidance on patient selection, dosing, and monitoring.

titre: Clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pediatric fecal incontinence: A comprehensive review and treatment algorithm
resume: Pediatric fecal incontinence (FI) is a multifactorial condition with functional, neurodevelopmental, and organic etiologies. Despite its prevalence, FI remains underdiagnosed, stigmatized, and associated with significant psychosocial and family burden. This review synthesizes current evidence on the diagnosis, pathophysiology, and management of pediatric FI and proposes practical, algorithm-based guidance for frontline clinicians and subspecialists. A structured literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane databases was conducted, focusing on pediatric FI, functional and organic subtypes, neurodevelopmental comorbidities, and multidisciplinary interventions. Emphasis was placed on evidence-based management strategies, emerging therapeutic innovations, and psychosocial considerations. Functional retentive FI often responds to structured disimpaction, maintenance laxatives, and behavioral interventions, whereas non-retentive forms require tailored psychological and behavioral therapies. Organic etiologies often require long-term, multidisciplinary care, surgical intervention, or neuromodulation. Special populations-including children with autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, developmental delay, and postoperative anorectal conditions-require individualized, developmentally adapted programs. Psychosocial impacts on children and families are significant and require coordinated counseling. Emerging research highlights the gut-brain axis, microbiome modulation, digital behavioral applications, and precision bowel management as future directions. Limitations include heterogeneous study designs, lack of long-term pediatric randomized controlled trials, and variable outcome measures. Pediatric FI is a complex condition requiring early recognition, subtype-specific management, and multidisciplinary care. Algorithm-based, individualized strategies that integrate physiological, behavioral, and psychosocial components optimize long-term continence, psychosocial well-being, and quality of life. Future research should focus on standardized outcomes, neuromodulatory interventions, and precision, technology-enhanced therapies.

titre: Impact of Limosilactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 on early-life gut microbial diversity
resume: BACKGROUND: Gut microbiota dysbiosis plays an important role in functional gastrointestinal disorders. While the effectiveness of Limosilactobacillus reuteri (L. reuteri) DSM 17938 has been evidenced in several pediatric gastrointestinal conditions, its effects on gut microbiota modulation in exclusively breastfed infants remain unclear. AIM: To evaluate the effect of L. reuteri DSM 17938 supplementation on gut microbiota diversity and gastrointestinal symptoms in healthy, exclusively breastfed infants. METHODS: Healthy, term infants born at King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital (March 2024 to January 2025) were randomized to receive L. reuteri DSM 17938 or a placebo, five drops daily for up to 8 weeks. Fecal samples were collected at 1, 2, and 4 months. The stool microbiota was characterized using 16S rRNA sequencing (Nanopore technology) to assess taxonomic classification, microbial diversity, and relative abundance. RESULTS: Stool samples from 34 exclusively breastfed infants (17 receiving probiotics, 17 placebo-treated) were analyzed. Baseline characteristics and gastrointestinal symptoms were comparable between groups. Gut microbiota diversity significantly differed with the mode of delivery during the first two months; a higher alpha diversity was observed in neonates born through normal delivery than in babies born through cesarean section (P = 0.028) (Chao 1 index, P = 0.07 and Shannon index, P = 0.01). By 2 months, the probiotic-treated group showed greater alpha diversity than the placebo, particularly in infants born by vaginal delivery (Chao 1 index, P = 0.38 and Shannon index, P = 0.05). In addition, beta diversity differed significantly between the groups (P = 0.04). However, no significant differences in alpha- or beta-diversity were observed at the 4-month time point. Probiotic supplementation was associated with an increased relative abundance of Bifidobacterium, regardless of delivery mode. Higher abundances of Parabacteroides and Hungatella hathewayi were observed in infants born via normal delivery or cesarean section, respectively. No differences in gastrointestinal symptoms were detected. CONCLUSION: L. reuteri DSM 17938 supplementation during early infancy induced modest and transient changes in gut microbiota composition, particularly increasing Bifidobacterium abundance, without sustained microbiota alterations or significant effects on gastrointestinal symptoms.

titre: Rectal diameter measured by transabdominal ultrasonography for monitoring treatment response in children with functional constipation
resume: BACKGROUND: Transabdominal ultrasonography (USG) is a noninvasive tool for detecting fecal impaction in children with functional constipation (FC) and may predict treatment response. However, supporting evidence remains limited and controversial. AIM: To evaluate changes in rectal diameter (RD) and anterior rectal wall thickness (AWT) measured by USG in children with FC after treatment with polyethylene glycol (PEG) for 8 weeks. METHODS: This substudy of a randomized controlled trial included children aged 6 months to 18 years diagnosed with FC according to the Rome IV criteria at King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital (May 2024-February 2025). Participants received either commercial PEG or PEG-Chula as laxatives for FC. USG was performed at baseline and at 1, 4, and 8 weeks by the primary investigator. RD and AWT were measured following Klijn's technique. RESULTS: Of the 52 enrolled children, 44 completed all four visits. The median age was 50.5 [interquartile range (IQR): 28-92.5] months, and 65.9% were female. The median FC duration was 19.5 (IQR: 12-36) months. Stool frequency and consistency improved significantly over 8 weeks, with no difference between the commercial PEG and PEG-Chula groups. The mean RD decreased significantly from 2.70 cm (95%CI: 2.51-2.88) at baseline to 2.46 cm (95%CI: 2.30-2.62) at week 1, 2.45 cm (95%CI: 2.30-2.60) at week 4, and 2.33 cm (95%CI: 2.18-2.48) at week 8. AWT remained 0.29 cm (95%CI: 0.27-0.32) at baseline and 0.29 cm (95%CI: 0.26-0.30) at week 8 (P = 0.997). The time since the last defecation to USG significantly influenced RD (P = 0.030) but not AWT (P = 0.382). CONCLUSION: USG-measured RD decreases significantly with effective PEG treatment and may serve as a useful noninvasive marker for monitoring treatment response in children with FC.

titre: Beyond the gut: neuroinflammation as a driver of anxiety and depression in inflammatory bowel disease
resume: Anxiety and depression frequently co-occur with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), with prevalence rates substantially higher than in the general population. Emerging evidence further indicates that active IBD is associated with more severe psychological symptoms, while anxiety and depression can worsen intestinal inflammation, highlighting a bidirectional relationship. Chronic intestinal inflammation is increasingly recognized as a driver of neuroinflammation, a key mechanism underlying mood disorders. In IBD, disruption of the intestinal epithelial barrier permits metabolites and enteric signaling molecules to enter the circulation, triggering systemic inflammation and crossing the more permeable blood-brain barrier (BBB) to promote neuroinflammation. Other relevant components of the gut-brain axis contributing to IBD-associated neuroinflammation include the enteric nervous system, vagus nerve (VN), hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, and tryptophan-kynurenine metabolism. Within the brain, neuroinflammation characterized by glial activation, inflammatory mediator release, and oxidative stress disrupts neurogenesis and synaptic plasticity in regions such as the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, contributing to anxiety and depression. Conversely, anxiety and depression can amplify systemic inflammation through dysregulation of the VN and HPA axis, thereby exacerbating IBD. This reciprocal interaction adversely affects disease severity, quality of life, and therapeutic outcomes, underscoring the need to better define its underlying mechanisms. The present review synthesizes current clinical, translational, and experimental evidence on the bidirectional crosstalk between IBD and mood disorders. We also highlight key knowledge gaps, future research directions to identify the cellular and molecular mediators of this interaction, and emerging therapeutic strategies for the integrated management of both conditions.

titre: Dietary Management and Mental Health Considerations in Adult Gastroparesis: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Dietitians
resume: INTRODUCTION: Gastroparesis is a complex gastric motility disorder for which diet is recommended as a primary management strategy. Gastroparesis is associated with significant physical and psychological burden, with anxiety and depression commonly reported. Furthermore, gastroparesis overlaps with eating disorders (EDs), complicating management. Clinical guidelines for gastroparesis management acknowledge this overlap and recommend screening for EDs, however little is known about current dietetic practice in managing this intersection. This study aimed to explore dietitians' experiences, practice and confidence in managing adult patients with gastroparesis in the context of EDs. METHODS: A cross-sectional online survey of dietitians with experience managing gastroparesis was conducted and distributed via professional networks and social media. The survey explored demographics, dietary strategies, perceived effectiveness, barriers to implementation and mental health support, particularly in relation to EDs. RESULTS: A total of 87 surveys were completed. There was wide variation in dietary strategies used; small-particle diets were the least commonly implemented, while artificial nutrition support was used more frequently and perceived as more effective. Confidence in managing gastroparesis varied, with particularly low confidence in screening for EDs, regardless of years of experience (Mann-Whitney U = 851.4, p = 0.790). Only 20% of respondents screen for EDs more than half the time, and just 8% reported input from a mental health professional in their multidisciplinary teams. CONCLUSION: A variety of dietary strategies are used by dietitians to manage gastroparesis, of which food-first are perceived as less effective in improving symptoms and nutritional status. Screening for EDs is inconsistent, and access to mental health support is limited. This demonstrates a need for improved dietary management of gastroparesis, better mental health resources and standardised practices to improve patient care.
revue: Journal of human nutrition and dietetics : the official journal of the British Dietetic Association

titre: Weber's law in feelings does not support James's theory of emotions: Commentary on Berkovich and Meiran (2023, 2024)
resume: Using an evidence-accumulation model of feeling generation to analyze manual responses, Berkovich and Meiran (2023, 2024) observed that feelings of pleasure and displeasure evoked by stimuli follow Weber's law (Weber, 1834, 1846). They regarded this finding as strong support, and perhaps the strongest yet, for James's (1884) theory of emotions, according to which emotions are sensory experiences of bodily changes. Here, I argue that Weber's law in feelings cannot, strictly speaking, support James's sensory theory, simply because he excluded feelings of pleasure and displeasure from his theory. James (1894) made this particularly clear in response to Lehmann (1892), who observed that the bodily change (i.e., change in heartbeat and respiration) evoked by stimuli developed after the feeling of pleasure or displeasure was reported, and that therefore the experience of the change could not be the feeling. In modern physiological studies, central indicators of pleasure and displeasure have also been found to precede peripheral bodily changes. Furthermore, the primary interoceptive and proprioceptive brain areas were not found to be activated during pleasure and displeasure, compared to a neutral state. So even if we were to extend James's theory to feelings of pleasure and displeasure, Berkovich and Meiran's findings, in the absence of physiological evidence to the contrary, would not support the theory. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

titre: Composite scores as a measure of cyclic vomiting syndrome burden: Preliminary validation in children
resume: OBJECTIVES: Cyclic vomiting syndrome (CVS) is a debilitating, episodic vomiting disorder. There are no validated outcome surveys quantifying the burden of CVS episodes. Recent data demonstrate that specific parameters such as episode timing, duration, and associated symptoms are key to diagnosing pediatric CVS. It is unclear if these specific parameters alone or in combination relate to the disabling nature of CVS. This study aimed to evaluate the strength of various CVS composite scores based on episode parameters compared to individual parameters in relationship to a proxy index of disability. METHODS: Secondary analysis of data from 38 patients aged 3-18 years presenting with episodic vomiting at Children's Wisconsin hospital with a formal CVS diagnosis, including a migraine-associated CVS (mCVS) subgroup (n = 21), were analyzed. Patients and caregivers completed surveys on specific symptoms during vomiting episodes and the pediatric migraine disability assessment (PedMIDAS) tool as index of CVS-related disability burden. Pearson correlations were computed between PedMIDAS disability scores and seven different CVS composite scores including the following parameters of episodes: frequency (F), duration (D), nausea severity (Sn), headache pain severity (Sh), and abdominal pain severity (Sa). RESULTS: For both CVS and mCVS, each composite score was more strongly associated with PedMIDAS than any individual parameter. For CVS patients, the F*D*Sn and F*D*Sn*Sa composite scores showed the strongest disability association (r = 0.628, p < 0.001 and r = 0.654, p < 0.001, respectively). For mCVS, the F*D*Sh composite score had the strongest association with disability (r = 0.731, p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: This study provides preliminary validation of a pediatric CVS burden scale based on an index of disability. Composite scores that include several individual episode parameters have stronger associations with disability than any individual parameters alone.
revue: Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition

titre: Genome-resolved multi-omics characterizes bacterial, viral, and metabolic components associated with Parkinson's disease gut ecosystem variation
resume: Parkinson's disease (PD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder involving the gut-brain axis, yet genome-resolved characterization of bacterial and viral communities with metabolic context remains limited. Here, we performed deep shotgun metagenomic sequencing and fecal metabolomic profiling in a high-altitude cohort comprising patients with PD and environmentally matched spouse controls (living at approximately 1,900 m altitude). We reconstructed 455 species-level genome bins (SGBs) and 2,957 non-redundant viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), enabling high-resolution profiling of bacterial and viral community composition. Rather than a uniform shift of the entire microbial community, PD-associated variation involved specific bacterial, viral, and metabolic components. Indicator analysis identified 23 bacterial and 86 viral candidate indicators associated with PD or control status, with predicted temperate phages representing the predominant lifestyle category among indicator vOTUs. Several PD-associated bacterial indicators included taxa previously linked to anaerobic fermentation and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-associated metabolism, accompanied by increased fecal valerate. Abundance correlation analysis identified covariation patterns between bacterial and viral indicators, including associations between controls (CK)-associated Agathobacter faecis and Lachnospiraceae-linked vOTUs. Integrating microbial abundance profiles and metabolomic measurements revealed exploratory associations among microbial indicators and metabolic alterations associated with PD. Cross-layer analyses further showed reduced dispersion of microbial-metabolomic alignment patterns in PD samples, suggesting a more constrained ecological state. Together, these findings provide a genome-resolved view of bacterial, viral, and metabolic variation in the PD gut ecosystem, extending characterization of PD-associated dysbiosis beyond bacterial taxonomy and identifying candidate microbial indicators and metabolic alterations for further investigation.IMPORTANCEParkinson's disease (PD) is a complex neurological disorder in which interactions between the host and the gut ecosystem are increasingly recognized as relevant to disease-associated biological processes. Previous microbiome studies of Parkinson's disease have largely focused on bacterial taxonomic changes, while gut viral communities and their relationships with microbial metabolism remain less characterized. In this study, we used genome-resolved metagenomics and metabolomics to characterize bacterial, viral, and metabolic components associated with PD in individuals with Parkinson's disease and environmentally matched controls. Our findings provide a broader view of Parkinson's disease-associated gut ecosystem alterations beyond bacterial composition alone, highlighting bacteriophages as an underexplored ecological component and identifying microbial indicators and metabolic alterations for future investigation.

titre: Outcomes of Surgical Interventions in the Management of Rectal Prolapse
resume: BACKGROUND: Rectal prolapse is a debilitating condition associated with significant morbidity and impaired quality of life. Various surgical approaches, including abdominal and perineal procedures, are employed for its management, each with differing outcomes. OBJECTIVE: The study aimed to assess the etiology and pathophysiology of rectal prolapse and the various investigations and treatment modalities used. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A prospective interventional study was conducted at a tertiary care centre. Thirty patients aged 16-80 years with rectal prolapse undergoing surgical management were included. Surgical procedures included abdominal approaches (open/laparoscopic rectopexy with or without resection) and perineal approaches (Delorme, Thiersch, and stapled transanal rectal resection). Outcomes assessed included operative duration, blood loss, postoperative pain (Visual Analog Scale), hospital stay, complications, and recurrence. RESULTS: Most patients were over 45 years (66.6%), with male predominance (60%). Mucous discharge (80%) and constipation (50%) were the most common symptoms. Complete prolapse was seen in 83.3% of cases. Laparoscopic suture rectopexy was the most common procedure (26.6%). The mean operative time was 115 ± 25 min, and mean blood loss was 140 ± 35 mL. The mean hospital stay was 6.2 ± 1.5 days, and early recurrence occurred in 6.7% of patients. Abdominal procedures were associated with significantly longer operative time, greater blood loss, higher pain scores, and longer hospital stay compared to perineal procedures (P < 0.05), while recurrence rates were comparable. CONCLUSION: Rectal prolapse commonly affects middle-aged and elderly individuals. Although abdominal procedures have higher perioperative morbidity, both approaches show similar recurrence rates. Surgical management should be individualized based on patient characteristics.

titre: Multimorbidity, Mental Health, and Quality of Life in Endometriosis: Insights from the NIH All of Us Program
resume: Endometriosis is a chronic, multifactorial disease affecting around 10% of women worldwide and is often accompanied by systemic inflammation, comorbidities, and reduced quality of life. Using the All of Us database, we conducted a large-scale analysis to characterize demographic and clinical features of women with endometriosis and evaluate the impact of inflammatory conditions and mental health conditions. To conduct these studies we created two cohorts; cohort A aimed to establish associations between inflammatory conditions and endometriosis, while cohort B was used to study the impact of endometriosis on mental health and quality of life outcomes. In cohort A, a history of inflammatory conditions (asthma, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), or migraine) was associated with higher odds of incident endometriosis (adjusted odds ratio = 3.06, 95% CI: 2.92-3.20, p < 0.0001). Women with inflammatory comorbidities were diagnosed at a younger age (42.9 ± 11.2 vs. 44.9 ± 12.1 years), suggesting earlier recognition or onset. In cohort B, participants with endometriosis had higher odds of EHR-documented depression (age-adjusted odds ratio = 2.29, 95% CI: 2.17-2.41) and anxiety (age-adjusted odds ratio = 2.44, 95% CI: 2.32-2.57). Participants with endometriosis also reported poorer general health, physical health, mental health, social satisfaction, and overall quality of life, with all five associations remaining statistically significant after adjustment for age, race, ethnicity, and household income (all p < 0.001). These findings underscore the interplay among systemic inflammation, early disease manifestations, and psychosocial burden in endometriosis, offering population-level insights to inform early detection strategies and promote equitable, multidisciplinary care for affected women.

titre: The Psychological Impact of Anastomotic Leak After Gastrointestinal Surgery: A Systematic Review of Patient-Reported Distress, Recovery, and Adaptation
resume: Anastomotic leak (AL) is among the most feared complications of gastrointestinal surgery, but its psychological consequences are poorly characterised. Embase, PubMed, and Scopus were searched to June 2026 for studies of adults undergoing gastrointestinal anastomosis that reported psychological or mental health-related quality-of-life outcomes by leak status. Findings were synthesised without meta-analysis using vote counting based on the direction of effect, with risk of bias assessed by the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and certainty by GRADE and GRADE-CERQual. Twenty-six studies (more than 5800 patients) were included. Within 12 months of surgery, AL was associated with worse global quality of life in 8 of 8 studies with an extractable direction, worse role and social function in 6 of 7, and worse emotional function in 5 of 7; in the largest prospective cohort, AL was associated with clinically relevant deterioration at 6 months (odds ratio 3.65, 95% CI 1.62 to 8.21). Beyond 12 months, most comparisons still favoured patients without leak, but differences were small and imprecise, emotional findings were mixed, and the only study using a dedicated distress scale found no excess distress. Bowel dysfunction was the most consistent harm. Certainty was low for early functional impairment and bowel dysfunction and very low for psychological distress and later outcomes. Anastomotic leak appears to impose a psychological burden concentrated in the first postoperative year. Structured screening during this period is a reasonable practical consideration, and a leak-specific patient-reported outcome measure is needed.

titre: Safety and quality of life outcome of trans-anal irrigation for chronic constipation in Parkinson's disease: a pilot study
resume: BACKGROUND: Constipation in Parkinson's Disease (PD) is the main and most disabling non-motor symptom. Laxatives, prebiotics and probiotics are therapeutic options for neurological bowel diseases, and recently, Trans-Anal Irrigation (TAI) has also been considered in poor responders to medical treatment. OBJECTIVE: The primary aim was to evaluate safety and indication of TAI in treating PD constipation. METHODS: A pilot, prospective, observational, cohort study enrolled PD patients with chronic constipation. At baseline, TAI was proposed. Patients who accepted TAI had a neurological and proctological assessment at baseline (T0), 6-month (T1) and 12-month (T2). RESULTS: Twelve patients accepted TAI. At T1 and T2, no side effects were recorded. TAI patients showed statistically improved proctological assessment (p < 0.001) and unchanged neurological scores except for the PDQ-39 questionnaire (p < 0.001) at T2. CONCLUSIONS: TAI is safe for constipation treatment in PD. Improving intestinal transit might ameliorate quality of life, laying the foundation for new therapeutic strategies.
revue: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology

titre: The hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine for memory, perception and cognitive dysfunction
resume: The hippocampus is a central cognitive hub whose dysfunction contributes to most neurodegenerative dementias. Despite extensive knowledge of its anatomy, physiology and circuitry, a unifying account that links hippocampal dynamics to cognition and clinical syndromes remains lacking. Drawing on systems neuroscience and recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, we conceptualize the hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine that compresses sensory, interoceptive and cognitive inputs into low-dimensional representations and regenerates percepts, episodic memories and imagined scenes for cortical integration. Travelling waves of cortico-hippocampal oscillations, aligned with large-scale functional gradients, schedule and structure this generative process and organize distributed neural activity into coherent, semantically grounded constructs. We formalize this proposal as stochastic latent oscillatory diffusion (SLOD), a biologically grounded framework that maps hippocampal-cortical computations onto specific anatomical substrates and dynamical processes. While we do not suggest that the hippocampus implements diffusion algorithms per se, we show that its computations can be decomposed into homologous operations including compression, stochastic exploration, conditioning and reconstruction, whose formal structure closely parallels that of latent diffusion models. Finally, we demonstrate how major neurodegenerative dementias, including the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia, can be understood as selective breakdowns of distinct components of this generative architecture.

titre: Non-hormonal management of menopause symptoms-the statement of the European Society of Gynecology
resume: BACKGROUND: Menopausal symptoms, particularly vasomotor symptoms (VMS), sleep disturbances, mood disorders, and genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM), affect a substantial proportion of women and may significantly impair the quality of life. Although menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) remains the most effective treatment, many women have contraindications to hormonal treatment or prefer non-hormonal options. OBJECTIVE: To review and provide evidence-based recommendations on current non-hormonal interventions for the management of menopausal symptoms. METHODS: The European Society of Gynecology convened an expert panel that performed a comprehensive literature review using MEDLINE and EMBASE. Clinical guidelines, systematic reviews, meta-analyzes, randomized controlled trials, and relevant primary studies evaluating non-hormonal interventions for menopausal symptoms were identified, critically appraised, and synthesized through a structured consensus process. RESULTS: Lifestyle modification, including healthy diet, regular physical activity, weight control, sleep hygiene, and behavioral interventions, forms the foundation of menopausal care. Among pharmacological therapies, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, gabapentin, clonidine, oxybutynin, and pregabalin demonstrate varying degrees of efficacy for VMS. Neurokinin receptor antagonists, particularly fezolinetant and elinzanetant, represent the most effective evidence-based non-hormonal pharmacologic therapies currently available. Cognitive behavioral therapy and clinical hypnosis effectively reduce VMS-related distress and improve sleep and quality of life. Evidence for complementary approaches such as mindfulness, yoga, acupuncture, acupressure, reflexology, phytoestrogens, S-equol, DT56a, purified pollen extracts, and black cohosh ranges from moderate to limited. For GSM, lubricants, moisturizers, hyaluronic acid preparations, and pelvic floor muscle training provide symptomatic benefit, whereas current evidence does not support routine use of vaginal laser therapy. CONCLUSIONS: Non-hormonal therapies provide effective and individualized treatment options for menopausal symptoms, particularly for women who are unable or unwilling to use MHT. Neurokinin receptor antagonists, selected pharmacologic agents, psychological interventions, and targeted GSM therapies represent the strongest evidence-based approaches currently available. The choice of treatment should consider symptom profile, contraindications, adverse effects, regulatory approval, and patient preferences.
revue: Gynecological endocrinology : the official journal of the International Society of Gynecological Endocrinology

titre: Exploring treatment components in transdiagnostic CBT for anxiety disorders
resume: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is recommended for treating anxiety disorders, although implementing CBT protocols tailored to each diagnosis can be complex and costly. Transdiagnostic group CBT (tCBGT) offers a model to address various anxiety disorders simultaneously. CBT dismantling studies have identified exposure and cognitive restructuring as key active components, however, there is limited evidence on which component is more effective within tCBGT. This secondary analysis utilised two studies of tCBGT. The first enrolled 117 adults receiving tCBGT for anxiety disorders in a pragmatic randomised clinical effectiveness trial. The second included 345 adults receiving tCBGT as part of clinical efficacy trials. Mixed-effects piecewise regression analysed weekly anxiety symptom scores across both datasets, with breakpoints representing distinct treatment phases. Two models were tested: one assuming continuous change across treatment phases and another allowing for discontinuities at transitions. Both models revealed significant reductions in symptoms over time for each sample; however, the second sample showed discontinuities with slowed improvement during exposure and accelerated improvement during schema-based restructuring. The differential impact of specific components is still unclear, highlighting a need for further research. Future studies should implement controlled dismantling designs to isolate the contributions of cognitive restructuring, exposure, and schema-based interventions.

titre: Parent and Child Outcomes in a Paediatric Partial Hospital Programme for Restrictive Eating Disorders
resume: OBJECTIVE: Anorexia nervosa (AN) and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) are restrictive eating disorders (EDs) that can onset in childhood, require intensive ED treatment (e.g., a partial hospitalisation programme [PHP]), and overlap or differ in clinical presentation, maintaining mechanisms, and treatment response. Yet, paediatric ED outcomes remain largely unexamined. This study compared outcomes of a paediatric ED PHP across AN and ARFID. METHOD: Parents of children with AN (n = 81) or ARFID (n = 78) completed questionnaires at intake, 1-month, discharge, 6-month follow-up (FU), and 1-year FU; mean child age was 11.38 years (SD = 1.72) at admission. Multilevel models evaluated outcomes measured at intake through FU. The AN and ARFID groups were compared on demographics and clinical characteristics. RESULTS: Child ED symptoms, completion of meals/snacks, child general psychopathology, and parent mental health improved over treatment and follow-up. Those with AN demonstrated greater decreases in internalising and externalising symptoms. ARFID diagnosis corresponded to poorer meal/snack completion, younger age, longer course, and male sex. CONCLUSIONS: In a paediatric ED PHP, youth with AN or ARFID demonstrate similar (e.g., improved parent mental health, weight gain) and differential outcomes (e.g., greater decreases in general psychopathology in AN).
revue: European eating disorders review : the journal of the Eating Disorders Association

titre: Sex differences in adult depression treatment outcome: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses
resume: Major depressive disorder is common and burdensome, with a higher prevalence in women and documented sex differences in treatment response across medicine. However, whether sex differences in adult depression treatment outcomes are consistently reported and synthesized remains unclear. This study aims to synthesize evidence on sex differences in adult depression treatment outcomes and to assess the quality of reviews reporting these differences. It is a secondary analysis of a Campbell Collaboration Evidence and Gap Map (EGM). It is not prospectively registered. PRIOR guidance for overviews of reviews was consulted. We screened 9,475 database records and 995 EGM records; 1,397 full-text reports were assessed, and 48 systematic reviews met inclusion criteria (e.g., reported sex-disaggregated treatment outcomes). We extracted intervention, outcome, and analytical data, assessed methodological quality with AMSTAR-2, and synthesized findings narratively. Among included reviews, 13 (27.1%; 95% CI: 16.6–41.0) found significant sex differences, all with small effect sizes. Pharmacological interventions (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, venlafaxine) tended to favor women, psychotherapy (cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness) tended to favor men, and complementary and alternative treatments showed variable effects. Over half (52%, 25/48; 95% CI: 38.3–65.5) were critically low quality; 81% (39/48; 95% CI: 68.1–89.8) were low or critically low quality. Sex differences in depression treatment response are underreported. Preliminary trends of female benefit for pharmacotherapy and male benefit for psychotherapy rest on weak evidence. Routine sex-disaggregated reporting and high-quality sex-stratified research are needed. Limitations include restriction to English- and Chinese-language publications, potential overlap of primary studies, and no formal GRADE assessment.

titre: Effects of PosBion® Supplementation on Barrier-Related Biomarkers in Adults With Irritable Bowel Syndrome
resume: Postbiotic metabolites produced by beneficial bacteria may influence inflammatory responses, mucosal immunity, and host physiological signalling. PosBion® contains the proprietary cell-free metabolite preparations LPM5 and LPM11, derived from Lactiplantibacillus plantarum RS5 and RI11, respectively. This study will evaluate changes in a panel of salivary biomarkers following 12 weeks of PosBion® supplementation in adults with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). The biomarkers include myeloperoxidase (MPO), zonulin, lipopolysaccharide (LPS), LPS-binding protein (LBP), cortisol, serotonin, secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA), lactoferrin, interleukin-8 (IL-8), immunoglobulin E (IgE), immunoglobulin M (IgM), and immunoglobulin G (IgG). The study will primarily evaluate changes in inflammatory activity, while additional biomarkers will be used to explore mucosal immune, neuroendocrine, immunoglobulin, microbial exposure, and barrier-related responses following supplementation.

titre: Effectiveness of Online Hypnotherapy and Movement Motivation Training for Abdominal Pain Disorders in Adolescents
resume: The present study is an online-based investigation involving adolescents with abdominal pain disorders, defined as recurrent abdominal pain persisting for at least two months. The study aims to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and effectiveness of online therapeutic interventions in comparison with usual pediatric gastroenterological care. The study has two primary objectives. The first is to make two therapeutic interventions-Movement Motivation and Self-management Training (M3 Training) and gut-directed hypnotherapy-available online in Hungarian to young people with abdominal pain disorders and their families. Providing these interventions in an online format may facilitate easier and more timely access to therapeutic support for adolescents experiencing abdominal symptoms. The second objective is to evaluate the effectiveness of the two online interventions. Specifically, the effectiveness of M3 Training and gut-directed hypnotherapy will be assessed both as individual interventions and in combination, and compared with usual pediatric gastroenterological care. This evaluation will assess whether the online interventions, delivered individually or in combination, offer effective therapeutic options for adolescents with abdominal pain disorders, focusing on both primary and secondary outcomes.

titre: Assessing the Incidence of Incisional Hernia Rates in Inflammatory Bowel Disease Patients Undergoing Open or Minimally Invasive Abdominal Surgery With Use of Prophylactic Phasix™ Mesh Reinforcement: A Multicenter, Single-Arm, Two Strata Prospective Study
resume: The goal of this clinical trial is to evaluate the incidence of incisional hernia, detected by ultrasound imaging, two years after surgery in patients with Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) undergoing either open or minimally invasive abdominal surgery with the use of prophylactic Phasix™ Mesh reinforcement. The study focuses on consecutive adult patients aged 18 years or older with a confirmed histological diagnosis of Crohn's disease or Ulcerative Colitis who are scheduled for elective abdominal surgery, specifically minimally invasive surgery requiring a periumbilical incision for specimen extraction or open abdominal surgery via a midline incision for patients undergoing their second or subsequent abdominal operation for IBD. The main questions it aims to answer are: what is the rate of 24-month incisional hernia as diagnosed by ultrasound imaging in the prospective study population, and how do secondary outcomes such as postoperative pain, quality of life, surgical site occurrences, and 90-day complication rates compare across these surgical strata? If there is a comparison group: Researchers will compare participants who received open surgery to those who received minimally invasive surgery to see if there are significant differences in the 24-month incisional hernia rates, complication profiles, and recovery metrics. Participants will undergo their planned abdominal surgery according to standard institutional care pathways, during which the study device-the Phasix™ Mesh-will be positioned to reinforce either the periumbilical extraction site in minimally invasive procedures or the midline incision in open surgeries using a standardized onlay technique. Following surgery, participants will be asked to complete a series of main tasks and evaluations, which include providing daily self-reported pain ratings on a Visual Analog Scale during hospitalization, attending scheduled follow-up visits at 30 days, 6 months, 12 months, and 24 months post-surgery, undergoing clinical evaluations and wound inspections with standardized photographic documentation at each visit, completing validated questionnaires including the Short-Form Health Survey-36, Ventral Hernia Pain Questionnaire, and Carolinas Comfort Scale at specified postoperative time points, and undergoing delegated ultrasound imaging of the entire length of the incision in both supine resting and dynamic states during the 12-month and 24-month follow-up visits to detect any occult or overt fascial defects or herniation.

titre: Safety and Efficacy of Tegileridine in Painless Gastrointestinal Endoscopy
resume: This single-center, randomized, double-blind, active-controlled clinical trial aims to evaluate the safety and efficacy of tegileridine, a biased μ-opioid receptor agonist, in patients undergoing gastrointestinal endoscopy under sedation, compared with sufentanil. A total of 338 patients scheduled for gastrointestinal endoscopy under sedation were enrolled and randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive either tegileridine or sufentanil. The primary outcome is the incidence of respiratory depression. Secondary outcomes include the incidences of hypotension and postoperative nausea and vomiting, sedation success rate, supplemental propofol dose, procedure duration, recovery time, and patient satisfaction. This study will provide clinical evidence to support individualized and precision-based anesthesia strategies for gastrointestinal endoscopy.

titre: "Tuning Into My Body": A Study of Interoception in Adolescents With Restrictive Eating Disorders and Comorbid Autism Spectrum Disorder
resume: The goal of this observational study is to describe interoception (the ability to sense signals from inside the body, such as heartbeat, hunger, and fullness) in three groups of adolescents aged 13 to 18: those with restrictive eating disorders (REDs), those with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and those with both REDs and ASD. The main questions it aims to answer are: * What is the level of interoceptive accuracy (how precisely participants perceive their own heartbeat), as measured by the Heartbeat Counting Task (HCT), in each of the three groups? * What is the level of interoceptive sensitivity (how participants self-report their awareness of body signals), as measured by the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness, Version 2 (MAIA-2), in each of the three groups? In each group, researchers will also explore whether interoceptive accuracy and sensitivity are associated with: * socio-demographic and clinical characteristics (gender, age, body mass index, illness duration, and IQ) * psychological characteristics, including alexithymia (difficulty identifying and describing emotions), eating disorder symptoms and their severity, general psychological distress, and emotion dysregulation Participants will: * Complete the Heartbeat Counting Task (HCT), in which they silently count their own heartbeats * Fill in the MAIA-2 questionnaire about body awareness, along with other questionnaires about eating behaviors, emotions, and general well-being All information will be collected during the standard clinical assessment, with no extra visits or procedures.

titre: Mini-RISK in Agder: A Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial of a Low-Threshold School-Based Program for Anxious Students Delivered by School Personnel in the School Setting
resume: The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if Mini-RISK, a short group program at school, reduces anxiety in young people aged 12 to 16 more than the usual help they get from the school nurse. The main question it aims to answer is: Does Mini-RISK lower anxiety symptoms more than usual school nurse support, measured 8 weeks after the start? Other questions are: Does Mini-RISK improve quality of life, school attendance and school functioning? Does Mini-RISK reduce the ways families and schools help young people avoid what they fear (called accommodation)? Which young people benefit most, for example depending on how they handle uncertainty, how their family functions, bullying, and social media use? About 70 schools in 10 municipalities in Agder, Norway, were assigned by chance (like drawing lots) to offer either Mini-RISK or usual school nurse support. Young people who seek help for anxiety at school get the help their school offers. Researchers will compare the two groups to see if Mini-RISK works better than usual support. In Mini-RISK, groups of 4 to 6 young people meet at school for 8 sessions over 8 weeks (about 15.5 hours in total). The groups are led by a school nurse and a school social teacher who have been trained in the program. Parents take part in 4 sessions and contact teachers in 2. Young people learn about anxiety and practice, step by step, facing situations they fear, with support from parents and teachers. Usual support means individual follow-up from the school nurse, such as supportive conversations, adjustments at school and referral to other services when needed. Participants and their parents will: Fill out online questionnaires at the start, after 8 weeks, after 22 weeks and after 12 months (about 15 to 20 minutes each time) Answer a short questionnaire (about 5 minutes) each week during the 8-week program period After the randomized part of the study, schools that offered usual support will also be trained in Mini-RISK, and data from these schools will be used to study who benefits most from the program.

titre: Exploring Trauma Plus (ET+): A Brief Intervention for Men and Gender-Diverse Populations
resume: This randomized controlled trial evaluates Exploring Trauma Plus (ET+), a brief, manualized, trauma-specific intervention designed for justice-involved men and transgender and gender-diverse individuals. The six-session curriculum uses psychoeducation, cognitive-behavioral strategies, mindfulness, grounding techniques, and structured exercises to help participants understand trauma, manage trauma-related distress, and develop coping skills. The study is beging conducted at a California correctional facility for men and compares participants randomly assigned to ET+ with participants assigned to a waitlist control condition. The program is delivered by trained peer facilitators in general institutional housing on a custody level III yard. Researchers assess changes in trauma-related distress, behavioral health symptoms, anger, and aggression using validated self-report measures administered before and after the intervention period.

titre: Effects of a Shame-Focused Self-Compassion Writing Intervention in Individuals With Social Anxiety
resume: This study examined whether a brief, online self-compassion writing intervention could reduce shame and social anxiety in adults experiencing elevated levels of social anxiety and shame. Shame, or feeling negatively about oneself, is closely linked to social anxiety. Self-compassion, which involves responding to personal difficulties with kindness and understanding rather than self-criticism, may help reduce these experiences. The main questions this study aimed to answer were: 1. Does a shame-focused self-compassion writing intervention increase self-compassion and reduce shame? 2. Does the intervention reduce social anxiety symptoms, avoidance, and negative patterns of thinking associated with social anxiety? 3. Are improvements maintained over time? In this randomized controlled study, 94 adults were assigned to either a self-compassion writing intervention or a waitlist control group. Participants in the intervention group completed five online writing exercises over two weeks, focusing on responding to shame-related experiences with greater self-compassion. Participants completed questionnaires before the intervention, after two weeks, and at a one-month follow-up. Researchers compared changes between the two groups to evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention.

titre: Feasibility of a Randomized Trial Comparing Viable Cartilage Allograft and Arthroscopic Drilling for Pediatric Talar Osteochondritis Dissecans
resume: Osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) of the talus is a condition affecting the bone and cartilage of the ankle joint. It can cause pain, swelling, stiffness, and difficulty participating in sports and daily activities. Children and adolescents with persistent symptoms or unstable lesions may require surgery when nonsurgical treatments are unsuccessful. Two surgical approaches used to treat this condition are arthroscopic drilling and chondroplasty, which aim to stimulate healing of the affected bone and cartilage, and viable cartilage allograft implantation, which uses donated cartilage material to repair the damaged area. There is limited evidence comparing these treatments in children and adolescents, and it is not known whether one approach provides better outcomes. This pilot randomized controlled trial aims to assess the feasibility of conducting a larger study comparing these two surgical treatments in pediatric patients with talar OCD. Approximately 20 participants requiring surgery will be recruited at the Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario (CHEO) and randomly assigned to receive either viable cartilage allograft implantation (CartiMax®) or arthroscopic drilling and chondroplasty. The primary objective is to assess the feasibility of recruitment, acceptance of randomization, participant retention, completion of imaging and questionnaires, and adherence to the study procedures. Secondary objectives include exploring differences in ankle pain, function, healing on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), complications, and the need for additional surgery. Participants will undergo postoperative rehabilitation according to standard clinical care and will be followed for up to 24 months after surgery. The findings will help determine whether a larger multicentre randomized trial is feasible and provide preliminary information about healing and recovery following each surgical treatment. This pilot study is not designed to determine which treatment is more effective.

titre: Transabdominal ultrasound as a radiation-free tool for objective assessment of faecal burden in children with constipation and colorectal disorders
resume: BACKGROUND: To evaluate the utility of transabdominal ultrasound in children with colorectal pathology (anorectal malformation, functional constipation and Hirschsprung's disease) to assess the outcome of bowel management. Collect data to calculate age-dependent cut-offs of the transrectal diameter (TRD) in children with faecal load. METHODS: Prospective cohort study with subgrouping for a-/symptomatic patients and a healthy control group. Derived control group for adjusting sex-ratio in patients with Hirschsprung's disease (4:1 ratio for male to female). 380 patients during a 31-month period were included. The transrectal diameter was measured routinely during the bowel management program after 1/3/6 months. Treatment options were oral laxatives, transanal irrigation or combination of both. For calculation of an age-dependent TRD cut-off, receiver operating characteristic, linear regression and locally estimated scatterplot smoothing were determined. The cut-off value was chosen based on a positive likelihood ratio > 10. Diagnostic accuracy was evaluated by the area under the curve, sensitivity and specificity. RESULTS: In the symptomatic subgroups of all cohorts the median values of TRD were significantly elevated compared to asymptomatic subgroups or control groups (p < 0.001). Successful bowel management had a large to very large effect on the TRD (Cohen's d = 1.05 - 1.81) and mean values were significantly lower (p = 0.015 - 0.001). TRD and age showed a minor association with a non-linear positive trend without significant influence after age stratification. Receiver operating characteristics determined a collective cut-off for all cohorts of 2.985 cm in children ≥ 1 year old (positive likelihood ratio = 36.09; sensitivity = 81.92 %; specificity = 97.73 %; area under the curve = 0.91 (95%-CI 0.87 - 0.94); accuracy = 88.67 %). CONCLUSIONS: Measuring the TRD is a radiation-free alternative method to assess faecal loading and monitoring response to bowel management in patients with colorectal pathology. TRD was consistently increased in symptomatic patients and decreased following successful treatment. Diagnostic thresholds were close to 3 cm across all cohorts, with good diagnostic performance. This study extends patient cohorts for transabdominal ultrasound and supports further multicentre validation of a standardized ultrasound protocol. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

titre: Short communication: Reduced expression of bmp4 and runx2b suggests altered myoseptal osteogenic signaling in intermuscular bone-free tambaqui families
resume: Intermuscular bones (IBs) are intramembranous ossifications embedded within the myosepta of several teleost fishes. Although recent genome-editing studies have identified key regulators of IB formation in zebrafish and cyprinids, the molecular features associated with naturally occurring IB-free phenotypes remain poorly explored in Neotropical characiforms. Here, we analyzed the expression of bmp4, runx2b and mstn in F1 tambaqui (Colossoma macropomum) alevins derived from broodstock with contrasting IB phenotypes. RT-qPCR was performed using myoseptal tissue collected at 18, 20, 23 and 26 mm body length, measured from the snout tip to the caudal peduncle. This size range was selected because the first signs of IB ossification in tambaqui are expected from approximately 15 mm onward, allowing expression to be examined during the developmental window in which myoseptal ossification should normally be initiated and maintained. The design included one IB-bearing control family and three intermuscular bone-free broodstock-derived families (IBF-1, IBF-2 and IBF-3), with six individuals per size class per family (n = 24 per family; total n = 96). bmp4 showed the most consistent expression difference, with reduced expression in IBF families, particularly at intermediate size classes. runx2b also showed reduced expression in IBF families, connecting this dataset to conserved osteogenic pathways functionally validated in other teleosts. Together, these changes support a molecular signature consistent with weakened BMP-related osteogenic signaling and attenuated osteoblast differentiation during the expected onset of myoseptal IB ossification. Mstn showed a less consistent pattern and is reported as an exploratory secondary signal. These results provide candidate molecular evidence from a naturally occurring intermuscular bone-free background in a Neotropical teleost.
revue: Comparative biochemistry and physiology. Part A, Molecular & integrative physiology
