titre: Exclude or expose in irritable bowel syndrome study: what works for whom and how? Protocol for a randomised controlled trial of internet-delivered FODMAP diet versus exposure-based cognitive behavioural therapy
resume: INTRODUCTION: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a disorder of gut-brain interaction characterised by abdominal pain and altered bowel habits and is associated with reduced quality of life. Although several treatments are effective at the group level, treatment responses vary substantially between individuals, highlighting the need for personalised approaches. This trial investigates moderators and mediators of treatment response to two established IBS interventions to determine for whom treatments are most effective and how they exert their effects. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This parallel-group randomised controlled trial will enrol 235 adults with IBS from community, primary and tertiary care across Australia and the US. Participants will be randomised to a 12 week online fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides and polyols (FODMAP) diet intervention targeting reduction of fermentable carbohydrate intake or an exposure-based cognitive behavioural therapy (E-CBT) programme targeting symptom-related avoidance behaviours, each with therapist support (dietitian or psychologist, respectively). The primary objective is to assess moderators and mediators of treatment response on gastrointestinal symptom severity, measured using the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS-IBS), assessed weekly from baseline to week 12. Pre-specified moderators and mediators include gastrointestinal-specific anxiety and avoidance behaviour and total FODMAP intake; treatment preference will also be examined as a moderator. Treatment expectancy and credibility and therapeutic alliance will be assessed as covariates accounting for non-specific treatment effects. Secondary outcomes, assessed at baseline, post-treatment (12 weeks) and 3- and 6-month post-intervention follow-up, include IBS-specific symptom severity (measured using the IBS-Symptom Severity Scale, IBS-SSS), IBS-related quality of life, eating-related symptoms, psychological symptoms, extraintestinal symptom distress, stool frequency and consistency and gut microbiome composition and function. We will also assess gastrointestinal symptom severity by the GSRS-IBS at 3- and 6-month follow-up to assess maintenance. Linear mixed-effects models will assess treatment effects and moderation. Latent growth curve modelling and time-lagged mixed-effects models will examine mediation. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval was obtained from the University of Melbourne Human Research Ethics Committee (Project ID: 31186). This manuscript is based on protocol V.4.0 (06–04-26). Recruitment is ongoing. Results will be disseminated via peer-reviewed publications and presentations at scientific meetings. TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT06940596.

titre: l-Arginine Ameliorates IBS-D by Modulating the Ligilactobacillus murinus-LCA-FXR/eNOS Signaling Axis
resume: l-Arginine is a semiessential amino acid with diverse metabolic functions and has been implicated in gastrointestinal health through interactions with the gut microbiota; however, its therapeutic potential in diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) remains unclear. Here, an IBS-D mouse model was established in C57BL/6J mice, and multiomics analyses combined with in vivo and in vitro validation were performed to investigate the mechanisms underlying l-arginine-mediated protection. l-Arginine supplementation significantly alleviated IBS-D-like symptoms and improved intestinal barrier function. Transcriptomic analysis revealed the activation of the FXR/PI3K/AKT/eNOS signaling pathway, which was associated with enhanced nitric oxide production. Integrated metagenomic and transcriptomic analyses identified Ligilactobacillus murinus (L. murinus) as a key microbiota component associated with bile acid metabolism and eNOS expression. Furthermore, L. murinus transplantation reproduced the beneficial effects of l-arginine, and metabolomic analysis identified lithocholic acid (LCA) as a microbiota-derived metabolite involved in this process. In vitro experiments demonstrated that LCA alleviated lipopolysaccharide-induced epithelial inflammation and barrier dysfunction via FXR/eNOS activation. Collectively, these findings reveal that l-arginine ameliorates IBS-D through microbiota remodeling, LCA-mediated bile acid regulation, and activation of the colonic FXR/PI3K/AKT/eNOS axis, highlighting its potential as a microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategy.
revue: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry

titre: Neuroimaging of Anxiety in Mild Cognitive Impairment: Integrating Structural, Functional, Molecular, and Network Perspectives-A Narrative Review
resume: This narrative review summarizes neuroimaging evidence on the neurobiological correlates of anxiety symptoms in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) across the Alzheimer's disease continuum. A literature search was conducted in PubMed from 1 January 2015 to 30 June 2026. Structural magnetic resonance imaging studies link anxiety to atrophy in medial temporal and prefrontal-limbic regions, with white matter disruption in the cingulum bundle and uncinate fasciculus. Functional magnetic resonance imaging shows altered interactions among the default mode network, salience network, and central executive network. Molecular imaging points to limbic glucose hypometabolism, amyloid deposition, and neuroinflammation. Emerging vascular and peripheral biomarker data further implicate blood-brain barrier disruption and gut-brain axis alterations. Most of the literature is cross-sectional and relies on heterogeneous anxiety assessments. Findings are further complicated by symptom overlap with depression and other neuropsychiatric manifestations, and anxiety-specific imaging studies in MCI are relatively scarce. Direct evidence specific to anxiety in MCI remains limited; some findings discussed here are derived from studies of Alzheimer's disease dementia or general neuropsychiatric symptoms and should be interpreted accordingly. Longitudinal multimodal designs, standardized anxiety-specific instruments, and integrative models linking symptom dimensions to imaging and fluid biomarkers are needed to disentangle whether anxiety in MCI represents an early marker of neurodegeneration, a disease-course modifier, or both.

titre: Natural Glycosides in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Multi-Target Mechanisms via the Gut-Brain Axis
resume: The multifactorial complexity of neurodegenerative diseases (NDs), including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, limits the efficacy of single-target therapies. Natural glycosides exhibit promising neuroprotective potential, but their clinical translation is hindered by poor oral bioavailability and limited blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration. The gut-brain axis offers a framework for understanding their potential biological effects beyond direct central exposure. This review explores the multi-target mechanisms of natural glycosides in NDs, focusing on their interactions with the gut-brain axis. A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect for studies published up to June 2026. Relevant literature on glycosides, NDs, gut microbiota, microbial biotransformation, pharmacokinetics, and neuroprotective mechanisms was critically reviewed. Natural glycosides may affect ND-related processes through gut-mediated and systemic/central mechanisms. Poorly absorbed glycosides can interact with intestinal microbiota, potentially modulating microbial composition, intestinal barrier integrity, and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) production. Microbial biotransformation may generate metabolites with altered physicochemical properties and systemic exposure, potentially enhancing central nervous system accessibility in a compound-specific manner. Experimental evidence also suggests effects on neuroinflammation, mitochondrial homeostasis, autophagy, and synaptic function. However, most findings remain preclinical, with limited direct human evidence. The gut-brain axis provides a valuable perspective for understanding the biological activities of natural glycosides despite their limited oral bioavailability and BBB penetration. Further pharmacokinetic studies, causal investigations of microbiota-mediated effects, and controlled clinical trials are needed to establish their therapeutic potential in NDs.

titre: Traditional Chinese Medicine for Hepatocellular Carcinoma: An Evidence-Mapped Narrative Review of Clinical Certainty, Mechanisms, and Translational Gaps
resume: This evidence-mapped narrative review evaluates traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) across clinical, preclinical, computational, and theoretical evidence. The original search cutoff was June 2026, and the evidence map comprised 139 bibliographic records, originally distributed between 89 main-text references and 50 supplementary records. Targeted literature verification during revision supplemented this map with treatment benchmarks and relevant clinical studies. Certainty judgments are preliminary narrative assessments, not formal outcome-level GRADE ratings. TACE plus Chinese herbal medicine and selected standardized preparations show the most consistent, low-to-moderate preliminary clinical signal, mainly for short-term tumor response and quality-of-life-related outcomes. Individual survival-endpoint trials, including an Rg3-TACE trial and a multicenter postoperative Huaier trial, warrant separate consideration and do not establish a class-wide survival benefit. Clinical reports of TCM plus targeted agents exist, but their methodological limitations prevent firm conclusions. No prospective clinical efficacy evidence for TCM combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors was identified in this review. Mechanistic studies support hypotheses involving cell death, the tumor microenvironment, and the gut-liver axis; heterogeneous models and limited causal or exposure validation constrain translation. Postoperative prevention, palliative care, and pattern-based prescribing remain incompletely supported. Priorities are reproducible searches, product-specific multicenter trials with survival or validated patient-reported endpoints, pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic characterization, nutritional assessment, and staged safety evaluation before immunotherapy combination trials.

titre: Tuberculous Salpingo-Oophoritis Mimicking Ovarian Malignancy: A Case Report of a Diagnostic Dilemma
resume: Female genital tuberculosis (FGTB) is an uncommon form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis that poses a significant diagnostic challenge because it frequently mimics ovarian malignancy clinically, radiologically, and biochemically. We report the case of a 34-year-old multiparous woman who presented 66 days after cesarean delivery with progressive lower abdominal pain and a tender pelvic mass. Pelvic ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a complex left adnexal mass suspicious for ovarian malignancy, while serum CA-125 was elevated, further reinforcing the presumptive diagnosis. The patient subsequently underwent exploratory laparotomy with left salpingo-oophorectomy. Histopathological examination revealed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid granulomas, Langhans giant cells, and caseous necrosis, confirming tuberculous salpingo-oophoritis without evidence of malignancy. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient completed a standard 6-month anti-tuberculosis regimen with complete clinical recovery and progressive normalization of CA-125 levels during follow-up. This case highlights the diagnostic dilemma posed by FGTB, particularly in tuberculosis-endemic regions where the disease may closely resemble ovarian cancer. Elevated CA-125 should therefore be interpreted cautiously in premenopausal women, as it is a nonspecific marker that may also reflect benign inflammatory conditions. A high index of suspicion for FGTB, coupled with careful integration of clinical, radiological, and epidemiological findings into preoperative decision-making, is essential to facilitate timely diagnosis, appropriate management, prompt initiation of anti-tuberculosis therapy, and avoidance of unnecessary extensive surgical intervention while minimizing long-term reproductive morbidity.

titre: Oral bacterial lysate treatment for prevention of recurrent wheeze following severe bronchiolitis: protocol for an international multicentre randomised, placebo-controlled trial (BLIPA)
resume: BACKGROUND: Bronchiolitis is a common condition caused by a viral acute lower respiratory infection (ALRI) in infants. Severe bronchiolitis requiring hospitalisation is associated with increased risk of preschool wheeze and school-age asthma. Early exposure to microbial products modulating immune system development may help prevent later wheeze. Thus, this study evaluates whether an oral bacterial lysate after bronchiolitis hospitalisation reduces subsequent wheezing episodes. METHODS: This international multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tests bacterial lysate (OM85-BV; Broncho-Vaxom®) in infants after hospitalisation for bronchiolitis. Safety and efficacy will be assessed, and a subset will undergo exploratory mechanistic analyses. For 12-24 months post-discharge, parents/guardians will give one capsule of OM85-BV or placebo daily for 10 consecutive days each month. RESULTS: The primary endpoint is the number of parent/guardian-reported wheeze episodes 12-months after starting OM85-BV or placebo. Secondary outcomes at 12 or 24-months follow-up include clinical outcomes, parent-proxy quality-of-life scores, incidence of atopy, recurrent wheeze needing asthma medication, wheeze-related hospitalisations, number of ALRI episodes, and mechanistic data on systemic immune pathways and nasopharyngeal and gut microbiota. CONCLUSIONS: This international multicentre study will determine whether oral OM85-BV given for 10 consecutive days each month for 12-24 months reduces parent/guardian-reported recurrent wheeze episodes post-hospitalisation for bronchiolitis. TRIAL REGISTRATION (4): AZNCTR ACTRN12621001556831 (5/10/2021) and clinicaltrials.gov NCT05064631 (20/08/2020). Prospectively Registered. Approval to use the IMP in this clinical trial was provided by the Australian Government Therapeutic Goods Agency under the clinical trials notification scheme (TGA CTN: CT-2021-CTN-02639-1). IMPACT: Our study addresses a large unmet clinical need and research gap related to reducing recurrent wheeze in infants post-hospitalisation for bronchiolitis. If our hypothesis is correct, this study may lead to an implementable intervention to improve health outcomes by reducing recurrent wheeze episodes in infants and young children. Reductions in recurrent wheeze might also reduce the incidence of childhood asthma and improve the lung health trajectories of children hospitalised with severe bronchiolitis.

titre: French protocol for the diagnosis and management of chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis
resume: Chronic Nonbacterial Osteomyelitis (CNO) is a primary, non-infectious inflammatory bone disorder predominantly affecting children (median age 10 years), with a female predominance. It presents as bone pain with an inflammatory pattern, sometimes accompanied by localised swelling, and follows a relapsing-remitting course. Typical lesions involve the metaphysis of the lower limbs, while clavicular, mandibular, and vertebral involvement may also occur, the latter often being asymptomatic. Cutaneous manifestations (such as palmoplantar pustulosis), articular features, or gut inflammation may coexist, placing the disease within the broader spectrum of Synovitis, Acne, Pustulosis, Hyperostosis, and Osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. Diagnosis is based on imaging, with whole-body MRI being the gold standard in children. It reveals multiple, symmetric inflammatory bone lesions often exceeding the clinically apparent sites. Bone biopsy is reserved for atypical or unifocal presentations or when a diagnostic uncertainty persists. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are the first-line treatment. In refractory cases or in patients with vertebral involvement, second-line therapies - including intravenous bisphosphonates or TNF inhibitors - may be considered off-label. Management primarily aims to control pain and preserve quality of life. Overall prognosis is favourable, with spontaneous remission in most patients after a median disease duration of four years. However, up to 50% of patients still experience flares after five years, and orthopaedic sequelae or spinal deformities may persist. General practitioners play a key role in early recognition, appropriate referral to specialist care, avoidance of unnecessary bone biopsies, and initial therapeutic management.

titre: Longitudinal cohort study of immune-mediated inflammatory diseases within the systems medicine framework of the DREAM Centre: a study protocol
resume: INTRODUCTION: Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) are chronic disorders characterised by dysregulated immune responses affecting multiple organ systems, including the skin, joints and gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Progression across organ systems contributes to clinical heterogeneity and complicates prediction of disease course and treatment response. Systems medicine approaches integrating longitudinal clinical data with molecular profiling provide a framework to address these challenges. The DREAM (Dermatology REsearch Across Multiple disciplines) Centre applies a systems medicine approach to improve the understanding and prediction of disease trajectories and treatment response across IMIDs. The Centre aims to establish the MultiOrgan Systemic Autoimmune Inflammatory Conditions (MOSAIC) cohort as an integrated platform for this research. This protocol describes the first clinical component of MOSAIC, focusing on long-term follow-up of patients with multiorgan IMIDs. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This study is designed as a longitudinal follow-up study of a cohort previously enrolled in a randomised controlled trial at Aarhus University Hospital (2019–2022). The original trial enrolled patients diagnosed with at least two concurrent IMIDs affecting the skin (psoriasis, hidradenitis suppurativa), the joints (psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis) or the GI tract (inflammatory bowel disease). All 213 participants will be invited to a single follow-up visit. Assessments include standardised clinical examinations, validated patient-reported outcomes and biological sampling. The primary outcomes are inflammatory disease activity. Secondary outcomes include mental health, quality of life, physical function, work productivity and cardiovascular risk. Exploratory analyses will integrate multiomics data to identify clinical and molecular markers of disease progression and treatment response. ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: The study is approved by the Central Denmark Regional Ethics Committees (1-10-72-185-25). Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, scientific conferences and relevant patient organisations.

titre: Toxicity and patient-reported quality of life through 12 months following pelvis-inclusive once-weekly stereotactic body radiotherapy versus conventional IMRT for high-risk prostate cancer: updated results of the SRAM randomized phase II trial
resume: AIM: To compare toxicity through 12 months and patient-reported quality of life following pelvis-inclusive stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) versus conventional intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) in men with high-risk prostate cancer enrolled in the SRAM trial (NCT03938649). METHODS: Men with node-negative high-risk prostate cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to pelvis-inclusive SBRT or IMRT. SBRT was delivered 40 Gy to the prostate and 25 Gy to the pelvis in five once-weekly fractions; IMRT comprised 50 Gy to the prostate and pelvis followed by a 26 Gy prostate boost. Gastrointestinal (GI) and genitourinary (GU) toxicities were graded using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.0. Patient-reported outcomes were assessed using the Expanded Prostate Cancer Index (EPIC) and International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS). RESULTS: Among 121 evaluable patients, 60 received SBRT and 61 IMRT. Between 6 and 12 months after radiotherapy, grade ≥2 GI and GU toxicity occurred in 16.7 % versus 13.1 % (p = 0.583) and 11.7 % versus 16.4 % (p = 0.455) of patients, respectively, including one grade 3 rectal hemorrhage after SBRT. EPIC bowel scores were lower in the SBRT group at 9 months (83.2 vs. 92.4; p = 0.0022) and 12 months (82.5 vs. 90.1; p = 0.0181), reflecting greater declines from baseline. Other EPIC domains and IPSS outcomes were broadly similar between groups. CONCLUSION: Once-weekly pelvis-inclusive SBRT showed no significant difference in grade ≥2 GI and GU toxicity compared with conventional IMRT at 6-12 months, but was associated with worse patient-reported bowel quality of life at 9-12 months.
revue: Radiotherapy and oncology : journal of the European Society for Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology

titre: Food avoidance, disordered eating behaviors, and eating disorders in inflammatory bowel disease: a systematic review of prevalence and associated factors
resume: BACKGROUND: People living with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) commonly modify their diet, but when restriction becomes persistent or rigid, it may reflect one of a spectrum of disordered eating behavior(s). OBJECTIVE: To better understand restrictive eating behaviors in IBD, this systematic review synthesized how food avoidance, disordered eating behaviors and eating disorders are defined and measured, estimated their prevalence, and identified associated factors in adults with IBD. METHODS: Six databases (CENTRAL, EMBASE, MEDLINE, APA PsycINFO, CINAHL and AMED) were searched from inception to January 2026. Eligible studies were full-text, quantitative studies assessing restrictive eating behaviors and/or associated factors in adults with IBD. RESULTS: Thirty-three studies were included. There was substantial heterogeneity in measurement and definition of restrictive eating in IBD. Food avoidance was commonly reported (36-97%), particularly when framed around symptom avoidance or disease flares. Prevalence of disordered eating behaviors ranged from 4.8-77%, with limited evidence on diagnosed eating disorders. Restrictive eating was more frequently reported in Crohn's disease and during periods of active disease. Psychological factors, including gastrointestinal-specific anxiety, general psychological distress and restrictive dietary beliefs, were consistently associated with restrictive behaviors, often independently of disease activity. CONCLUSIONS: Restrictive eating behaviors are commonly reported in adults with IBD. However, inconsistent terminology and reliance on non-validated or non-disease-specific measures limit interpretation and clinical application. Greater conceptual clarity and development of clinically meaningful assessment tools are needed to distinguish adaptive dietary self-management from more rigid, potentially harmful eating patterns and to inform appropriate dietetic and psychosocial support.
revue: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics

titre: Symptom Monitoring With Patient-Reported Outcomes During Curative-Intent Radiation Treatment
resume: PURPOSE: Although symptom self-reporting improves clinical outcomes in patients with metastatic cancer receiving outpatient chemotherapy, the effects are not well established for patients undergoing radiation therapy (RT). In this randomized study, we assessed the impact of patient symptom self-reporting using the mobile Patient-Reported Outcomes version of the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events Administration system (mPROS) application during curative-intent RT with concurrent chemotherapy for gastrointestinal, gynecological, lung, central nervous system, and head and neck cancers on health-related quality of life. METHODS AND MATERIALS: Enrolled patients were randomly assigned to symptom self-reporting with mPROS (experimental [EXP]) or usual care (control [CON]). EXP arm participants were asked to report symptoms at least weekly; severe or worsening symptoms triggered alerts to the clinical team. Participants remained in the study until 3 months after completion of RT. The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System - 29 (PROMIS-29) was administered at baseline, completion of RT (end-of-treatment [EOT]), and 3 months after RT completion. Patient assessment of the usefulness of mPROS was measured via a 24-question exit survey using a 7-point Likert scale. RESULTS: There were 59 subjects enrolled, of which 55 (n = 28 EXP and n = 27 CON; mean age, 62.0 years; 69.1% male) completed at least 1 PROMIS-29. On average, EXP participants logged symptoms twice per week, with a mean of 15 severe attributes and 11 unique symptoms reported. There were no significant differences between mean changes in PROMIS-29 physical (EXP, ∆ -6.03 vs CON ∆ -4.04; P = .45) or mental (EXP ∆ -2.82 vs CON ∆ -2.17; P = .78) function scores from baseline to EOT. Likewise, there were no significant differences between median changes in PROMIS-29 physical (EXP ∆ -3.87 vs CON ∆ -2.22; P = .29) or mental (EXP ∆ -1.74 vs CON ∆ -1.39; P = .77) function scores from baseline to EOT. On multivariable linear regression adjusting for age, sex, race, ethnicity, and education, treatment arm was not a statistically significant predictor of physical [F(1,30) = 0.81; P = .38] or mental [F(1,30) = 0.00; P = .98] health scores at EOT. On the exit survey, mean scores for selected questions descriptively indicated high satisfaction and were as follows: care team understanding symptoms (6.27), feeling more involved in care (6.36), help with symptom tracking (6.18), and recommending mPROS to other patients (6.09). CONCLUSIONS: Use of mPROS to monitor symptoms, compared with usual care, did not result in statistically significant differences in physical or mental health-related quality of life. However, patients in the EXP group expressed high satisfaction with self-reporting, feeling more engaged in their cancer care, and helping them keep track of symptoms.

titre: Alexithymia in persons with neurodegenerative disease is associated with worse relationship quality for their care partners via shared negative affect
resume: Difficulty identifying and describing one's emotions (i.e., alexithymia) is associated with greater negative affect and poorer relationship quality and is common in people with neurodegenerative diseases (PWNDs). The pathways connecting alexithymia and poor relationship quality are not clear, but one candidate could be shared affect. This study investigates: 1) whether alexithymia in PWNDs was associated with worse relationship quality, 2) whether shared negative or positive affect were associated with relationship quality, and 3) the extent to which shared affect explained the relationship between alexithymia and relationship quality. Trained coders viewed video recordings of PWNDs and their spousal care partners (CPs) (N = 225) engaging in a 10-minute conversation about a relationship conflict and continuously rated the emotional valence of each dyad member. Results revealed that greater alexithymia in PWNDs was associated with worse relationship quality. Path analyses showed that greater shared negative, but not positive affect, partially explained this association.
revue: Clinical psychological science : a journal of the Association for Psychological Science

titre: Effects of resistance training on neuronal response to visual food cues in adults with overweight/obesity
resume: BACKGROUND: Individuals with overweight/obesity show altered neuronal response to food cues, but how exercise affects this response remains unclear. This study examined resistance training (RT) effects on neuronal response to visual food cues and eating behaviors in adults with overweight/obesity. We hypothesized RT would be associated with decreased response in brain regions involved in regulating energy intake and decreased ad libitum intake, with brain and behavioral changes correlated. Exploratory analyses evaluated RT effects on eating behaviors and whole-brain response and compared RT with a 12-week diet intervention. METHODS: Participants (N = 19) completed a visual food cues task during functional magnetic resonance imaging in fasted and fed states, before and after a 12-week RT program. Paired t-tests examined RT effects on response to high-calorie foods versus non-food objects in regions of interest (ROIs; dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, insula, nucleus accumbens), energy intake, Three Factor Eating Questionnaire, and whole-brain response. Repeated measures correlations examined associations between changes in ROIs and energy intake. Linear mixed models compared RT and diet (N = 17). RESULTS: RT was associated with decreased dietary disinhibition (p = 0.009) and increased restraint (p = 0.023). No significant within-group effects were observed on neuronal response, energy intake, or associations between the two. Between-group analyses demonstrated (1) increased restraint across groups (p = 0.017), with a stronger effect for diet, and (2) a significant group*time interaction in right posterior insula and left primary somatosensory cortex (p < 0.001), with decreased response following RT and increased response following diet. CONCLUSIONS: Despite an absence of observed changes in predefined ROIs or energy intake, RT may promote self-regulatory eating behaviors in adults with overweight/obesity. Exploratory analyses suggest RT and diet may have distinct effects on neuronal response to food cues, with RT decreasing and diet increasing response in interoceptive and sensory processing regions. Findings should be interpreted with caution, however, given the small, non-randomized sample. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT02047721 and NCT03985787.

titre: Janus in Thermosensation: The Dual Interoceptive-Exteroceptive Nature of Thermal Signals in Body Ownership
resume: Thermosensation has traditionally been studied for its essential role in survival, enabling detection of environmental thermal stimuli and the maintenance of thermal homeostasis. Interestingly, unlike most sensory systems, thermosensation provides information about both the external world and the body's internal physiological state. In this review, we conceptualize these two dimensions as exteroceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the thermal properties of external objects and the environment, and interoceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the body's thermal state. Growing evidence suggests that this dual nature serves functions that extend beyond survival and homeostasis. Alterations in both thermal perception and thermoregulation have been associated with changes in body ownership, the experience that one's body belongs to oneself, while manipulations of thermal signals can influence ownership itself. Here, we review the physiological and neural bases of exteroceptive and interoceptive thermosensation, from peripheral encoding to central processing, and examine their relationship with body ownership in healthy and clinical populations. We discuss evidence suggesting partially distinct yet potentially convergent neural substrates for these two dimensions of thermosensation, highlighting the insular cortex and its broader connectivity network as a candidate through which thermal information may sustain body ownership. Finally, we consider how emerging neurotechnologies offer new opportunities to investigate the contribution of thermosensation to body ownership while also opening novel avenues for neurorehabilitation. We propose that thermosensation represents an underexplored contributor to body ownership, opening new avenues for future research on how bodily and environmental thermal signals are integrated to support the sense of self.
revue: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience

titre: Six Challenges for a Mechanistic Science of Human Interoception
resume: Human interoception has become a major focus of systems, cognitive, and clinical neuroscience. Work across the past decade has shown that signals originating within the body shape perception, emotion, cognition, behavior, and health. Despite rapid methodological and conceptual progress, which substantially expanded our understanding of how bodily signals are processed and represented, much of the field remains constrained by descriptive methods. As these approaches passively assess bodily signals or subjective awareness, they have limited ability to establish causal mechanisms or translate interoceptive findings into clinically informative frameworks. Here, we identify six challenges and corresponding methodological directions for advancing human interoception research: strengthening integration of animal and human models, developing causal perturbation paradigms, capturing interoception in ecologically valid contexts, standardizing multidimensional measurement across bodily systems, adjudicating between computational accounts, and translating mechanistic insights into clinically informative models of health and disease. These challenges are best understood as linked requirements for moving interoception research from relevance to mechanism. Together, they highlight the need to move beyond predominantly static, passive, and single-modality approaches toward studies that can test how internal bodily signals relate to neural activity, behavior, and health.
revue: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience

titre: Emotional awareness in children and adolescents with functional somatic disorders: a systematic review
resume: INTRODUCTION: Functional somatic symptoms (FSS) and functional somatic disorders (FSDs) are common in children and adolescents and are associated with reduced quality of life. Emotional awareness (EA) has been proposed as a psychological factor potentially associated with FSS/FSDs. This review investigated the association between EA and FSS/FSDs in children and adolescents. METHODS: PubMed, PsycINFO, Embase, and Scopus were systematically searched using predefined terms related to EA and FSS/FSDs in children and adolescents (0-18 years). Title/abstract screening, full-text review, and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. RESULTS: Of 1,579 records identified, 17 studies comprising 7,023 participants met the inclusion criteria. Sixteen studies included questionnaire-based measures of EA and generally indicated greater difficulties in several aspects of EA among children and adolescents with FSS/FSDs compared with healthy or clinical controls or peers with varying levels of somatic complaints. The most consistent finding was greater Difficulty Identifying Emotions. Three studies included task-based measures, with differences observed in Difficulty Verbally Expressing Emotions and Experiencing Negative Emotions. CONCLUSIONS: Children and adolescents with FSS/FSDs show greater difficulties in several aspects of EA, with the most consistent association observed for Difficulty Identifying Emotions. However, substantial heterogeneity in populations, measures, comparison groups, and study quality limits the strength of the conclusions. The findings provide a rationale for further investigating the role of EA in pediatric FSS/FSD, including whether EA may represent a relevant treatment target. Future research should use longitudinal designs, integrate questionnaire- and task-based measures, and account for psychiatric comorbidities.

titre: Barriers to Complementary and Integrative Health Use Among Veterans on Long-Term Opioid Therapy
resume: BACKGROUND: Complementary and integrative health (CIH) therapies are increasingly promoted within the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) as nonpharmacologic approaches and adjuncts to long-term opioid therapy (LTOT) for chronic pain. However, uptake remains modest, and barriers to initiation and continuation are poorly understood. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 126 Veterans with chronic pain on LTOT who had no CIH utilization documented in VHA electronic health records between July 1, 2017, and December 31, 2022. Participants were sampled from a national VHA cohort of over 280,000 Veterans. Respondents reported familiarity with nine CIH services-acupuncture, biofeedback, guided imagery, clinical hypnosis, therapeutic massage, meditation, tai chi/qi gong, yoga, and chiropractic care-as well as prior use and reasons for non-use or discontinuation. Barriers were summarized overall and stratified by age, sex, and race. RESULTS: Fewer than 10% of Veterans reported regular use of most modalities, with chiropractic care as the exception (23% regular use). Common reasons for non-use included lack of knowledge about eligibility, uncertainty about how to begin, and skepticism about effectiveness. Discontinuation was most often attributed to perceived ineffectiveness, cost, and logistical challenges. Younger Veterans more frequently reported not knowing they were eligible or how to start, while White Veterans more often cited doubts about effectiveness, and Black Veterans reported discomfort with particular modalities. Self-practice therapies (yoga and meditation) were more commonly practiced at home; whereas hands-on therapies (acupuncture, chiropractic care, and massage) were largely accessed in community settings where cost and logistics were prominent barriers. CONCLUSIONS: Substantial barriers remain to CIH service engagement among Veterans on LTOT, spanning awareness, logistics, and personal comfort. Targeted education, streamlined referrals, and strategies to manage early expectations may improve uptake and sustainment.
revue: Journal of integrative and complementary medicine

titre: Effects and mechanisms of mindfulness acceptance commitment training on anxiety and cognitive flexibility in elite taekwondo athletes: A randomized controlled trial
resume: Competitive anxiety is a common challenge in elite taekwondo, where athletes must regulate pressure and rapidly adapt to changing tactical demands. This randomized controlled trial examined the effects of Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment (MAC) training on competitive anxiety and cognitive flexibility in elite taekwondo athletes. Eighty athletes were randomly assigned to an 8-week MAC group (n = 40) or an active Psychological Skills Training control group (PST; n = 40). Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0), immediately post-intervention (T1), and 3-month follow-up (T2) using self-report questionnaires and a computerized task-switching paradigm. Significant Group × Time interactions were found for cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety, self-confidence, cognitive flexibility, and task-switching switch cost (all p < .01), indicating that changes differed between groups over time. The MAC group showed larger improvements in anxiety-related outcomes, self-confidence, and cognitive flexibility, with medium-to-large effects and the strongest effect for reduced switch cost (d = 1.67). Mediation analyses suggested that increased mindfulness and reduced experiential avoidance partially explained these changes. These findings provide preliminary evidence that MAC training may improve psychological regulation and adaptive cognitive functioning in elite taekwondo athletes, although further studies with larger samples and competition-based assessments are warranted.

titre: Mindfulness-based stress reduction for sleep quality and emotional state in menopause-related insomnia symptoms
resume: This study examined the efficacy and safety of mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) for menopause-related insomnia symptoms, with a focus on anxiety, depression, sleep quality, coping styles and quality of life. Eighty-two patients with menopause-related insomnia symptoms were randomized into an experimental group (n = 41, MBSR plus routine health intervention) and a control group (n = 41, routine health intervention) for a 12-week intervention. Emotional state, sleep quality, disease coping styles and quality of life were assessed using standardized scales, with intervention adherence and adverse events recorded as secondary outcomes. Compared with routine care alone, the MBSR group achieved significantly larger decreases in Self-Rating Anxiety Scale and Self-Rating Depression Scale scores, lower Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores, more positive improvements in disease coping styles and more pronounced gains in several quality-of-life dimensions, particularly physical, psychological and social functioning (p 0.05). The adverse event incidence was below 5% in both groups, with no serious adverse events reported. This study confirms that 12-week MBSR is a safe and effective intervention for improving sleep quality, negative emotions, coping styles and quality of life in patients with menopause-related insomnia symptoms. Menopause-related insomnia symptoms are a common issue for women aged 45–60 years, often linked to anxiety, depression and poor quality of life, with current treatments having limitations like side effects or low adherence. This 12-week study tested mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) plus routine care in 41 women with menopause-related insomnia symptoms (vs. 41 with routine care only). MBSR combined offline group training and online self-practice, covering breath awareness, body scanning, emotion regulation and daily mindfulness integration. Results showed that MBSR reduced anxiety scores by 15.4% and depression scores by 15.5%, and improved sleep quality (25.5% Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index score reduction, especially sleep latency/efficiency) far better than routine care alone. MBSR also boosted active disease coping, with notable gains observed in several quality-of-life dimensions, particularly physical, psychological and social functioning. The intervention had high adherence (offline 90.24%, online 87.80%) and low mild adverse events (<5%), with no serious issues. In short, 12-week MBSR is a safe, effective non-pharmacological approach to improve sleep, ease negative emotions and enhance well-being for women with menopause-related insomnia symptoms.
revue: Climacteric : the journal of the International Menopause Society

titre: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy modulates dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activation during self-referential processing in obsessive-compulsive disorder
resume: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) has emerged as a promising strategy for patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) who do not fully respond to cognitive behavioral therapy. However, the neurobiological mechanisms underlying the effects of MBCT remain unclear. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is a critical tool for identifying brain changes associated with therapeutic interventions. We aimed to identify the neurobiological underpinnings of MBCT for clinically complex OCD by evaluating task-based fMRI during self-referential processing. Thirty-one patients with OCD (i.e., 15 randomized to a 3-month MBCT program and 16 to a treatment-as-usual group) underwent task-based fMRI scanning sessions focused on self-referential processing at baseline and after 3 months. During the fMRI sessions, participants completed a self-referential processing task, where they responded "yes" or "no" to whether an adjective described themselves. A flexible factorial model and within-group paired t-tests were used to evaluate the impact of the treatment group on longitudinal changes in brain activation. Our analyses revealed a group-by-time interaction in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) activity during self-referential processing. Patients with OCD treated with MBCT showed a reduction in dlPFC activation. An exploratory psychophysiological interaction analysis did not identify significant group-by-time changes in task-dependent functional connectivity between the dlPFC and regions within the default mode network. This study highlights that MBCT was associated with reduced dlPFC recruitment during self-referential processing in OCD, potentially reflecting less reliance on executive control during self-referential judgments. This dlPFC down-shift offers a plausible neurobiological correlate of MBCT effects in OCD.

titre: Why Patients with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder Have Difficulty Inhibiting Responses: A Dual-Path Hypothesis
resume: BACKGROUND: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is characterized by impaired response inhibition, yet the mechanisms underlying this impairment remain unclear. Building on Resource-Control Theory and Christoff et al's (2016) dynamic framework of mind-wandering (MW), we propose a dual-path hypothesis of response inhibition. This model suggests that MW may have different associations with inhibitory control depending on whether it is linked to relatively goal-directed internal thought or to repetitive thoughts such as rumination and obsession. METHODS: A total of 134 patients with OCD and 70 healthy controls (HCs) were enrolled. All participants completed the stop-signal task (SST). Mind-wandering was assessed using the Mind-Wandering Questionnaire (MWQ), while inhibitory control was evaluated using conventional indices, including stop-signal reaction time (SSRT) and stop-signal delay (SSD), together with intraindividual response-time variability (IIRTV), an index of attentional control. Group differences were examined using standard statistical tests, and structural equation modeling (SEM) was used to test the proposed dual-path model. RESULTS: Compared with HCs, patients with OCD showed poorer inhibitory control, reflected by shorter SSD, longer SSRT, and higher IIRTV. Go-trial accuracy and reaction time did not differ significantly between groups. SEM supported two indirect pathways from MW to inhibition: one through lower IIRTV and shorter SSRT, and another through rumination or obsession, increased IIRTV, and longer SSRT. CONCLUSION: The findings provide preliminary support for a dual-path account of response inhibition in OCD. Inhibition difficulties may reflect dynamic associations among MW, repetitive thought, and attentional control, rather than global cognitive decline.

titre: Capturing Habits in Humans: Neural Circuitry, Computations, and Clinical Mechanisms
resume: Habits allow repeated behaviors to be executed efficiently, but habitual control can contribute to maladaptive inflexibility when it dominates despite changing goals or consequences. This review examines recent advances in understanding habitual control across neural circuits, computation, clinical phenotypes, and measurement. We first consider dorsomedial striatal mechanisms that support action-outcome learning and flexible goal-directed behavior and how chronic stress can alter striatal inputs to bias learning toward habitual control. Progress on what computational reinforcement-learning accounts for arbitration between goal-directed and habitual systems is described along prefrontal mechanisms guiding model-based control, action perseveration, and compulsivity in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). A wider behavioral spectrum beyond action initiation is provided, reviewing emerging work on habitual inhibition and frontostriatal circuit dynamics of avoidance in OCD. Recent laboratory paradigms aim to reveal habit formation more sensitively than traditional outcome-devaluation paradigms, whereas real-world digital approaches use smartphones, wearables, and intensive longitudinal measurement to track habit formation and expression in everyday life. Integrating these approaches can help link habits to physiology, symptoms and neural circuits across laboratory to real-world and clinical contexts.
revue: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience

titre: Comparative efficacy and tolerability of pharmacological interventions for the acute treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder across the lifespan: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
resume: BACKGROUND: Pharmacological treatment is recommended for obsessive-compulsive disorder. Several options are available, yet little is known on comparative effects of individual medications. We aimed to elucidate the efficacy and tolerability of pharmacotherapy for people with obsessive-compulsive disorder, across the lifespan. METHODS: We did a systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing short-term pharmacological interventions for obsessive-compulsive disorder. We searched multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, PsycInfo, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, for literature on licensed or recommended pharmacological treatments for obsessive-compulsive disorder, without age restrictions, from database inception up to March 11, 2026. We included double-blind, randomised controlled trials with outcomes between 8 and 16 weeks. Two reviewers independently and in duplicate extracted outcomes, with a quality check done by a third reviewer. Primary outcomes were efficacy, defined as change from baseline score, and tolerability, defined as the proportion of participants discontinuing treatment due to adverse events. Separately for children and adolescents (aged 0-17 years) and adults (aged ≥18 years), we calculated standardised mean differences (SMDs) and odds ratios (ORs) with random-effects pairwise and network meta-analysis. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework. People with lived experience of obsessive-compulsive disorder were involved in the entire review process, including protocol development, writing, and interpretation of the findings. The study was preregistered in Open Science Framework (identifier 4V3GS). FINDINGS: We included 52 randomised controlled trials with 7316 participants. Nine trials were included for children and adolescents (N=822; median age 12·5 years [IQR 11·6-13·2]; 352 [55%] male and 285 [45%] female among 637 participants with reported sex distribution). 43 trials were included for adults (N=6494; median age 36·4 years [35·0-37·9]; 3105 [49%] male and 3200 [51%] female among 6305 participants with reported sex distribution). Data on ethnicity were reported in 15 (29%) of 52 randomised controlled trials, using inconsistent definitions. In children and adolescents, clomipramine was more efficacious than placebo (SMD -1·19, 95% CI -1·73 to -0·64, CINeMA low), as were sertraline (-0·52, -0·80 to -0·02, low), fluoxetine (-0·43, -0·76 to -0·10, low), and fluvoxamine (-0·39, -0·71 to -0·07, low). Clomipramine was more efficacious than fluoxetine (SMD -0·75, 95% CI -1·39 to -0·11; very low), fluvoxamine (-0·79, -1·43 to -0·16; very low), paroxetine (-0·87, -1·51 to -0·22; very low), and sertraline (-0·87, -1·51 to -0·22; very low). Only sertraline was less tolerable than placebo (OR 4·51, 95% CI 1·36 to 14·96; low). In adults, clomipramine (SMD -0·71, 95% CI -0·88 to -0·54; high), fluvoxamine (-0·63, -0·83 to -0·43; high), paroxetine (-0·51, -0·73 to -0·29; moderate), sertraline (-0·49, -0·70 to -0·28; moderate), escitalopram (-0·43, -0·85 to -0·02; moderate), and fluoxetine (-0·37, -0·6 to -0·08; moderate) were more efficacious than placebo, and clomipramine was more efficacious than fluoxetine (-0·34, -0·65 to -0·04; low). Clomipramine (OR 4·65, 95% CI 3·27 to 6·60; moderate), fluvoxamine (2·73, 1·77 to 4·20; moderate), fluoxetine (2·52, 1·27 to 4·98; moderate), sertraline (2·23, 1·49 to 3·34; moderate), and paroxetine (1·99, 1·36 to 2·93; moderate) were less tolerable than placebo. Clomipramine was less tolerable than all active comparators (OR range 1·70 to 3·50; moderate) except fluoxetine (moderate) and venlafaxine (low). INTERPRETATION: Clomipramine showed the largest estimated efficacy for obsessive-compulsive disorder but had a lower tolerability than SSRIs. The evidence of its superiority over individual SSRIs was more pronounced in children and adolescents. Our findings suggest that the trade-off between efficacy and tolerability should be discussed within an individualised, shared, decision-making framework. FUNDING: None.

titre: Associations between typhoon exposure and mental disorders: a population-based ecological time-series study
resume: Typhoons impose multi-dimensional impacts on society, yet the broad spectrum of subsequent mental health morbidity remains under-investigated in large-scale populations. This study aimed to explore the longitudinal association between typhoon exposure and the outpatient department visits for various mental disorders. We conducted a population-based retrospective cohort study in Taiwan. Quasi-Poisson regression models analyzed lagged associations between landfall typhoons and daily outpatient department (OPD) visits for major depressive disorder (MDD), anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, substance use disorder (SUD), bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. Significant associations were found for all studied disorders except schizophrenia. The strongest impact occurred during weeks 4-6 post-typhoon (IRRs: 1.01-1.16). A "dose-response" relationship was observed during the first week, where higher typhoon intensity correlated with increased clinical mental health visits. Females exhibited significantly higher OPD visit for SUD than males across the observation period. Typhoon exposure significantly elevates the risk of diverse mental disorders, with effects peaking after the immediate emergency phase. These findings necessitate a transition toward integrated and climate-resilient mental health frameworks that prioritize targeted screening during the 4-to-6-week post-disaster window.

titre: Endosomal signalling of protease-activated receptor-2 amplifies histamine-induced pain of irritable bowel syndrome
Determinants of Long-Term Bowel Function and Quality of Life Following PSARP for Anorectal Malformations
resume: Abstract Purpose Anorectal malformations (ARM) are associated with substantial variability in long-term bowel function. Although anatomical severity and associated anomalies are identified determinants of outcome, the influence of surgical timing remains controversial. This study evaluated predictors of long-term bowel function and health-related quality of life following posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP). Methods A national single-center cross-sectional study included patients with ARM treated by PSARP between 1997 and 2019 and aged ≥ 3 years at follow-up. Functional outcomes were assessed using the Bowel Function Score (BFS), and health-related quality of life using the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL). Associations between outcomes, surgical timing, ARM subtype, and associated anomalies were assessed using uni- and multivariable analyses. Results Fifty-six patients were included (57% female). Median BFS was 16.0 (IQR 12.8–19.0); 39% achieved normal bowel function (BFS ≥ 18). Constipation and soiling were present in 46% and 57% of patients, respectively. Bowel function differed significantly among ARM subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis H = 17.07, p = 0.004). In multivariable analysis, spinal anomalies were independently associated with lower BFS (β − 5.38, p = 0.009), whereas age at definitive reconstruction was not associated with bowel function (p = 0.286). Better bowel function correlated with higher PedsQL scores (ρ = 0.43, p = 0.002). Conclusion Long-term bowel function after PSARP is primarily determined by anatomical and neurological factors rather than surgical timing. Better bowel function is associated with improved quality of life, supporting long-term multidisciplinary follow-up in patients with ARM.

titre: Aperiodic Exponent as an EEG Marker of Interoceptive Attention during Gastric Fullness
resume: Gastric interoceptive attention to internal, bodily signals such as hunger, satiety, and fullness are important for regulating feeding behaviors. However, abnormal processing or sensitivity to these can lead to disorders that result in overly restrictive or excessive consumption, highlighting the need for better understanding of the cortical processing of these cues. Specifically, understanding cortical representations of self-perceived gastric fullness have yet to be studied in humans. In this work, we demonstrate that consistently across individuals, the broadband power spectral density of EEG signals, as quantified by the aperiodic exponent, flattens after individuals drink water until fullness. Simultaneous measures of the stomach and heart demonstrate increased vagal drive to peripheral organs. We further find that changes in cortical aperiodic exponent patterns are associated with changes in the frequency of gastric oscillations. Overall, this suggests that the EEG aperiodic exponent may be a useful noninvasive biomarker for assessing gastric interoceptive attention.

titre: Distributional Connexed Cognition (DCC): An Experience-Driven Architecture for Artificial Agents
resume: Abstract Current artificial intelligence is fundamentally data-driven, relying on human-imposed training sets and hard-coded algorithmic rules that lack the capacity for autonomous, experience-based adaptation. To address this, I propose an Experience-Driven AI architecture where system behavior emerges from autonomous, accumulated experiential traces rather than pre-programmed datasets. Grounded in the neuro-functional principles of the brain and strictly constrained by the CISR (Co, I-layer, S-layer, R-layer) meta-theoretical framework, I first synthesize neuroscientific evidence regarding interoception, exteroception, prioprioception and endogenous signals, dopaminergic gating and channels (the gray and white matters), and the "free won't" veto mechanism (dFMC) to construct Connexed Cognition which is a continuous, pre-conscious integration process mapping multi-source signals. I then formalize this into the Connexed Conscious Architecture (CCA) , a four-stage pipeline (Orientation, Competition, Binding, Evaluation) that synthesizes existing five major consciousness theories into a unified functional model. Finally, I operationalize this theory via Distributional Connexed Cognition (DCC), a design method featuring a distributed, modality-specific memory architecture and an associated experience registration process. To manage decision making, DCC implements two nested decision loops: a rapid dFMC micro-loop for local alternative prediction search after a local veto, and the macro-loop for global re-observation when micro-loop becomes in-feasible. Through preliminary A1 experiments, we demonstrate three primary contributions: 1. Bayesian Correlation: The system autonomously selects actions by matching current static observations against historical traces via a localized Bayesian distance metric, rather than executing explicit rules. 2. Recursive Condensation: Over repeated cycles, new traces overlap with old ones. The system transforms raw experiential traces into condensed knowledge. Through algorithmic memory collapse (simulating synaptic pruning), non-core elements fade, shrinking Bayesian distances and transforming raw matching into generalized, situation-specific knowledge. 3. Autonomous Analogy: Unlike Large Language Models that "regurgitate" human data, A1 generates self-referential analogies derived purely from its own experiential history, demonstrating functional self-agency. Crucially, we address the philosophical boundary of AI consciousness. While the recursive refinement of S-layer functions technically reconstructs and functionally approximates the triggering conditions of the I-layer, it does not violate CISR’s non-identity axiom. It does not generate actual phenomenology. Instead, it establishes a novel technical foundation for AI accountability, where autonomous actions are justified by, and grounded in, the system's own unique experiential history.

titre: From transdiagnostic compulsivity to clinical applications: a computational psychiatry approach to bridge research and clinic
resume: Compulsivity, the maladaptive persistence of behaviour despite adverse consequences, is central to obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and has been increasingly conceptualised as a transdiagnostic dimension spanning multiple neuropsychiatric disorders. Research within computational psychiatry has linked dimensional compulsivity to two candidate mechanisms: impaired goal-directed control and elevated metacognitive confidence. Here, we take a clinical perspective addressing how insights from these findings can be brought into practice. We first ask how dimensional compulsivity measures should be interpreted with respect to clinical presentations and discuss conflicts between the general population findings and clinical data. We highlight several challenges facing clinical implementation: effect sizes are small, goal-directed control has not been shown to change with either pharmacotherapy or psychological therapy, and the overconfidence associated with dimensional compulsivity contrasts with the reduced confidence reported in patients with OCD. We argue these discrepancies are informative rather than disqualifying and set out a translational roadmap for mechanistically informed detection and transdiagnostic intervention. Specifically, we suggest that screening and digital monitoring of dimensional compulsivity, combined with cognitive and mechanistic phenotyping to guide psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy, may ultimately improve outcomes across diagnostic boundaries.

titre: PSYCHOLOGICAL, DIGITAL, DIETARY AND MICROBIOTA-TARGETED INTERVENTIONS FOR FUNCTIONAL ABDOMINAL PAIN DISORDERS IN CHILDREN: A STRUCTURED REVIEW OF 2025–2026 EVIDENCE
resume: Functional abdominal pain disorders (FAPDs) are among the most common gastrointestinal complaints in children, and the evidence supporting individual treatments has been described as broad but shallow. This structured narrative review (IMRAD format) aimed to summarize recent evidence on psychological, digital, dietary and microbiota-targeted interventions for FAPDs in children and to outline implications for medical institutions. PubMed was searched on 11 November 2026 with three topic-specific queries; titles and abstracts of 75 unique records were screened and 23 publications from 2025–2026 were included: two guidance documents, six systematic reviews or meta-analyses, eight randomized controlled trials (RCTs), four uncontrolled or secondary-analysis studies of remotely delivered therapies, two qualitative studies and one cross-sectional study. The pooled prevalence of FAPDs in children was 10.89%. Internet-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy improved gastrointestinal symptoms, also in children with psychiatric comorbidity (n=120; sustained at 6 months) and in a further cohort of 87 youths (SMD 1.17), and web-based hypnotherapy in a primary-care RCT (n=152) produced earlier relief at 3 and 6 months, although the difference at 12 months was not significant. An educational website (RCT, n=166) reduced pain-related disability. Probiotics gave modest benefit (complete symptom resolution 35.3% vs 22.8%; number needed to treat 7), while evidence for Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 was inconsistent. Peppermint oil was not superior to placebo (RCT, n=228); psyllium fiber (n=109) and fecal microbiota transplantation (n=32) showed promising but preliminary results. Remotely delivered psychological and educational programs currently have the most consistent signals, whereas dietary and microbiota-targeted options remain mixed and are supported by small trials. Medical institutions can prioritize Rome IV-based diagnosis, parent-inclusive education and access to adapted remote psychological programs.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Neutralidade na Alíquota e Neutralidade na Carga: o Imposto Seletivo de 2027 e a base do IBS, da CBS e do ICMS
resume: Uma medida reprodutível da distância entre as duas leituras de 'manter a carga do IPI', de 2027 a 2033. Working Paper 03/2026 — Série de Pesquisa Tributação Seletiva (Luiz F. Research — Quantificação Aplicada). Instrumento de demonstração: IS-01 (modelo is.neutralidade-ipi v1.1.0). Papers anteriores da série: Working Papers 01/2026 e 02/2026. Working paper metodológico. titre: The gut microbiota-gut-brain axis in sepsis-associated encephalopathy: pathogenesis and therapeutic potential of probiotics
resume: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) represents one of the most severe complications of sepsis, characterized by diffuse neurological dysfunction. It significantly increases patient mortality and can lead to long-term neuropsychiatric sequelae, including cognitive deficits, anxiety, and depression, thereby imposing a substantial societal burden. Currently, the clinical diagnosis of SAE relies primarily on subjective assessment scales, and effective specific therapies are lacking, underscoring the need for further elucidation of its pathological mechanisms. Recent studies indicate that gut dysbiosis plays a pivotal role in the development of SAE. Consequently, probiotic-based microbiome intervention strategies offer a novel approach to SAE prevention and treatment by reshaping the gut microbiota, restoring beneficial metabolite levels, and inhibiting harmful immune cell migration. This review aims to systematically summarize the latest mechanistic studies on the gut microbiota-gut-brain axis in SAE. It focuses on evaluating the experimental evidence and potential clinical value of microbiological therapies, particularly probiotics, while outlining future challenges and translational research directions in this field. The goal is to provide a theoretical basis for developing precise intervention strategies for SAE.

titre: Microbiome dysbiosis and phytochemical interactions in Alzheimer's disease: the oral–gut–brain axis
resume: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by amyloid-β deposition, tau hyperphosphorylation, chronic neuroinflammation, and progressive cognitive decline. Increasing evidence suggests that, beyond classical neuropathology, alterations in the oral and gut microbiota contribute to AD through interconnected inflammatory, metabolic, immune, and epigenetic mechanisms. This review synthesizes recent findings on the oral–gut–brain axis, highlighting how oral dysbiosis may influence gut microbial ecology and how gut microbial metabolites mediate communication between the gastrointestinal tract and the CNS. Particular emphasis is placed on microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), lipopolysaccharide, trimethylamine N-oxide, bile acids, tryptophan-derived metabolites, vitamins, and neurotransmitter-related compounds, which regulate blood–brain barrier integrity, immune cell activation, microglial function, and neuronal survival. We further discuss how these metabolites modify host epigenetic machinery through histone acetylation, DNA methylation, and non-coding RNA regulation, thereby providing a mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis and AD pathogenesis. The review also examines the reciprocal interactions between dietary phytochemicals and the gut microbiota, demonstrating that microbial biotransformation is often required to generate bioactive metabolites with improved bioavailability, blood–brain barrier penetration, and neuroprotective efficacy. Consequently, individual differences in microbial metabolic capacity may underlie the heterogeneous responses observed in clinical studies of nutraceutical interventions. Finally, we propose that integrating microbiome modulation, microbial metabolite profiling, epigenetic regulation, and microbiome-dependent phytochemical bioactivation offers a promising framework for developing personalized therapeutic strategies. Future research combining longitudinal human cohorts with multi-omics approaches and mechanistic studies will be essential to establish causality and translate microbiome-informed interventions into effective disease-modifying therapies for Alzheimer's disease.

titre: The Pancreas–Gut–Microbiome–Pain Axis in Chronic Pancreatitis: Linking Dysmotility, Dysbiosis, Visceral Hypersensitivity, and Persistent Pain — A Scoping Review
resume: This scoping review systematically maps and critically integrates clinical, physiological, and mechanistic evidence linking chronic pancreatitis (CP) and pancreatic pain with gastrointestinal dysmotility, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), intestinal dysbiosis, microbial metabolites, intestinal barrier and immune signalling, visceral hypersensitivity, and peripheral and central pain processing. The review distinguishes direct and associative human evidence in CP from mechanistic human and translational evidence obtained outside CP. Its objectives are to identify established, emerging, and currently untested relationships; define major methodological and mechanistic evidence gaps; and develop a provisional, hypothesis-generating VIBRA Pancreas–Gut–Microbiome–Pain framework for future prospective mechanistic and interventional research.

titre: Association of clinically determined extended perioperative antibiotic therapy with postoperative neurocognitive outcomes in older adults: a prospective cohort study with microbiome and biomarker analyses
resume: Postoperative neurocognitive decline is common in older surgical patients and has multiple determinants, including patient vulnerability, operative stress, inflammation, infection, and perioperative complications. The gut microbiota may contribute to systemic and central inflammatory signalling through the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Human data linking clinically determined perioperative antibiotic exposure with postoperative cognition remain limited. This prospective cohort study examined whether patients receiving extended therapy had different neurocognitive, microbiome, short-chain fatty acid, and inflammatory profiles than patients receiving standard prophylaxis. This prospective observational cohort study enrolled 156 patients aged ≥ 60 years undergoing elective non-cardiac surgery at Loudi Central Hospital from January 2022 to January 2024. The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Loudi Central Hospital (2021CH003274), and all participants provided written informed consent. Participants were classified by clinically determined antibiotic duration as standard prophylaxis (SP; ≤24 h) or extended therapy (ET; >24 h). Neuropsychological testing was performed at baseline and on postoperative days (PODs) 3, 7, and 30; the primary outcome was test-defined postoperative neurocognitive decline at POD 7. Multivariable logistic regression and propensity-score matching adjusted for measured baseline and perioperative covariates. Fecal microbiota, fecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and serum inflammatory and exploratory perioperative stress markers were also assessed. Test-defined neurocognitive decline at POD 7 occurred in 33/78 patients (42.3%) in the ET group and 19/78 (24.4%) in the SP group (relative risk 1.73, 95% CI 1.12–2.68; P = 0.013). The association remained in the reported multivariable model (adjusted odds ratio 2.34, 95% CI 1.18–4.64; P = 0.015) and in the propensity-matched sensitivity analysis (odds ratio 2.08, 95% CI 1.02–4.26; P = 0.044). Compared with SP, patients receiving ET also had lower Shannon diversity, larger reductions in selected SCFA-associated genera, lower fecal butyrate, and higher systemic inflammatory markers. Lower butyrate and higher lipopolysaccharide-binding protein were associated with greater cognitive decline. Because ET was prescribed for contamination or postoperative infection and was associated with greater clinical complexity, these findings do not isolate an effect of antibiotic duration itself. Patients who received clinically determined extended perioperative antibiotic therapy had a higher frequency of postoperative neurocognitive decline and a different microbiome, SCFA, and inflammatory profile than patients receiving standard prophylaxis. These observations are biologically coherent but do not establish that antibiotic duration caused the cognitive or biological differences because treatment indication, surgical complexity, antibiotic spectrum, and other perioperative factors were incompletely separable. Clinically indicated antibiotics should not be withheld on the basis of these results. Future multicenter studies should evaluate infectious and neurocognitive outcomes together and, where clinical equipoise exists, compare acceptable antibiotic-duration strategies while measuring the factors that determine treatment duration.

titre: Extracellular vesicles of Fusobacterium nucleatum induce anxiety and depression by triggering neuroinflammation via IL-1β
resume: Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) is an opportunistic Gram-negative oral bacterium that is associated with periodontitis. Fn can induce inflammation outside of the oral cavity via bacterial translocation to other organs, and extracellular vesicles (EVs) released by the bacterium have been implicated in mediating this inflammation. However, the effects of Fn EVs on the brain have not been explored in detail. Here, we investigated the neuropathological effects of Fn EVs. Fn EVs induced neuroinflammation, characterized by microglial activation and alteration of inhibitory synaptic transmission, which was associated with anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors. Administration of Fn EVs increased IL-1β release, and pharmacological inhibition of IL-1β ameliorated the Fn EVs-induced behavioral abnormalities. Our data indicate that Fn EVs have the capacity to trigger neuroinflammation via the IL-1β pathway, contributing to depression and anxiety, highlighting the potential of Fn EVs to mediate pathogenic neuroinflammation via the microbiome-gut/oral-brain axis in neurological/psychiatric disorders.

titre: Depression is associated with endometrial polyp occurrence and convergent gut microbiota-mitochondrial alterations: a multi-omics case-control study
resume: Endometrial polyps (EPs) affect 7.8%–34.9% of women and cause abnormal uterine bleeding and reproductive failure, yet their pathogenesis is unclear. Depression is over-represented among women with EPs but is usually read as reactive distress; whether that association involves the gut microbiota and mitochondrial biology is unknown. We combined a hospital-based case–control analysis (n = 466), faecal full-length 16S rRNA and blood leukocyte RNA-seq in 30 participants (PD n = 11, PND n = 12, NPND n = 7), and a chronic restraint stress (CRS) mouse model with bacterial supplementation. Depression was significantly associated with higher odds of EP in the full cohort (unadjusted OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.55–3.34; P PND > NPND), together with downregulation of GDF15, HIC1, TCF7L2 and ICAM1 . In mice, restraint stress was accompanied by stromal proliferation exceeding that in estradiol-treated controls and by reduced uterine TOMM20; oral F. prausnitzii given after stress was associated with higher TOMM20 and lower proliferation, whereas E. lenta was not. These findings place a convergent gut microbiota–mitochondrial axis at the intersection of depression and endometrial proliferation, and nominate candidate taxa and transcripts for hypothesis-driven validation. Limitations: multi-omics profiling included 30 participants (11, 12 and 7) with no depression-only cell; microbial functions were predicted by PICRUSt2 and no metabolite was measured; medication use, diet, physical activity, sleep and hormonal status were incompletely captured; and each bacterial group contained three animals. The axis proposed here is therefore hypothesis-generating and requires longitudinal, metabolomic and tissue-specific validation.
revue: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

titre: Interoception in trans and gender diverse people: A scoping review
Examining the Associations Among Interoceptive Awareness, Exposure to Violence, and Mental Health in Youth
resume: This study will examine the relationship between interoceptive accuracy, violence exposure, and mental health in adolescents. Participants will complete questionnaires, an ECG cardiac interoception task, and brief daily surveys for two weeks. Additionally, we will examine different forms of violence exposure such as witnessing, or encountering community violence and the association with interoceptive accuracy while also looking at depression, anxiety & PTSD symptoms. The results may help understand how adverse experiences during this important stage of development relate to body awareness and mental health.

titre: Yet Again on the Somatic Specificity of Discrete Emotions: Associations Between Bodily Sensations, Interoception, and Mental Health
resume: Background. While theoretical models suggest that emotions are fundamentally embodied, empirical research often relies on localized laboratory monitoring or macro-level topographical maps that fail to capture the qualitative modality of visceral signals. Our cross-sectional study deconstructs the bodily profiles of discrete emotions, associating them with distress, somatic complaints, and self-reported interoceptive awareness. Methods. Healthy individuals (N = 127, mean age = 32.2 years) completed a questionnaire operationalizing 32 bodily sensations experienced concurrently with nine emotions (anger, fear, disgust, sadness, happiness, surprise, shame, guilt, resentment), alongside standardized scales (MHC-SF, DASS-21, GBB-24, MAIA-R). Results. Generalized Estimating Equations demonstrated category-level somatic specificity. Fear tracked cardiac activity; anger clustered with musculoskeletal tension (clenched jaws); disgust exhibited gastrointestinal patterns. For complex emotions, shame mapped onto facial and vasomotor shifts (feverish state), while resentment demonstrated a somatic convergence of sadness (tearing and throat constriction) coupled with cardiovascular activation (heart racing). Guilt and shame emerged as "Lump in the throat" and "Weight on the chest". The total volume and intensity of sensations were related to stress, anxiety, depression, and functional physical complaints, negatively associated with well-being. Conclusions. Discrete affective experience is grounded in differentiated bodily sensations. Hypervigilant bodily monitoring might reflect somatic distress under psychological tension.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: A Revised Polish Version of The Toronto Alexithymia Scale-20 (TAS-20-POL-R): Translation and Validation
Emotion Perception in Individuals with Dissociative Disorders, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, Personality Disorders and Non-Clinical Adults
