resume: Following current diagnostic criteria (DSM-5), individuals with Complex Dissociative Disorders (CDD), that is, Other Specified Dissociative Disorder (OSDD) or Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID), are characterized by identity fragmentation, meaning they report the experience of having two or more distinct identity states with accompanying differences in behaviors, perceptions, cognitions and/or memories. Although identity fragmentation is considered a core feature of CDD, its nature and underlying mechanisms remain debated. Following the practice-based trauma model of CDD (Nijenhuis et al., 2010; van der Hart et al., 2006), identity fragmentation is conceptualized as a coping response to severe trauma experienced in childhood where two types of identities are distinguished: trauma-fixated and trauma-avoidant. Trauma-fixated identities are considered to be ‘stuck’ in the past trauma and experience the traumatic events as still happening or as about to be happening, while trauma-avoidant adult identities are considered to not be aware of the trauma and focus on the responsibilities of the individual’s adult daily life (e.g., working, parenting). Accordingly, individuals with CDD in a trauma-fixated identity state (i.e., when self-reporting remembering memories of past traumatic experiences) are expected to show stronger trauma-related cognitions and behaviors, akin to individuals with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), than when in their trauma-avoidant identity state (i.e., when self-reporting amnesia for past traumatic events). However, these theoretical assumptions have not been systematically tested, and it remains unclear to what extent individuals with CDD differ from individuals with related disorders, such as personality disorders and PTSD, in various aspects of cognitive functioning. The current study is part of a larger project aiming to investigate the nature of various aspects of cognitive functioning in individuals with CDD. In the present study different aspects of emotion perception are compared (a) within individuals with CDD between different identity states and (b) between individuals with CDD, PTSD related to childhood traumatic experiences before the age of 12, personality disorders (borderline [BPD] and avoidant [APD]) and non-clinical adults using a performance-based emotion perception task and a self-report questionnaire on alexithymia (i.e., difficulty to identity feelings, distinguish between emotions and bodily sensations of arousal and describing one’s feelings to others). Previous research indicated that individuals with PTSD show several impairments in emotion perception, including difficulty processing both positive and negative emotions correctly, less sensitivity for negative emotions, and heightened alexithymia (Couette et al., 2020; Poljac et al., 2011). Individuals with BPD also showed impairments in emotion perception, however, while positive, neutral and fearful emotional stimuli were less accurately perceived, they tended to be more accurate in identifying anger and disgust (Domes et al., 2011; Meehan et al., 2017). For individuals with APD, research indicates a specific impairment in accurately processing fearful emotional stimuli (Rosenthal et al., 2011). Generally, individuals with personality pathology have been shown to report low emotional awareness, reflected in – among other factors – heightened alexithymia (Derks et al., 2017; Simonsen et al., 2021).
auteurs: Robin P. A. van der Linde

titre: Experimental Hypnosis: State of the Art and Position Paper of a Panel of Experts
revue: Advances in Social Sciences Research Journal

titre: Comparative effects of combined behavioral intervention and ericksonian hypnotherapy in alcohol use disorder: a randomized controlled trial
resume: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a chronic, relapsing condition associated with psychological, behavioral, and social impairment. Individualized, experiential psychotherapies such as Ericksonian Hypnotherapy (EH) have a limited randomized evidence base in AUD. This three-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial compared Combined Behavioral Intervention (CBI), EH, and a psychoeducational control condition (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06916754). Ninety adults meeting DSM-5 criteria for AUD were randomized 1:1:1; both active interventions were delivered individually over 12 weekly sessions. Prespecified primary outcomes were three Timeline Follow-Back indices covering the preceding 30 days: drinking days, heavy drinking days, and drinks per drinking day. Craving, depressive and anxiety symptoms, quality of life, and readiness for change were secondary and exploratory. The primary analysis was an intention-to-treat linear mixed-effects model including all randomized participants, with completer and multiple-imputation analyses as sensitivity analyses; multiplicity was controlled across the confirmatory family of primary outcomes. Both active interventions produced significantly greater improvement than control across all primary alcohol-use outcomes and across the exploratory secondary domains, with moderate-to-large between-group effects. Contrasts between the two active treatments favored EH on craving-related cognitions, obsessive craving, and anxiety severity, but these comparisons were exploratory, were not powered a priori, and are reported as preliminary. Differences between the active treatments on alcohol-use outcomes were not statistically significant, which should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence. The findings support structured psychotherapy for AUD and identify Ericksonian Hypnotherapy as a treatment package warranting adequately powered comparative evaluation.

titre: The effectiveness of AI-based cognitive behavioral therapy chatbots for anxiety and depression symptoms: a systematic review and meta-analysis
resume: Background AI chatbots are increasingly being used to provide accessible psychological support. However, the effectiveness of chatbot-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety and depressive symptoms remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of artificial intelligence chatbot-based cognitive behavioral therapy on anxiety and depressive symptoms. Method A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Cochrane Library, CNKI, VIP, Wanfang, and CBM databases was conducted from their inception to July 8th, 2025. Updated search on August 25, 2026. Meta-analysis was conducted using Stata version 18.0 and RevMan version 5.4. The ES for the treatment effect was calculated using the SMD . Results Ten studies involving a total of 1,301 participants. The results of the meta-analysis showed that the CBT of AI chatbots could significantly improve depressive symptoms at the end of the intervention ( d = −0.40, 95% CI : −0.62 ~ −0.17, P = 0.0005). In contrast, the intervention did not significantly improve anxiety symptoms ( d = −0.029, 95% CI : −0.145 ~ 0.087, P = 0.623), with no substantial heterogeneity detected ( I 2 = 0%). The subgroup analysis for depressive symptoms indicated significant effects were observed in participant age stratification, intervention Duration, and Control group intervention. However, some subgroup estimates were based on a small number of studies, so the data should be interpreted with caution. Conclusion This meta-analysis emphasizes that AI-based chatbots for CBT may have great potential in contributing to the alleviation of depressive symptoms. Given the small number of included studies and the high heterogeneity, the results should be interpreted with caution. More high-quality RCTs are needed in the future to further validate these findings and explore their long-term benefits. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251089835 .

titre: Efficacy of mindfulness-based interventions and biofeedback for migraine management: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
resume: Objective This systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials aims to analyze the efficacy of mindfulness-based interventions and biofeedback on headache frequency, pain intensity, headache-related disability, psychological distress, and quality of life in adult patients with migraine. Methods The review followed the PRISMA statement and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261381587). A structured search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, and PsycInfo for RCTs published in English between May 2016 and May 2026. Seven clinical trials ( n = 535 participants) met the inclusion criteria. Methodological quality and risk of bias were evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool. Results The pooled analysis for headache frequency ( n = 6 studies) showed no statistically significant differences between groups (MD = −0.59; 95% CI: −1.81 to 0.62; p = 0.34). Conversely, significant improvements favoring the experimental groups were found for headache-related disability measured with the HIT-6 scale ( n = 6 studies; MD = −2.28; 95% CI: −4.47 to −0.08; p = 0.04), pain intensity ( n = 3 studies; SMD = −0.39; 95% CI: −0.64 to −0.14; p = 0.002), and health-related quality of life ( n = 3 studies; MD = +5.21; 95% CI: 1.95 to 8.47; p = 0.002). No statistically significant differences were observed for anxiety ( p = 0.30) or depression ( p = 0.88). Conclusion Interventions incorporating Mindfulness-Based Interventions and Biofeedback do not significantly reduce objective migraine attack frequency compared to control conditions, nor do they yield distinct differences in affective outcomes (anxiety/depression)—which may partly reflect subclinical baseline depression scores in episodic cohorts, active-comparator effects, and instrument heterogeneity. However, they exhibit statistically significant efficacy in decreasing subjective pain intensity, mitigating headache-related functional disability, and restoring health-related quality of life, supporting their role as valuable complementary strategies for self-regulation and clinical coping in migraine management. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261381587 , Identifier: CRD420261381587.

titre: Nurse-delivered cognitive behavioural therapy for anxiety in cardiac disease versus usual care: a randomised superiority trial
resume: Background Anxiety is common in patients with cardiac disease and is linked to poorer quality of life and adverse clinical outcomes. This trial investigated whether nurse-delivered individual cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) plus usual care reduces anxiety compared with usual care alone in cardiac patients. Methods The Heart & Mind Trial was an investigator-initiated, randomised clinical superiority trial with blinded outcome assessment. Patients aged ≥ 18 years with cardiac disease and clinically significant anxiety according to the Structured Clinical Interview for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (SCID) were randomised 1:1 to individual CBT plus usual care or usual care alone across four Danish university hospitals and stratified by cardiac diagnosis, recruitment site and anxiety severity, enabling prespecified analyses across the three major cardiac diagnostic groups. Randomisation was conducted in blocks of four. The intervention nurse was informed of the assigned group. Outcome assessors were blinded to group allocation. The primary outcome was anxiety severity measured by Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale-Anxiety (HADS-A) score at 5-month follow-up. The primary efficacy analyses were performed according to the intention-to-treat principle using a linear regression model. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, ID NCT04582734. The trial has been completed. Findings Between May 1, 2021, and May 31, 2023, 336 patients were randomised (165 assigned to the intervention group and 171 to the control group). 134 patients (40%) were female and 202 (60%) males. The mean age was 61.3 (SD 11.8). Of the 336 patients, 304 (90.5%) completed 5-month follow-up. At 5 months, the intervention group had significantly lower anxiety levels with a HADS-A mean difference score of −3.01 (95% confidence interval, −3.77; −2.26) (Cohen's d=1.11). One serious adverse event (death) occurred during the trial and was not considered related to the intervention. Interpretation Nurse-delivered individual CBT effectively reduced anxiety in cardiac patients with clinically significant anxiety compared to usual care without CBT, addressing an important and often unmet clinical need and suggesting its relevance for routine cardiac care. Funding The Novo Nordisk Foundation, The Capital Region of Denmark and The Danish Nurses' Association's Nursing Research Fund.

titre: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for Pregnant Women: A Scoping Review
resume: Background: Pregnancy represents a period of elevated vulnerability to psychological distress. Anxiety and depression affect a large proportion of pregnant individuals, and symptoms may persist into the postpartum period. Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), a third-wave cognitive behavioral therapy that aims to enhance psychological flexibility, has been increasingly adopted to improve psychological well-being in pregnancy. However, the existing evidence on the scope and characteristics of ACT-based interventions for pregnant women has not been comprehensively mapped. Methods: This scoping review adopted the five-stage framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley and was reported following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A comprehensive search of eight English and three Chinese databases was conducted from database inception to 30 September 2026. Studies evaluating ACT-based interventions targeting pregnant women were eligible for inclusion. Results: Fourteen studies published between 2015 and 2025, involving a total of 862 participants (mean age: 29.70 years; mean gestational age: 28.82 weeks), were included. Quasi-experimental designs were most common (n = 8), followed by randomized controlled trials (n = 4) and mixed-methods studies (n = 2). Across the included studies, 24 distinct outcomes were assessed using 37 measurements. The most frequently assessed outcomes included pregnancy-related anxiety, coping strategies, psychological flexibility, and fear of childbirth. Findings suggested that ACT-based interventions may enhance psychological flexibility and alleviate psychological symptoms. However, considerable heterogeneity was observed in intervention characteristics and outcome assessment, alongside limited reporting of intervention development and treatment fidelity. Conclusions: ACT shows promise for promoting psychological well-being during pregnancy. Nevertheless, future research should prioritize well-designed randomized controlled trials, standardized intervention and outcome reporting, longer-term follow-up assessments, and transparent documentation of intervention development and fidelity to strengthen the evidence base, enhance reproducibility, and support clinical translation.

titre: New Directions in Culturally Informed OCD Assessment and Treatment
Untangling the Yarn Further: Methodological Considerations in Characterizing Dynamic OCD–Trauma Intersections
A qualitative study on the considerations and experiences in mental health care for older adults with affective disorders, anxiety disorders, OCD, or PTSD
resume: The aim of this study is to explore perceptions of older adults with affective disorders, anxiety disorders, OCD, or PTSD in specialized mental health care. This consists of considerations, perceptions, experiences and attitudes before treatment and during treatment. To this end, a qualitative study including interviews will be performed.

titre: A Theoretical Study on the Common Mechanism Between Repetitive Reward-Seeking Behavior in Digital Environments and Stereotyped Behavior in OCD and ASD(デジタル環境下における反復的報酬探索行動と強迫性障害・自閉スペクトラム症における常同行動の共通メカニズムに関する理論的考察)
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Impactos do Transtorno Obsessivo-Compulsivo (TOC) em universitários: uma revisão sistemática
resume: O Transtorno Obsessivo-Compulsivo (TOC) é uma condição psiquiátrica caracterizada por obsessões e compulsões recorrentes que geram sofrimento clínico e prejuízo funcional significativos. No contexto do ensino superior, a exposição a elevadas demandas acadêmicas e estressores psicossociais torna os estudantes vulneráveis ao surgimento e ao agravamento dessa sintomatologia, justificando a investigação de seus desdobramentos nessa população. O objetivo deste estudo foi analisar, por meio de uma revisão sistemática da literatura produzida entre 2015 e 2025, a prevalência e os impactos do TOC em estudantes universitários, bem como propor aplicações práticas de intervenção. A metodologia seguiu as diretrizes do protocolo PRISMA, mediante busca na base de dados PubMed utilizando os descritores controlados "Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder", "Quality of Life" e "Students" combinados pelo operador booleano AND. De um total de 40 registros identificados, nove estudos atenderam integralmente aos critérios de elegibilidade e compuseram a amostra final, totalizando 4.495 participantes (66,3% do sexo feminino). Os resultados demonstraram ampla variabilidade na prevalência de sintomas obsessivo-compulsivos entre universitários (de 3,8% a 43,0%), influenciada pela heterogeneidade dos instrumentos avaliativos e por recortes socioculturais e pandêmicos. Verificou-se correlação negativa consistente entre a gravidade dos sintomas de TOC e os escores de qualidade de vida, com maior comprometimento nos domínios da saúde psicológica, relações sociais, qualidade do sono e sintomas depressivos, além de associações com adições digitais e transtornos alimentares. Conclui-se que o período universitário coincide epidemiologicamente com a faixa etária de início do transtorno e de menor acesso a tratamento, evidenciando a necessidade de estratégias institucionais de rastreamento precoce e da oferta de intervenções viáveis de primeira linha, como a terapia cognitivo-comportamental baseada na internet.
auteurs: José Alberto Fernandes Gomes dos Santos

titre: Clinical Positioning of Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors as Gut-Brain Neuromodulators in Irritable Bowel Syndrome: A Comprehensive Review of Mechanisms, Effectiveness, Tolerability, and Treatment Challenges
resume: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a disorder of gut-brain interaction in which serotonergic signaling contributes to symptom generation and modulation. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have been proposed as gut-brain neuromodulators because they act on both central and peripheral serotonin pathways. Physiological studies suggest that SSRIs enhance gastric and small bowel transit, although their effects on visceral sensitivity and abdominal pain remain inconsistent. Recent meta-analysis indicates that SSRIs may provide a modest benefit for abdominal pain; however, the certainty of the evidence is low, and no significant improvement has been demonstrated for global IBS symptoms. Findings across randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and meta-analyses remain inconsistent, reflecting substantial heterogeneity in study design, patient populations, and outcome measures. The potential role of SSRIs may differ according to the IBS subtype. By accelerating gastrointestinal transit, SSRIs may be more suitable for constipation-predominant IBS, whereas tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), which slow transit, may be preferable for diarrhea-predominant IBS. However, evidence supporting subtype-specific efficacy remains limited. Further well-designed RCTs evaluating treatment effects according to IBS phenotype are therefore needed. Current guidelines generally recommend TCAs, which have stronger evidence for efficacy, as first-line neuromodulators and SSRIs as alternative options. In clinical practice, treatment selection should extend beyond efficacy alone and consider bowel habit subtype, predominant symptoms, psychological comorbidities, adverse-effect vulnerability, patient preferences, and the likelihood of treatment acceptance, adherence, and persistence. SSRIs are well tolerated medications and may be particularly useful in selected patients, including those with IBS-constipation or coexisting anxiety, within a personalized, phenotype-informed treatment approach. Prescribers should recognize that patients may face several barriers to accepting and adhering to neuromodulators in IBS including concerns about taking an "antidepressant" for a gastrointestinal disorder, fear of adverse effects, perceived stigma, and misunderstanding of the gut-brain mechanism. Therefore, clinician-patient education and ongoing adherence monitoring are essential.

titre: Discrimination and Irritable Bowel Syndrome Diagnosis Among a Multi-Ethnic Sample
resume: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a diagnosis of the gut-brain interaction (DGBI) characterized by abdominal pain/discomfort and alterations in bowel habits. Its etiology is typically attributed to disruptions in the gut-brain axis. While extensive research has established significant associations with facets of mental health (e.g., trauma, anxiety), less is known about IBS in a cross-cultural context and the social determinants of health that may affect its presentation. The purpose of this study was to investigate the role of discrimination with the likelihood of obtaining an IBS diagnosis among a diverse sample. A logistic regression was conducted among 980 Black, Asian, Latinx, and Arab/Middle Eastern North African groups. Results revealed that racial discrimination [OR = 1.04, 95% CI = 1.01, 1.07, p = .012] emerged as a significant predictor of IBS diagnosis. Sex did not emerge as a significant predictor. Implications for health care are discussed. Providers should approach IBS through a biopsychosocial lens while considering discrimination as a social determinant of health that may be related to provider-patient interactions or the physiological toll of discrimination.
revue: Journal of immigrant and minority health

titre: Correction to Efficacy of Tenapanor in Treating Patients With Irritable Bowel Syndrome With Constipation: A 12-Week, Placebo-Controlled Phase 3 Trial (T3MPO-1)
A Hyaluronic Acid-Stabilized Zinc-Loaded Probiotic Mitigates Nanoplastic Toxicity across the Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis
resume: Nanoplastics are emerging stressors that perturb host physiology across the gut-immune-brain continuum, yet scalable interventions remain limited. Here, we engineer ZG@EcN@HA, a biohybrid living system created by vacuum-assisted intracellular loading of zinc gluconate into Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) followed by an outer hyaluronic acid (HA) shell. This architecture preserves probiotic culturability under gastric challenge and supports sustained zinc availability in intestinal conditions. In zebrafish chronically exposed to polystyrene nanoplastics, we observe reproducible neurobehavioral impairment coupled with inflammatory activation, redox imbalance, barrier stress, neurotransmitter dysregulation, and multiorgan histopathology. ZG@EcN@HA yields the most coherent rescue compared with single-component controls, restoring behavioral outputs and realigning immune-redox-neurochemical readouts. ASV-based profiling shows recovery of microbial diversity and a shift toward a control-like community structure, including reduced dominance of inflammation-linked taxa. Intestinal transcriptomics and integrative correlation analyses further support normalization of barrier/metabolic programs and attenuation of innate inflammatory signaling. Together, the data identify a materials-enabled strategy for microbiota-gut-brain protection against chronic nanoplastic stress.

titre: The Gut-Brain Axis in Binge Eating Disorder: From Pathophysiological Mechanisms to Emerging Therapeutic Targets
resume: Binge-eating disorder (BED) is one of the most prevalent eating disorders worldwide; however, current pharmacological and psychological interventions provide limited long-term efficacy. Increasing evidence indicates that dysregulation of the gut-brain axis (GBA) via altered gut microbiota, impaired hormonal signaling, vagal dysfunction, and HPA axis hyperactivity disrupts energy homeostasis and feeding regulation in BED. These interconnected abnormalities may contribute to impaired satiety perception, enhance reward-driven eating behaviors, perpetuate stress-induced binge episodes, and may be associated with metabolic dysregulation, thereby contributing to obesity susceptibility in individuals with BED. In this review, we summarize recent clinical and preclinical advances on GBA involvement in BED pathogenesis and discuss emerging therapeutic strategies targeting this regulatory network. We pay particular attention to microbial metabolites, endocrine signaling, immune regulation, and neural pathways involved in appetite control and reward processing. Furthermore, we evaluate novel GBA-targeted interventions, including probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists, and vagus nerve stimulation (VNS), with emphasis on their underlying mechanisms, current evidence, and translational challenges. Finally, we propose an integrated framework for future research, highlighting the importance of large-scale longitudinal studies and biomarker-guided patient stratification to improve therapeutic precision. Targeting the gut-brain axis represents a promising investigational approach for BED management; however, clinical validation and biomarker-guided strategies remain necessary before its translation into routine practice.

titre: Mechanistic role of functional bacterial amyloids (FuBAs) in inflammatory responses, ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) impairment, and cross-seedings with host amyloids
resume: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by disruption of protein homeostasis, aggregation, inflammation, and neuronal resilience, with age affecting disease susceptibility. Bacterial amyloids, such as curli, Fap, TasA, and phenol-soluble modulins, are functional amyloids that aid in biofilm formation and potentially interact with host proteins and innate immune pathways. They are cross-β-sheet proteins that interact with other proteins from different species, and experimental data show that some bacterial amyloids promote the aggregation of amyloid-β and α-synuclein. Various fuBA effects along the gut-brain axis depend on microbial production, retention in the gut, barrier integrity, clearance from the system, immune status, and tissue susceptibility. The activation of innate immune mechanisms, such as Toll-like receptor signaling, by FuBAs or related microbial signals could lead to inflammation and oxidative stress. The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is another aspect of cellular protein quality control that could be further compromised by increased amyloid burden. To date, direct FuBA-mediated proteasome inhibition remains poorly established. To this end, this review separates direct evidence, indirect effects of aggregation/inflammatory stress, and mechanistic precedents from studies on human amyloid. Structural biology, immunology, and proteostasis research will be combined, and FuBAs will be investigated as potential upstream modulators of the neurodegenerative proteinopathies. We assess whether FuBAs directly influence UPS function in intestinal, peripheral, or neural compartments, and discuss possible therapeutic strategies, including microbiome modulation, barrier repair, immunomodulation, and proteasome stimulation. FuBAs can alter neuronal proteostasis in both amyloid-related disorders and other neurodegenerative processes, but not necessarily act as triggers of these processes.

titre: Shared host-genetic architecture between gut microbiota and internalizing psychopathology
resume: It is unknown whether gut microbial composition causally influences mental illness. Using genetic variants as instruments (Mendelian randomization, MR), we tested the genetically predicted effects of 211 gut microbial taxa on nine psychiatric and psychopathology-related phenotypes. Of 1,898 valid tests, seven taxon-outcome associations (five clades) passed false-discovery-rate correction (FDR < 0.05). All involved depression, neuroticism or insomnia, the three most precisely estimated outcomes. The strongest, a protective association of the Mollicutes/Tenericutes clade with depression (odds ratio 0.93 per SD of log-abundance, p = 1.5 × 10-6), survived every multiple-testing correction. The associations persisted with weak-instrument-robust estimators, stricter instrument selection and leave-one-out analysis, and reverse-direction MR found no effect of psychiatric liability on these taxa. In independent samples, the depression association had the same direction but was weaker and non-significant (one-sided p = 0.13), and the neuroticism and insomnia associations, tested with limited power, did not replicate. Bayesian colocalization (posterior probability of a shared variant < 0.05 at every locus) and CAUSE (0 of 45 pairs causal) did not support causation at individual loci. In factor-level MR within a Genomic SEM model, Mollicutes/Tenericutes was associated with a latent internalizing factor, and Butyrivibrio and Negativicutes/Selenomonadales with internalizing-specific variance beyond a general psychopathology factor. Psychotic-factor estimates were null but imprecise, and specificity relative to less well-powered phenotypes remains unresolved. Selected gut taxa and internalizing psychopathology appear to share host-genetic influences, and the evidence does not support direct effects of these taxa on the disorders.

titre: Nutrition Care Strategies at the Intersection of Menopause and Obesity Pharmacotherapy
resume: The premenopause to menopause transition, known as perimenopause, is a critical period of metabolic vulnerability, characterized by hormonal changes, shifts in body composition, and increased cardiometabolic risk. Concurrently, incretin mimetic pharmacotherapies have emerged as highly effective treatments for obesity, achieving weight reductions that are approximating those previously observed only after bariatric surgery. While these agents confer substantial benefits, their mechanisms-appetite suppression, delayed gastric emptying, and enhanced satiety-introduce nutritional risks that intersect with pre-existing vulnerabilities of women experiencing this transition. Reduced energy intake and inadequate micronutrient intake, combined with estrogen deficiency, heighten the risk for osteoporosis and sarcopenic obesity. Likewise, gastrointestinal adverse events further compromise dietary quality and hydration, while aging physiology amplifies susceptibility to malnutrition. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on nutritional risks during perimenopause in the context of incretin mimetic pharmacotherapy, highlighting overlapping pathways that influence musculoskeletal health, metabolic resilience, and quality of life. Clinical strategies to mitigate these risks, including protein optimization, micronutrient monitoring, menopausal hormone therapy (osteoporosis/musculoskeletal health), and multidisciplinary care, are discussed alongside research priorities to inform targeted nutrition frameworks. Addressing these gaps is essential to ensure safe, effective, and sustainable obesity management for women in midlife and beyond.

titre: The probability of self-related stimuli modulates heartbeat-evoked potentials
resume: Interoception, the cortical processing of visceral signals, has been proposed as a foundation of self-processing. Heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEPs) provide a measure of interoceptive processing and have been linked to self-processing, but whether HEP modulations reflect self-specificity rather than familiarity and depend on probabilistic context remains unclear. We recorded EEG and ECG during passive listening to subject's own names (SON), familiar names (FN), and unfamiliar name (UN) under equal- and biased-probability conditions. In the equal-probability condition, HEP amplitudes were more positive for SON than for FN and UN over centro-parietal-occipital sites at 164-242 and 258-296 ms after the R peak, whereas FN and UN did not differ. This self-specific pattern was not detected under biased probabilities. Within-name comparisons revealed probability-related HEP effects for SON and UN with distinct spatiotemporal characteristics, indicating that stimulus probability did not produce a uniform effect across name types. The late positive potential showed a comparable probability-dependent self-specific pattern, and SON-evoked LPP amplitudes positively covaried with HEP amplitudes during SON perception across conditions. These findings indicate that self-specific HEP modulations depend on probabilistic context and is associated with relatively late external self-related processing, highlighting a context-sensitive relationship between interoceptive and external self-related processing.

titre: Static and dynamic intrinsic brain activity in eyes-closed and eyes-open resting-state conditions
resume: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data are typically acquired under eyes-closed (EC) or eyes-open (EO) conditions, which are thought to reflect interoceptive and exteroceptive brain states. However, evidence for condition-dependent differences has largely relied on static analyses that provide limited information about temporal variability. Here, we investigated eye-state modulation of intrinsic brain activity by integrating multimetric static and dynamic analyses across multiple spatial scales. Static measures, including the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), fractional ALFF (fALFF), regional homogeneity (ReHo), and degree centrality (DC), were estimated to characterize low-frequency amplitude, relative spectral contribution, local synchronization, and network centrality. A sliding-window approach was used to calculate ALFF, fALFF, ReHo, and DC within successive windows, and their variability across windows was quantified. Static analyses revealed spatial differences between EC and EO across visual, sensorimotor, temporal, prefrontal, parietal, and subcortical regions. A particularly consistent finding across the static metrics was greater middle occipital gyrus involvement during EO. However, fALFF also showed an EC-related increase in the left calcarine cortex, indicating regionally heterogeneous effects within the occipital cortex. Dynamic analyses showed greater variability during EC in selected posterior visual regions, most consistently for dALFF and dReHo variability, whereas dfALFF and dDC variability were more sensitive to window length, mean adjustment, and spatial standardization. These findings demonstrate that eye state modulates intrinsic brain function through coordinated changes in both whole-scan measures and temporal variability across multiple spatial scales, highlighting the importance of jointly considering static and dynamic properties when investigating the neural organization of resting-state activity.

titre: Conceptualizing the process of experiential acceptance during an episode of anxiety: A qualitative study of individuals with prior experience in mindfulness- and acceptance-based interventions
resume: INTRODUCTION: Experiential acceptance refers to the capacity to be open to internal experiences without attempting to change or avoid them. Although acceptance is a core emotion regulation strategy within mindfulness- and acceptance-based interventions (MABIs) and a protective factor for mental health, its conceptualization and implementation remain unclear and ambiguous. The aim of this study was to clarify and develop a model of accepting anxiety as experienced by individuals with prior experience in MABIs. METHOD: Twenty-six participants from a non-clinical sample with varying levels of prior experience in MABIs took part in semi-structured interviews exploring their experience of accepting anxiety. Data collection and analysis followed the principles of Grounded Theory to generate a data-driven model of the acceptance process. RESULTS: We identified a five-stage dynamic model involving distinct processes: observing through the body with attentional focus on interoceptive experience; identifying and acknowledging anxiety; validating and normalizing the experience through validation and self-compassion; observing from an observer stance characterized by decentering; and maintaining flexible contact with the experience via interoceptive exposure and nonreactivity. We also identified facilitating factors that support engagement in the acceptance process. CONCLUSION: These findings refine the understanding of acceptance as a multidimensional emotion regulation process by highlighting an active dynamic involving multiple mechanisms underlying the acceptance of anxiety. As experienced by individuals with prior MABI experience, this model provides a framework for developing more targeted clinical interventions and for investigating individual and contextual variability in these subprocesses.

titre: Towards a comprehensive understanding of the processes underlying phenomenological continuity
resume: The sense that ourself is continuous over time is a ubiquitous human experience. Although episodic autobiographical memory (AM) makes some contribution to one's subjective sense of self-continuity-also known as I-self continuity or phenomenological continuity-there is growing evidence that individuals with memory disorders report intact phenomenological continuity. These observations suggest that additional processes must also contribute to phenomenological continuity. This systematic search and critical review aimed to identify candidate bodily and psychological processes underlying phenomenological continuity, with a focus on processes beyond AM. A systematic search of three databases (PsycINFO, PubMed and Web of Science) yielded 153 publications that provided evidence of several processes contributing to phenomenological continuity: interoception, embodiment, temporality, a stable life trajectory and nostalgia. Alongside episodic AM, these processes provide multiple sources of constancy integrated across differing timescales. In addition, we identified several processes that indirectly influence the saliency and expression of phenomenological continuity, such as ageing, socio-cultural factors and narrative processes. These findings extend existing models of self-continuity, providing a more comprehensive overview of the processes that, along with memory, underpin phenomenological continuity. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.
revue: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences

titre: Making sense of sensation: a framework of interoceptive attribution and appraisal with clinical applications
resume: Interoception provides a link between bodily states and cognitive and affective processes across both unconscious and conscious domains and is fundamental for a coherent sense of self. While previous research linking interoception to mental health has predominantly focused on interoceptive accuracy, attention, self-beliefs and insight, we argue that the higher-order interpretation of consciously perceived bodily signals plays a fundamental and underexplored role in this relationship. We propose a framework delineating two higher-order processes-interoceptive attribution and appraisal-which constitute the interpretation of interoceptive sensations that reach conscious awareness. We outline key factors that modulate attention, attribution and appraisal, and evidence the relevance of this framework to mental health conditions. Given that these processes are accessible to cognition, they represent an important target for existing psychotherapeutic interventions. We integrate such interventions within our framework, highlighting their potential to enhance interoception-based therapeutic approaches. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.
revue: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences

titre: How does the developing mind construct a self?
resume: Our capacity to think about ourselves is a developmental achievement that, when it emerges, profoundly changes cognition. Currently, there are few, if any mechanistic accounts of where a concept of self could come from, and empirical investigation within contemporary developmental science is surprisingly absent. Drawing on a wealth of data from cognitive neuroscience and developmental psychology, I propose a new mechanistic account of the ontogeny of our reflective self-awareness anchored in infants' interoceptive signals. This is a social cognitive account in which infants' expectations about others' attention are deeply entwined with the modulating effect that others' attention has on infants' awareness of their interoceptive state, together providing the impetus for infants to generate a conceptual representation of self de novo. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.
revue: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences

titre: Tuning in: how interoception shapes body image across early adolescence
resume: Early adolescence is a critical time marked by dynamic changes in physiology, appearance and social environment. These changes are also reflected in how adolescents perceive themselves, including their bodies. The transition through pubertal stages allows us to consider the development of the self from the perspective of how body perception, both from within and from the outside, changes. Although research in adults and post-puberty adolescents suggests that lower interoceptive accuracy is associated with greater body-image concerns, how these factors interact during puberty remains unknown. We tested a sample of 181 girls (ages 10-14 years) spanning across a broad range of pubertal stages, on measures of interoceptive accuracy and behavioural and self-report measures of body image. Lower interoceptive accuracy predicted greater body-image dissatisfaction. Moreover, this relationship was moderated by pubertal stage, showing that the protective effect of higher interoceptive accuracy against body-image dissatisfaction was stronger during more advanced stages of puberty. Our findings show that interoceptive influences extend from the basic multisensory integration to conscious attitudes about our body during a critical developmental period, highlighting the positive role that better interoception can play in mental health. This article is part of the discussion meeting issue 'From being to identity: analysis and synthesis of the self'.
revue: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences

titre: From suicidal ideation to hope: Perceived mental health transformation following a culturally adapted multiple family group therapy for adolescents living with HIV in Ghana - A qualitative process evaluation
resume: Adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV) in sub-Saharan Africa experience profound mental health challenges including depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation. Evidence-based psychological interventions specifically designed for this population remain scarce, particularly family-based approaches in resource-limited settingsThis study explored ALHIV's perceived mental health transformation following participation in culturally adapted Multiple Family Group Therapy (MFGT) in Ghana.Qualitative study nested within a randomized controlled trial (NCT06701942) conducted in Lower Manya Krobo District, Ghana. Nineteen ALHIV who completed the 10-MFGT core content sessions. MFGT intervention participated in three focus group discussions. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis.Three major themes emerged: (1) Pre-Intervention Mental Health Crisis, (2) Psychological Change Mechanisms, and (3) Mental Health Transformation. Pre-intervention, ALHIV described experiencing profound mental health crisis-level distress including active suicidal ideation with method-specific planning, emotional dysregulation, and existential foreclosure. Intervention mechanisms facilitating transformation included cognitive reframing through culturally resonant metaphors, dual-level universality (peer and intergenerational family), biomedical knowledge (U = U) as psychological intervention, and emotional catharsis in safe spaces. Post-intervention, participants described substantial perceived improvements in mental health characterized by reduced suicidal ideation, emotional regulation gains, reduced anxiety, and greater psychological peace.Culturally adapted family-based group therapy was associated with meaningful mental health improvements, including reduced suicidal ideation. Participants described shifts in emotional wellbeing, coping, and family cohesion, though the qualitative design precludes causal claims. Findings support the feasibility of task-shifted, family-centered interventions in resource-limited settings and underscore the need to integrate mental health screening and family-based support into HIV diagnosis protocols. Trial registration Clinical trials.gov (NCT06701942).

titre: Effectiveness of LGBTQ targeted cognitive behavioral therapy on mental health outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis protocol
resume: INTRODUCTION: Sexual and gender minority populations experience disproportionately high rates of mental disorders due, in large part, to their chronic exposure to stigma, discrimination, and minority stress. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an established evidence-based psychotherapy; however, conventional CBT was primarily developed among predominantly cisgender, heterosexual individuals and not often addresses identity-specific stressors relevant to LGBTQ individuals. Emerging adaptations of LGBTQ-affirmative CBT integrate components that affirm sexual and gender minority identities and target minority stress. Although the number of investigations testing such interventions has increased, evidence remains fragmented across studies. To our knowledge, no systematic review has examined the efficacy of LGBTQ targeted CBT on improving mental health outcomes. OBJECTIVE: This systematic review aims to synthesize empirical evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating the effectiveness of LGBTQ targeted CBT interventions in reducing mental health symptoms among sexual and gender minority adults. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A comprehensive search will be conducted across PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, the Cochrane Library, and Scopus, supplemented by gray-literature searches. Eligible studies include RCTs conducted on adults aged 18-65 and evaluating LGBTQ targeted CBT compared with usual care, waitlist, or active controls. Outcomes include depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorder symptom changes at post-intervention and follow-up. Data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment will be performed independently by two reviewers, with risk of bias assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. Where feasible, meta-analyses using random-effects models in R will estimate standardized mean differences or risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Overall efficacy and potential moderators, such as intervention delivery mode and duration, will be investigated. EXPECTED CONTRIBUTION: By consolidating the evidence base for LGBTQ targeted CBT, this review will clarify its efficacy, identify key intervention features associated with improved outcomes, and provide guidance for evidence-based mental health care for sexual and gender minority populations. PROSPERO REGISTRATION: This protocol has been pre-registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO: CRD420251173207).

titre: Transdiagnostic variation in age-related patterns of rich-club organization across neurodevelopmental and related mental health conditions
resume: Rich-club organization is a topographical property of functional brain networks where highly connected regions are more densely interconnected. The rich-club has been shown to be vital for supporting cognitive functioning, and differences have been associated with a wide range of mental health and developmental conditions. This type of organization undergoes complex changes across development, and we have previously shown that males and females have strikingly distinct age-related changes. While disruptions in its development have been related to neurodevelopmental conditions and related mental health conditions such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), the diagnostic- and sex-specific age-related patterns remain unexplored. These conditions also have heterogeneous and overlapping neurobiology and phenotype, and thus transdiagnostic approaches may be most suitable for addressing the complexities. Here, we combine the temporal advantages of magnetoencephalography (MEG) with a data-driven, transdiagnostic approach to parse the heterogeneity of age-related variation in rich-club organization in 386 neurodivergent (116 ADHD, 231 autism, 39 OCD) and 231 neurotypical children and youth, stratified by biological sex. In males and females, subgroups with distinct age-related patterns of rich-club organization did not align cleanly with the diagnostic categories. These patterns were frequency specific, separating the female subgroups in the alpha and gamma bands and the male subgroups in the theta, alpha, beta, and high gamma bands. While the female subgroups differed in their proportions of autistic and neurotypical individuals, all diagnostic categories were represented across the subgroups. The female subgroups also differed in intelligence, while the male subgroups differed in hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms. Together, our findings indicate that frequency-specific, age-related variation in rich-club organization is largely shared across neurotypical and neurodivergent children and youth, rather than delineating diagnostic categories, and highlight the importance of considering sex when studying the biological constructs underlying neurodivergence.

titre: Cancer morbidity and mortality in individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder: a population-based and sibling cohort study in Sweden and Denmark
resume: BACKGROUND: Assessing the risk of cancer morbidity and mortality in individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is important to identify potential disparities in cancer incidence and prognosis. In this study, we aimed to assess the overall and site-specific cancer risk among individuals with OCD, as well as their cancer-specific and all-cause mortality following a cancer diagnosis. METHODS: This cohort study used population-based matched cohorts and sibling-matched cohorts from Sweden (people born between 1932 and 2010) and Denmark (1932-2009). OCD diagnoses were derived by the Swedish National Patient Register and the Danish Psychiatric Central Register. Each individual with OCD was matched with 20 individuals without OCD on sex, birth year, and calendar time and, in separate analyses, with their OCD-free full siblings. Follow-up began at the index date (OCD diagnosis or matching date) and continued until an incident cancer diagnosis, death, emigration, or end of follow-up (December 31, 2016, in Sweden, or 2015, in Denmark). To assess mortality risk in the Swedish population-matched cohort, individuals diagnosed with cancer were subsequently followed from cancer diagnosis until death, emigration, or end of follow-up. RESULTS: In the population-based matched cohorts, 1,372 (2.4%) of 57,239 individuals with OCD and 30,376 (2.7%) of 1,144,780 unaffected individuals developed cancer. OCD was not associated with overall cancer risk (pooled HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.94-1.04). In Sweden, OCD was associated with a lower risk of prostate cancer (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65-0.97) and melanoma (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.51-0.89). Following a cancer diagnosis, individuals with OCD showed no clear difference in cancer-specific mortality (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.97-1.25), but showed higher all-cause mortality (HR 1.27, 95% CI 1.14-1.42), compared with individuals without OCD. CONCLUSIONS: OCD was not associated with overall cancer risk or cancer-specific mortality. However, it was associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality after cancer diagnosis. There does not seem to be a higher-than-expected cancer burden in this population. However, the higher all-cause mortality after a cancer diagnosis suggests that clinical attention should be directed toward managing comorbid conditions to bridge the mortality gap.

titre: 18-years Follow-up after Mosaicplasty in Adolescent Athletes with Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Elbow
resume: BACKGROUND: Autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty is an established surgical treatment of unstable osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesions of the elbow. However, the information on the long-term outcomes is lacking. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the long-term clinical and radiographic results after autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty in the treatment of OCD of the elbow. METHODS: This prospective long-term follow-up study is an extension of previously published data on 10 patients treated with autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty due to advanced, unstable OCD at the capitellum from 2003-2007. Objective and patient-reported outcomes were evaluated including Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Oxford Elbow Score, Quick-Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (Quick-DASH), Timmerman-Andrews Score, a Subjective Elbow Value, and Range of Motion (ROM). Radiographic signs of osteoarthritis were graded according to the Kellgren-Lawrence classification. RESULTS: At mean 18 years (range 16.0-19.7) five patients were available for follow-up. Mean age at follow-up was 34.4, and all five patients were women. MEPS was a median 100 (range 85-100). Activities of daily life were mildly affected in two patients. Two patients had non-symptomatic osteoarthritis grade 1 and 2. Patients experienced a functioning and near-normal elbow. CONCLUSION: The long-term results after mosaicplasty are encouraging, and we find it reasonable to recommend mosaicplasty as the surgical treatment in this group of female patients with advanced, unstable OCD lesions of the elbow. However, it is of concern that two out of five patients had non-symptomatic early radiographic signs of osteoarthritis at an early age. As this study has an inclusion rate of 50 % of the original cohort, attrition bias must be taken into consideration. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, case series, treatment study.
revue: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery

titre: Intermittent Fasting as a Potential Therapeutic Approach for Irritable Bowel Syndrome: A Mechanistic Perspective
resume: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a gastrointestinal disorder that is highly prevalent, often accompanied by considerable comorbidities and that places a substantial burden both on individuals and healthcare systems. Treatments are usually aimed at addressing symptoms but often fall short of long-term relief. Current dietary strategies primarily focus on what patients should avoid eating, while the potential physiological importance of when food is consumed has received little attention in IBS research. We hypothesize that gastrointestinal symptoms may, at least partially, be affected by a cumulative burden of epithelial injury as well as insufficient time for mucosal maintenance and repair. This paper explores the hypothesis that intermittent fasting regimens could represent underexplored therapeutic strategies for reducing IBS symptoms by promoting gut renewal and restoring homeostasis. We review the multifactorial pathophysiology of IBS and explore how fasting may impact relevant biological mechanisms. Several lines of evidence, from both preclinical and clinical studies, indicate that intermittent fasting may reduce inflammation, regulate gut motility and reshape the microbiota, thereby strengthening the gut barrier and dampening immune responses. Fasting also induces autophagy, a key cellular recycling process essential for intestinal barrier maintenance and microbial defense, which may be impaired in IBS. Hence, intermittent fasting may reduce cumulative epithelial injury and allow time for repair to alleviate symptoms in IBS. Although no randomized controlled trials on fasting regimens and IBS are available, evidence from related populations and mechanistic research supports further exploration of this accessible, low-cost approach.

titre: Bacterial Preconditioning Differentially Reshapes Neuronal Responses to Intermittent and Continuous Hypoxia-Like Stress
resume: Abstract The microbiota–gut–brain axis exposes the nervous system to microbial information, but whether such exposure becomes part of the biological history that shapes later neuronal stress responses remains unknown. Here, we tested whether transient direct exposure to live Lactiplantibacillus plantarum ( L. plantarum ) alters how differentiated B35 neuronal cells subsequently respond to hypoxia-like metabolic stress. We compared two trajectories combining chemical HIF stabilization with nutrient restriction: an intermittent, sublethal condition with recovery periods (MHX), relevant to recurrent vascular insufficiency, and a continuous severe condition (SHX). These trajectories generated distinct structural, metabolic and transcriptional states. Prior L. plantarum exposure was associated with higher MTT-derived metabolic viability after MHX but not SHX, and induced broader transcriptional reorganization under MHX (167 versus 64 differentially expressed genes), engaging signaling and cytoskeletal programs together with pathways linked to negative regulation of apoptosis and oxidative-stress-induced cell death. Only one bacterially responsive gene was shared between the two stress trajectories. Thus, L. plantarum did not impose a fixed neuroprotective program. Instead, prior microbial exposure acted as a biological input whose consequences depended on the subsequent stress trajectory. These findings establish neuron–bacteria communication as history-dependent and define an adaptive range in which microbial signals can influence neuronal responses before metabolic stress becomes overwhelming—a principle relevant to preventive intervention during recurrent vascular stress.

titre: The role of Sacral TENS in Improving Continence and Quality of Life in Children with Anorectal Malformations: A six-year Follow-up
resume: Abstract PURPOSE Anorectal malformations are congenital defects of the posterior intestinal development, leading to structural and functional abnormalities of the rectum and/or anal canal. Typically, these patients develop long-term constipation or fecal incontinence, which can be challenging to manage. Sacral transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) is a non-invasive technical alternative initially studied for bladder elimination disorders and has been increasingly established as a tool for treating intestinal dysfunctions. This study aims to observe outcomes in patients who underwent surgery for anorectal malformations and received TENS therapy. METHODS: A longitudinal and retrospective observational study (2018 to 2024). Included children with corrected anorectal malformation, aged 4 to 15 years who underwent TENS therapy. The analysis considered medication use, quality of life through the Paulista Continence Score, and anorectal manometry at three time points: before TENS application, four weeks and six years post TENS. RESULTS: Eleven children were included, 6 had low anorectal malformations and 5 had high anorectal malformations. Among these patients, 81.81% used some type of laxative or bowel management before application, and six years after the treatment, the immediate post-results remained, only 27.27% of patients used some type of laxative or bowel management. Applying São Paulo Continence Score 36.36% were classified as a continent before TENS, increasing to 75% continence six years after TENS. The number of Paulista score had shown improvement through time (χ² (2) = 29.7, p < 0.001). Post-TENS and late follow-up scores were significantly lower than pre-TENS scores (post vs. pre: p = 0.005; late vs. pre: p < 0.001), and late follow-up scores were also significantly lower than post-TENS scores (late vs. post: p = 0.012). Manometric evaluation did not show statistical significance when analyzing resting pressure and average contraction pressure, neither intra-rectal volumes across the three time points. CONCLUSION: patients with anorectal malformation improved clinical outcomes with TENS therapy and can be used for treating elimination disorders.

titre: Factors Associated with Anastomotic Leak After Colostomy Reversal in Northwest Ethiopia: A Retrospective Case–Control Study
resume: Abstract Anastomotic leak is a feared complication after gastrointestinal surgery; however, the risk factors following colostomy reversal in low-resource settings remain poorly defined. We conducted an institution-based case–control study at Debre Markos Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, northwest Ethiopia, using data from all patients who underwent colostomy reversal between 1 January 2016 and 31 December 2024. Cases were patients with a documented anastomotic leak during the index hospitalization or within 30 days postoperatively, while controls had no anastomotic leak. Data were extracted using a pretested checklist and analyzed using binary logistic regression. Of 225 eligible patients, 56 (24.9%) developed an anastomotic leak. Factors independently associated with anastomotic leak were residence more than 60 km from the hospital (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 8.45, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.43–20.83), colostomy duration of less than 3 months (AOR = 2.53, 95% CI: 1.10–5.82), comorbid illness (AOR = 5.15, 95% CI: 1.97–13.49), significant intraoperative adhesions (AOR = 2.73, 95% CI: 1.15–6.49), a short distal stump (AOR = 2.82, 95% CI: 1.18–6.74), iatrogenic bowel injury (AOR = 3.20, 95% CI: 1.09–9.46), failure to pass flatus within 72 hours (AOR = 5.84, 95% CI: 1.63–20.91), and other postoperative complications (AOR = 3.48, 95% CI: 1.03–11.73). Anastomotic leak after colostomy reversal is influenced by patient-related, geographic, intraoperative, and postoperative factors, several of which are modifiable. Preoperative optimization, appropriate timing of reversal, meticulous adhesiolysis, avoidance of bowel injury, careful assessment of the distal stump, and vigilant postoperative monitoring may reduce leak-related morbidity and mortality in similar resource-constrained settings.

titre: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Non-Inferiority Trial Comparing Microbial and Porcine Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy in Chronic Pancreatitis (Np-Pert Trial) - Protocol
resume: Abstract Background Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is a progressive inflammatory disorder causing irreversible pancreatic damage, eventually resulting in pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI). This may lead to malabsorption, malnutrition, weight loss, and impaired quality of life. Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) is the standard treatment for PEI and is predominantly derived from porcine sources. However, religious, ethical, dietary, and supply-related concerns highlight the need for effective non-porcine alternatives. Microbial based pancreatic enzymes have shown promising safety and efficacy in preliminary studies, but evidence in CP remains limited. Objective To compare the efficacy and safety of non-porcine microbial -based pancreatin with standard porcine-based pancreatin in patients with PEI secondary to CP. Methods This investigator-initiated, randomized, double-blind, single-center, non-inferiority trial will enroll 134 adults with CP-associated PEI (defined as having a faecal elastase 1.4. After a two-week washout period, participants will be randomized 1:1 to receive either microbial-based or porcine-based pancreatin for 12 weeks. The primary outcome is the change from baseline in the PEI-Q score at 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes include nutritional status, anthropometric measures, gastrointestinal symptoms, pain scores, stool consistency, glycemic parameters, laboratory markers, and quality of life. Discussion This study aims to evaluate whether microbial-based pancreatin is non-inferior to porcine-based therapy and may provide a culturally acceptable and sustainable alternative for managing CP-related PEI.

titre: Capturing continuous spectrotemporal pupil–brain coupling with simultaneous wearable EEG/Eye tracking
resume: Spontaneous fluctuations in pupil diameter are closely linked to neural dynamics, yet most evidence for pupil–brain coupling has been obtained in conventional laboratory settings. We therefore asked whether the spectrotemporal and directional organization of such coupling can be captured with wearable systems to test their use in naturalistic settings. Using combined lightweight mobile EEG (MUSE) and eye tracking (Tobii Pro Glasses 3) devices, we investigated resting-state pupil–brain coupling and explored interoceptive attention to determine whether the core organizational principles observed with stationary equipment are detectable within and preserved across continuous recording states. Cross-correlation, mutual information, and Granger causality analyses revealed that pupil–brain coupling displayed clear frequency-dependent organization. Lower EEG frequencies (2-12Hz) preceded pupil dynamics by roughly 764ms, while higher frequencies showed a distinct coupling range. Granger-causality analysis further indicated predominantly EEG-to-pupil directional coupling. Similar observations were made during interoception. Overall, these findings align well and extend previous evidence on spontaneous pupil–brain coupling, demonstrating that lightweight and movable wearable devices are suitable to characterize spectrotemporal and directional pupil– brain interactions. In turn, these results encourage future fundamental and translational research in naturalistic environments.

titre: Somatic symptom burden is associated with anger internalization measured as reduced reactive aggression
resume: Objectives Difficulties in emotion regulation, including anger suppression, have been linked to more severe somatic symptoms in patients with chronic pain. Because this evidence comes mainly from clinical samples, it remains unclear whether such difficulties precede or follow symptom chronification. We examined whether somatic symptom burden is associated with reduced reactive aggression, as a behavioral marker of anger internalization. Method Forty-four healthy adults (25 females) completed the Taylor Aggression Paradigm, a competitive reaction-time task in which they selected noise intensity delivered to a fictitious opponent across three provocation conditions (low, moderate, and high). somatic symptom burden was evaluated using the Somatic Symptom Scale-8 (SSS-8) and Patient Health Questionnaire-15 (PHQ-15). Alexithymia was evaluated using the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20). Results Participants with higher somatic symptom burden selected lower noise intensities overall, with significant differences at low and moderate provocation levels. Difficulty identifying feelings tended to be positively associated with somatic symptom burden, whereas alexithymia was not associated with reactive aggression. Discussion These findings suggest that inhibited retaliation, previously reported in chronic pain patients, may already be present in healthy individuals with higher somatic symptom burden, potentially aiding early identification of chronic pain risk. Difficulty distinguishing emotions from bodily sensations may also contribute to somatic symptom expression.

titre: Anxiety and Depressive Symptom Trajectories During Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Incorporating Gratitude Touch: Implications for Multimodal Mental Health Care
resume: Background: /Objectives: Brief nonpharmacological exercises may complement psychotherapy within multimodal mental health care, although their specific contribution to symptom change requires controlled evaluation. We described 12-month psychological symptom trajectories in women receiving cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) that included the Gratitude Touch exercise. Methods: This single-group, non-randomized study included 50 women aged 25–45 years. Weekly individual CBT sessions incorporated tactile contact with each finger, verbalized gratitude, and brief bodily observation. DASS-21, Endler Multidimensional Anxiety Scales (EMAS), and Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) scores were assessed at baseline and at 3, 6, and 12 months. Longitudinal differences were examined using Friedman tests and Bonferroni-adjusted Wilcoxon comparisons. Results: Mean DASS-21 Anxiety scores decreased from 13.30 at baseline to 8.72 at 3 months, then increased to 11.44 at 6 months and 11.94 at 12 months. The reported omnibus difference was significant (χ²(3) = 127.40, adjusted p < 0.001; Kendall’s W = 0.8493). Depression and stress subscales showed a similar early decrease followed by partial rebound. EMAS-S and BDI-II means decreased at intermediate assessments but matched baseline values at 12 months; conflicting paired-test summaries limit interpretation of these endpoints. Conclusions: The cohort showed temporal symptom variation during combined nonpharmacological therapy, rather than consistent improvement across all measures. Without a CBT-only comparison, the added contribution of Gratitude Touch and its clinical significance remain undetermined.

titre: Altered pre-supplementary motor area recruitment during semantic inhibition in individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits
resume: Background: Inhibitory control dysfunction has been implicated in obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), but neuroimaging research has focused predominantly on motor response inhibition. Whether obsessive–compulsive traits are associated with altered neural recruitment during semantic inhibition remains unclear. Methods: Forty right-handed participants with lower or elevated obsessive–compulsive traits performed an fMRI adaptation of the Hayling Sentence Completion Task. Participants either selected an expected sentence completion (initiation) or suppressed this strongly prepotent response to select an unrelated word (inhibition). Whole-brain and anatomically defined region-of-interest (ROI) analyses examined task-related activation and Group × Condition interactions, with particular interest in the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) and SMA proper. Results: Semantic inhibition produced a robust behavioural cost in reaction times and error rates, with no significant differences between groups. Whole-brain analysis identified the strongest inhibition-related activation in the left preSMA. The exploratory Group × Condition analysis also yielded its peak interaction in this region. Anatomically defined ROI analysis showed a significant Group × Condition interaction in the preSMA after family-wise error correction (t = 2.56, pFWE = .012), reflecting a larger inhibition-related increase in controls compared to individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits. The corresponding interaction in SMA proper did not reach statistical significance (t = 1.74, pFWE = .084). Conclusions: Elevated obsessive–compulsive traits were associated with altered preSMA recruitment during semantic inhibition in absence of behavioural impairment. This extends neural markers of obsessive–compulsive alterations from the domain of motor inhibition to that of semantic inhibition.

titre: Association between serum ghrelin concentrations and depression severity in patients with irritable bowel syndrome: a clinic-based case–control study
resume: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disease commonly associated with psychological comorbidities. Ghrelin, a gut-derived peptide hormone participated in gut-brain axis regulation, may play a role in both gastrointestinal and emotional symptoms. This study aimed to investigate the association between ghrelin levels in serum and depression severity in a Northwestern Iranian patients with IBS. In this case–control study, 140 IBS patients (diagnosed based on Rome III criteria) and 115 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were enrolled. Depression severity was assessed using the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II). Also, serum ghrelin concentrations were measured via an enzyme-linked immune-sorbent assay (ELISA). Statistical analyses included independent t-test, ANOVA, linear regression, and Pearson’s correlation analysis. Our results showed that IBS patients had significantly lower ghrelin levels compared to healthy controls ( P = 0.001). IBS patients with minimal, mild, moderate, or severe depressive symptoms (≥ 29) exhibited lower ghrelin levels than controls with mild depression (All, P = 0.00). Serum ghrelin levels were inversely correlated with IBS severity ( r = − 0.18, P = 0.001). Also, serum ghrelin remained a significant predictor of BDI-II score (standardized β = −0.442, P < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, serum ghrelin remained independently associated with depression severity after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI ( P < 0.001). Decreased ghrelin levels in IBS patients are linked to higher depression severity and this issue is the major driver of disease severity. These findings suggest a potential role of the gut–brain axis in the IBS and psychological symptoms interactions. However, further research is needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms since causal relationships cannot be inferred based on the cross-sectional study.

titre: Diet and synbiotics in the gut–immune–brain axis: implications for gastrointestinal and psychological health
resume: The gut microbiota participates in gut–immune–brain communication through metabolic, immune, neural and endocrine pathways. Dietary patterns and microbiota-directed interventions, including prebiotics, probiotics and synbiotics, may affect these pathways, but biological responses do not necessarily translate into clinical benefit. We examine mechanistic and human evidence, focusing on disorders of gut–brain interaction, particularly irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and on psychological outcomes. Selected synbiotic trials report improvements in gastrointestinal symptoms, although formulations, populations, comparators and endpoints differ substantially. Evidence for psychological benefit is less consistent and remains limited by small or uncontrolled studies. Human milk oligosaccharides illustrate the potential for selective substrate use, but their clinical value in adults requires further testing. Future trials should specify the intended clinical effect, select appropriate comparators and measure microbial, metabolic and host responses alongside validated symptoms.

titre: Sattvic Diet and Gut-Brain Axis Scoping Review
resume: Scoping review to compare the impact of a Sattvic diet on the Gut-Brain axis and other secondary markers of health.

titre: Gut-brain axis and neuroinflammation: mechanisms, interactions, and recent advances
resume: In recent years, the gut-brain axis (GBA), an essential bidirectional communication network linking the gut microbiota and central nervous system (CNS) functions, has attracted increasing research interest at the intersection of microbiology and neuroscience. This pathway is involved in multiple physiological and pathological conditions including emotion regulation, cognitive function and neuroinflammation through neural, immune, endocrine and metabolic mechanisms. Based on human observational studies, animal models and in-vitro experiments, there is evidence that gut dysbiosis is also related to intestinal barrier dysfunction, altered microbial metabolites and neuroinflammatory response. Evidence is largely preclinical or mechanistic, whereas human data are currently more limited for causal relationships. Signal transfer involves three components: the vagus nerve, immune mediators and the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Microbiota-targeted interventions have been shown to yield proportionally consistent mechanistic benefits in preclinical models, whereas human intervention studies remain heterogeneous and show mixed positive and null outcomes—among these microbiota-targeted interventions there are probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), and dietary modulation. Hence, their clinical utility for neuroinflammatory disorders is only preliminary and needs to be validated in bigger, placebo-controlled trials. Although the present studies are confronted with difficulties, which include unclear causality and great individual variations among subjects, GBA research has been gradually moving into a novel stage from the perspective of mechanistic explanation and precision intervention along with advancements in multi-omics technologies and artificial intelligence, generating new theoretical hypotheses and translational significance for the prevention or treatment of neuroinflammatory diseases.

titre: Research Progress on Using Non-drug Traditional Chinese Medicine Interventions to Treat Parkinson's Disease by Regulating the Gut-Brain Axis
resume: Conventional Western medical treatments for Parkinson's disease (PD) still have limitations in terms of maintaining efficacy and managing adverse reactions; the "microbiota-gut-brain" axis offers a new perspective in this regard. The Braak hypothesis suggests that α-synuclein can enter the brain via the vagus nerve, and damage to the intestinal barrier and TLR4-mediated intestinal inflammation are key links in neurodegeneration along the gut-brain axis. This article reviewed the mechanisms and clinical evidence supporting the prevention and treatment of PD through therapies such as acupuncture (body, electroacupuncture, scalp, ocular, and abdominal), moxibustion, Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) exercises, and auricular acupuncture. In terms of mechanism, the evidence is fairly clear for electroacupuncture. It upregulated colonic GPR40/43, elevated GLP-1, and activated neuroprotective pathways such as PI3K-AKT-GSK3β through the gut microbiota–brain axis. By comparison, animal studies on other therapies mostly described broader effects, including modulation of the microbiota, repair of intestinal permeability, and inhibition of enteric inflammation. Clinical observations also suggested some symptom improvement. These therapies appear to improve motor symptoms and, to varying degrees,non-motor symptoms such as constipation, insomnia, and depression. One study reported an overall efficacy rate of 93.3% for ocular acupuncture, which was higher than the 75.6% observed for body acupuncture (single study). Still, this comparison should be treated cautiously. Most of the available evidence came from animal experiments and small-sample observational studies, with few direct cross-comparisons between therapies.
