For that reason, the gut-brain axis mechanisms involved in ocular acupuncture and scalp acupuncture still need closer examination and confirmation in large-sample multicenter studies.

titre: Traditional Indian Plant-Based Dietary Patterns and the Gut–Brain Axis: A Scoping Review of Sattvic, Jain, Hindu Vegetarian and Vegan Diets
resume: Scoping review to compare the impact of a Sattvik diet on the Gut-Brain axis and other secondary markers of health.

titre: Gut Microbiota and Emotional Eating Behavior: Neuropsychological Pathways Involving Stress, Anxiety and Depression
resume: Emotional eating is described as eating without feeling physically hungry to cope with stress, anxiety and negative emotions. Hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis activity associated with stress, anxiety and depression, along with changes in cortisol levels and neurobiological processes that regulate appetite and reward mechanisms, can trigger emotional eating behavior. The gut microbiota may influence emotional eating through modulation of hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis activity, as hypothesized from a neuropsychological perspective. The aim of this review is to evaluate the neurobiological and neuropsychological mechanisms associated with stress, anxiety and depression that may play a role in the potential relationship between the gut microbiota and emotional eating; to provide a comprehensive perspective on the current evidence regarding these mechanisms. The gut microbiota is a dynamic ecosystem that regulates metabolic, immune and neuroendocrine homeostasis through host-microbiota interactions. The gut microbiota may influence the gut–brain axis through the metabolism of short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan and GABA, along with BDNF and FXR/TGR5 signaling pathways, thereby regulating emotional eating behaviors associated with stress, anxiety and depression. As a result, alterations in the gut microbiota can affect emotional eating associated with stress, anxiety and depression through various pathways. Current evidence is largely based on in vitro and animal studies, while human studies are mostly observational, limiting causal inferences regarding the relationships between gut microbiota, depression, anxiety, and stress. Future studies should address the impact of the gut microbiota on emotional eating through individualized intervention studies that evaluate stress, anxiety and depression.

titre: Editorial: Impact of gut probiotic metabolites on human metabolic diseases
resume: irritable bowel syndrome, a multifactorial disorder with abdominal pain, altered bowel habits and multifaceted interactions among the gut microbiome. The importance of evaluating probiotic efficiency at the strain level rather than at the species level, with particular emphasis on their metabolites, notably short-chain fatty acids, is highlighted. Inadequate dietary control and incomplete strain, dose, and biomarker assessments limit the application of probiotics for IBD (Mora Guzmán et al., 2026) .The effects of probiotics, Lactobacillus plantarum strain LP-115 and Bifidobacterium bifidum strain BB-06, on gut microbiota functions were investigated among liver failure cases. Rats supplemented with probiotics showed increased levels of SCFAs and decreased levels of toxic metabolites, such as ammonia. Shotgun metagenomic reconstruction of faecal DNA provided comprehensive insights into the metabolic potential of the microbiome (Luo et al., 2026).The effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Lactobacillus plantarum, and Bifidobacterium longum on intestinal barrier function and hepatic injury in an animal model of fulminant liver failure (FLF) has been reported in this study. Probiotic treatment reduced intestinal hyperpermeability and restored tight junction integrity. In addition, probiotics reduced serum levels of alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, bilirubin, ammonia, oxidative stress markers and pro-inflammatory cytokines.Histopathological examination of liver tissue showed reduced hepatocellular injury and apoptosis.Probiotics may represent an effective therapeutic approach for protecting against FLF (C. Wu et al., 2026).Random forest models classified disease stages with 89.3% accuracy and identified key microbial markers, providing microbiome signatures as potential diagnostic, severity, and personalized therapeutic tools for H. pylori-related diseases. H. pylori eradication therapy along with probiotics might enhance eradication rates, reduce the side effects associated with antibiotics, help to preserve gut and oral microbiota and support their use as adjunctive therapy (X. Wu et al., 2025). Saccharomyces boulardii CNCM I-745 reduces IL-6 and TNF-α levels, increases intestinal occludin expression, and improves gut microbial composition and diversity in a rat model of sepsis. It stimulated the growth of beneficial bacteria and inhibited the growth of harmful bacteria, suggesting a potential to block disruption of the intestinal barrier and inflammation (Liu et al., 2025).In a double-blind randomized controlled trial, probiotics improved irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) symptoms by modulating increased fecal acetate, propionate, and butyrate levels; enhancing intestinal barrier integrity and tight-junction protein expression; and decreasing inflammation. Higher SCFA levels were associated with symptom improvement, highlighting the possible role of SCFAs in probiotic benefits. Overall, probiotics seem safe and effective for treating IBS through SCFA production, barrier strengthening, and anti-inflammatory effects (E. Li et al., 2025). A network metaanalysis of 29 randomized controlled trials with 4,389 patients showed that fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) had the best improvement in bowel movements and stool consistency and acupuncture had a good clinical response. Probiotics had the lowest risk of adverse events. This study supports FMT, with or without acupuncture, as a promising treatment for functional constipation, but further high-quality studies are needed (Tan et al., 2025).The gut microbiome is a key factor influencing host energy metabolism. The review highlights the role of probiotic-fermented herbal residues in managing obesity by revealing the biological processes that improve bioactive compounds and their bioavailability by modulating the gut-liver axis. The combined herbal medicine and modern biotechnology will be a promising approach for managing metabolic disorders (Tian et al., 2026). The multi-omics approach assessed the impact of probiotic supplementation on gut microbiota composition and metabolomic profiles in women with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).Administration of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium significantly changed the gut microbiota and increased the levels of SCFAs, particularly butyrate and acetate. Gene expression analysis using RT-PCR showed a 2.5-to 1.9-fold increase in insulin receptor and AKT expression, suggesting greater insulin sensitivity; however, gut barrier genes (ZO-1 and CLDN1) also increased. Probiotic supplementation may be a non-invasive, safer therapeutic approach for GDM by improving insulin sensitivity and gut health (Su et al., 2026).The meta-analysis covers 46 randomized controlled trials with 3,580 participants with either type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Probiotic/synbiotic administration significantly decreased CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α, along with increased IL-10 and SCFA levels. Probiotic/synbiotic and SCFA supplementation may be a better diabetes care strategy (Xie et al., 2025).Another meta-analysis showed that microbial metabolites from probiotics interact with host proteins and tissue-specific pathways affecting gastrointestinal and metabolic health. Network and transcriptomic analyzes revealed important metabolite-gene relationships involving 10-hydroxy-cis-12-octadecenoic acid, glycodeoxycholic acid and N-(1-carbamoyl-2-phenyl-ethyl) butyramide. These findings identify molecular connections between microbial metabolites and host function that can inform microbiome-directed therapies and precision nutrition approaches to improve metabolic health (Yao et al., 2025).Potential host targets and biological functions of probiotic-based metabolites were identified using an integrative network-based approach based on metabolite-protein interactions and tissue-specific transcriptomics. High-degree genes including SLC27A4, LCN12 and APOD were highly expressed in gastrointestinal tract tissues, suggesting their involvement in host-microbe interactions. Metabolitespecific analysis showed different expression patterns. 10-hydroxy-cis-12-octadecenoic acid demonstrated a relationship to sialyltransferases and neuraminidase, glycodeoxycholic acid was related to bile acid metabolism and lipid transport and N-(1-carbamoyl-2-phenyl-ethyl) butyramide was related to detoxification pathways (Ma & Zhang, 2025).The systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effectiveness of probiotic-derived metabolitetargeted interventions on hormonal and metabolic outcomes in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Experimental treatments included synbiotics, probiotics, sodium butyrate, Akkermansia muciniphila, and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) compositions, and all interventions lasted at least 8 weeks. Pooled data analysis showed a significant decrease in total testosterone, LH/FSH, fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR, with a slight increase in HDL cholesterol (Maddirevula et al., 2025).A total of 46 randomized controlled trials involving more than 12,500 pregnant women suggest that probiotic supplementation may reduce gestational weight gain and postpartum weight retention and improve fasting glucose, HOMA-IR, total cholesterol, and LDL. This study reveals that probiotics are a promising non-pharmacological strategy for improving maternal metabolic health and reducing adverse pregnancy outcomes in obese women through multiple pathways (Jia et al., 2025).A randomized double-blind and placebo-controlled trial assessed multistrain probiotics (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Bifidobacterium longum) administered to 84 subjects who had closed tibial shaft fractures, through 3-dimensional microcomputed tomography (CT) measurements of BV/TV. Exploratory analyses showed that probiotics were associated with earlier weight-bearing, reduced pain at week 2, and higher RUST scores at 12 weeks. These results suggest that perioperative probiotic administration could not only promote fracture healing but also accelerate functional recovery, likely mediated by gut-bone axis-based immunomodulatory effects. Thus, probiotics can positively impact fracture care as an adjunct to standard treatment (Huang et al., 2026).Another study explored the role of probiotics in sarcopenia using data from NHANES and the UK Biobank, integrated with in vitro C2C12 myotube experiments, molecular docking, and machinelearning models. Individuals who regularly consume probiotics have higher handgrip strength and fatfree mass, and lower signs of inflammation, than those who do not. Probiotic-conditioned media greatly promoted muscle cell fusion, increased cell diameter, and increased expression of the muscle regulatory genes MyoD, Myogenin, and MyHC; it also reduced NF-κB and TNF-α while boosting PGC-1 levels. Butyrate showed strong interactions with AMPK, mTOR and NF-B. Thus, probiotics could help preserve muscle via immune responses and microbiota-controlled metabolic and muscleanabolism pathways (Wang et al., 2026).The study evaluated the impact of gut microbiome changes on postoperative recovery in postmenopausal women by examining stool samples using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and QIIME2.Analysis of alpha and beta diversity exhibited major changes in microbial composition, with a predominance of Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, associated with improved functional outcomes and faster recovery. Conversely, Proteobacteria and Escherichia were linked to delayed healing and worse clinical outcomes. Based on microbial abundance, a random forest machine learning model achieved 85% accuracy in predicting clinical recovery, suggesting that gut microbiome signatures may serve as key biomarkers and provide a basis for microbiome-based personalized strategies to accelerate postoperative recovery and enhance long-term musculoskeletal health. Furthermore, microbiome composition correlates with various important surgical parameters such as bone healing and infection rate (Pan et al., 2026).A meta-analysis evaluated the effects of different doses and intervention durations of different probiotic strains on bone metabolism. The review states that probiotic supplementation boosts bone formation and decreases bone resorption in patients with osteoporosis. Formulations with probiotic consortia and higher doses showed significant improvements, especially in postmenopausal women, suggesting that probiotics may be a promising adjunctive approach to improve bone health. The changes observed in bone resorption markers indicate the beneficial effects of probiotics on bone health. Probiotics are not considered a primary treatment for osteoporosis, but could support maintaining bone health (Yuan et al., 2026).The human gastrointestinal tract (GIT) is colonized by a complex microbial community which plays major roles in host physiology, metabolism, immunity and neurobehavioral functions. This study highlights the bidirectional gut-brain axis, in which the gut microbiota influences neural signalling, stress responses, and emotional regulation. Dysbiosis of this gut microbiota has been linked with psychiatric, neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders such as anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, major depressive disorder, and schizophrenia. Psychobiotics are promising microbiomebased interventions for supporting mental health. These benefits may arise from modulation of neurotransmitter production, SCFA signaling, immune responses, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity. FMT restores the natural gut microbiota and relieves the symptoms of mental illness via modulating inflammatory pathways. These emerging therapies, psychobiotics and FMT, may be promising strategies for managing mental health disorders (Selta et al., 2026).The study assessed the effect of washed microbiota transplantation (WMT) and investigated the changes in gut microbiota in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Thirty-eight ASD children who underwent a full course of WMT from a single donor were evaluated before and 4 weeks after treatment by clinical rating scales and 16S rRNA gene sequencing. WMT significantly improved core ASD symptoms, sleep, and GI symptoms. In addition, the therapeutic effect was related to the gut microbiota of both the donor and recipient before therapy, suggesting that donor-recipient microbiota compatibility may influence the effect of WMT in ASD (Quan et al., 2026).The multi-omics study provides mechanistic evidence supporting the neuromodulatory effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and Bifidobacterium longum 1714. L. rhamnosus GG mainly boosts GABAergic and SCFA-based synaptic pathways, whereas B. longum 1714 influences the tryptophanserotonin-immune axis. Additionally, in vitro validation demonstrated increased GABA and serotonin release, reduced ROS levels, and enrichment of anti-inflammatory transcripts in EVs. These findings reveal the therapeutic potential of L. rhamnosus GG and B. longum 1714 for neurological health (Jin et al., 2026).The effect of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG was evaluated in sepsis-induced lung injury by assessing the gut-lung axis. Probiotic supplementation in Wistar rats endangered by caecal ligation and puncture improved pulmonary function, lung histology, and respiratory parameters. Probiotic culture also restored the gut microbiota and reduced hypoxemia and inflammation. Thus, efficient therapeutic probiotics will greatly increase the success of treatment and improve the patient's quality of life and survival (Wang et al., 2026).A single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated the effects of probiotic lozenges in children with adenoid hypertrophy and otitis media with effusion receiving standard nonsurgical management. Probiotic treatment significantly improved tympanogram classification compared with placebo, with favorable changes in tympanometric and audiological parameters, including DPOAE conversion. Probiotic treatment may improve auditory function by promoting probiotic colonization and inhibiting pathogens, supporting the potential of probiotic bacteria as a safe adjunct for conservative management of pediatric otitis media with effusion (Shi et al., 2026).Network pharmacology and bioinformatics analysis identified 110 gut microbiota-derived metabolites with 6,860 potential human target genes and 268 overlapping otitis media associated genes. Enrichment analyzes of these targets to inflammatory and immune pathways provided molecular evidence for microbial metabolites as candidate therapeutics (Zheng & Jin, 2025). Reanalysis of the public dataset GSE43764 identified the effect of oral Lactobacillus pentosus B240 on innate immunity against H1N1 influenza via modulation of the glutathione-ROS pathway and the macrophage type I IFN axis. Probiotic supplementation was associated with improved baseline antioxidant and oxidative stress regulatory pathways, associated with coordinated activation of GSH-ROS, Nrf2, macrophage activation and type I IFN responses. Differential and co-expression analyzes showed regulated expression of genes involved in glutathione metabolism, oxidative stress, macrophage activity, interferon signaling, and antiviral defense. Mixed probiotics significantly reduced lung damage and pathological inflammation and enhanced immune cell function and systemic immune response (Ye & Zhang, 2025).The therapeutic potential of probiotics, Lactobacillus rhamnosus, L. plantarum, and Bifidobacterium longum, along with their heat-killed preparations, extracellular vesicles, and metabolite extracts, to control HPV-associated head and neck cancer is demonstrated using microbiome, immunological, and computational approaches. Probiotic treatment improved immune regulation and epithelial barrier function and decreased cancer cell viability by inducing apoptosis. Their therapeutic potential was also supported by increased caspase activity and immunoregulatory cytokines. These results suggest that live probiotic cultures and their various forms and metabolites could be promising adjunctive therapies for HPV-associated head and neck cancer (Jiang et al., 2026).A randomized controlled trial (RCT) investigated the effects of comprehensive nursing care combined with probiotic intervention on improving gut health in patients with malignancies. After 8 weeks of intervention, the observation group had better gastrointestinal function and nutritional status, reduced non-infectious complications and improved quality of life among patients undergoing chemotherapy.This study found therapeutic value in probiotics combined with comprehensive nursing care for patients with gastrointestinal malignancies (Huang et al., 2026).The retrospective study investigated how a probiotic-rich diet combined with an enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) nursing pathway, affects postoperative recovery in patients with laryngeal cancer.The treatment with probiotic formulation containing Lactobacillus acidophilus LA-5, Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. Lactis BB12 led to higher recovery rates in energy and protein intake in the early postoperative phase through the gastrointestinal tract. Inflammatory markers CRP, IL-6, and leukocyte count had increased, and albumin and prealbumin levels had declined. The probability of complications, including pneumonia, wound infection and pharyngocutaneous fistula, was much reduced. Hospital stay and antibiotic use were reduced (Wei et al., 2025).In this meta-analysis of 18 randomized controlled trials with 1,246 women with endometrial cancer (EC), probiotics increased gut microbiota diversity, increased beneficial bacteria, and reduced gastrointestinal complications. Probiotics also improved well-being and reduced IL-6 and TNF-α levels. Multi-strain formulations, higher doses (≥10¹⁰ CFU/day) and longer interventions had greater benefits, supporting probiotics as a potential adjunctive therapy (Chen et al., 2025).This review explores the significant role of Akkermansia muciniphila, an important gut commensal, in maintaining gut immune homeostasis and metabolic balance. The molecular mechanisms underlying the anti-inflammatory effects of A. muciniphila involve intestinal barrier enhancement, immune modulation, metabolite-mediated signaling and reshaping the gut microbiota. This review also notes that pasteurized preparations and bioactive metabolites can have therapeutic effects alongside live bacterial cultures (Xie et al., 2026). This review highlights the phenylketonuria pathophysiology, gut probiotics, phenylalanine amino acid metabolism, and the therapeutic potential of probiotics. Pre-and probiotic-based approaches could benefit phenylketonuria treatment by increasing microbial diversity and making the microbiome more resilient, enabling the intestine to resist disturbances and prevent losses in functional diversity (Kalla Veedu et al., 2025).Though gut microbiome and their metabolites ae gaining more attention and popularity, the interpretation and therapeutic strategy of the available data are limited due to less availability of clinical translations. Molecular docking, computational projections, and in vitro investigations provide mechanistic insights, but they do not adequately replicate physiological circumstances or prove clinical relevance. Such in silico studies require experimental validation for identified biomarkers and predicted metabolite-protein interactions. It is yet unclear how microbial metabolites, live probiotics, microbial consortia, and host responses relate to one another. Furthermore, conclusions drawn from certain strains, formulations and disease models cannot be applied to all probiotic treatments. In this research topic, the published in vitro and in silico studies indicate potential probiotic activities, metabolites, host targets and biological pathways but cannot be used to establish a therapeutic efficacy per se. Reported animal studies suggest potential physiologic effects of B. fragilis, such as modulation of inflammation, injury to organs, intestinal barrier integrity and microbial metabolism, but these findings need to be validated in human volunteers. titre: The effect of a one-session slow breathing exercise on emotional reactivity, heart rate, and blood pressure in alexithymic vs. non-alexithymic individuals
resume: Alexithymic individuals experience difficulties in emotion regulation at both emotional and somatic levels. Some studies suggest that breathing interventions might compensate for these impairments. The main aim of the present study was to test whether a one-session breathing exercise affects emotional reactivity, blood pressure, and heart rate in alexithymic vs. non-alexithymic individuals. Based on their TAS-20 scores from the screening part of the study ( n = 210), participants were allocated to an alexithymic ( n = 27) or non-alexithymic group ( n = 29). They underwent negative mood induction and they were randomly allocated to one of the breathing training conditions (faster – 12 breaths/minute vs. slower – 6 breaths/minute). Their mood, heart rate, and blood pressure were measured 3 times throughout the study. The results revealed a marginally significant interaction between alexithymia and breathing exercise for the arousal dimension of emotional reactivity. Alexithymic participants who underwent slower breathing reported lower arousal, akin to non-alexithymic participants but contrary to participants after faster breathing, who reported higher arousal. Additionally, alexithymic participants, after the slower-breathing exercise, experienced a significant drop in HR. We did not observe any significant effects on blood pressure. The present findings suggest that breathing-based strategies may warrant further investigation as a simple approach to supporting emotional and physiological recovery in individuals with alexithymic traits. Given the preliminary nature of the evidence, these findings require confirmation in larger, adequately powered studies.

titre: Dissociation, Trauma, Interoception, and Sleep: A Network Analysis
resume: Dissociation, as a multidimensional psychological construct, encompasses a broad spectrum of experiences, ranging from everyday detachment and lapses in attention to severe clinical symptoms observed in dissociative disorders and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD; ​Danböck et al., 2025)​. Current evidence indicates the transdiagnostic nature of dissociative symptoms ​(Ellickson-Larew et al., 2020; Lyssenko et al., 2018)​, which may co-occur across various forms of psychopathology. Competing models of dissociation etiology—the posttraumatic model (PTM) and the sociocognitive model (SCM)—have been proposed, yet consensus between them remains unresolved ​(Lynn et al., 2024)​. The present study investigates relationships between dissociative symptoms and variables derived from both theoretical frameworks (PTM and SCM) within a single sample, aiming to elucidate multidirectional associations among dissociation, trauma exposure, posttraumatic symptomatology, interoception, and sleep quality. Existing evidence suggests that these variables are highly interconnected. Of particular interest is the link between dissociation and atypical interoception ​(Fani et al., 2023; Kaldewaij et al., 2024; Maqueda et al., 2015; Michal et al., 2014; Millman et al., 2023; Pick et al., 2020; Schäflein et al., 2018; Woelk & Garfinkel, 2024)​, which has been conceptualized as a potential “P factor”​(Smith et al., 2024)​ contributing to broad vulnerability in mental disorders ​(Brewer et al., 2021)​. Interoceptive dysfunctions have also been observed in individuals with PTSD ​(Leech et al., 2024)​. Furthermore, accumulating evidence suggests that sleep disturbances represent an important mechanism contributing to dissociative experiences ​(Arora et al., 2020; Eiser, 2024; Giesbrecht et al., 2007; Lopez et al., 2023; Quaedackers et al., 2022; Selvi et al., 2017; van der Kloet et al., 2012; Van Der Kloet et al., 2012)​. Several studies have documented significant associations between sleep quality and interoceptive processing ​(Alfì et al., 2025; Arora et al., 2021; Asaoka et al., 2025; Bynum & Brindle, 2025; Julie et al., 2025; Seo et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2016; Wei & Van Someren, 2020)​. Sleep disturbances are particularly prevalent among individuals with PTSD ​(Miller et al., 2020; Palagini et al., 2022)​. Taken together, substantial evidence points to complex, multidirectional relationships among dissociative symptoms, interoceptive functioning, sleep quality, and posttraumatic symptomatology. These variables may share a common underlying mechanism—namely, stress-related dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system and its communication with the central nervous system ​(Beutler et al., 2022; Siciliano et al., 2022)​.

titre: Relationship between Alexithymia and Chronic Stress by Compassionate Goals
No Words for Intergroup Feelings: Intergroup Empathy Mediates the Relationship Between Alexithymia and Intergroup Relations
resume: ABSTRACT Alexithymia is linked to poor interpersonal relations; less is known about its role in intergroup relations. We examined which of its facets predict negative intergroup relations, and whether dispositional and intergroup empathy mediate these associations. We also tested whether alexithymia is associated with general social impairment or disproportionately poorer intergroup relations relative to interpersonal relations. White British heterosexual men ( N = 302) participated in a preregistered cross‐sectional online survey on experiences with gay men. Alexithymia was measured with the Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS‐20) and the Perth Alexithymia Questionnaire (PAQ), and dispositional and intergroup empathic concern (EC) and perspective‐taking (PT) were assessed using the Interpersonal Reactivity Index. Results first showed an intergroup bias: Individuals reported lower PT, greater affective prejudice, lower behavioral intentions, and lower self‐disclosure toward outgroup than ingroup members. Individuals higher on the alexithymia externally oriented thinking (EOT) facet rated both ingroup and outgroup members more negatively on affective prejudice, stereotypes, and behavioral intentions than individuals with lower alexithymia‐EOT. They also reported lower self‐disclosure in both interpersonal and intergroup relations. Finally, lower intergroup (but not trait) EC and PT mediated the negative relationship between alexithymia‐EOT and outgroup attitudes (affective, cognitive, behavioral), across both the TAS‐20 and PAQ. These findings suggest that alexithymia is linked to broader social difficulties, and highlight the importance of targeting intergroup empathy in efforts to reduce negative outgroup attitudes among individuals high in alexithymia‐EOT.

titre: The Effectiveness of Group-Based Positive Youth Development Training on Attachment to Parents and Alexithymia in Male Adolescents with a Tendency Toward Addiction in Isfahan
resume: Objective: This study aimed to determine the effectiveness of group-based Positive Youth Development training on attachment to parents and alexithymia among male adolescents with a tendency toward addiction in Isfahan. Methods and Materials: This quasi-experimental study used a pretest–posttest–follow-up design with a control group. The statistical population included male lower-secondary students with a tendency toward addiction in Isfahan during the 2023–2024 academic year. Thirty eligible adolescents were selected through purposive sampling and randomly assigned to experimental and control groups. The experimental group received twelve 90-minute weekly sessions of Positive Youth Development training, while the control group remained on a waiting list. Data were collected using the Inventory of Parent and Peer Attachment and the Toronto Alexithymia Scale. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures analysis of variance and Bonferroni post-hoc tests. Findings: Repeated-measures ANOVA indicated a significant time effect for attachment to mother, attachment to father, and alexithymia. The results showed that the intervention produced a significant improvement in attachment to mother and a significant reduction in alexithymia from pretest to posttest and follow-up. However, the between-group effect for attachment to father was not significant, and Bonferroni comparisons confirmed that changes in attachment to father were not statistically meaningful. The intervention effects for attachment to mother and alexithymia remained stable at follow-up. Conclusion: Group-based Positive Youth Development training can be considered an effective preventive and corrective intervention for improving attachment to mothers and reducing alexithymia in male adolescents with a tendency toward addiction. However, improving attachment to fathers may require longer, family-based, or father-inclusive interventions.
revue: Journal of Adolescent and Youth Psychological Studies (JAYPS)

titre: Restoring embodied safety through martial arts: Japanese ju-jitsu [JJJ] for embodied reappraisal & psychosocial function in a woman with trauma
resume: Background: Martial Arts halls are important community-mental health hubs. Japanese Ju Jitsu (JJJ) delivered with clear consent rules, breath/voice work, & positional-control may cultivate Interoceptive Awareness (IA), embodied reappraisal, & thus emotion regulation in trauma & survivors of violence. Case: A 51-year-old woman with mental-health trauma from adolescent-sexual violence completed a brief JJJ-informed program. Outcomes included the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (MAIA) and a hermeneutic-phenomenological interview. Intervention: Six 60 - 75-minute sessions over six weeks emphasizing diaphragmatic-pressure-control, boundary-setting voice cues, kata-based drills, & self-regulated positional scenarios, integrated with therapist-guided self-awareness & embodied reappraisal. Outcomes: MAIA showed notable gains in Emotional Awareness, Body Listening, & Self-Regulation; qualitative data indicated resolution of nightmares, improved sleep, & greater agency. Discussion: The current case study provides a framework to guide Martial Arts instructors in supporting students with trauma histories. Mind-Body & Nervous-system clinicians (e.g., Exercise Physiologists & Physiotherapists) are important for participant support.

titre: Hipnose terapêutica como tratamento para o estresse acadêmico: uma revisão bibliográfica
resume: Introduction: Academic stress is a prevalent issue in the university setting, affecting student performance, mental health, and retention. Therapeutic hypnosis has emerged as a complementary intervention with a growing body of evidence. This research aims to synthesize the scientific literature on the effectiveness of hypnosis in managing academic stress, with a focus on findings from Cuba and the rest of the world. Materials and Methods: A narrative review was conducted by searching databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and SciELO, as well as institutional repositories. Systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and experimental studies published between 2000 and 2026 were selected. Results: International findings consistently show significant reductions in test anxiety and perceived stress, alongside improvements in executive function and emotional regulation. In Cuba, a quasi-experimental study demonstrated that hypnotherapy modified personality traits and reduced vulnerability to stress among law students. Discussion: Hypnosis acts through cognitive-behavioral and psychophysiological mechanisms, making it a viable, cost-effective, and low-risk alternative. Conclusions: The evidence supports the inclusion of hypnosis in university wellness programs; however, further randomized controlled trials—with long-term follow-up and tailored to the Cuban context—are required.

titre: Pharmacokinetic--pharmacodynamic blueprints for the anaesthetized adult digital twin: a coupled five-layer specification with an open reference implementation
resume: General anaesthesia is a multi-drug intervention, yet the pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) models that guide it are applied one drug at a time. As precision anaesthesia and closed-loop control move toward clinical reality, this fragmentation becomes a central obstacle: no reference maps validated PK/PD models across drug classes onto the clinical signals they drive, specifies the interactions that couple them, and states the result precisely enough to be implemented. This review addresses that gap in three steps. First, the validated single-agent models for hypnotics, opioids, neuromuscular blockers, vasoactive drugs and volatile agents are consolidated into a covariate-aware selection guide that includes the organ-function covariates omitted by anthropometric models. Second, the resulting architecture is converted into a complete mathematical specification: an enumerated state vector with units and initial conditions, an input vector that includes surgical stimulus, the equations of five pharmacodynamic layers (hypnosis, nociception, respiratory safety, haemodynamics, neuromuscular blockade), the mechanistic couplings that link them, and an observation model that treats the bispectral index as a confounded measurement of a latent hypnotic state rather than as that state itself. Third, an open reference implementation supports three in-silico demonstrations: a coupled clinical case, a quantification of what monitor feedback adds to an open-loop population prediction, and a Fisher-information analysis of which parameters are identifiable from which signals. Individualising the twin on twenty minutes of monitoring reduced the median error of a subsequent fifteen-minute-ahead bispectral index prediction from 18.4% to 5.8%, while leaving the underlying effect-site concentration no better estimated, which delimits both the value and the limits of model-based prediction. A prioritised research agenda follows. The framework is a pharmacological substrate and an in-silico test-bench, not a clinically validated device.

titre: Does self-esteem act as a mechanism of change within Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for young people with Social Anxiety? A systematic review and meta-analysis
Psychological distress during the first 12 months post-upper limb fracture: systematic review and meta-analysis
resume: Abstract Background and purpose Upper limb fractures cause substantial disability and loss of independence, creating a growing burden in an ageing population. The purpose was to systematically review the evidence to determine how psychological distress may change during the initial 12 months following post-upper limb fracture. Methods A systematic review of published and unpublished literature databases was performed to 25th August 2026. Studies presenting data on psychological distress were eligible. Data were appraised using the Downs and Black Appraisal tool, with analysis through meta-analysis comparing scores from fracture to early- (two to six weeks) and longer-term (six to 12 months) follow-up. Results 28 studies ( n = 5,638 people) were eligible and included. There was a significant decrease in depression from early recovery to up to 12 months (Standardised Mean Difference (SMD): 0.65; 95% confidence intervals (CI): 0.43–0.86; N = 2,230), and anxiety (SMD: 0.51; 95% CI: 0.43–0.59; N = 1229). Overall, methodological quality was moderate, with inadequate adjustment for confounding (24 studies) and limited accounting for loss to follow-up (26 studies) identified as common limitations. Kinesiophobia scores were lower at six- to 12-month follow-up compared with the initial fracture assessment (MD: 8.32; 95% CI: 7.26–9.38; N = 1,072). Pain catastrophising scores were lower at six- to 12-month follow-up compared with the initial fracture assessment (MD: 2.05; 95% CI: 1.66–2.43; N = 1,803), although the difference in effect estimates between shorter- and longer-term follow-up was not statistically significant ( p = 0.26). Conclusion Psychological distress was reported following upper-limb fracture, at a population level, anxiety, depression, kinesiophobia and pain catastrophising generally decreased during the first 12 months following fracture. However, kinesiophobia and pain-catastrophising scores did not reach clinically important levels. Further research is required to determine the prevalence and trajectories of clinically important distress and to identify individuals at greatest risk. Clinicians should remain alert to symptoms of anxiety, depression, fear of movement and fear of falling, particularly where recovery is delayed. They should consider further assessment or referral where clinically indicated. Evidence is currently insufficient to recommend universal screening or a specific psychological intervention. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

titre: Virtual reality exposure therapy for anxiety and trauma-related disorders: clinical evidence, behavioral sensing, and implementation priorities
resume: Virtual reality exposure therapy (VRET) provides a controlled environment for delivering exposure to feared cues. Evidence supports benefit over inactive controls for selected specific phobias and social-anxiety presentations, but nonsignificant differences from active treatment do not establish equivalence. This critical narrative review integrates systematic reviews, representative randomized trials, mechanistic studies, and measurement and implementation frameworks. We distinguish diagnosed social anxiety disorder from performance-focused and symptom-selected samples, and exposure-based treatment from VR distraction or relaxation. PTSD findings require particular caution because military cohorts, trauma cues, and treatment histories may not represent civilian clinical populations. Behavioral and physiological signals are examined at four levels: technical capture, experimental association, clinical validity, and incremental clinical utility. Feasible recording and associations with arousal or attention do not establish that a signal measures therapeutic learning or improves treatment decisions. We propose a clinician-governed precision VRET loop as a conceptual framework requiring prospective evaluation, rather than a clinically validated adaptive intervention. Research priorities include appropriately designed comparative trials, explicit diagnostic characterization, standardized intervention and hardware reporting, purpose-specific measurement validation, systematic harms assessment, longer follow-up, and implementation and economic evaluation. VRET should be evaluated as a defined exposure intervention for a specified population and care setting, with patient choice and accountable clinical oversight.

titre: Beyond AI Chatbots: A Human-AI Collaboration Framework for Anxiety Support in University Counseling Services- a Systematic Review (Preprint)
resume: BACKGROUND Anxiety is among the most common mental health problems experienced by university students, while university counseling services face demand that human staff alone cannot meet. Chatbots based on artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) are increasingly offered as a solution, but evidence on how AI works alongside counselors remains scattered. OBJECTIVE This systematic review aims to synthesize evidence on the functions of AI in anxiety support, human-AI collaboration models, and safety and ethical requirements, and then derive a framework for university counseling services. METHODS Searches were conducted in Scopus, PubMed, ERIC, and Lens.org on October 28, 2026, for English-language journal articles published 2021-2026 examining AI systems for mental health support and involving university students, young adults, counselors, or counseling services. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020. Risk of bias was assessed using the JBI checklist according to design, the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool 2018, and PROBAST. Findings were synthesized thematically and narratively using Whittemore and Knafl's integrative approach. RESULTS Of 368 records, 75 studies reported in 76 articles met the inclusion criteria: 8 qualitative studies, 11 cross-sectional and survey studies, 8 comparative experimental and observational studies, 18 system development, mixed methods, and prediction model studies, and 30 reviews and conceptual papers. Only 14 studies measured anxiety directly. Qualitative and survey studies consistently position AI as a complement and expect human judgment in crises. Experimental studies show short-term anxiety reduction; a systematic review of 31 trials reported an SMD of -0.37 (95% CI -0.58 to -0.17), with the greatest improvements in clinician-supported AI-assisted CBT. System development and prediction model studies report high performance, but mostly on simulated or public data and at high risk of bias. Risk of bias was low in 24 studies, moderate in 30, and high in 21. CONCLUSIONS Evidence supports AI as a risk-tiered complement within counselor-controlled services, rather than as a standalone chatbot. We propose a Human-AI Collaborative Anxiety Support (HACAS) framework with four tiers of service, counselor decision-making at every escalation point, and a governance foundation. This framework needs prospective testing.

titre: The Neural Basis of Emotion Regulation: A Review of Prefrontal-Limbic Mechanisms and Their Implications for Psychotherapy
resume: Emotion regulation involves the strategies by which people adjust the strength, time course, or display of emotional responses. This review integrates psychological theory, functional neuroimaging, meta-analytic evidence, and intervention studies to characterize the neurocognitive basis for emotion regulation,which emerges from dynamic interactions among distributed brain networks. Regulation depends on context-sensitive activity in the amygdala, insula, and cingulate cortex during emotion generation, whereas intentional control engages lateral and medial prefrontal regions that maintain goals, interpret events, and shift attention or meaning. Effective regulation therefore relies on information integration rather than the inhibition of one brain region by another. Depression and anxiety involve maladaptive regulation patterns and ineffective prefrontal-limbic interaction, although these alterations are heterogeneous and non-specific to particular diagnoses. Cognitive behavioral therapy, exposure therapy, and mindfulness-based interventions may alter appraisals, salience, self-referential processing, and neural connectivity. However, small samples, heterogeneous tasks, and the correlational nature of functional imaging constrain causal and clinical inference. Future work should adopt integrated, longitudinal, multimodal, and ecologically valid designs to identify individual-level predictors of treatment outcomel.
revue: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media

titre: Connectopic Mapping of Striatal and Hippocampus-Amygdala Gradients in OCD
resume: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a chronic psychiatric condition characterized by intrusive, unwanted thoughts or images, and repetitive or ritualistic behaviors (American Psychiatric, 2022). Functional alterations in OCD are well documented, particularly within corticostriatal-thalamocortical (CSTC) and frontolimbic circuitry and associate with symptom severity and clinical features (Bruin et al., 2023; Li & Mody, 2016; Thorsen, Hagland, et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019). Neurotransmitters such as dopamine and serotonin are considered key modulators of this circuitry, but evidence for neurotransmitter alterations in OCD is inconsistent (Dougherty et al., 2018; Mota et al., 2026). Specifically, alterations in striatal dopaminergic markers are repeatedly reported in OCD, though with varying directionality of effects (Mota et al., 2026). Further, reduced serotonin transporters across CSTC and limbic regions have been observed in OCD, and serotonin appears closely linked to anxiety and symptom severity, although null findings are also noted (Dougherty et al., 2018). Serotonergic and dopaminergic alterations in OCD are particularly relevant considering that serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first-line pharmacotherapy, whereas dopamine antagonist augmentation benefits a subset of patients.(de Oliveira et al., 2023). However, directly characterizing these neurotransmitter alterations using PET imaging with radioligands is resource-intensive and difficult to implement in large cohorts. Connectopic mapping utilizes standard resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) to map dominant and non-dominant voxel-wise fingerprints of connectivity within a region of interest. Where standard resting-state fMRI analysis is typically constrained by the assumptions of homogenous regions, predefined single seed or network se connectopic mapping can provide insight into fine-grained patterns for both the dominant and non-dominant functional connectivity gradients of the region of interest to the rest of the brain. Connectopic gradients reflect how each voxel within a region is functionally connected to the rest of the brain. By capturing both dominant and secondary patterns of connectivity variation, connectopic provides a complementary framework for investigating subtle alterations in the functional organization of brain regions. Dominant striatal connectopic gradients have recently been linked to OCD symptom severity in a smaller cohort (Webb et al., 2025), while striatal and amygdala-hippocampus connectopic projection maps can provide insight into topographical patterns of connectivity across networks, i.e., reward processing, sensorimotor or limbic networks (Marquand et al., 2017; Mulders et al., 2022; Nordin et al., 2025). Importantly, the non-dominant modes have been shown to spatial corresponds to dopamine transporter (DAT) density in the striatum, and to 5-HT1A receptor density in the hippocampus-amygdala complex in human neuroimaging samples, including healthy adults and individuals from a range of psychiatric cohorts (Haak et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2026; Oldehinkel et al., 2022). The current study will utilize datasets from the global OCD study, a worldwide initiative with harmonized data collection and analysis pipelines of ethno-culturally diverse samples of medication-free (6-week wash-out) individuals with OCD, unaffected siblings of individuals with OCD and healthy controls from five international sites (Simpson et al., 2020), to gain insight into connectopic gradients of the striatum and amygdala-hippocampus in OCD. Including unaffected siblings may help elucidate whether alterations in functional gradients reflect familial vulnerability to OCD or are more specifically associated with clinical symptoms. The objectives of the current investigation are to characterize dominant and non-dominant functional gradients (spatially corresponding to DAT and 5-HT1A) of the striatum and hippocampus-amygdala complex in individuals with OCD compared to unaffected siblings of individuals with OCD and healthy controls (HCs), and to examine whether these gradients are associated with clinical measures (i.e., depression, anxiety, OC symptom severity).

titre: Chronic intracranial neural dynamics forecast treatment response and therapeutic engagement during deep brain stimulation for OCD
resume: Clinical improvement following psychiatric neuromodulation often requires weeks to months, creating prolonged uncertainty during treatment optimization. Identifying early neural signatures of therapeutic response could provide objective evidence of target engagement and accelerate optimization. We analyzed nearly 120,000 patient-hours of chronic ventral striatal recordings from 24 patients undergoing deep brain stimulation for treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder. We derived a measure of neural predictability to quantify the temporal regularity of low-frequency power, implemented in a manner suitable for prospective computation. Clinical responders exhibited rapid reductions in neural predictability within two weeks of stimulation, months before they achieved clinical response. The magnitude of this early neural change correlated significantly with eventual symptom reduction. Baseline circadian features of ventral striatal activity also distinguished responders from non-responders before stimulation. Together, these findings establish a framework for leveraging chronic neural sensing to inform therapeutic target engagement and longitudinal monitoring of treatment response.
revue: USC Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute

titre: Perinatal mood and anxiety disorders and adverse perinatal outcomes: a retrospective cohort study
resume: Perinatal mood and anxiety disorders (PMADs) are common mental health complications of pregnancy, affecting approximately 1 in 5 women in the US. Serious mental illness (SMI) is less common and clinically distinct. We examined associations between the number of documented PMAD conditions and, separately, SMI with adverse perinatal outcomes, and whether associations varied by race/ethnicity and chronic hypertension. This retrospective cohort study included 46,729 singleton births delivered at a tertiary obstetric hospital in South–Central Louisiana from 2017 to 2022. PMAD included anxiety, depression, panic disorder, and obsessive–compulsive disorder, while SMI included bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and postpartum psychosis. Conditions were identified from medical records and modeled as distinct exposure groups. PMAD burden was categorized as 0, 1, 2, or ≥ 3 documented conditions, while SMI was modeled as any versus none. Outcomes included preterm birth (PTB), low birthweight (LBW), cesarean delivery, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP), gestational diabetes, delivery complications, postpartum hemorrhage, and postpartum readmission. Modified Poisson regression estimated adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), accounting for maternal characteristics and repeated deliveries. Of 46,729 births, 70.6% had no documented PMAD or SMI, 26.9% had PMAD only, 0.4% had SMI only, and 2.2% had both. Risk generally increased with the number of documented PMAD conditions. Women with ≥ 3 PMAD conditions had increased risk of PTB (aRR = 1.54, 95% CI = 1.32–1.79), LBW (aRR = 1.33, 95% CI = 1.09–1.62), cesarean delivery (aRR = 1.11, 95% CI = 1.01–1.22), HDP (aRR = 1.16, 95% CI = 1.01–1.33), and delivery complications (aRR = 1.43, 95% CI = 1.14–1.79). After adjustment for PMAD burden, SMI was associated with LBW, while associations with other outcomes were less precise. Anxiety was associated with increased risk across all eight outcomes, although depression and bipolar disorder showed larger point estimates for selected outcomes. Associations varied by race/ethnicity for six outcomes and by chronic hypertension for four. Greater documented PMAD burden was generally associated with higher risk of several adverse perinatal outcomes after accounting for SMI. Associations also differed across individual mental health conditions and maternal risk groups. These findings highlight heterogeneity in perinatal mental health risks and support distinguishing specific conditions rather than treating diagnosis counts as clinical severity. Not applicable.

titre: Evaluation of the Efficacy of Different Homemade Kefir Formulations in Improving Symptoms of Functional Chronic Constipation in Chilean Adults
resume: Functional chronic constipation is a common digestive disorder in Chilean adults. It causes infrequent or difficult bowel movements, abdominal discomfort and a feeling of incomplete evacuation, and it can impair quality of life. Kefir is a fermented milk made with grains that contain lactic acid bacteria and yeasts. It has been proposed as a dietary option to relieve constipation, but its effects may depend on how it is prepared. The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether daily intake of two homemade kefir formulations, one made with whole milk and one made with skim milk, improves constipation symptoms and quality of life in adults with functional chronic constipation, compared with dietary counseling alone. Thirty adults of both sexes diagnosed with functional chronic constipation according to the Rome IV criteria will be randomly assigned to one of three groups (10 per group): Whole-milk kefir (KLE) Skim-milk kefir (KLD) Control group receiving nutritional counseling based on the Chilean Dietary Guidelines only Participants in the kefir groups will follow a gradual dose increase (50, 100, 150 and up to 200 mL/day) for 4 weeks. Both kefir formulations will be prepared under standardized conditions (6% grain inoculation, 48-hour fermentation) and characterized for their nutritional, microbiological and sensory properties before the trial. The primary outcome will be constipation-specific quality of life, measured with the PAC-QOL questionnaire. Secondary outcomes will include constipation symptoms (Rome IV criteria), stool consistency (Bristol Stool Form Scale) and generic health-related quality of life (EQ-5D). Dietary intake (24-hour recall and food frequency questionnaire) and physical activity (GPAQ) will be recorded as potential confounders. All assessments will be done before and after the intervention. The researchers expect that participants who drink kefir will improve their constipation symptoms and quality of life more than those who receive counseling only. They also expect a greater improvement with the whole-milk kefir

titre: Single Vs Double Stapling Technique & Intracorporeal Vs Transanal Purse-String in Low Anterior Resection for Rectal Cancer: An Adjusted Comparative RCT Evaluating Anastomotic Leak, Oncological and Patient-Reported Outcomes
resume: This study compares ways of joining the bowel after surgery for rectal cancer. It aims to find out whether using a single-stapling technique leads to fewer bowel leaks than using a double-stapling technique. It also compares two ways of placing the closing stitch used in the single-stapling technique. The study will include 124 adults having planned surgery to remove rectal cancer while preserving the anus. After removing the affected part of the rectum, the surgeon joins the remaining bowel. A leak can occur if this join does not heal properly. Participants will be assigned by chance during surgery to one of two techniques: Double stapling: the surgeon closes the remaining rectum with a straight stapler, then uses a circular stapler to join the bowel. Single stapling: the surgeon closes the remaining rectum with a drawstring-like stitch, then uses a circular stapler to join the bowel. Participants assigned to single stapling will have a second assignment by chance. The surgeon will place the closing stitch either from inside the abdomen or through the anus. The main outcome is a bowel leak that requires treatment within 30 days after surgery. Researchers will also compare other complications, recovery, findings from the removed cancer tissue, and whether the cancer returns locally during the first year. Participants will be followed for 12 months after surgery. They will complete questionnaires about bowel function, bowel control, and quality of life at 6 and 12 months.

titre: Multicenter Open-label Randomized Trial With an Active Control Group to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Polisorb® MP in the Complex Therapy of Patients With Atopic Dermatitis
resume: This multicenter, open-label, randomized Phase III clinical trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of adding Polisorb® MP, an oral colloidal silicon dioxide adsorbent, to basic therapy in adults with mild to moderate atopic dermatitis. The study included 161 patients in the efficacy analysis. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either basic therapy alone (81 patients) or basic therapy in combination with Polisorb® MP (80 patients). Basic therapy included skin care with emollients and pharmacological treatment, including cetirizine and topical pimecrolimus. The treatment period lasted 14 days, followed by an observation period. The primary endpoint was the change in the SCORAD index from baseline to Day 14. Itch intensity, dermatology-related quality of life, EASI and IGA scores were also assessed. Both groups showed improvement in disease severity during treatment. The mean SCORAD score decreased by 21.5 points in patients receiving Polisorb® MP in addition to basic therapy, compared with 17.7 points in patients receiving basic therapy alone. The difference between the groups was statistically significant (p = 0.0028), favoring the addition of Polisorb® MP. Improvements in itch intensity and IGA scores also favored combination therapy, while differences between groups in EASI changes and changes in dermatology-related quality of life were not statistically significant. A total of 34 adverse events were reported in 26 patients. No serious adverse events or deaths were reported. Gastrointestinal events, particularly constipation, were more frequent in the Polisorb® MP group. Other reported events included difficulty with defecation, abdominal discomfort, bloating, dry mouth and nausea. No new or unexpected safety concerns specific to Polisorb® MP were identified during the study. The findings indicate that adding Polisorb® MP to basic therapy was associated with a greater reduction in SCORAD scores over 14 days than basic therapy alone. The results should be interpreted in the context of the open-label design and the short treatment period.

titre: ESBo-SCI: Abdominal Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation to Treat Neurogenic Bowel Dysfunction in Chronic SCI
resume: Difficulty with bowel movements is one of the most serious side effects of spinal cord injury and one that most severely restricts everyday life. Many people affected take 30 to 60 minutes, or considerably longer, to pass stools. This is accompanied by a significantly slowed bowel transit, which often leads to a feeling of fullness, flatulence and chronic pain. The study investigates a method suitable for everyday use to support bowel function: electrical stimulation of the abdominal muscles. This involves applying adhesive electrodes to the abdomen and controlling them via a small device. The treatment is carried out independently at home - 30 minutes before each planned bowel movement. Two stimulation settings are being compared: i) Motor stimulation: The current strength causes a noticeable contraction of the abdominal muscles. ii) Sensory stimulation: The intensity is lower and is perceived merely as a gentle tingling sensation. The procedure is divided into several phases. Before stimulation begins, baseline values are recorded during a two-week pre-observation phase. Subsequently, both stimulation methods are applied one after the other for 12 weeks each, interspersed with a six-week break without stimulation. Which participant starts with which type of stimulation is determined at random. A final six-week follow-up phase assesses whether any improvements achieved persist after the end of treatment. During the study, participants will keep a diary and, together with specialists, complete two questionnaires. Bowel transit time will be measured in a simple and safe manner (using maize grains and a capsule containing blue food colouring). In addition, stool samples will be collected at five specified time points to analyse changes in the gut microbiota. The aim is to evaluate a gentle, practical method that facilitates the bowel movement process, promotes gut health and noticeably improves the quality of life of people with spinal cord injury.

titre: A Direct-to-consumer Dissemination Campaign About Exposure to Increase Treatment Access
resume: The goal of this pilot randomized study is to learn whether a dissemination campaign co-designed with a community advisory board helps caregivers of children with anxiety and related disorders seek exposure therapy, compared with standard information. Participants are caregivers of children ages 4 to 18 with current anxiety, OCD, or traumatic stress symptoms. The main questions it aims to answer are: Does the dissemination campaign improve caregivers' knowledge of exposure therapy, attitudes toward it, perceived norms about seeking it, and confidence that they can find an exposure therapist, compared with dissemination-as-usual? Does the dissemination campaign increase caregivers' intentions to seek exposure therapy for their child, compared with dissemination-as-usual? Researchers will compare the dissemination campaign to dissemination-as-usual, which is links to professional organization websites and advice to contact their insurance company or search an online therapist directory. Participants will: * Complete an online survey about their help-seeking intentions, knowledge, attitudes, norms, and confidence * Be randomly assigned to review either the dissemination campaign or dissemination-as-usual materials for at least 10 minutes * Complete the same survey again right after reviewing the materials * Possibly be invited to a 15-minute phone interview 2 months later about whether they sought treatment for their child and what barriers they faced

titre: Estudiantes Felices y Florecientes
resume: This study evaluated the effectiveness of a university-level Flourishing Curriculum on students' well-being in Colombia using two rigorous designs: a cluster randomized study (Study 1, n = 389 control vs. n = 614 intervention) and an individually randomized controlled trial (Study 2, n = 77 control vs. n = 75 intervention). Both studies followed the same experimental and measurement structure. The nine-week-long curriculum integrated evidence-based components targeting meaning in life, forgiveness, humility, mindfulness, self-control, resilience, leadership, positive relationships, and spirituality, and was implemented within the standard academic course structure followed by students at the university. The control condition completed the measures but completed their usual coursework. The assessment battery included Spanish-language versions of established psychological measures. These instruments had either been previously validated for use in Spanish-speaking populations or had been back-translated into Spanish by researchers at Universidad del Sinú for prior studies conducted in Colombia. The investigators selected a set of 20 theory-driven and curriculum-informed outcome variables corresponding to two levels of anticipated change. First, investigators assessed constructs targeted by each of the nine curriculum modules, including coherence, purpose, and significance as three central dimensions of meaning in life, trait forgivingness, trait humility, mindfulness, self-control, resilience, leadership, loneliness, and transcendent spirituality. Second, constructs were assessed reflecting more distal outcomes that the flourishing curriculum is intended to support, including depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, stress overload, and a brief measure of multidimensional flourishing that yielded an overall flourishing score and five domain-specific scores: happiness and life satisfaction; mental and physical health; meaning and purpose; character and virtue; and close social relationships. Mean scores were computed for all outcome variables. In addition, following each module of the Flourishing Curriculum, students in the intervention group also completed a five-item course evaluation assessing satisfaction with the learning experience.
