titre: Sarcopenia in Alcoholic Liver Disease: Molecular Mechanisms, Clinical Consequences, and Emerging Therapeutic Strategies
resume: Alcoholic liver disease (ALD) remains a major cause of chronic liver disease worldwide and is associated with substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden. Among its extrahepatic complications, sarcopenia has emerged as a key determinant of disease progression, liver transplantation outcomes, and overall survival. This review provides an updated and critical overview of the epidemiology, pathophysiological mechanisms, clinical significance, diagnostic challenges, and evolving therapeutic strategies for ALD-associated sarcopenia. Current evidence indicates that skeletal muscle loss results from the interplay of direct ethanolinduced myotoxicity, malnutrition, chronic inflammation, insulin resistance, hormonal dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and impaired muscle regeneration. Emerging molecular insights, including stabilization of hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), accelerated post-mitotic senescence, and dysregulation of the gut-liver-muscle axis, further expand our understanding of disease pathogenesis. The review also critically examines the methodological heterogeneity in sarcopenia diagnosis, highlighting the limitations of existing imaging modalities and consensus-based diagnostic criteria, particularly in patients with fluid retention and advanced liver disease. Clinically, ALD-associated sarcopenia is consistently associated with hepatic decompensation, reduced transplant-free survival, poorer post-transplant outcomes, functional decline, and diminished quality of life. Although nutritional support, exercise, pharmacological interventions, and microbiota-targeted therapies have shown encouraging results, heterogeneous evidence, patient-related barriers, and a lack of ALD-specific therapeutic recommendations limit their translation into routine clinical practice. Finally, we discuss emerging concepts of phenotypic heterogeneity, including myosteatosis, and highlight the potential of multiomics approaches and precision medicine to improve risk stratification and enable individualized therapeutic strategies. By integrating recent mechanistic advances with critical diagnostic and therapeutic perspectives, this review provides an updated ALD-focused framework to guide future research and clinical management.
revue: Recent advances in inflammation & allergy drug discovery

titre: Impact of Impedance Planimetry on Optimized Therapeutic Assessment in Complex Benign Esophageal Stenosis - A Prospective, Randomized Trial
resume: BACKGROUND: Accurate evaluation of complex benign esophageal stenosis is essential for successful endoscopic dilation, yet conventional methods are either subjective or involve radiation exposure. This study investigated whether impedance planimetry (EndoFLIP) optimizes stricture geometry assessment compared with conventional nonradiographic methods and whether it improves patient outcomes. PATIENTS AND METHODS: Totally 22 adult patients with symptomatic benign esophageal strictures were allocated to either a planimetry group or a control group. In the planimetry group, FLIP measurements were obtained before and after dilation in addition to standard endoscopic evaluation, whereas the control group underwent conventional assessment alone. Symptoms and quality of life were evaluated using the SWAL-QOL questionnaire pre- and 14 days postprocedure. RESULTS: EndoFLIP measurements revealed significant increases in diameter, cross-sectional area, and distensibility following dilation. Compared with FLIP, stricture length was underestimated endoscopically by an average of 14.4 mm and post-therapeutic diameter was overestimated by 1.2 mm based on the final dilator size. G-SWAL-QOL total scores improved in both groups, whereas symptom scores and tolerance of solid food improved significantly in the planimetry group only. CONCLUSION: The use of impedance planimetry enabled a standardized and radiation-free assessment of complex benign esophageal stenosis and may contribute to optimizing the treatment of complex benign strictures of the upper gastrointestinal tract.

titre: Appearance-related anxiety and mental health in celiac disease: Distinct psychosomatic patterns compared with healthy adults
resume: BACKGROUND: Although psychological distress is well documented in celiac disease (CD), the contribution of appearance-related anxiety to overall mental health in this clinical population remains unclear. This study aimed to assess the relationship between appearance-related anxiety and mental health in adults with CD compared with healthy controls. METHODS: The study included 96 adults with CD and 96 healthy controls. Participants completed the Physical Appearance State and Trait Anxiety Scale (PASTAS) and the 28-item General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-28). RESULTS: Mean total PASTAS scores did not differ significantly between CD and control groups (6.9 ± 6.7 vs. 8.1 ± 10.1). In contrast, CD patients reported significantly higher somatic symptoms (8.0 ± 3.5 vs. 6.7 ± 4.4; p = 0.031) and anxiety-insomnia (7.0 ± 3.3 vs. 5.8 ± 3.2; p = 0.009), while depressive symptoms were higher in controls (4.3 ± 4.7 vs. 3.0 ± 4.1; p = 0.031). Correlations between PASTAS and GHQ-28 scores were significant in controls, particularly for somatic and depressive symptoms, but largely absent in the CD group. Sten-based analysis showed that low overall psychological distress predominated in CD, whereas moderate scores were more frequent in controls (p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Appearance-related anxiety does not differentiate adults with CD from healthy controls and is less strongly associated with general mental health in CD. Psychological distress in CD manifests primarily through somatic and anxiety-related symptoms rather than body image concerns, highlighting the importance of addressing disease-specific stressors in clinical care.

titre: Comparative evaluation of edible Bifidobacterium species in repairing 5-fluorouracil induced intestinal microenvironment damage
resume: Chemotherapy-induced disruption of the intestinal microenvironment severely compromises both the quality of life and clinical prognosis of cancer patients. Despite the potential of edible Bifidobacterium to alleviate chemotherapy-associated intestinal damage, substantial inter-species comparisons remain to be clarified to support the rational selection of probiotic candidates. In this study, a 5-fluorouracil (5-FU)-induced mouse model of intestinal damage was established to comparatively evaluate the effects of six edible Bifidobacterium species. Our results revealed distinct responses in the protective efficacy of Bifidobacterium against 5-FU-induced microenvironmental damage. Notably, intervention with Bifidobacterium longum subsp. longum (BLL) attenuated 5-FU-induced weight loss and reductions in food intake, while also alleviating diarrhea. BLL supplementation was associated with improved intestinal barrier-related gene expression, reduced inflammatory responses in colonic tissues, and altered gut microbiota composition. These protective effects were accompanied by shifts in the relative abundance of specific bacterial taxa, including Enterococcus, Ruminococcaceae UCG_014, and Ruminococcus 2, as well as changes in cholic acid and deoxycholic acid levels. In contrast, B. bifidum and B. adolescentis supplementation was associated with lower endpoint survival and less favorable intestinal outcomes. Further experiments using representative mucin-utilizing bacteria indicated that mucin-utilization capacity alone may not fully explain the differential responses observed among bacterial interventions. These findings provide insights into the rational selection of Bifidobacterium species for future probiotic development targeting chemotherapy-associated intestinal injury.

titre: Obliterative versus Reconstructive Surgery for Advanced Pelvic Organ Prolapse in Older Women: A Systematic Review for Preference-Sensitive Surgical Decision-Making
resume: INTRODUCTION AND HYPOTHESIS: The choice between obliterative and reconstructive surgery for older women with advanced pelvic organ prolapse is preference sensitive. This review synthesized comparative evidence across perioperative safety, durability, urinary, bowel/anorectal, and patient-reported outcomes. METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched through 1 May 2026. English-language comparative studies in older advanced-prolapse populations were included. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data, assessed risk of bias using Risk Of Bias In Nonrandomized Studies of Interventions, and rated certainty using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation. Findings were narratively synthesized because of heterogeneity. RESULTS: Of 664 records, 29 reports representing 27 study families were included. Safety outcomes were reported in 23 reports, durability/recurrence in 16, urinary outcomes in 12, bowel/anorectal outcomes in 9, and broad patient-reported outcomes/quality of life in 10. Twelve of the 14 non-overlapping comparisons reported shorter operative time after obliterative surgery; blood loss favored obliteration in 8 of the 12 comparisons and hospital stay in 5 out of 11. Overall complications were not consistently lower. Anatomical/composite durability numerically favored obliteration in 7 out of 10 comparisons, and recurrence-related reoperation was lower in 7 out of 8. Urinary, bowel, and patient-reported outcomes were inconsistent or similar. Certainty was low for operative time and very low for other key outcomes. CONCLUSION: Current evidence supports a more definitive conclusion about lower procedural burden, particularly shorter operative time, than about global complications, anatomical superiority, or functional outcomes. Findings should inform counseling that integrates frailty, comorbidity, sexual goals, functional symptoms, durability expectations, treatment burden, and patient preference.

titre: Mechanisms of impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia: Lessons from neuroimaging
resume: Hypoglycaemia is a physiological stress and the body generates symptom and hormonal responses that alert the individual and protect them. Protection from hypoglycaemia requires three layers of defence. Firstly, a physiological counter-regulatory response that is designed to correct glucose through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; secondly awareness-the ability to perceive symptoms and attribute them to hypoglycaemia; and thirdly a behavioural and emotional response that serves as motivation to avoid subsequent episodes. Impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia (IAH) affects up to a third of people with type 1 diabetes and increases the risk of severe hypoglycaemia. The traditional model of IAH suggests this is a physiological habituation response caused by recurrent episodes that can be reversed on meticulous avoidance of hypoglycaemia. Recent data, especially from neuroimaging, suggests important roles for regions of the brain involved in salience, attention and interoception, implying a more nuanced view of IAH that may involve deficits in each of these areas. This may explain why simple hypoglycaemia avoidance using technology may not suffice to restore awareness, requiring a more holistic approach that addresses key cognitive barriers.
revue: Diabetic medicine : a journal of the British Diabetic Association

titre: Sleep complaints in alexithymia reflect non-specific negative affectivity
resume: Alexithymia is the inability to identify and describe emotions, associated with an increased risk of somatic and psychiatric disease. Alexithymia is also characterized by reduced subjective sleep quality. However, it is not well-known whether this reduction in sleep quality reflects physiological changes in sleep, a specific alteration in perceived sleep quality not captured by objective metrics, or a non-specific spillover of the negative affective style which characterizes alexithymia. In BSETS, a large (N = 228) in-home EEG study of naturalistic sleep, we found that alexithymia symptoms are associated with worse habitual (AIS) and current (GSQS) subjective sleep quality (βAIS = 0.207, pAIS = 0.002, βGSQS = 0.203, pGSQS = 0.002). However, we observed no significant association between alexithymia and EEG-based sleep efficiency (β = -0.017, p = 0.791). The association with subjective sleep quality was almost completely attenuated when controlling for either depressive symptoms (PHQ-9, βAIS = 0.001, pAIS = 0.982, βGSQS = 0.044, pGSQS = 0.486) or trait neuroticism (ZKPQ, BFI-44, βAIS = 0.057, pAIS = 0.442, βGSQS = 0.048, pGSQS = 0.514). A possible exception is the alexithymia dimension Difficulty Identifying Feelings, partially reflecting complaints about the labeling of interoceptive experiences, which was associated with lower subjective sleep quality even after some covariate control. This pattern of findings suggests that alexithymia is characterized only by alterations of subjective sleep quality, and even these reflect a non-specific increase in negative affect which influences self-reports of sleep quality, rather than a specific reduction in perceived sleep quality itself.

titre: Visual and interoceptive factors shape affective and aesthetic evaluations of body postures
resume: The influence of internal body rhythms, such as heartbeats, on affective and cognitive processes remains an area of research, informing how bodily states shape perception of the world. Studies of facial expression evaluation show that emotional (negative vs. neutral) faces are detected more easily and perceived as more intense when presented during systole rather than diastole, two phases of the cardiac cycle. Whether similar cardiac phase effects extend to affective and aesthetic evaluations of human bodies remains unclear. In this preregistered study, participants without dance training rated upright and inverted body postures from motion capture recordings of contemporary dancers for emotional intensity and likability. Each image was presented during either the participant's ventricular systole or diastole. We assessed interoceptive accuracy (via the Heartbeat Counting Task; HBCT) and collected emotional valence and bodily arousal ratings for each stimulus. Contrary to predictions, emotional intensity and likability did not increase during systole. Instead, we found that cardiac-related effects were conditional. Emotional intensity was positively associated with bodily arousal, except for inverted postures during systole. How this relationship depended on orientation was modulated by HBCT performance. Likability was positively associated with valence, with this relationship becoming stronger as HBCT performance increased. These findings suggest cardiac-related factors may contribute to affective and aesthetic evaluations of dance-like body postures, as a function of body orientation, stimulus affective characteristics, and individual differences in heartbeat perception. They indicate that ongoing physiological states may shape how others are evaluated beyond facial information, extending to both affective and aesthetic domains.

titre: Unguided bibliotherapy and digital self-help interventions based on cognitive behavioural therapy for university students with gaze-related anxiety and social anxiety symptoms: a randomised controlled trial
resume: Individual cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for social anxiety disorder is effective, but CBT has not become widespread enough. Since young people with social anxiety also experience above a certain level distress and functional impairment, the development of readily available CBT-based self-help interventions is urgently needed. The objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of two five-week, unguided CBT-based self-help interventions in reducing gaze-related anxiety and social anxiety symptoms among university students with elevated gaze-related anxiety. A three-arm, randomised controlled trial was conducted in Japan from April to December 2025. University students with gaze-related anxiety were randomly assigned to bibliotherapy (Bib) or unguided digital self-help interventions (DSI), or to a six-month waitlist control. Social anxiety symptoms were evaluated using several self-report scales, and assessments were conducted at baseline, post-intervention, and at two follow-ups. Of 252 university students enrolled, 244 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analyses, which used linear mixed-effects models. For the primary outcome, the adjusted mean difference in the Gaze Anxiety Rating Scale at post-intervention was -10.09 (95% CI: -14.61 to -5.56, Hedges' g = -0.66) for Bib and - 6.95 (95% CI: -12.11 to -1.79, Hedges' g = -0.47) for DSI, both showing a significantly greater reduction compared to the waitlist control. Similarly, for a secondary outcome, the adjusted mean difference in the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale at post-intervention was -13.57 (95% CI: -20.86 to -6.29, Hedges' g = -0.55) for Bib and - 12.47 (95% CI: -20.78 to -4.17, Hedges' g = -0.53) for DSI, which were also significantly higher than the waitlist control. The effectiveness of these two interventions in reducing social anxiety symptoms compared to the waitlist control was maintained at the 3-month and 6-month follow-ups. These findings support brief unguided CBT-based self-help as a potentially accessible low-intensity option for university students with elevated social anxiety symptoms.

titre: Feasibility and Preliminary Efficacy of a Digital Cognitive-Behavioral and Expressive Writing Intervention for Fear of Cancer Recurrence in Young Breast Cancer Survivors: A Quasi-Experimental Study
resume: OBJECTIVE: To examine the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of a 4-week digital intervention combining cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and expressive writing for reducing fear of cancer recurrence (FCR) among young breast cancer survivors (YBCSs). METHODS: A quasi-experimental, two-group repeated-measures design was employed. The intervention group (n = 14) participated in a 4-week online program with weekly CBT-based group sessions and 20-minute expressive writing sessions on four consecutive days each week (16 sessions in total), whereas the control group (n = 16) received weekly educational materials. Outcomes, including FCR, anxiety, depression, cancer coping, and post-traumatic stress symptoms, were assessed at baseline, immediately postintervention, and 4 weeks postintervention. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA. RESULTS: Feasibility was supported by a 100% recruitment rate and 100% retention after baseline, with group session attendance (90%), expressive writing completion (95.6%), and weekly telephone consultation completion (80%) all exceeding benchmarks. A significant group × time interaction was observed for FCR (F = 4.888, P = .011), with greater reductions in the intervention group than in the control group over time. Group × time interactions did not reach statistical significance for anxiety, depression, cancer coping, or post-traumatic stress symptoms. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrated high feasibility and provided preliminary evidence of a potential benefit of the intervention for reducing FCR among YBCSs. Future randomized controlled trials with larger samples are warranted to confirm these findings and further investigate the mechanisms underlying the intervention effects. IMPLICATION FOR NURSING PRACTICE: Oncology nurses may consider incorporating accessible, developmentally tailored digital interventions as a potential component of survivorship care for YBCSs.

titre: MDMA-assisted therapy for social anxiety disorder: A randomized, open-label, wait-list controlled trial
resume: BACKGROUND: ±3, 4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) has positive effects on socio-emotional processing and MDMA-Assisted Therapy (MDMA-AT) showed promise for treating Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) in a previous placebo-controlled trial. AIMS: Develop a preliminary estimate of clinical response and safety for MDMA-AT versus waitlist in adults with SAD. Secondary aims included refinement of a standardized psychotherapy manual and assessment of candidate therapeutic processes. METHOD: This randomized, open-label, wait-list controlled clinical trial recruited and enrolled 20 participants diagnosed with SAD from April 2022 to March 2024. They were randomly assigned to either immediate treatment with MDMA-AT or a 16-week waitlist condition followed by MDMA-AT equivalent to the immediate treatment arm. MDMA-AT consisted of three 90-min preparation sessions, two MDMA sessions, and six 90-min integration sessions. The preregistered primary outcome was the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale; secondary outcomes were functioning, shame, acceptance, belongingness, self-concealment, and self-compassion. RESULTS: Across 20 participants (45% women, 40% men, 15% transgender; 85% White; mean age 38) we observed a mean difference on the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale at 16-week primary outcome of -43.3 (SD = 14.7; 95% CI, -29.5 to -57.1; p < .0001; Hedges' g = 2.8) indicating greater improvement in the MDMA-AT condition. No serious adverse events occurred; adverse events were mild to moderate and transient. CONCLUSIONS: MDMA-AT resulted in a significant reduction in social anxiety symptoms and improvement in functioning compared to waitlist. There were no serious adverse events. Findings provide preliminary data for clinical response, safety, and feasibility of MDMA-AT for SAD, supporting the need for further investigation. Trial Registration https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05138068.

titre: Does Neurobiological Evidence Support the Diagnostic Distinction Between Hoarding Disorder and OCD? A Critical Narrative Review of Genetic, Neuroimaging, and Neuropsychological Findings
resume: BACKGROUND: Hoarding symptoms were long regarded as one dimension of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but DSM-5 (2013) classified hoarding disorder (HD) as a separate diagnosis. This review asks whether neurobiological evidence, including studies published after the reclassification, adequately supports that decision. METHODS: This critical narrative review searched PubMed and Web of Science (January 2010 to July 2026, plus foundational studies found by citation tracing) and was structured according to the SANRA criteria. Genetic, neuroimaging, and neuropsychological evidence was judged against four questions: is hoarding a separable trait within OCD; do groups differ biologically on average; is any difference specific to hoarding; and can the evidence classify an individual patient? MAIN FINDINGS: Twin studies suggest that hoarding-related traits have a heritability of about 26%-48%, and one genome-wide association study reported an SNP-based heritability of 11%. These estimates come from different models and are not directly comparable; they are compatible with a heritable, polygenic trait but do not by themselves show a disorder-specific genetic architecture. A small number of PET, structural MRI, functional MRI, and EEG studies report differences associated with hoarding, including seven direct HD-OCD comparisons, but samples are small, diagnostic criteria vary, and findings have not converged. An exploratory computational study has compared genetic signals for the two phenotypes, but no direct comparison of risk variants exists. Neuropsychological findings were inconsistent: the most recent systematic review found no significant impairment on most cognitive tests in HD. CONCLUSIONS: Current neurobiological evidence provides only supplementary, not definitive, support for the diagnostic distinction between HD and OCD. It points to group-level biological heterogeneity, but it does not establish a distinct etiology or individual-level diagnostic utility. Larger studies using standardized DSM-5 criteria and direct HD-OCD comparisons are needed.

titre: Brainstem functional connectivity integrates microbiome-gut-brain signals in healthy older adults: a cross-sectional evaluation and a randomised controlled probiotic trial
resume: ABSTRACT Background Despite increasing interest in the gut-brain axis, the role of the autonomic nervous system and the brainstem in human gut-brain signalling remain largely unknown. Objective To characterise resting state functional connectivity (FC) of the brainstem in healthy older adults and to examine its association with a variety of factors relevant to ageing and the gut-brain axis, and to assess if brainstem FC is altered by probiotic intervention. Design Randomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial in 60–80-year-olds (55 women/28 men) with six-weeks Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus HN001 intervention in a non-encapsulated and microencapsulated formulation. Brainstem-optimised functional magnetic resonance imaging was performed before and after intervention. Results At baseline, age correlated positively with FC of locus coeruleus (LC) and dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) with pre-/postcentral gyrus, as well as of periaqueductal gray (PAG) with temporal/supramarginal gyrus and planum temporale. FC of PAG with precuneus cortex and cingulate gyrus correlated with cognitive status and mood. Perceived stress correlated with FC between nucleus tractus solitarius and occipital cortex, angular/temporal gyrus. FC of DRN differed between men and women. All p Conclusion Brainstem-to-cortex FC at rest correlates with several phenotypic characteristics implicated in healthy ageing and may be modifiable by probiotic supplementation. KEY MESSAGES What is already known on this topic: Gut-derived signals, including those related to gut microbiota modulations, influence brain function. Whether and how those signals are transmitted via the autonomic nervous system and integrated via the brainstem remains largely unexplored in humans. What this study adds: Brainstem-to-cortex functional connectivity, originating especially from the periaqueductal gray and locus coeruleus, was associated with age, cognitive status and psychological symptoms; and functional connectivity especially of the locus coeruleus was also affected by probiotic intervention. How this study might affect research, practice or policy: From a human gut-brain perspective, imaging the brainstem may add to the understanding of the role of the autonomic nervous system in (patho-)physiological processes and modes-of-action of intervention effects. This may have clinical implications for conditions with disturbed signalling along this axis.

titre: An expansive internal chemosensory system in the insect abdomen implicates Gustatory Receptors in diverse aspects of interoception
resume: SUMMARY Taste and olfactory receptors are gatekeepers that convey chemical information about the external environment. Their role in chemosensory systems has been extensively studied in several model system, which established their role in triggering discrete behavioral as well as physiological responses related to feeding and social interactions. Over time, cases of chemoreceptors expressed internally in organs not linked to the external chemosensory systems of taste and olfaction have been reported. Here, we present the existence of a complex internal chemosensory system in the abdomen of Drosophila melanogaster. We show that the adult fruit fly harbors a complex internal chemosensory system, composed of about 80 to 100 abdominal chemosensory neurons (ACSNs) expressing approximately 20 different Gustatory receptor ( Gr ) genes, including all sugar receptor and several members of the less conserved bitter receptor genes. The cells expressing specific Gr genes are stereotypically arranged along the entire circumference of the abdominal body wall, in proximity of muscle and fat layers. The ACSN fall into at least nine different subtypes based on co-expression analysis, projection trajectories into the Abdominal Ganglion (AG) and location of cell somata. Identification of different subpopulation of ASCNs expressing discrete combinations of Gr genes indicates that these receptor complexes have new, previously not considered roles in interoception, including monitoring of different nutrients, detection of cell metabolites and their byproducts and chemicals associated with pathogens.

titre: Neuroscience-informed Psychoeducation for Anorexia Nervosa: From Genetics to Neuroplasticity
resume: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a debilitating and often chronic disorder associated with significant morbidity and mortality. In recent decades, research on AN has identified key neurobiological pathways and brain regions that likely contribute to risk for and maintenance of the disorder and its symptoms. These include alterations in neurocircuitry underlying fear, motivation and reward, interoception, habit formation, and cognitive control, in addition to the detrimental effects of malnutrition on brain structure and function. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) for AN can be integrated with existing therapeutic approaches to improve patients’ and families’ understanding of the disorder and engagement in treatment. This chapter outlines content, strategies, and considerations for the effective implementation of NIPE in the treatment of AN.

titre: Investigating Cerebral and Systemic Haemodynamics During Hypnosis with Time-Domain Optical Imaging
resume: Clinical hypnosis can relieve pain and anxiety, yet its cerebral and systemic physiological mechanisms remain unclear. Portable optical imaging offers a means to investigate both, provided systemic vascular changes are distinguished from cortical activity. We tested whether time-domain diffuse optical tomography (TD-DOT), which provides separate superficial and model-assigned intracranial estimates, withstands a challenge from each recording’s own scalp field. In processed continuous-wave near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) hypnosis recordings (26 participants), low-frequency oxyhaemoglobin variability decreased by 21.8% (P = 0.0067), whereas a network effect did not survive global-signal regression. In a time-domain NIRS auditory cohort (49 participants, two visits), withheld short channels matched reconstructed scalp more closely than intracranial estimates (t(48) = 16.5). In the auditory cohort, scalp-only injection reproduced an apparent intracranial HbR phase lead, whereas attenuated 0.02–0.07-Hz HbO/HbT transfer differed from the specified leakage null (P < 10⁻⁶). In three exploratory hypnosis sessions (novice, intermediate and experienced participants), heart-rate fluctuations at 0.04–0.15 Hz were lower than during induction in all nine phase comparisons, and directly measured forehead pulsatility increased in two participants. These findings support leakage-aware optical monitoring during hypnosis, while intracranial source identity and hypnosis-specific effects require independent validation.

titre: Testing implications of the network theory of mental disorders in intensive short-term treatment
resume: Importance. Network theory is increasingly used to inform targeted and personalized treatment by identifying symptoms and interactions that maintain psychopathology. Yet, its prediction that successful treatment should weaken symptom interactions remains insufficiently tested.Objective. To examine whether temporal interactions among depression and anxiety symptoms and global network connectivity decrease during short, intensive inpatient/day-clinic treatment, as predicted by network theory.Design. Preregistered secondary analysis of OPTIMA, a randomized controlled trial conducted September 2017 to October 2020; analyses were conducted January 2025 to May 2026.Setting. Single-center inpatient and day-clinic treatment in Germany with weekly symptom assessments.Participants. Adults aged 18 to 75 years with moderate to severe depression without psychotic symptoms. Of 1370 patients assessed, 292 were randomized, and 288 were included in this analysis.Interventions. Seven weeks of schema therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, or individual supportive therapy, with up to 2 individual and 2 group sessions weekly plus clinically indicated pharmacotherapy and concomitant care.Main Outcomes and Measures: Changes in temporal interactions among 6 core depression and anxiety symptoms and in global network connectivity, estimated using a time-varying longitudinal network model. Exploratory stability landscapes characterized changes in network-implied symptom states.Results. Among 288 participants (mean [SD] age, 43.6 [13.6] years; 55.6% female), only 3 of 36 temporal symptom associations changed substantially, although symptom severity decreased. Mean absolute network strength did not substantially decrease from 0.55 (95% CI, 0.47-0.64) at treatment start to 0.46 (95% CI, 0.38-0.54) after 7 weeks. Still, the network model could explain symptom trajectories well (Bayesian pseudo-R² ranging from 0.43 to 0.54) and exploratory network-implied stability landscapes indicated a system shift toward lower-symptom states.Conclusions and Relevance. These findings provide limited support for the prediction that successful treatment reduces global connectivity in short, intensive treatment settings. In such settings, treatment-related change in symptom severity may be reflected in a reduction in general likelihood of symptom occurrence, but not necessarily in changes in symptom interactions, raising questions about long-term vulnerability. On the other hand, global symptom connectivity alone may not sufficiently characterize a healthy symptom system, and the role of specific symptom interactions warrants further investigation.Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03287362.

titre: Cholecystectomy among patients with irritable bowel syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
resume: Background Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and gallbladder disease share overlapping symptoms that may contribute to diagnostic uncertainty and unnecessary cholecystectomy. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether patients with IBS are more likely to undergo cholecystectomy than those without IBS. Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Google Scholar was conducted through June 3, 2026. Observational studies comparing cholecystectomy among adults with and without IBS were included. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed to calculate pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, influence diagnostics, meta-regression, publication bias assessment, and risk-of-bias evaluation were conducted. Results Ten studies met the inclusion criteria for the systematic review, and nine studies comprising 181,848 participants and 6,249 cholecystectomy events were included in the meta-analysis. Patients with IBS had significantly higher odds of undergoing cholecystectomy than controls (OR = 2.57, 95% CI 1.36–4.85; p = 0.009). Between-study heterogeneity was substantial (I 2 = 98.1%), but the association remained robust across leave-one-out sensitivity analyses. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression demonstrated that study design, geographic region, IBS diagnostic criteria, study quality, and sample size did not significantly influence the pooled effect estimate. No evidence of publication bias was detected, and the included studies were generally of good methodological quality. Conclusions Patients with IBS have significantly higher odds of undergoing cholecystectomy than individuals without IBS. These findings support careful evaluation of biliary symptoms in patients with IBS to improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize patient selection for surgery, and reduce unnecessary cholecystectomy. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261412571 , identifier CRD420261412571.

titre: Gut Microbiota–Metabolite Signaling in Irritable Bowel Syndrome: From Mechanisms and Candidate Metabotypes to Precision Therapeutics
resume: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a heterogeneous disorder of gut–brain interaction in which the same bowel-habit subtype can arise from different biological processes. This narrative review maps microbiota-related bile acids, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan metabolites, lipopolysaccharide (LPS), neuroactive amines, and fatty acid ethanolamides to host sensors and barrier, immune, motor, and sensory outcomes. Its contribution is a pathway-specific assessment of the evidence needed for clinical use: analytical and temporal reproducibility, demonstration of the proposed mechanism in humans, and prediction of differential treatment benefit. We distinguish descriptive associations, preclinical mechanisms, human pharmacodynamic effects, and validated treatment-selection biomarkers. Bile acid dysregulation offers the most developed connection between a measurable physiological abnormality and a tractable pathway, although biomarker changes do not establish symptom benefit or validate every proposed selection threshold. Most other candidate metabotypes lack externally validated classification rules and prospective treatment-by-biomarker interaction evidence. Diet, transit, medications, sex and hormonal context, and subtype transitions can modify both microbial function and measured metabolite exposure. Accordingly, proposed metabotypes remain research constructs. We integrate microbial transformations and endocrine cross-talk with an evidence ledger that identifies the missing human and predictive links, providing a testable agenda for mechanism-based treatment rather than a clinically validated prescribing algorithm.

titre: What is the evidence of the impact of contraception methods on symptom management in patients with Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) and/or Endometriosis?
resume: Contraceptive methods, particularly hormonal ones, are directly supported by evidence for symptom management in patients with endometriosis, though not specifically for IBS. They are effective in reducing pain and menstrual-related symptoms, with choices guided by patient preference and clinical profiles.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Are there systematic reviews or meta-analyses on the relationship between exam-related anxiety and the exacerbation of irritable bowel syndrome in university students?
resume: No direct evidence for the relationship between exam-related anxiety and IBS exacerbation in university students was identified, but existing studies indicate that anxiety, in general, is associated with IBS among students.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: IBS BAG
resume: The IBS BAG includes teams from IBS (Grenoble) and external groups from CEA-Cadarache (St Paul lez Durance), CEA-Grenoble, CERMAV (Grenoble) et IRBA (Brétigny-sur-Orge). We study the structure-function relationships of proteins and biological macromolecular complexes with a focus on human health, biotechnology and methodology. Most of the projects are a continuation of the MX-2686 proposal and can be grouped under the following themes: host-pathogen interaction, new therapeutic targets, fundamental cellular mechanisms, membrane proteins, biotechnological applications and methodology. Some of these projects use integrative approaches (X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM, SAXS and NMR) together with other biophysical and biochemical studies and, more recently, the use of AI (e.g. AlphaFold, Chai-1) to fully understand the complexity of the biological systems under study.

titre: Distinct gut microbiota and bile acid profiles in pediatric inflammatory bowel disease versus functional gastrointestinal disorders: potential for non-invasive discrimination
resume: Differentiating pediatric inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) from functional gastrointestinal disorders (FGID) is clinically challenging due to symptom overlap. This study aims to identify and compare distinct gut microbial and fecal bile acid profiles between these conditions to identify potential non-invasive discriminatory biomarkers for differentiating these conditions. In this case-control study, fecal samples from 33 pediatric IBD patients and 28 FGID patients were analyzed. Gut microbiota composition was assessed via 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing, and bile acid profiles were quantified using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Statistical analyses included diversity indices, differential abundance analysis, and Spearman correlation to explore microbiota-bile acid-inflammatory marker relationships. The IBD group exhibited significantly lower gut microbial alpha diversity and distinct beta diversity compared to the FGID group. Microbiota dysbiosis in IBD was characterized by depletion of Firmicutes and the genus Blautia , and enrichment of Proteobacteria and Escherichia-Shigella . Metabolically, IBD fecal samples showed elevated primary bile acids (e.g., cholic acid) and reduced secondary bile acids (e.g., deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid). Notably, bacteria enriched in FGID (e.g., Blautia ) positively correlated with secondary bile acids, and both were inversely correlated with inflammatory markers. Pediatric IBD and FGID demonstrate significantly different and interconnected gut microbial and bile acid metabolic profiles. The identified features, including specific bacteria and bile acids, warrant further validation as a non-invasive candidate biomarker panel with potential utility in differentiating these disorders. Not applicable (This is an observational cohort study without interventional treatment).

titre: Beyond emotional hunger: exploring the microbiota-gut-brain axis as a proposed mechanistic framework for emotional eating
resume: Emotional eating (EE), characterized by food intake in response to affective states rather than physiological hunger, has traditionally been conceptualized through psychological models of stress, emotion dysregulation, and reward-driven behaviour. These frameworks, however, do not fully explain interindividual differences in vulnerability or the persistence of maladaptive eating patterns. This narrative review critically examines the microbiota–gut–brain axis as a potential mechanistic framework linking psychological, neurobiological, and nutritional determinants of emotional eating. Evidence from psychology, neuroscience, microbiology, and nutritional psychiatry is integrated to evaluate the roles of hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis activation, reward processing, neurotransmitter metabolism, immune signaling, appetite-related hormones, and microbial metabolites. Emerging findings suggest that gut microbial composition and function may influence mood, stress responsivity, food craving, and eating behaviour through neural, endocrine, immune, and metabolic pathways. Most of this evidence, however, derives from animal models, mechanistic in vitro work, or human studies of stress, depression, obesity and general appetite regulation; comparatively few studies have measured emotional eating itself as an outcome, and the pathways described should therefore be read as candidate rather than established mechanisms. Dietary patterns may further modify these interactions by shaping microbial diversity, inflammatory tone, and metabolite production. Although current evidence is consistent with a plausible bidirectional relationship between gut–brain signaling and emotional eating, direct causal evidence in humans remains limited and the direction of the association is unresolved. EE should therefore be understood as a multidimensional biopsychological phenomenon. Future longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to clarify causal pathways and evaluate integrated psychological, nutritional, and microbiome-targeted strategies for personalized prevention and management in diverse clinical populations.

titre: Intolerance of uncertainty as a core driver of anxiety and depression: The mediating role of the gut–brain axis
resume: Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) is the tendency to react negatively to situations that are unclear, unpredictable, or lacking in information, and it is now regarded as a transdiagnostic risk factor for anxiety and depression. Research on the microbiota–gut–brain axis shows that the gut and brain communicate constantly and that disturbances in this communication accompany anxiety and depressive symptoms, yet the two literatures have developed largely apart. This study integrates them in a conceptual model in which IU (independent variable) influences anxiety and depression (dependent variables) partly through the gut–brain axis (mediator), via stress-system, immune–inflammatory, and behavioural pathways. Six hypotheses are derived and then illustrated in a simulation-based demonstration using a synthetic dataset (N = 400) analysed with parallel mediation, covarying age and gender, and 5,000 bootstrap resamples. In the simulated data, IU predicted gut–brain axis symptom burden (β = .42), which in turn predicted anxiety (β = .21) and depression (β = .31) over and above IU. A‍‍‍ significant part of an effect was mediated indirectly by anxiety (ab =.091, 95% CI [.047,.138]; 22% mediated) and depression (ab =.131, 95% CI [.081,.184]; 44% mediated), suggesting partial mediation. In terms of its implications, the paper also concludes by pointing out issues of assessment, psychological treatment, and integrated care while suggesting that the model should be tested in a real, longitudinal sample.
revue: Research Journal of Human and Social Aspects

titre: From gut education to central infiltration: microbiota-driven immune trafficking along the gut-brain axis
resume: The classical paradigm of central nervous system (CNS) immune privilege has evolved toward recognizing a dynamic, multi-organ neuroimmune axis. In recent years, the gastrointestinal tract has been widely recognized as a major immune reservoir, where rather than functioning as a localized physical barrier, the gastrointestinal mucosa acts as a vital educational center that instructs systemic immune responses. Within the gut-associated lymphoid tissue, dietary inputs, microbial metabolites, and commensal colonization imprint intestinal adaptive and innate immune cells with distinct functional phenotypes and migratory signatures. Through coordinated molecular mechanisms, these gut-educated immune cells egress from the mucosa to reach distant sites, with the CNS representing a critical destination. In experimental models, under homeostatic conditions, gut-derived signals direct the physiological seeding of central border zones and parenchyma, where specialized populations maintain baseline tissue surveillance, reinforce barrier integrity, and calibrate neurodevelopmental behaviors. Conversely, pathobiont expansion, loss of short-chain fatty acid-producing commensals, and mucosal barrier disruption predominantly promote pathogenic gut priming, transforming gut-resident cells into autoreactive or pro-inflammatory effectors that breach central neurovascular borders. Once inside the CNS, these gut immune cells can contribute to neurodegeneration, ischemic injury, and neuroinflammatory pathology. However, this migration is not always destructive; specific gut-educated populations are simultaneously deployed to central boundaries to execute anti-inflammatory and counter-regulatory protection. By tracing this microbiota-driven intestinal priming to central infiltration, we highlight shared homing mechanisms identified mainly in preclinical models (mouse models, germ-free and photoconvertible animals), while outlining translational challenges in establishing their role in human neuroinflammatory pathology.

titre: Bacterial Metabolites
resume: The gut microbiota produces metabolites that are involved in maintaining host physiological functions by exerting local effects on other microorganisms, intestinal epithelial cells, enteric nervous system, and immune cells. Emerging research is focused on understanding how microbial metabolites interact with the blood intestinal barrier, circulating immune cells and the blood brain barrier to induce their direct and indirect effects on host physiology and behavior. Indeed, the gut microbiota forms a critical component of the microbiota-gut-brain axis and alterations in gut microbiota composition can result in changes in microbial metabolite production that impact communication in the axis. This chapter addresses the diverse nature of microbial metabolites in terms of their composition, microbial origins, and site of production. We also describe the role of bacterial metabolites in modulating the microbiota-gut-brain axis, as revealed by looking at behavioral, immunological, and gastrointestinal readouts from preclinical models and human studies. Finally, the chapter outlines how various multi-omic methods have been employed to mine microbial metabolites for mental health. The chapter also addresses challenges and biases faced when multi-omic technologies are being employed to study the role of microbial metabolites on host physiology.

titre: Cannabis Hyperemesis Syndrome and its Connections with the Endocannabinoid System, Brain, and Gut Microbiome: A Scoping Review
resume: This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on bidirectional interactions among the gut microbiome, gut-brain axis, and endocannabinoid system (ECS), and proposes an integrated mechanistic framework by which chronic cannabis exposure may disrupt gastrointestinal and neuroimmune homeostasis, contributing to CHS development. This narrative synthesis integrates preclinical and clinical evidence on the pathophysiology of CHS, endocannabinoid signaling, gut microbiome composition and function, gastrointestinal physiology, and gut-brain communication. Particular emphasis was placed on interactions among the intestinal microbiome, enteric nervous system, immune system, and central nervous system, as well as their potential modulation by chronic cannabinoid exposure. The interactions among the gut microbiome, gut-brain axis, and ECS represent a potentially important but understudied dimension of CHS pathophysiology. An integrated understanding of these systems may provide new insights into individual susceptibility, disease progression, and the paradoxical gastrointestinal effects of chronic cannabis exposure. These interactions may ultimately identify novel biological targets and inform the development of mechanism-based therapeutic strategies beyond symptomatic management and cannabis abstinence.

titre: Correction: Predictors of ustekinumab intensified dose escalation in inflammatory bowel disease: a real-world (UST-predict) study
resume: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), affects over three million adults in the United States, with incidence rates continuing to rise globally (Dahlhamer et al., 2016). The chronic, relapsing nature of these conditions significantly impacts patients' quality of life and poses substantial healthcare costs, with annual direct medical expenses exceeding $14 billion in the United States alone (Burisch, 2025). Sustainable care strategies are needed including early biologic use, biosimilar adoption, and escalation of doses are essential to improve patient outcomes.The advent of biologic therapies has revolutionized IBD treatment, offering targeted approaches to control inflammation and achieve sustained remission. Ustekinumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting the p40 subunit shared by interleukin-12 and interleukin-23, represents a novel mechanism of action in the IBD therapeutic armamentarium (Benson et al., 2011). Initially approved for psoriasis, ustekinumab demonstrated efficacy in IBD through pivotal clinical trials, leading to regulatory approval for both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis (Janssen Biotech and I nc, 2016;Alorfi et al., 2023). The standard dosing regimen consists of weight-based intravenous induction followed by subcutaneous maintenance therapy at 90 mg every 8 weeks.Despite the proven efficacy of ustekinumab in clinical trials, realworld experience reveals that a substantial proportion of patients experience loss of response or suboptimal clinical outcomes during maintenance therapy. Studies indicate that primary non-response occurs in approximately 20%-30% of patients, while secondary loss of response affects an additional 20%-40% of initial responders over time (Ito et al., 2020). This phenomenon of diminishing therapeutic effectiveness leads to considerable clinical challenges and highlights the need for optimized dosing strategies.Current literature demonstrates variable approaches to managing loss of response to ustekinumab, with limited standardized guidance on dose optimization strategies. While therapeutic drug monitoring has revealed correlations between serum ustekinumab concentrations and clinical outcomes, the optimal approach to dose escalation remains incompletely defined. Notably, some real-world dose escalation practices have labeled recommendations, including adjustments such as increasing ustekinumab from every 8 weeks to every 4 (Panaccione et al., 2023).This study aims to evaluate clinical outcomes and predictive factors supporting ustekinumab dose escalation strategies in IBD patients with loss of response or suboptimal outcomes. The objectives are to assess the efficacy of shortened dosing intervals, define optimal criteria for candidate selection, and examine the safety profile of intensified ustekinumab regimens.This is a retrospective single center study was conducted in a specialized gastroenterology tertiary center and performed in accordance with Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines (von et al., 2008).Data extraction from medical records was performed between 20th and 30th of September 2025 to include all patients with IBD who were on ustekinumab treatment between September 2019 to August 2025. The inclusion criteria were as follows: adults aged 18 years or older with a confirmed diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), where the diagnosis was made according to the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11, version 2025). Patients were considered to have IBD if they had ICD-11 code DD70 corresponding to Crohn's disease (CD) or ICD-11 code DD71 corresponding to ulcerative colitis (UC). Eligible patients should have received at least one dose of ustekinumab induction IV dose and been maintained on 80 mg S.C every 8 weeks. Additionally, patients should have had moderate to severe exacerbation when started on ustkinumab defined as Crohn's Disease Activity Index (CDAI) score of 220-450. Outcome was assessed after 8 weeks or more of receiving the first ustekinumab 80 mg S.C maintenance dose.Exclusion criteria included patients with primary nonresponse (those who had only received IV induction and were then switched to another medication), pregnant females, patients with concomitant autoimmune diseases (such as psoriasis), and patients taking dual biologics agents (e.g., ustekinumab and another biologics). Additionally, patients with missing data and those without follow-up data were excluded.Patients' demographics and IBD related parameters were extracted from electronic medical health records. Several clinical and demographic variables were collected and examined as potential predictors of ustekinumab dose escalation and time to escalation. These included disease duration, duration of ustekinumab therapy (in months), prior use of biologic medication before initiating ustekinumab, number of prior biologic therapies, steroid use within 12 months prior to ustekinumab initiation, prior or concomitant immunomodulator use, age, sex, and inflammation (presence of at least one of the following: C-reactive protein (CRP) ≥10 mg/L, fecal calprotectin ≥250 μg/g, or albumin <35 g/L).Ethical approval for this study was obtained on 9 October 2024 from the standing committee for the coordination of health and medical research at the ministry of health of Kuwait (IRB No. 2917/2024) and as per the updated guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki (64th WMA General Assembly, Fortaleza, Brazil, October 2013) and the US Federal Policy for the Protection of Human Subjects.The primary outcome of this study was to assess potential factors associated with ustekinumab dose escalation-defined as an increase in dosing frequency to every 4 weeks among patients with IBD. Outcomes were measured separately for those with CD and UC. Dose escalation status (escalated vs. not escalated) served as the dependent variable in the logistic regression analysis.The secondary outcome was to investigate factors associated with the time to ustekinumab dose escalation among patients with CD who underwent dose intensification during the course of treatment (to every 4 weeks regimen). The time to escalation, measured in months from treatment initiation to dose adjustment, was analyzed using multivariable linear regression.Descriptive statistics were conducted to summarize the study variables. Categorical variables were reported as frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were expressed as medians with interquartile ranges (IQR). To compare differences between study groups, the chi-square test was used for categorical variables, and the Mann-Whitney U test was used for continuous variables.Stepwise multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted separately for patients with UC and CD to identify factors associated with ustekinumab dose escalation. All logistic regression models were adjusted for age, sex, and inflammation (defined as CRP ≥10 mg/L, fecal calprotectin ≥250 μg/g, or albumin <35 g/L). Additionally, a subgroup analysis was performed among patients with CD who had dose escalation to explore potential factors influencing the time to dose escalation. Natural logarithmic transformation (log10) was applied to the dependent variable (ustekinumab dose escalation in months) to account for the skewness in the continuous time-to-escalation variable in the multivariable linear regression model.Results of the logistic regression models are reported as odds ratios (ORs) using a null value of OR = 1. Linear regression analysis was presented as unstandardized beta coefficients (B), representing the change in the log-transformed outcome per unit increase in each predictor. To aid interpretability, the exponentiated beta values (exp [B] -or antilog[B]-) were also calculated, representing the multiplicative effect on the original (non-transformed) time to escalation. All estimates were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and a two-sided p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics (Version 29.0; Armonk, NY: IBM Corp.).Total of 165 patients with CD were included in the analysis. The median age was 31 years (IQR 24-39), and 87 (52.7%) were male. The median disease duration prior to initiation of ustekinumab therapy was 5 years (IQR 2-11). About 53 (32.1%) of the patients were biologic-naïve, while 72 (43.6%) had received immunomodulators before starting ustekinumab therapy, and 36 (21.8%) had used steroids within 12 months prior to starting ustekinumab. A total of 69 (41.8%) of the patients underwent dose escalation during the follow-up period. The median duration of therapy since ustekinumab initiation was 43 months (IQR 23-84). Inflammatory markers included a median CRP level of 7 mg/L (IQR 3-14.5) and median fecal calprotectin of 90 μg/g (IQR 56-361.5). Serum albumin levels showed highly clustered values, with a median of 40 g/L (IQR 40-40).UC patients were 41 in total. The median age was 30 years (IQR 25-40.5), and 22 (53.7%) were male. The median disease duration prior to starting ustekinumab was 4 years (IQR 2-7.5). A total of 18 (43.9%) of patients were biologic-naïve, 21 (51.2%) had received immunomodulators previously, and 15 (36.6%) had used steroids within 12 months prior to ustekinumab initiation. Dose escalation occurred in 14 (34.15%) of patients during follow-up. The median duration since starting ustekinumab was 34 months (IQR 12-65). Inflammatory markers included a median CRP level of 4 mg/L (IQR 2.35-15) and median fecal calprotectin of 89 μg/g (IQR 55.5-359). Serum albumin values were highly clustered, with a median of 40 g/L (IQR 40-40). All demographic information is summarized in Table 1.Among patients with UC (Supplementary Table S1A), extensive colitis (E3) was the most prevalent disease subtype, accounting for 49% (approximately 20 patients). Left-sided colitis (E2) followed with 34% (14 patients), while ulcerative proctitis (E1) accounted for 19% (8 patients). In contrast, among patients with CD (Supplementary Table S1B), ileal subtype (L1) was the most common, observed in 52% (86 patients). Ileocolonic disease (L3) and colonic disease (L2) represented 36% (59 patients) and 10% (17 patients), respectively. Upper gastrointestinal involvement (L4) was rare, occurring in only 2% (3 patients). Perianal disease was reported in 16.8% (28 patients). Regarding disease behavior, inflammatory type (B1) was predominant at 47% (78 patients), followed by penetrating (B3) in 32% (53 patients) and stricturing (B2) in 21% (35 patients).Among 165 patients with CD, 69 (41.8%) required ustekinumab dose escalation to every 4 weeks. Patients who underwent dose escalation had a significantly longer disease duration compared to those without escalation (median 6 [IQR 4-13] vs. 4 [IQR 2-8] years; P = 0.003). They were also less likely to be biologic-naïve (18.8% vs. 42.7%; P = 0.005) and more likely to have prior immunomodulator use (59.4% vs. 32.3%; P = 0.001).The median time to dose escalation was 9 months (IQR 3-18). No significant differences were observed in age, sex, steroid use, duration of ustekinumab therapy, or baseline inflammatory markers between groups (Supplementary Table S2A; Figures 1A,B).Among 41 patients with UC, 14 (34.1%) required dose escalation. No statistically significant differences were observed between patients with and without dose escalation in baseline demographics, disease characteristics, prior treatments, or inflammatory markers (Supplementary Table S2B; Figures 2A,B).Among patients with CD, patients who had received prior biologic therapy were approximately three times more likely to require ustekinumab dose escalation compared to biologic-naïve patients (OR = 3.05; 95% CI: 1.31-7.14; p = 0.01). Similarly, patients with a history of immunomodulator use prior to initiating ustekinumab were twice as likely to undergo dose escalation (OR = 2.07; 95% CI: 1.00-4.29; p = 0.05). In contrast, other factors, including patient age, sex, duration of ustekinumab use, and the presence of inflammation, were not significantly associated with the likelihood of dose escalation (Supplementary Table S3). Conversely, in patients with ulcerative colitis, none of the evaluated variables, including prior biologic or immunomodulator use, were significantly associated with the likelihood of ustekinumab dose escalation (Supplementary Table S4).Post hoc analysis was conducted in the subgroup of CD patients who underwent ustekinumab dose escalation. None of the evaluated predictors were significantly associated with the time to escalation. Prior biologic use (Exp[B] = 1.82; B = 0.60; 95% CI: -6.20 to 7.40; p = 0.86) and prior immunomodulator use (Exp[B] = 0.18; B = -1.73; 95% CI: -6.86 to 3.40; p = 0.50) did not demonstrate a statistically significant effect. Similarly, the duration of ustekinumab use was not a significant predictor (Exp[B] = 1.00; B = 0.00; 95% CI: -0.06 to 0.61; p = 0.95). All models were adjusted for age, sex, and biochemical inflammation (Supplementary Table S5; Figure 3). Post hoc analysis was not conducted among patients with UC because of the small sample size.This study reveals important disease-specific differences in factors predicting ustekinumab dose escalation between CD and UC patients. The primary finding demonstrates that prior biologic exposure and immunomodulator use significantly predict dose escalation in patients with CD but not in UC, highlighting the need for tailored therapeutic approaches based on disease and treatment history. Despite the availability of potent biologic therapies, improvising therapeutic strategies remains compelling today. Persistent disease activity in many patients necessitates approaches that aim to achieve deep remission while minimizing dependence on corticosteroids or surgical intervention (Lamb et al., 2019).The findings in patients with CD show that patients with prior biologic exposure have 3-fold increased odds of requiring dose escalation (OR 3.05, p = 0.01), while those with prior immunomodulator use have a 2-fold increased risk (OR 2.07, p = 0.05). These findings suggest that prior treatment exposure is a clinically meaningful predictor of dose escalation in CD patients on ustekinumab.The biological mechanisms underlying this association are likely multifactorial. Previous exposure to biologics may reflect a more refractory disease phenotype or alterations in inflammatory signaling pathways. Additionally, pharmacokinetic variability, including differences in drug clearance and serum ustekinumab concentrations, may contribute to reduced therapeutic response. This is supported by findings from Battat et al., who demonstrated that lower ustekinumab drug levels are associated with poorer clinical outcomes in Crohn's disease (Battat et al., 2017). While the mechanistic basis for this association, such as prior immunological priming or altered inflammatory pathway activity requires prospective pharmacokinetic investigation, our data support the use of treatment history as a practical clinical factor when anticipating the need for dose intensification. Prior immunomodulator use may create lasting changes in immune function that affect subsequent biologic requirements, potentially through long-term immunosuppressive effects or alterations in cytokine networks (Adorini, 2003).In contrast, patients with UC showed no significant predictors for dose escalation among the evaluated factors, which may reflect fundamental biological differences between CD and UC in their response to IL-12/23 pathway inhibition.The 59.4% rate of prior immunomodulator use in escalated CD patients versus 32.3% in non-escalated patients (p = 0.001) represents an 84% relative increase in prior immunomodulator exposure among those requiring dose intensification. The significantly longer disease duration in dose-escalated CD patients (median 6 vs. 4 years, p = 0.003) represents a 50% longer inflammatory burden before ustekinumab initiation. The longer disease duration likely reflects cumulative structural damage, fibrosis, and altered tissues that impairs drug distribution and necessitates higher drug concentrations for therapeutic effect. Interestingly, while baseline inflammatory markers showed non-significant trends toward higher values in escalated CD patients (CRP 7.8 vs. 6.5 mg/L, p = 0.131; fecal calprotectin 115 vs. 88 μg/g, p = 0.099), these parameters were not predictive of escalation needs with ustikenumab as suggested (Gisbert and Chaparro, 2020). The median time to dose escalation of 9 months (IQR 3-18) in CD patients closely matches recent international experience, where studies report escalation timing ranging from 6 to 9 months (Rehman et al., 2025). Contrasting sharply with CD findings, UC patients showed no significant differences between escalated and non-escalated groups across all evaluated variables. The nearly identical biologic-naïve rates (42.9% vs. 44.4%, p = 0.923) and non-significant differences in prior immunomodulator use (64.3% vs. 44.4%, p = 0.228) suggest pathophysiological differences between CD and UC in their response to ustekinumab. However, the shorter median time to escalation in UC patients (4.5 vs. 9 months in CD) may reflect different inflammatory kinetics or treatment response patterns between the two diseases.Our findings are consistent with previous real-world evidence demonstrating that ustekinumab dose escalation is frequently required in patients with IBD (Petrov et al., 2025). In a multicenter retrospective cohort, dose escalation was necessary in 55.5% of patients, with male sex identified as the only independent predictor of escalation. Importantly, dose intensification was clinically effective, resulting in steroid-free clinical remission in 66.1% of patients, normalization of C-reactive protein in 55.8%, and endoscopic healing in 35.8%. These findings support the role of ustekinumab dose escalation as an effective strategy for recapturing response in patients experiencing secondary loss of response.A systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 real-world cohort studies included 925 patients with CD, and it demonstrated that ustekinumab dose escalation successfully recaptured clinical response in 55% of patients with inadequate response or secondary loss of response to standard dosing (Meserve et al., 2022). Additionally, 61% achieved an endoscopic response, including 29% who attained endoscopic remission. Dose interval shortening alone was effective in restoring response in 57% of patients, although no consistent predictors of successful dose escalation were identified. Collectively, these data support ustekinumab dose intensification as an effective strategy for managing loss of response in clinical practice.The observed differences in ustekinumab dose escalation between CD and UC likely reflect fundamental differences in disease biology and treatment response. CD is characterized by transmural inflammation, greater disease heterogeneity, and involvement of any segment of the gastrointestinal tract, all of which contribute to increased inflammatory burden and pharmacokinetic variability that may necessitate dose intensification. In contrast, UC is limited to the colonic mucosa and generally exhibits a more homogeneous disease phenotype, which may result in different therapeutic requirements and response patterns to IL-12/23 inhibition. These biological differences may also explain why prior biologic exposure and immunomodulator use predicted dose escalation in CD but not in UC. Furthermore, differences in therapeutic goals and clinical decision-making may have contributed to the observed variation. Clinicians may be more inclined to escalate ustekinumab in CD to achieve transmural healing and prevent progressive structural complications, whereas in UC, persistent disease activity may more often prompt a switch to an alternative mechanism of action rather than dose intensification. the small UC cohort may have limited our to significant and prospective studies are needed to define factors associated with ustekinumab optimization in this study has important clinical for IBD in Kuwait and healthcare findings suggest that patients with CD who have received biologic therapy, or have a longer disease duration are more likely to require ustekinumab dose escalation, to identify patients early and monitoring during maintenance therapy. these predictors may therapeutic optimization before significant disease or In contrast, the of predictors in UC that treatment should on rather than baseline clinical real-world study evidence to support treatment strategies and may treatment and for IBD of this study include the of both CD and UC in a real-world and the use of clinical and treatment history factors to identify predictors of escalation.
