Despite maximal safe surgical resection followed by radiotherapy and temozolomide-based chemotherapy, disease recurrence remains a major therapeutic challenge. Increasing evidence suggests that the gut microbiota can regulate systemic immunity, host metabolism, and inflammatory signalling through the microbiota–gut–brain axis [1–3]. However, the extent to which these mechanisms directly influence human glioblastoma remains incompletely established. This review examines the proposed gut microbiota–microglia–glioblastoma axis through an integrated framework encompassing microbial metabolites, peripheral immune signalling, blood–brain barrier regulation, microglial plasticity, and glioblastoma-associated macrophage (GAM) metabolism. Particular emphasis is placed on short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan–kynurenine metabolism, aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling, microbial-associated molecular patterns, and inflammatory pathways involving Toll-like receptors, NF-κB, NLRP3 inflammasomes, and colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R). Pharmacological opportunities include myeloid-cell reprogramming, selective inflammatory pathway modulation, microbiome-directed interventions, and rational combinations with standard anticancer therapies. Recent reviews published in 2025–2026 have further highlighted the potential relationship between microbiome-associated signals and glioblastoma immunobiology [4–8]. Nevertheless, evidence differs substantially across human observational studies, experimental models, and mechanistic investigations. Confounding by antibiotics, corticosteroids, diet, treatment exposure, and tumour-associated physiological changes remains important. This review proposes a translational framework integrating longitudinal microbiome profiling, metabolomics, single-cell analysis, spatial transcriptomics, and pharmacological target validation. Establishing whether microbial signals causally modify tumour-associated myeloid cells will be essential before microbiome-informed strategies can be translated into clinical glioblastoma management.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: A Scoping Review Protocol for Unravelling the Relationships Between Colonialism, Gut Health, and Neurodegeneration Among Indigenous Populations
resume: The gut-brain axis is an emerging topic of interest in modern understandings of human physiology and metabolism, connecting the nervous system, digestive system, immune system, and the trillions of microbes that reside within our gut and digestive tract. This emerging area of research can be used to broaden our understanding of wholistic brain health, yet a research gap remains in the application of these theories to understanding the prevalence of neurodegeneration in Indigenous populations. This scoping review protocol aims to produce a review that provides a broad understanding of the availability of literature and evidence that addresses our research question. Through this evidence synthesis, we aim to inform future research in neurodegeneration among Indigenous populations.

titre: Effect of Care Brochure and Progressive Muscle Relaxation on Heartburn and Quality of Life among Antenatal Women: A Quasi-experimental Study
resume: Introduction: Heart Burn is one of the most common gastrointestinal problems during pregnancy and it is mostly caused by physiological and hormonal changes. It can adversely affect maternal comfort, everyday activities, sleep, and general Quality of Life (QoL). Pregnancy-related discomforts can be safely and effectively managed with non pharmacological therapies. Aim: To evaluate the effect of care brochure and progressive muscle relaxation on heart burn and QoL among pregnant women. Materials and Methods: The present quasi-experimental study was conducted in the Obstetrics and Gynaecology Outpatient Department of Amala Institute of Medical Sciences, a tertiary care hospital, Kerala, South India, from October 2023 to June 2024. A total of 250 antenatal women with heart burn were selected using consecutive sampling, with 125 participants in each intervention and control group. The intervention group received a self-care brochure comprising lifestyle and dietary modifications along with training in progressive muscle relaxation, while the control group received routine antenatal care. Heart burn symptoms were assessed using the Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease Symptom Assessment Scale (GSAS), and QoL was measured using the QoL/GRAV Questionnaire before and after the intervention. The Mann-Whitney U test was used to compare two independent groups. Results: Baseline sociodemographic and obstetric characteristics were comparable between the intervention and control groups, with no statistically significant differences in most assessed variables, except occupational status (p=0.037). The findings indicated that women in the intervention group experienced fewer heart burn symptoms, with a median {Interquartile Range (IQR)} score of 4 (2), compared with 7 (2) among those in the control group. Heart burn-related distress was also lower in the intervention group, with a median (IQR) score of 1 (0.25), compared with 2 (0.488) in the control group. After the intervention, overall QoL improved substantially (p<0.05). The intervention group demonstrated better QoL, reflected by a lower median (IQR) QoL score of 26 (3), compared with 34 (2) in the control group. Conclusion: Self-care practices that include dietary and lifestyle changes, along with progressive muscle relaxation, are safe, effective, and affordable non pharmacological treatments for reducing heart burn symptoms and improving pregnant women’s QoL.
revue: JOURNAL OF CLINICAL AND DIAGNOSTIC RESEARCH

titre: Interoceptive Pathways Linking Childhood Maltreatment to Adult Affective, Somatosensory, and Sleep Symptoms
resume: This study examines whether childhood maltreatment is associated with adult psychopathology symptoms through differences in the way individuals experience and interpret bodily sensations. The study uses existing data from the EPIC dataset to test a preregistered secondary-data analysis of the relationship between childhood maltreatment severity, interoceptive processes, and adult mental and physical health symptoms. The primary predictor is cumulative childhood maltreatment severity, assessed using the Maltreatment and Abuse Chronology of Exposure (MACE) measure. Two dimensions of interoceptive experience are examined as potential mediators: distress associated with bodily sensations, operationalized using the Body Signals Beliefs Questionnaire (BSBQ) (Stephenson, E. et al., in prep), and difficulty interpreting bodily sensations, assessed using the Interoceptive Sensory Questionnaire (ISQ) (Fiene et al. 2018). These processes are hypothesized to represent related but distinguishable pathways through which early adverse experiences may become associated with later psychopathology. Four adult outcomes are examined: depressive symptoms (BDI), anxiety symptoms (GAD), somatic symptoms (Common Mental Disorders Screening Questionnaire (CMDQ)), and sleep disturbance (PSQI). The primary analyses use parallel mediation models to estimate the associations of childhood maltreatment severity with each outcome through BSBQ distress and ISQ scores while accounting for age, gender, and difficulties in identifying feelings (Toronto Alexithymia Scale). Indirect effects will be estimated using nonparametric bootstrap confidence intervals. Missing data will be handled using full-information maximum likelihood, with complete-case analyses conducted as a sensitivity analysis. The primary hypotheses are that greater childhood maltreatment severity will be associated with greater interoceptive distress and difficulty interpreting bodily sensations, and that these interoceptive processes will in turn be associated with greater depression, anxiety, somatic symptoms, and sleep disturbance. The study will also test whether the associations between childhood maltreatment and adult outcomes are statistically consistent with indirect pathways through these two interoceptive processes. Additional exploratory analyses will examine whether socioeconomic status moderates associations between childhood maltreatment and interoceptive processes, whether other measures of interoceptive clarity and visceral awareness are related to the proposed pathways, whether momentary somatic-affective coupling in daily diary data is associated with individual differences in interoceptive experience and psychopathology, and whether different forms of childhood maltreatment show distinct patterns of association (MACE Subscales). Because the data are observational and the primary analyses are based on existing cross-sectional measures, the mediation analyses are intended to evaluate patterns of statistical association consistent with the proposed theoretical model rather than establish causal mediation. Confirmatory and exploratory analyses will be clearly distinguished, and all confirmatory analyses will follow the analysis plan specified in this registration.

titre: THE ROLE OF ALEXITHYMIA AND EMOTION REGULATION DIFFICULTIES IN PREDICTING PSYCHOSOMATIC SYMPTOMS AMONG UNIVERSITY STUDENTS
resume: Psychosomatic symptoms – Physical illnesses such as headaches, stomach and fatigue are common in the university students, associated with scientific impairments, and impaired quality of life, which are not fully explained by medical pathology. This document develops and tests a mediation model in which Alexithymia, a characteristic that is characterized by difficult identification and description of your own emotions, indirectly predicts psychosomatic symptoms through emotion regulation issues. Starting from the Process Model of Emotion Regulation (Gross, 1998), the deficit-in-emotional processing account from alexithymia (Taylor, Bagby, & Parker, 1997) and somatosensory amplification theory, this paper suspects that alexithymia impairs students’ capacity to regulate emotional experience and that this regulatory impairment is manifesting itself again as physical symptomatology. Based on the sample size of 250 university students and validated self-reporting measures (the Toronto Alexithymia Scale Sema20, the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale and the Patient Health Questionnaire Sema15), a mediation analysis (Hayes' PROCESS Model 4, 5,000 bootstrap resamples) indicated that alexithymia positively associated was emotion regulation difficulties (β = .77, p < .001) and that it is positively associated with psychosomatic symptoms (β = .46, p < .001). The indirect effect of alexithymia on psychosomatic symptoms through emotion regulation problems was significant (β = .36, 95% CI [26, .46]) and continued to have a significant direct effect (β = .33, p < .001) indicative of partial mediation. The complete model represented 55.4% of the psychosomatic symptoms variance. These findings underpin emotional regulation difficulties as an important mechanism link alexithymia of physical symptoms in university students and suggest that emotional regulation focused interventions could reduce psychosomatic complaints even among students who remain relatively alexithymic.

titre: The Adherence Paradox of Interoceptive Observation: Motivational Thresholds and Behavioral Constraints in Self-Directed Practice
resume: Background: Prior phenomenological accounts have described volitional fascial unbinding arising from prolonged interoceptive observation (Huang, 2026). However, phenomenological success does not guarantee sustained adherence in practice. Objective: This paper aims to analyze the behavioral and cognitive thresholds required for adherence to such endogenous observation protocols, rather than evaluating them as a therapeutic intervention. Analysis: We examine two primary behavioral barriers: the "motivation-intention gap" and the cognitive load of sustained attention. We propose that sustained adherence depends on the rare conjuncture of paired thresholds, following two distinct pathways: either exceptional baseline cognitive endurance alongside a powerful motivational catalyst, or targeted epistemic curiosity alongside substantial sunk costs. No single factor alone appears sufficient to sustain practice. We further explore trade-offs between "attentional anchoring" (suited for novices) and "targeted attentional focus with somatic relaxation" (an advanced strategy carrying greater risk of attentional drift). Conclusion: The protocol imposes substantial cognitive and motivational constraints, limiting its broader applicability across populations. These findings suggest that while valuable as a somatic practice, such observational approaches pose considerable challenges for widespread clinical referral, particularly given the apparent need for sustained external guidance during an ambiguous initial phase.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Fibromyalgia as a trauma-related functional syndrome: multimodal neurobiological basis, post-traumatic model, and interoceptive-emotional reprocessing
resume: Fibromyalgia (FM) is a heterogeneous condition that, in a substantial proportion of patients, resists a purely organic explanation. Following previous articles dedicated to diagnostic paradoxes, this work aims to develop a post-traumatic and functional therapeutic model. The central hypothesis is that, after excluding unrecognized organic conditions—primarily small fiber neuropathy, documented in approximately 40–50% of patients (Grayston et al., 2019; Marshall et al., 2025; Oaklander et al., 2013)—the residual core of what we call "fibromyalgia" may represent, in a significant portion of cases, the somatic expression of a trauma-related disorder or a post-traumatic spectrum. PTSD prevalence estimates in FM vary widely depending on samples and diagnostic criteria, from about 9% in large-scale retrospective studies up to over 70% in clinical samples selected for trauma (Gardoki-Souto et al., 2022; Rahangdale & Ferraro, 2025), but the direction of the association is constant. A 2025 review proposes that FM and PTSD share a common pathogenetic mechanism—salience network hyperactivity—and should be read as parts of the same spectrum (Luís et al., 2025). Early trauma would remain encoded in implicit memory, in limbic (amygdala) and interoceptive (right anterior insula) circuits, without sufficient integration with hippocampal and prefrontal circuits that allow contextualization and narration. This integration deficit produces a self-reinforcing circuit—metaphorically the "broken record," technically a self-sustained maladaptive attractor state—and finds correspondence in specific patterns documented by MRI, fMRI, EEG/MEG, and EMG. On this basis, the article presents an exploratory proposal for therapeutic integration combining targeted EMDR (validated technique) with Harmony Meditation and Analogic Meditation (meditative practices developed by the author, not yet validated by independent trials), discusses available evidence on meditation for chronic pain and central sensitization, and introduces the concept of the Incredulity Effect as an original construct—here proposed as an interpretative hypothesis—that can psychologically hinder remission.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Alexithymia and alexisomia in adolescents with functional neurological disorders: insights from brain network connectivity analysis – a study protocol
resume: Background Functional Neurological Disorder (FND) is a complex neuropsychiatric condition, characterized by diverse sensory and motor symptoms, and accompanied by significant pain and comorbidities. While previous research has explored FND primarily in adults, this study proposes to focus on adolescents, a critical developmental period where FND can emerge and impact various developmental milestones. The multifaceted nature of FND has led to the investigation of two underexplored compromised awareness traits: alexithymia (difficulty in emotional awareness) and alexisomia (difficulty in somatic awareness), and the relationship between them. Methods In the proposed study, we will apply a multidimensional model, to examine both subjective and objective aspects of alexithymia and alexisomia and their associations with FND symptoms. Finally, we will employ a comprehensive model of advanced neuroimaging techniques, including graph theory of both structural and functional connectivity, to investigate brain network patterns in adolescents with FND. Discussion By linking psychological constructs, such as emotional awareness, with neural connectivity, our novel theoretical and analytical approach will advance our understanding of the underlying neural mechanisms of awareness traits in adolescents with FND. This will assist in identifying potential biomarkers for early detection, refining diagnostic criteria, and informing the development of targeted interventions, contributing to potential improvement of clinical care and outcomes for adolescents with FND.

titre: The Mystery of Male-Female Perception: Two Dimensions of Vision, Body, Mind, and Love — A Conceptual Philosophical Study
resume: Human love, attraction, and interpersonal perception extend beyond visual beauty or mental constructs. They may involve bodily sensitivity, imagination, intellectual discernment, memory, conditioning, social environment, and the presence of another person. This conceptual philosophical study proposes two symbolic dimensions of perception: (1) vision-dominant perception—visual gaze → aesthetic perception → imagination → movement of desire; and (2) presence-dominant perception—proximity, gaze, voice, and demeanor → somatic perception → comfort, alertness, discomfort, or intimacy. The framework is placed in dialogue with Vedantic antahkarana, Samkhya, Tantric and Kashmiri Shaiva symbolism, Western phenomenology, and selected research on interoception. These dimensions are not universal gender laws, diagnostic categories, or claims of male-female psychological superiority. They are interpretive pathways that may appear in different people and contexts. The study distinguishes attraction from love, bodily response from reliable knowledge of another person’s intention, and comfort from consent. It argues that mutual dignity, autonomy, dialogue, and ethical discernment are indispensable to mature love. This paper is a conceptual philosophical inquiry, not an empirical experiment or a systematic review. Its proposed framework requires independent evaluation.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Exhibiting AI images: Unexpected outputs, linguistic inequalities, and curatorial possibilities
resume: Abstract Structured around latent data spaces that store masses of semantic associations, AI image generators have an intrinsic capacity to draw connections their users might not expect. Their outputs thus have the potential to engender characteristically anthropological epistemic shifts: subverting pernicious stereotypes, opening up horizons of possibility, and rendering the familiar strange. I demonstrate this with reference to World Hypnosis Convention , a collage of AI images that I developed for a public exhibition following long‐term fieldwork on the social imagination of hypnosis. While English‐language prompts generated highly standardized portraits of male stage performers, other languages elicited vivid, unexpected portraits that challenged rigid definitions of “hypnosis,” drew attention to the constitutive role of suggestion in social life, and invited critical perspectives on social institutions. World Hypnosis Convention thus demonstrates how AI images can support practices of anthropological exhibiting, while illuminating several limitations of AI image generation itself. In particular, it highlights the linguistic inequalities with which AI users can be faced: non‐English speakers may struggle to achieve the precision they may desire, whereas English speakers can miss out on lateral perspectives. Both issues warrant greater attention in critical anthropologies of AI and in future AI design.

titre: Erminio Di Pisa, il maestro della fascinazione istantanea. Biografia, metodo e testimonianze
resume: La monografia ricostruisce la figura di Erminio Di Pisa, ipnotista, astrologo e medium attivo a Milano nella seconda metà del Novecento (1° gennaio 1942 – 15 aprile 2002), specialista dell'ipnosi istantanea e della fascinazione, cioè dell'induzione di stati ipnotici soprattutto con lo sguardo. Il lavoro si fonda sulla lettura integrale dei suoi scritti conservati nell'archivio della Scuola – il Corso di ipno-magnetismo pratico (MEB, Torino, 1980), il Settenario di ipnosi superiore e L'ipnosi nel marketing, confluiti nel 2007 nel volume L'ipnosi dalla A alla Z (Anima Edizioni) – e sulla testimonianza diretta del dr. Marco Paret, suo allievo, che lo frequentò e ne osservò il lavoro. Si aggiungono la presentazione dello psichiatra Paolo Muzzana, i ricordi di amici e allievi raccolti nel 2026, il ricordo della famiglia in forma scritta e la tradizione della Scuola, trasmessa da Di Pisa al suo allievo, che collega Di Pisa al fascinatore belga Donato attraverso, con ogni probabilità, il suo assistente Jean-Lambert Pickman, un certo Morelli e il maestro milanese Dante Caravelli. Il testo descrive la vita di Di Pisa, il suo metodo (sguardo alla radice del naso, tre metodi di fascinazione, ipnosi istantanea, ipnosi «ad occhi aperti», magnetismo fisico con passi, imposizione delle mani e soffio, differenza fra l'ipnosi tradizionale del Corso e l'«ipnosi superiore» del Settenario, sedute a teatro, in radio e in televisione), le sue applicazioni terapeutiche e le cautele da lui stesso indicate. Quattro puntate del programma pomeridiano di Raidue «Segreti per voi», ottenute dalle Teche RAI e databili al 1993, documentano le sue dimostrazioni televisive. Le registrazioni di alcune serate in diretta su Telelombardia del 1999 mostrano l'applicazione dello stesso metodo al telefono, con i risultati dichiarati in diretta dai telespettatori, compresi i casi più difficili. Una sezione finale conclude con l'elenco delle fonti e delle ricerche in corso. La Scuola del dr. Marco Paret – ISI-CNV / Université Européenne (www.marcoparet.com) – porta avanti gli insegnamenti di Di Pisa d'accordo con la famiglia. This monograph reconstructs the profile of Erminio Di Pisa, a hypnotist, astrologer and medium active in Milan in the second half of the twentieth century (1 January 1942 – 15 April 2002), who specialised in instantaneous hypnosis and fascination, that is, the induction of hypnotic states mainly through the gaze. It is based on a comprehensive reading of his writings held in the School's archive – the Corso di ipno-magnetismo pratico (MEB, Turin, 1980), the Settenario di ipnosi superiore and L'ipnosi nel marketing, collected in the 2007 volume L'ipnosi dalla A alla Z (Anima Edizioni) – and on the first-hand testimony of Prof. Dr. Marco Paret, his direct student, who knew him and observed him at work. To these are added the foreword by the psychiatrist Paolo Muzzana, recollections of friends and students collected in 2026, the family's written remembrance, and the School's tradition, handed down by Di Pisa to Prof. Dr. Marco Paret, which links Di Pisa to the Belgian fascinator Donato, most probably through his assistant Jean-Lambert Pickman, a certain Morelli and the Milanese master Dante Caravelli. The text describes Di Pisa's life, his method (gaze at the root of the nose, three fascination methods, instantaneous hypnosis, eyes-open hypnosis, physical magnetism with passes, laying on of hands and breath, the difference between the traditional hypnosis of the Corso and the higher hypnosis of the Settenario, sessions in theatres, on radio and television), his therapeutic applications, and the precautions he himself recommended. Four episodes of the RAI 2 afternoon programme Segreti per voi, sourced from the RAI Teche archive and dating to 1993, document his television demonstrations. Recordings of live evening shows on Telelombardia from 1999 show the same method applied by telephone, with the results reported live by viewers, including the most difficult cases. A final section lists the sources and the ongoing research. The School of Prof. Dr. Marco Paret – ISI-CNV / Université Européenne (www.marcoparet.com) – carries on Di Pisa's teachings in agreement with his family.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Anxiety disorders and panic attacks: an umbrella review of meta-analyses on psychotherapy, medication, internet-based and exercise-based treatment, 2014–2023
resume: AbstractBackground. Anxiety disorders, including panic disorder, generalised anxiety disorder and social anxietydisorder, are the most common mental disorders. Panic attacks are frequent, highly distressing and often lead toemergency presentations. Effective psychological and pharmacological treatments are available, and their efficacyhas been examined in numerous meta-analyses that are rarely read together. Methods. Umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses of treatments for anxiety disorders in adults,with a focus on panic disorder and generalised anxiety disorder, covering cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT),other psychotherapies, medication, internet-based delivery, durability and physical activity. Structured search ofbibliographic records up to 2 November 2026. Published pooled estimates were extracted without re-pooling;methodological features were appraised descriptively. Results. Eight meta-analyses (2014–2023) were included, with up to 234 randomised trials and 37,333 patients peranalysis. Medication and psychotherapy both produced large pre–post improvements (Cohen’s d 2.02 and 1.22),but pre–post effects are inflated by high placebo response (d 1.29). Against psychological or pill placebo, CBTshowed a moderate effect on target symptoms (Hedges g 0.56). In panic disorder, CBT increased remissioncompared with waiting list (OR 3.0 after adjustment for small-study effects) and antidepressants reduced nonresponse compared with placebo (RR 0.72; number needed to treat 7). In generalised anxiety disorder, duloxetine,pregabalin, venlafaxine and escitalopram were effective and comparatively well tolerated. Gains afterpsychotherapy were maintained for up to two years. Guided internet-based CBT was as effective as face-to-face CBT(g –0.01). Physical activity reduced anxiety symptoms (median SMD –0.42). Conclusions. Anxiety disorders and panic disorder are highly treatable. CBT, selected antidepressants andpregabalin are effective first-line options, internet-based CBT extends access, and exercise is a useful adjunct. Trueeffects against placebo are moderate rather than large, which supports shared decision-making based onpreference, availability and tolerability. Author. Dirk de Pol, Editor-in-Chief, MedizinDoc (medizindoc.de), Berlin, Germany
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Efficacy of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy on Anxiety, Self-Criticism, and Body Image in Adolescent Female Athletes: A Randomised Controlled Trial
resume: This randomised controlled trial evaluated an eight-session, school-adapted Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) intervention among 62 adolescent female athletes from vocational high schools in Ahvaz, Iran. Participants with high competitive anxiety and low body image satisfaction were randomly assigned to the ACT group ( n = 31) or a waitlist control group ( n = 31). A pretest-posttest design with 3-month follow-up was used. Measures included the Sport Anxiety Scale-2, Forms of Self-Criticising/Attacking and Self-Reassuring Scale (short form), Multidimensional Body-Self Relations Questionnaire Appearance Scales, and Avoidance and Fusion Questionnaire for Youth. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed significant group × time interactions for all primary outcomes ( p < .001, partial η 2 = .33–.44). The ACT group exhibited reductions in competitive anxiety and self-criticism and improvements in body image satisfaction at posttest and follow-up. Exploratory mediation analyses indicated that intervention-related changes in psychological inflexibility were associated with changes in the outcomes; however, temporal precedence cannot be established and these findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating a causal mechanism. These results provide preliminary evidence that a brief, contextually adapted ACT programme was associated with improved psychological flexibility, reduced sport-related distress, and enhanced body image. Practical implications for school-based interventions are discussed.
revue: Journal of Psychologists and Counsellors in Schools

titre: Psychological Interventions for Depression in Nursing Students: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
resume: Depression is prevalent among nursing students and may adversely affect their academic performance, clinical competence, and well-being. We synthesized randomized trial evidence to determine whether psychological interventions alleviate depressive symptoms in undergraduate nursing students. PubMed, CINAHL, EMBASE, and CENTRAL were searched for randomized controlled trials published between January 2015 and June 2026. Two reviewers evaluated risk of bias with Cochrane RoB 2. We pooled standardized mean differences (SMDs) and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using random-effects models and explored variation by intervention category, academic year, and COVID-19 period. Nine trials were included in the systematic review and eight in the meta-analysis. Psychological interventions significantly reduced depressive symptoms compared with control conditions (SMD = −0.88, 95% CI = −1.32 to −0.43, p = 0.0001; I2 = 82%). Significant effects were observed for cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based interventions, and other psychological interventions, as well as across academic-year and pandemic-period subgroups; however, differences between subgroups were not statistically significant. Psychological interventions may reduce depressive symptoms among nursing students. Recurring educational features, including reflection, interaction, feedback, and behavioral practice, were noted in intervention descriptions; however, their contributions to intervention effects were not directly evaluated.

titre: Abstract 8677: Digital Exposure-Based Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Cardiac Anxiety Following Acute Coronary Syndrome Compared with a Lifestyle-Focused Intervention: A Randomized Controlled Trial
resume: Background: Cardiac anxiety is a specific form of psychological distress, characterized by fear, hypervigilance to cardiac-related sensations, recurrence, and avoidance behaviors in patients with cardiovascular disease. It affects approximately one-third of patients after acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and is associated with poorer quality of life (QoL), impaired recovery, poorer adherence to lifestyle recommendations and adverse cardiovascular prognosis. In a prior randomized controlled trial (RCT) we demonstrated that digital exposure-based cognitive behavioral therapy for cardiac anxiety (CA-CBT) reduced cardiac anxiety and improves disease-specific health status after ACS. Building on these findings, we evaluated CA-CBT n patients following ACS, against a therapist-guided lifestyle intervention, serving as an active comparator to account for non-specific treatment effects. Methods: In this RCT, patients with prior ACS (≥6 months post STEMI, NSTEMI or unstable angina) and significant cardiac anxiety, as per clinical interview, were randomized to eight weeks of therapist-guided digital CA-CBT or to a therapist-guided, digital cardiac lifestyle intervention (CLI). CA-CBT included psychoeducation, interoceptive and situational exposure to feared cardiac-related sensations and activities. CLI included psychoeducation and behavior change-support for health behaviors, including physical activity, without exposure components. The primary outcome was change in cardiac anxiety measured by the Cardiac Anxiety Questionnaire (CAQ) at post-treatment. Secondary outcomes included disease-specific QoL (HeartQoL). Analyses were conducted using mixed-effects models. Results: A total of 178 participants (mean age 64.3 years, 61% men) were randomized to CA-CBT (90) or CLI (88). Participants receiving CA-CBT demonstrated greater reductions in cardiac anxiety compared with CLI (B=-6.77, 95% CI [-8.16, -5.39], d=0.78; P<.001), along with greater improvements in both emotional and physical QoL domains (emotional domain: B=0.24, 95% CI [0.11, 0.37], d=0.31; P<.001; physical domain: B=0.20, 95% CI [0.11, 0.29], d=0.29; P<.001) at posttreatment. Treatment credibility ratings were similar between groups. Conclusions: Among patients with clinically significant post-ACS cardiac anxiety, therapist-guided digital exposure-based CBT resulted in greater improvements in cardiac anxiety and disease-specific emotional and physical QoL compared with a lifestyle-focused intervention. These findings support exposure-based CBT as a promising adjunctive strategy to improve psychological recovery and QoL following ACS. Ongoing analyses will further evaluate long-term outcomes, additional patient-reported outcomes, and adherence to secondary prevention lifestyle recommendations.

titre: School-based mindfulness interventions in children and adolescents: an umbrella review of systematic reviews, with implications for physical education
resume: Anxiety, depressive symptoms and stress-related difficulties have increased among school-aged children and adolescents, and the school has been identified as a priority setting for universal preventive strategies. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are increasingly implemented in schools, and Physical Education has been proposed as a suitable curricular space because it explicitly mobilises body awareness, attention and emotional self-regulation. A growing number of systematic reviews with meta-analysis are available, but they differ in populations, protocols, comparators and outcomes, and their conclusions are not uniform. This umbrella review aimed to (i) synthesise the evidence provided by systematic reviews with meta-analysis on the effects of school-based MBIs on emotional, behavioural and cognitive outcomes in children and adolescents aged 5–18 years; (ii) appraise the methodological quality of those reviews and the certainty of the evidence; (iii) examine the factors that moderate effectiveness; and (iv) identify gaps to guide future research. Umbrella review of systematic reviews with meta-analysis, conducted according to the Joanna Briggs Institute guidance for umbrella reviews and reported following the PRISMA 2020 statement. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261381514). PubMed, Cochrane Library and EBSCO were searched from January 2014 to 29 May 2026, with publications restricted to English and Spanish. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data and appraised methodological quality with AMSTAR-2; the overlap of primary studies across reviews was quantified using the corrected covered area. Because the included reviews overlapped and differed in populations, comparators and effect metrics, no new pooled analysis was conducted: findings were synthesised narratively and structured by outcome domain, and the certainty of the evidence for each domain was rated with the GRADE approach. Because the protocol-defined requirement for a quantitative synthesis was broadened during full-text screening (Sect. 2.4), reviews without a pooled effect size were also eligible; this deviation and its rationale are reported in the Methods. Nine reviews met the eligibility criteria, which were broadened during full-text screening to admit narrative and correlational syntheses alongside meta-analyses. Verification against the original publications showed that four reviews report a pooled quantitative effect [14, 8, 3, 6] and five synthesise their evidence narratively, correlationally, or through a levels-of-evidence rating [4, 7, 24, 25]; three reviews included wholly or partly clinical samples. The two meta-analyses most directly addressing anxiety disagreed: [14] reported a small significant effect (d = 0.16–0.30, attenuated under active comparators) while [8] reported a non-significant pooled effect (d = 0.013). Depressive symptoms improved in two reviews and were explicitly unimproved in the non-clinical subgroup of a third. Evidence for emotion regulation and emotional intelligence was mixed and partly correlational rather than experimental. The single review addressing cognitive functioning found a significant effect in fewer than half of its primary studies and could not isolate mindfulness from co-occurring intervention components. No review evaluated interventions delivered specifically within Physical Education. The evidence for school-based MBIs in children and adolescents is more uncertain, and less consistent across reviews, than earlier secondary citations of this literature suggest. At most, a small and inconsistent effect on anxiety is supported; evidence for other outcomes is weaker, indirect, or based on designs that cannot support a causal claim. No review provides direct evidence on Physical Education as a delivery context. These interventions should not be presented as a demonstrated solution to youth mental health difficulties on the basis of this evidence, and any recommendation to integrate them into Physical Education remains a hypothesis to be tested, not a conclusion to be drawn from the reviews synthesised here. Prospero CRD420261381514. Date 29/04/2026.

titre: Predictors and consequences of accommodation as an interpersonal maintenance factor of obsessive-compulsive disorder in daily life: A multi-method investigation
resume: THEORETICAL BACKGROUND: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a complex mental disorder associated with severe distress and impairments in all domains of life (Torres et al., 2006). One largely underutilized domain for a fuller understanding of the maintenance of OCD in adults is the interpersonal context. Even among loving couples, partners’ behavioral responses to OCD symptoms can inadvertently reinforce compulsions and obsessional beliefs via a set of behaviors termed family accommodation (Calvocoressi et al., 1995). Accommodation (ACC) refers to various ways partners attempt to prevent or alleviate patients’ distress by participating in rituals, enabling avoidance of obsessional stimuli and providing reassurance. ACC is presumed to be maintained via negative reinforcement cycles (short-term reductions of patient distress but long-term maintenance of symptoms), but no empirical findings are available to show whether patients and partners indeed experience short-term reductions in distress as a result of ACC. Additionally, few empirical findings to date explain why some partners accommodate more than others. Preliminary findings suggest that partners’ reactivity to patients’ vocally encoded emotional arousal during couple conversations is predictive of ACC. STUDY DESIGN & METHODS: This study consists of a combined laboratory and psychobiological paradigm which will provide insights into the multi-modal and multi-time scale antecedents and consequences of ACC. This will be a prospective, non-intervention, non-randomized study in which all participants undergo the same study procedures. We will recruit a sample of N=60 adults with a primary diagnosis of OCD and their romantic partners. Couples will complete a lab-based assessment including an OCD-related communication task, followed by a 5-day ecological momentary assessment in daily life focused on ACC, OCD symptoms and subjective/psychobiological stress, and a follow-up after 3 months. Assessments include clinical interviews, self-reports, salivary cortisol and alpha-amylase, and vocally encoded emotional arousal. RESEARCH AIM: Hypotheses and analyses focus on interpersonal reactivity to vocally encoded emotional arousal and psychobiological stress reactivity as antecedents of ACC, changes in psychobiological and subjective stress responses as a consequence of ACC, and long-term impacts on OCD symptoms. In sum, this paradigm will provide a detailed, ecologically valid picture of ACC, addressing the research gap regarding the interpersonal maintenance of adult OCD.

titre: What is the evidence for using an SSRI plus Lamotrigine in treatment-resistant OCD?
resume: Evidence shows that augmenting SSRIs with lamotrigine can significantly reduce OCD symptoms in treatment-resistant cases, suggesting it as a viable therapeutic strategy.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: The associations between the heterogeneity of behavioral disinhibition symptoms and quality of life in children with Tourette syndrome
resume: Abstract The presentation of behavioral disinhibition symptoms in children with Tourette syndrome (TS) is highly heterogeneous, with varying degrees of impact on their quality of life (QoL). The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between behavioral disinhibition symptoms and QoL in subgroups of children with TS. A total of 3,958 children (male/female = 3,004/954, age mean ± SD = 8.65 ± 2.17 years) were included. They were assessed for behavioral disinhibition through the symptoms of TS, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and oppositional defiant disorder (ODD). Initially, this study employed the latent profile analysis to classify individuals into different latent subgroups (profiles) based on disinhibition symptoms. Subsequently, for each profile, network analysis was performed to construct network structures of disinhibition symptoms and QoL, with the goal of identifying central and bridge symptoms within the network structure. Heterogeneity of behavioral disinhibition symptoms in children with TS was identified, resulting in three latent subgroups: profile 1: low (TS, OCD) + low (ADHD, ODD), profile 2: moderate (TS, OCD) + high (ADHD, ODD), and profile 3: high (TS, OCD) + moderate (ADHD, ODD). Network analyses revealed “psychological” and “inattentive symptoms” as central and bridge symptoms across all profiles. Unique central symptoms related to QoL were “physical and activities of daily living” for profile 1, “family” for profile 2, and “school and learning” for profile 3. The identification of common and unique central and bridge symptoms across all profiles provides new ideas for the development of personalized intervention targets.

titre: The Problem of Relapse and the Need for a New Recovery Model
resume: This chapter examines why relapse remains common in substance use recovery even among individuals who are motivated, insightful, and engaged in treatment. It argues that relapse is best understood not as a failure of knowledge or willpower, but as a learned response to internal distress, reinforced through repeated experiences of relief. Drawing on cognitive neuroscience, learning theory, relapse prevention, acceptance-based treatment, exposure principles, and comparisons with compulsive disorders such as obsessive–compulsive disorder and eating disorders, the chapter explains how craving, shame, physiological discomfort, experiential avoidance, and distress intolerance can narrow behavioral flexibility when recovery skills are most needed. Readers gain a conceptual foundation for understanding relapse as a problem of access under emotional load rather than inadequate commitment. The chapter also introduces the rationale for shifting from control-based strategies toward capacity-building approaches that help individuals remain present with distress without immediate escape, preparing readers for the EXACT Recovery Model developed in later chapters.

titre: Person-first, identity-first and condition-first language in depression research, 1991–2025: a Web of Science bibliometric analysis
resume: Writing guides in psychology and medicine have long asked authors to describe people as having a condition ("patients with depression") rather than as the condition ("depressives"). In depression research, the most common label is an adjective ("depressed patients"), which is grammatically identity-first but may describe a mood state rather than a diagnosis. Diagnosis-first forms such as "MDD patients" have also become common. This study describes how the grammatical form of person labels in the titles, abstracts, and author keywords of depression research changed between 1991 and 2025. Each label is classified as identity-first ("depressed patients", "depressives"), condition-first ("MDD patients", "depression patients"), or person-first ("patients with major depressive disorder", "people living with depression"). The classification is grammatical and descriptive, and no form is treated as stigmatising or preferred. A separate secondary category records language with a negative load, such as "suffering from depression". This investigation forms the fifth study in a series on person labels in psychiatric research, following bipolar disorder, obsessive–compulsive disorder, autism, and addiction.

titre: Person-first, identity-first and condition-first language in addiction research, 1991–2025: a Web of Science bibliometric analysis
resume: Addiction research has a long record of describing people by their substance use or behaviour ("addicts", "alcoholics", "drug abusers", "gamblers"). In 2010, a randomised study found that clinicians who read about a "substance abuser" judged that person as more culpable than clinicians who read about someone "with a substance use disorder" (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010). In 2014 the editors of Substance Abuse asked authors to use person-first language (Broyles et al., 2014), and in January 2017 the US Office of National Drug Control Policy asked federal agencies to replace terms such as "addict" and "abuser" (ONDCP, 2017). DSM-5 (2013) replaced substance "abuse" and "dependence" with "use disorder" and placed gambling disorder among the addictive disorders. We will describe how the grammatical form of person labels in the titles, abstracts and author keywords of addiction research changed between 1991 and 2025, across substance and behavioural addictions. Each label will be classified as identity-first ("addicts", "alcoholic patients"), condition-first ("opioid-dependent patients", "AUD patients") or person-first ("people with alcohol use disorder", "people who inject drugs"). The primary classification is grammatical and descriptive. A separate secondary category records slang and terms that published language guidance in this field identifies as pejorative (for example "junkie", "abuser", "clean"/"dirty" for test results). This is the fourth study in a series on person labels in psychiatric research, after studies on bipolar disorder, obsessive–compulsive disorder and autism.

titre: Brain and Obesity Longitudinal Development: Neurobiological Mechanisms of Semaglutide Treatment of Adolescent Obesity
resume: This single-site, prospective observational pilot study examines how clinically prescribed semaglutide is associated with changes in the adolescent brain, cognition, mood, interoception, and metabolic and biological markers. Adolescents 12 to 15 years old with obesity (body mass index at or above the 95th percentile for age and sex), whose own treating physician has independently decided to start weekly subcutaneous semaglutide (Wegovy) as part of routine care, complete multimodal assessments before starting the medication and again after approximately 6 months of treatment. Assessments at each timepoint include 3T structural and resting-state functional MRI, a neurobehavioral and interoceptive battery, and saliva and blood collection for biomarker analysis and biobanking; a semi-structured qualitative interview is conducted at the follow-up visit. The study does not provide, prescribe, or modify the medication-all treatment decisions are made by the participant's own physician. The primary goal is to characterize within-subject changes in resting-state functional connectivity, brain structure, cognition, and eating- and reward-related behavior associated with GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment during adolescence, and to interpret these measures relative to normative neuroimaging and cognitive data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study.

titre: Psilocybin FCR Early-Stage Breast Cancer
resume: This trial is designed to evaluate efficacy and psychological mechanisms of single-dose psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy (PAP) to treat fear of cancer recurrence (FCR), psychiatric (anxiety, depression) distress and quality-of-life (QOL), in 100 outpatients with early-stage breast cancer. The study will assess the strength and durability of therapeutic effects in a double-blind, parallel-design, placebo-controlled, two-center randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing a single 25mg oral 'high' dose of psilocybin to a single 5mg oral 'low dose psilocybin (active placebo), both delivered in conjunction with a psychotherapy platform.

titre: The Effect of Three-Minute Breathing Space Meditation on Stress, Anxiety, and Depression Among Postgraduate Students in Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM): A Randomized Controlled Trial
resume: Postgraduate students often experience psychological distress linked to academic demands, deadlines, research uncertainty, and financial or social pressures, and international students may face additional adjustment challenges. This study tests whether a brief, low-burden mindfulness practice - a three-minute Breathing Space Meditation (BSM) session, done four days a week for 8 weeks - can reduce stress, anxiety, and depression in postgraduate students at Universiti Putra Malaysia, compared with an active control activity that is matched in format and contact time but does not involve mindfulness training. Participants are randomly assigned to one of the two groups and are grouped by whether they are local or international students. The study also looks at whether the intervention affects stress hormone (cortisol) levels, a marker of inflammation (C-reactive protein), and a brain-wave measure linked to mood, and it collects brief daily check-ins on mood, stress, sleep, and academic pressures over the 8 weeks.

titre: Defecation-Related Relief of Dyspeptic Symptoms Identifies Patients More Likely to Have Irritable Bowel Syndrome
resume: In 1074 patients with disorders of gut–brain interaction, relief of dyspeptic symptoms after defecation or flatus was common (52%–55%), associated with physician-assigned irritable bowel syndrome (aOR≈2.4) and lower odds of physician-assigned functional dyspepsia. This modifier, absent from formal Rome IV functional dyspepsia criteria, may help identify an intestinal-like phenotype. ABSTRACT Background Disorders of gut–brain interaction (DGBI) are defined using symptom-based criteria after exclusion of structural disease. We evaluated whether relief of dyspeptic symptoms after bowel movements or flatus is associated with physician-assigned functional dyspepsia (FD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), lower gastrointestinal symptoms, and physician–Rome IV FD agreement. Methods We performed a cross-sectional analysis of the Asian-European GastroIntestinal Symptoms (AEGIS) cohort, including adults with physician-diagnosed DGBI across 11 countries. Dyspeptic symptom domains were defined as PDS-type symptoms (postprandial fullness and/or early satiation) and EPS-type symptoms (epigastric pain and/or burning). The exposure of interest was evacuation-related symptom relief (≥ 30% of episodes relieved by bowel movement and/or flatus). Primary outcomes were physician-assigned diagnoses of FD and IBS. Multivariable logistic regression models were adjusted for age, sex, BMI, geographic region, PAGI-SYM, and PHQ-12 scores. Results Among 1074 patients, PDS-type and EPS-type symptoms were reported by 60.7% and 53.6%, respectively. Evacuation-related relief was common (55.1% and 51.7%) and more frequent in patients with IBS-only than FD-only diagnoses. In adjusted analyses, evacuation-related relief was associated with higher odds of physician-assigned IBS (PDS aOR 2.38 [1.64–3.46]; EPS aOR 2.45 [1.69–3.57]) and lower odds of physician-assigned FD (PDS aOR 0.56 [0.39–0.81]; EPS aOR 0.53 [0.37–0.75]). It was also associated with discordance between physician-assigned and Rome IV FD classifications (PDS aOR 1.91 [1.22–2.99]; EPS aOR 1.82 [1.14–2.90]). Conclusion Evacuation-related relief of dyspeptic symptoms is common and is associated with physician-assigned IBS, lower odds of physician-assigned FD, and discordance between physician-based and Rome IV FD classifications, suggesting that this symptom modifier may contribute to clinical phenotyping beyond current Rome criteria.

titre: Targeting the Gut-Brain Axis in Functional Dyspepsia: Buspirone and Mirtazapine Improve Anxiety and PAGI-SYM Scores
resume: Buspirone and mirtazapine were more effective than pantoprazole in reducing anxiety and improving symptoms in functional dyspepsia, suggesting anti-anxiety medications may help manage both the psychological and gastrointestinal aspects of the disorder. ABSTRACT Background Functional dyspepsia is a chronic gastrointestinal disorder with uncertain causes, often linked to anxiety and depression, which can worsen symptoms and hinder treatment success. Although psychological therapies and antidepressants have shown some benefit, the role of anti-anxiety medications remains unclear. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of buspirone and mirtazapine in reducing symptoms and improving the quality of life for patients with functional dyspepsia. Methods In a semi experimental study, 71 patients with functional dyspepsia were randomized to receive either buspirone 15 mg, mirtazapine 7.5 mg, or pantoprazole 40 mg once daily for 12 weeks. Outcomes—anxiety severity, dyspepsia symptom score, quality of life, and adverse events—were assessed at baseline and monthly. Efficacy was analyzed by repeated-measures ANOVA and adverse event rates by chi-square tests. Results Both buspirone and mirtazapine significantly outperformed pantoprazole alone in reducing anxiety (buspirone vs. control at 3 months, p = 0.01; both active treatments vs. control, p < 0.05) and in alleviating functional dyspepsia symptoms by Week 12 (both vs. control, p < 0.05), with no difference between the two active drugs. Conclusions This study suggests that buspirone and mirtazapine are effective in reducing anxiety and improving symptoms in patients with functional dyspepsia. These findings highlight the potential role of anti-anxiety medications in managing both the psychological and gastrointestinal aspects of this disorder.

titre: Corticotropin-Releasing Factor: A Key Player in Intestinal Barrier Dysfunction of Diarrhea-Predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome-A Narrative Mechanistic Review
resume: Corticotropin-Releasing Factor (CRF) plays a crucial role in the pathophysiology of diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) primarily by disrupting intestinal barrier function. In this narrative review of PubMed and Web of Science literature published through January 2026, we summarize the mechanisms by which CRF mediates intestinal barrier dysfunction in IBS-D and discuss potential therapeutic strategies. This review examines the mechanisms by which CRF impairs the intestinal barrier through several signaling pathways, including GC/NR3C1, MAPK/ERK, and Rho/ROCK/MLC. These pathways cause the downregulation of tight junction proteins, increased intestinal permeability, and dysregulated immune responses. Additionally, CRF induces immune inflammation via TLR signaling and promotes the activation of immune cells, further exacerbating barrier dysfunction. The disruption of epithelial barrier integrity is central to IBS-D, leading to visceral hypersensitivity and worsening gastrointestinal symptoms. Current therapeutic approaches for IBS-D often begin with lifestyle interventions. However, preclinical evidence suggests that interventions such as metformin, Eritoran, Puerarin, and anakinra may restore barrier integrity and alleviate symptoms by ameliorating CRF-mediated intestinal barrier dysfunction. Nevertheless, the mechanisms underlying CRF-induced IBS-D and the relevant therapeutic approaches have not been fully elucidated, and the available evidence is predominantly derived from animal and cell models, thus requiring further clinical validation. Future studies should further dissect CRF-related signaling pathways and develop intervention strategies aimed at restoring the intestinal barrier, thereby facilitating clinical translation and improving the prognosis of patients with IBS-D.

titre: ScRNA-Seq Reveals Jiangfu Zhixie Formula Alleviates IBS-D by Inhibiting Macrophage M1 Polarization through HIF-1α-Glycolysis Axis
resume: BACKGROUND: Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea (IBS-D) remains a challenging condition to manage due to its chronic nature and the limited long-term efficacy of current treatments. The traditional Chinese herbal formula Jiangfu Zhixie (JFZX) has shown clinical benefits, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. AIM: This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic effects of JFZX on IBS-D and elucidate its molecular mechanisms, focusing on macrophage polarization and the HIF-1α-glycolysis axis. METHODS: An IBS-D mouse model was established by senna leaf infusion combined with restraint stress. Mice were treated with varying doses of JFZX or pinaverium bromide (positive control) for 14 days. Diarrhea symptoms, visceral hypersensitivity, and intestinal barrier integrity were assessed. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed on colon tissues to analyze cellular composition and intercellular interactions. In vitro, LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages were treated with JFZX-medicated serum to evaluate M1 polarization, cytokine secretion (IL-1β, TNF-α), and expression of HIF-1α and glycolysis-related proteins (GLUT1, LDHA). RESULTS: JFZX treatment significantly ameliorated diarrhea, reduced visceral hypersensitivity, and restored intestinal barrier integrity in IBS-D mice, accompanied by upregulation of tight junction proteins ZO-1 and Occludin. scRNA-seq revealed that JFZX reshaped the colonic cellular landscape, attenuating myeloid-epithelial interactions and reducing the proportion of pro-inflammatory M1-like macrophages. Mechanistically, HIF-1α was identified as a key driver of M1 polarization in IBS-D. JFZX suppressed HIF-1α expression and its downstream glycolytic pathway (GLUT1, LDHA) both in vivo and in vitro, thereby inhibiting M1 macrophage polarization and decreasing IL-1β and TNF-α secretion in LPS-stimulated macrophages. CONCLUSION: JFZX alleviates IBS-D by inhibiting M1 macrophage polarization through suppression of the HIF-1α-glycolysis axis, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic agent for IBS-D and identifying HIF-1α as a promising target for intervention.

titre: Intestinal Permeability in Irritable Bowel Syndrome With and Without Comorbid Conditions: Results From the European DISCOvERIE Cohort
resume: BACKGROUND: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a disorder of gut-brain interaction often accompanied by psychiatric and/or somatic comorbidities. Intestinal-barrier dysfunction has been implicated in IBS pathophysiology. However, the contribution of psychiatric and somatic comorbidities to intestinal permeability remains unclear. We aimed to assess intestinal permeability in a large multicentric cohort of IBS patients with and without psychiatric and/or somatic comorbidities, compared with disease controls, and healthy subjects. METHODS: IBS patients and disease controls were recruited across nine European centres. Small intestinal and colonic permeabilities were assessed using the lactulose-mannitol-sucralose urinary excretion test. Urinary sugar concentrations were quantified by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Analyses were adjusted for relevant clinical and lifestyle confounders. RESULTS: The lactulose/mannitol (L/M) ratio, but not the percentage of sucralose (%S), was significantly increased in IBS patients (N = 418) compared with disease controls (N = 200), regardless of IBS subtype or sex. Notably, the increased L/M in IBS patients was primarly driven by a significant decrease in mannitol excretion. IBS patients with psychiatric or combined psychiatric and somatic comorbidities showed a higher L/M than their corresponding disease control groups. However, L/M values did not differ between IBS patients with and without comorbidities. Substantial between-centre variability in L/M ratios awas observed. DISCUSSION: Small intestinal, but not colonic, permeability, as reflected by an elevated L/M ratio, is increased in IBS patients. These alterations seem to be related to the presence of IBS per se rather than to comorbid conditions. Interestingly, substantial geographic variability was observed, which may reflect environmental or population-related factors influencing barrier function. Further investigations are needed to better understand the clinical relevance of these findings.

titre: Prevalence and Burden of Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction in Nigeria: Results From the Rome Foundation Global Epidemiology Study
resume: The study provides the first comprehensive national population-based prevalence of disorders of gut–brain interaction (DGBI) for Nigeria. We demonstrated that DGBI are prevalent and impactful in the Nigerian adult population and the northern region showed a higher burden of the DGBI. ABSTRACT Background Data on the prevalence and impact of disorders of gut–brain interaction (DGBI) are lacking for most parts of Africa, including Nigeria, the country with the largest population on the continent. This study aimed to investigate the prevalence and burden of DGBI among adults in the Nigerian general population. Methods Nigerian data from the Rome Foundation Global Epidemiology Study (RFGES) were obtained by trained interviewers using face-to-face household interviews. The questionnaire included the Rome IV diagnostic questionnaire to assess the presence of DGBI, psychological distress (PHQ-4), non-GI somatic symptom severity (PHQ-12), mental and physical quality of life (PROMIS-10), health care utilization, and dietary intake. Key Results One thousand six hundred and thirty-two individuals (48.6% females, mean age 44 (range 18–100) years) were sampled. The prevalence of any DGBI in Nigeria was 23.5% (95% CI: 21.5–25.6), with a higher prevalence in females (26.1%) than in males (21.0%). The highest prevalence of DGBI per gastrointestinal anatomical region was for bowel disorders (17.6%). The most prevalent individual DGBI diagnoses were functional dyspepsia (7.3%) and unspecified functional bowel disorder (6.6%). Compared to individuals without DGBI, individuals with DGBI were older, had reduced quality of life, increased psychological symptoms and associated healthcare utilization burden. There was a higher prevalence of any DGBI reported in the northern regions than in the southern regions. Conclusions DGBI are prevalent and impactful in Nigeria, in line with studies from other parts of the world that utilized the face-to-face survey methodology. More studies are needed to further understand the distribution and impact of DGBI in Nigeria and other similar countries around the world where they are understudied.

titre: Atopic biologic use and recalled irritable bowel syndrome symptom severity: A hypothesis generating retrospective survey evaluation
resume: Background: Case reports indicate that omalizumab may be therapeutic in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), but this has not been confirmed with follow-up studies. Objective: The present study sought to determine if biologics used to treat atopy have any effect on recalled IBS severity. Methods: All patients ≥ 12 years of age with IBS and currently taking an atopic biologic were sent a questionnaire that assesses IBS severity currently and before starting their atopic biologic. The IBS Symptom Severity Score (IBS-SSS) and IBS Adequate Relief metric were used to quantify IBS severity pre- and post-atopic biologic. Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon signed rank tests with Hodges-Lehman estimated median differences and 95% confidence intervals (CI) compared IBS-SSS pre- and post-atopic biologic start. Subset analyses of patients taking omalizumab or dupliumab were also conducted. Results: Sixteen patients (12% response rate) fully responded to the questionnaire (omalizumab, n = 7; dupilumab, n = 7; mepolizumab, n = 1; tezepelumab, n = 1). The majority were women (75%) with a median (range) age of 41 years (22-71 years). The frequency of respondents who reported adequate relief of their IBS did not differ pre- and post-atopic biologic start (p = 0.688), but patients reported significantly decreased IBS-SSS post-atopic biologic start (estimated median difference 70.0 [95% CI, 20.0-122.5]; z = -2.59, p = 0.0097). One patient (6%) taking omalizumab reported complete resolution of IBS symptoms. The majority of the patients (56%) reported a decrease of at least 50 in the IBS-SSS. Although subset analyses of patients taking omalizumab or dupilumab did not show statistically significant differences pre- and post-atopic biologic start, the estimated median IBS-SSS difference pre- and post-atopic biologic start was 93.8 (95% CI, -15.5 to 201.5) and 22.0 (95% CI, -27.5 to 149.0) for omalizumab and dupilumab, respectively. Conclusion: The patients with IBS reported improved recalled IBS severity after starting an atopic biologic, with patients taking omalizumab reporting a larger difference. Future controlled studies are needed to confirm this finding.

titre: Anticipated Threat Amplifies Esophageal Perception in the Absence of Peripheral Change
resume: BACKGROUND: Psychological processes may influence how gastrointestinal sensations are perceived and responded to, but their impact on esophageal symptom perception remains poorly understood. We developed and tested a novel stimulus-response paradigm to examine how anticipated threat influences behavioral responding, fear, and perceived intensity of esophageal sensations. METHODS: Healthy volunteers detected and rated neutral electrical stimulations to the distal esophagus under anticipated threat (potential pain) and control (no pain) conditions, pressing a response button (reaction time) and rating intensity and fear after each stimulus. To evaluate specificity, the paradigm was also applied to somatic hand stimulation. Linear mixed-effects models tested whether threat produced shorter reaction times and heightened fear and intensity ratings, and whether these effects differed by body location. KEY RESULTS: The sample included 46 participants. Participants rated stimuli in the threat condition as more intense and fear-evoking than control stimuli (both p < 0.0001), despite the stimuli being physically identical. Fear ratings were higher for esophageal than hand stimulation (p < 0.0001). Contrary to our hypothesis, response times were slower under threat (p = 0.0003) and for esophageal versus hand stimulation (p < 0.0001). Threat effects across all outcomes did not differ by body location p, suggesting a more general effect of threat across visceral and somatic stimulation. CONCLUSIONS & INFERENCES: Threat amplified perceived intensity and fear in response to neutral esophageal stimulation. Contrary to expectations, response times were slower under threat, suggesting threat may potentially interfere with rather than facilitate behavioral responding. These findings support a role for threat-related processes in esophageal symptom perception.

titre: The Vicious Cycle of Sleep Disruption and Inflammaging: Mechanisms, Consequences, and Therapeutic Opportunities
resume: Aging is characterized by two interdependent hallmarks: a chronic low-grade inflammatory state known as inflammaging, and a progressive deterioration of sleep and circadian rhythms. Emerging evidence indicates that these are not merely parallel processes but are mechanistically intertwined in a self-perpetuating cycle. This review synthesizes current knowledge on how age-related sleep and circadian disturbances exacerbate inflammaging through distinct molecular and cellular pathways. We examine the nocturnal dysregulation of the immune system, focusing on innate immune hyperactivation (e.g., via NLRP3 inflammasome and TLR4 signaling), cellular senescence (SASP), adaptive immune decline (T-cell aging), and disruption of systemic pathways such as the gut-brain axis. Clinical and epidemiological data link sleep disorders, particularly obstructive sleep apnea, to elevated inflammatory markers, accelerated epigenetic aging, and cognitive decline. Conversely, inflammaging impairs circadian regulatory structures, further degrading sleep quality. Interventions targeting the sleep-immune axis, including melatonin, circadian reinforcement, senotherapeutics, and lifestyle modifications, hold promise for mitigating inflammaging. We conclude that sleep disruption is not a passive symptom but an active driver of immunological aging, and propose that targeting this axis represents a viable strategy for promoting healthy longevity.

titre: A Comprehensive Assessment of the Multifaceted Impact of Inflammatory Bowel Disease on Quality of Life: Insights From the IBD-PODCAST Study
resume: INTRODUCTION: Inflammatory Bowel Diseases (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), are chronic gastrointestinal disorders, significantly affecting patients' daily lives. The "treat-to-target" approach emphasizes the enhancement of patients' quality of life (QoL) as a therapeutic target. This analysis aims to provide an overview of IBD's impact on QoL and further explore the burden related to EIMs, stool urgency, fatigue, and work productivity. METHODS: This analysis was part of the study IBD-PODCAST descriptive cross-sectional study including 2185 CD and UC patients from 10 countries. Suboptimal disease control (SDC) based on red flags from STRIDE II recommendations was assessed. The impact of IBD on patients' QoL was assessed, and the relationships of fecal urgency, fatigue, and work productivity to QoL were examined. Comorbidities, extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs), and therapeutic approaches and their effects on QoL were also evaluated. RESULTS: 52.2% of CD patients and 44.3% of UC patients experienced SDC. Impaired QoL was present in 70% of patients with SDC, regardless of advanced treatment use. 41.3% of CD patients and 39.4% of UC patients presented impaired QoL and 30.4% of CD patients and 27.6% of UC patients presented severely impaired QoL. Symptoms and signs of inflammation were more common among those with impaired QoL. Comorbidities (CD; 37.9% and UC; 36.1%) and EIMs (CD; 18.4% and UC; 13.5%) were linked to reduced QoL. Stool urgency was reported by 43.5% of patients, exacerbating QoL concerns. Fatigue and work productivity loss had an important impact on QoL, highlighting the significant burden of IBD. CONCLUSION: This study underlined the multifaceted impact of IBD. It emphasizes the need for a holistic disease management approach that prioritizes not only clinical parameters but also patients' QoL, fatigue, stool urgency and work productivity. A multidisciplinary approach is crucial to provide comprehensive care for the chronic effects for patients living with IBD.

titre: The Barriers and Facilitators for People With Bipolar Disorder Deciding to Attend and/or Complete Cancer Screening of the Cervix, Breast and Bowel: A Qualitative Study Using Normalisation Process Theory
resume: BACKGROUND: Bipolar disorder affects 1.3 million people in the United Kingdom. People with bipolar disorder are less likely, than the general population to attend and/or complete cancer screening. AIMS: To explore the barriers and facilitators towards thinking about, and/or completing cervical, breast and colorectal screening by people with bipolar disorder. METHODS: Semi-structured interviews with 27 people living with bipolar disorder in the North-East and Cumbria (January 2023 to June 2023). Deductive thematic analysis was completed using the constructs of Normalisation Process Theory (NPT). NPT was used to ensure recommendations from the study were developed through an implementation lens. RESULTS: Participants with bipolar disorder highlighted how their mental health influenced their decision to complete cancer screening, or not. Most participants understand what screening was and why it was important to complete screening. However, they described barriers such as anxiety, forgetfulness and fear in completing screening. As well as systemic barriers such as appointments not being at a good time, unfamiliar screening locations and discomfort in waiting rooms were also specifically highlighted for cervical and breast screening. Whilst for colorectal screening, home testing kits were seen as useful, participants felt unsupported in completing the kit, and feared completing the kit wrongly. CONCLUSIONS: The identification of barriers and facilitators to cancer screening has highlighted a clear need to increase awareness and providing tailored support for people with bipolar disorder. Offering multiple screening options could further improve screening participation among the group.

titre: Digestive Disease and Incident Depressive Symptoms in Middle-Aged and Older Chinese Adults: A Longitudinal Cohort Study Examining Grip Strength and Frailty
resume: BACKGROUND: Digestive diseases and depressive symptoms often co-occur, but whether physical vulnerability explains or modifies this association remains uncertain. METHODS: We analyzed 2011, 2013, 2015, and 2018 data from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. The primary cohort included 8412 adults aged at least 45 years without baseline depressive symptoms. Digestive disease was defined by a broad self-reported physician-diagnosis item, and incident depressive symptoms by a 10-item Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale score of at least 10. Discrete-time survival models with a complementary log-log link estimated hazard ratios; missing covariates were handled using 20 imputations. Secondary landmark analyses beginning in 2013 evaluated changes in grip strength and frailty index (FI) as potential mediators. Additional analyses assessed landmark-cohort selection, frailty-index construct overlap, effect modification, and incremental prediction. RESULTS: During follow-up, 3199 participants developed depressive symptoms. In the fully adjusted model, digestive disease was associated with a 15.7% higher discrete-time hazard (hazard ratio 1.157, 95% confidence interval 1.059-1.263). In the same 3003-person physical activity-observed sample, estimates were 1.093 without and 1.092 with physical activity adjustment. The standardized indirect risk ratios were 1.000 (0.995 to 1.004) for grip strength and 1.003 (0.998-1.011) for FI. Baseline vulnerability did not clearly modify the association, and incremental prediction gains were negligible. CONCLUSIONS: Broadly defined digestive disease was associated with a small increase in incident depressive symptoms. Secondary analyses did not provide clear evidence that change in grip strength or frailty mediated this association, and exploratory interaction and prediction analyses did not add clinically meaningful information.

titre: The Relationship Between Impulsivity and Neuropsychological Profile in Multiple Sclerosis
resume: INTRODUCTION: Impulsivity is increasingly recognized as a clinically relevant behavioral feature in people with multiple sclerosis (PwMS), but its neuropsychological correlates and the possible influence of intra-individual cognitive variability (IICV), an index of fluctuation in performance across tasks or within testing sessions, remain unclear. The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between impulsivity and neuropsychological profile in PwMS and to determine whether these associations persist after accounting for IICV. METHODS: Fifty-four PwMS underwent an assessment of cognitive abilities, including the Brief Repeatable Battery of Neuropsychological Tests. Behavioral measures included the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS‑11), Beck Depression Inventory‑II (BDI-II), Dimensional Apathy Scale (DAS), and Self‑Awareness Questionnaire (SAQ). IICV indices were derived from performance across memory, executive, and attention/processing speed using maximum discrepancy and intra-individual standard deviation metrics. Spearman correlations and hierarchical regression models were used to examine relations between impulsivity and other neuropsychological measures. RESULTS: Higher non-planning impulsivity was associated with poorer processing speed (SDMT: rho = -0.430, p = 0.001) and higher apathy (DAS Total: rho = 0.546, p < 0.001). Attentional impulsivity was associated with higher interoceptive sensibility (SAQ Total: rho = 0.405, p = 0.002), apathy (DAS Total: rho = 0.442, p = 0.001; DAS Executive: rho = 0.467, p < 0.001), and depressive symptoms (BDI-II: rho = 0.570, p < 0.001). Non-planning impulsivity remained an independent predictor of SDMT performance after adjustment for attention/processing-speed IICV (β = -0.363, p = 0.004). No significant associations were found for motor impulsivity. CONCLUSIONS: In PwMS, non-planning and attentional impulsivity appear to be associated with distinct cognitive and behavioral alterations, independently of IICV. Impulsivity could represent a clinically informative marker of top-down control dysfunction and a potential target for cognitive and behavioral interventions.

titre: Physiological Arousal During Alcohol Cue Exposure in Adult Drinkers: Sex Differences in Neural and Clinical Correlates: Alcohol Cue Exposure and Arousal
resume: Cue exposure contributes to craving and reinforces alcohol misuse, potentially by altering interoceptive processing and physiological arousal. However, few studies have reported changes in physiological arousal or their neural underpinnings in response to alcohol cues. Here, we addressed these questions in 94 adult drinkers (39 females; age mean ± SD: 59.1 ± 19.1 years and range: 19-85 years) who underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging and skin conductance recording during alcohol and neutral cue exposures and completed clinical assessments including the Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test (AUDIT; mean ± SD: 4.4 ± 5.5). Imaging data were processed with published routines and evaluated at a corrected threshold. The results showed significantly higher skin conductance response in 'alcohol>neutral' blocks (SCRAl-Ne) in females than in males. However, SCRAl-Ne was positively correlated with participants' AUDIT scores in males but not in females. SCRAl-Ne was also positively correlated with global positive alcohol expectancy and novelty seeking scores in males but not in females. A voxel-wise two sample test of the contrast 'alcohol>neutral' did not show any clusters with significant sex differences in cue reactivity. Whole-brain regression of the same contrast on AUDIT scores identified a large cluster in the perigenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC), with the beta estimates showing a significant positive correlation with the SCRAl-Ne, again in males only.
