These sex differences were all confirmed by slope tests. Thus, males with more drinking problems showed higher arousal as well as the pgACC response to alcohol cues in association with alcohol expectancy and novelty seeking. In chain mediation modelling, the pgACC response and alcohol expectancy interlinked SCRAl-Ne and AUDIT scores in males. In contrast, we failed to observe any significant neural or psychological correlates of physiological arousal, despite higher SCRAl-Ne, in females. With the caveat of a smaller sample size for females, these findings highlight sex and individual differences in physiological responses to alcohol cues and the neural and psychological underpinnings in male adult drinkers. Whether or how physiological arousal may play a role in the pathophysiology of alcohol misuse remains to be investigated for females.

titre: Functional Network Organization Underlying Individual Differences in False Feedback Susceptibility: A Graph Theoretical Analysis
resume: Individual differences in susceptibility to somatosensory false physiological feedback reflect variations in interoceptive processing, yet the underlying neural network mechanisms remain unclear. We analyzed resting-state functional connectivity using graph theoretical approaches in 41 healthy adults who completed a somatosensory false feedback paradigm. Nine regions of interest were defined from previous activation analyses, and network topology metrics including local efficiency, clustering coefficient, centrality measures, and path length were calculated across multiple thresholds. Three distinct patterns of network organization predicted false feedback susceptibility. Individuals more susceptible to false feedback showed: (1) increased posterior insula eccentricity, indicating network peripheralization of this key interoceptive region; (2) consistent orbitofrontal cortex segregation across multiple metrics including increased path length and decreased centrality measures; and (3) cerebellar network reconfiguration with reduced local efficiency but increased betweenness centrality. Somatosensory false feedback susceptibility reflects specific alterations in functional network topology, particularly reduced integration of interoceptive regions (posterior insula) and emotional appraisal systems (orbitofrontal cortex). These findings support a network-based model where interoceptive processing depends on efficient integration between visceral sensation, emotional evaluation, and cognitive control systems. Understanding these network properties may inform interventions targeting interoceptive awareness and emotional regulation.

titre: Investigating Interoceptive Beliefs in Individuals With Endometriosis
resume: BACKGROUND: Research has indicated that individuals experiencing chronic pain differ in their ability to sense and interpret signals arising from inside the body, termed interoception. It is unclear whether differences in interoception exist for those with endometriosis, a common condition where pain is a major symptom. METHODS: This study aimed to investigate whether interoceptive beliefs are altered in individuals with a diagnosis of endometriosis compared to those without, and whether pain experienced by those with endometriosis predicted interoceptive beliefs. Interoceptive beliefs were assessed in 247 participants with endometriosis and 98 participants without the condition. Those with endometriosis also reported their experience of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, and chronic pelvic pain. RESULTS: Individuals with endometriosis reported that they noticed more internal signals but had reduced trust in these signals and were more worried by them. They also reported that they try to distract themselves from internal sensations more than those without endometriosis. Increased pain intensity predicted higher scores in one facet of interoceptive beliefs, such that higher levels of pain were associated with higher awareness of internal sensations in individuals with endometriosis. CONCLUSIONS: These results indicate that those with endometriosis differ in their interoceptive beliefs and that these differences may be influenced by their pain experience. Given these findings largely align with changes observed in other conditions marked by pain, it is possible that interoceptive changes may represent a transdiagnostic characteristic across individuals experiencing pain. SIGNIFICANCE: This study addresses previously conflicted findings in the literature, providing a clearer picture of the changes in interoceptive beliefs present in people with endometriosis. Developing a stronger understanding of interoceptive functioning in this unique population may lead to opportunities to develop stronger interventions targeting bodily sensations in pain management in those with the condition.

titre: Sedative Potential of L (+)-Tartaric Acid: Behavioral Evidence With In Silico Insights Into Possible GABAergic Interaction
resume: PURPOSE: Insomnia is a prevalent neurological disorder often caused by stress, anxiety, and imbalances in the GABAergic system. Although benzodiazepines like diazepam (DZP) are commonly prescribed, their long-term use is associated with adverse effects, including dependence and impaired coordination. Therefore, there is growing interest in natural alternatives with safer pharmacological profiles. METHOD: This study aimed to investigate the sedative-like potential of L (+)-tartaric acid (LTA), a naturally occurring organic acid, through both in vivo and in silico approaches targeting the γ-aminobutyric acid A (GABAA) receptor. Sedative-like activity was evaluated in Swiss albino mice using thiopental sodium-induced sleeping time, open-field, and rotarod tests. FINDINGS: LTA significantly reduced sleep latency and prolonged sleep duration in a dose-dependent manner, with the higher dose (240 mg/kg) producing a more pronounced effect. Co-administration of LTA with DZP further enhanced thiopental-induced hypnosis. In the open-field test, LTA reduced locomotor and exploratory activities, as evidenced by decreases in square crossings, rearing, and grooming behaviors. Rotarod assessment demonstrated a dose-dependent reduction in motor coordination and neuromuscular performance, although the impairment remained less pronounced than that produced by DZP at the lower tested dose. Molecular docking revealed lower binding affinity than DZP but demonstrated multiple hydrogen-bond (HB) interactions with key amino acid (AA) residues of the GABAA receptor, suggesting a potentially stable receptor interaction. CONCLUSION: Collectively, the behavioral and computational findings indicate that LTA possesses sedative-like properties and may modulate GABAergic neurotransmission. Further mechanistic, pharmacokinetic, and electrophysiological studies are required to clarify its precise mode of action and therapeutic potential.

titre: The Impact of Psychological Therapies on Well-Being and Quality of Life in Adult Chronic Migraine Patients: A Systematic Review
resume: BACKGROUND: Chronic migraine is defined as ≥ 15 headache days per month, with at least 8 days meeting the migraine criteria. It profoundly impairs quality of life and is often accompanied by comorbid insomnia and emotional distress. Despite growing interest in psychological and behavioral interventions in chronic pain, these approaches remain understudied in chronic migraine. OBJECTIVE: To systematically review the impact of psychological and behavioral interventions on quality of life and well-being in adults with chronic migraine, and to compare intervention types across a range of clinical, psychological, and functional outcomes. METHODS: A systematic search of electronic databases was conducted to identify studies evaluating psychological interventions for adults with chronic migraine. Titles and abstracts were screened, followed by full-text review against predefined eligibility criteria. Due to heterogeneity in interventions and outcomes, a narrative synthesis was undertaken. Four studies were included, examining mindfulness-based interventions and cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBTi) across outcomes for migraine disability, well-being, and frequency. RESULTS: Mindfulness-based approaches demonstrated significant reductions in headache frequency and disability, along with improved pain acceptance and mood. Intervention therapy showed rapid and marked benefits; mindfulness following medication withdrawal saw improvements in psychological well-being and migraine frequency up to 12 months post intervention; combining mindfulness with transcranial direct current simulation (tDCS) suggested additive benefits. CBTi showed significant improvements in sleep quality, with delayed but meaningful reductions in headache days. Emotional outcomes such as depressive symptoms improved modestly; anxiety was less consistently affected. CONCLUSIONS: Empirical research evaluating psychological therapies for chronic migraine with well-being and quality of life outcomes is notably limited. However, existing evidence shows promising benefits for adults with chronic migraine, improving aspects of physical, emotional, and functional well-being. Mindfulness appears particularly effective in reducing migraine burden, while CBTi addresses sleep-related pathways. These findings support integrating these modalities into holistic, patient-centered migraine care. A stepping stone into the future of migraine management which highlights the potential of psychological therapy successfully improving well-being and quality of life in migraine management.

titre: Nurse-Led Stepped Care to Reduce Fear of Falling After Hip Fracture Surgery in Older Adults: A Non-Randomized Controlled Trial Protocol
resume: AIM: To evaluate whether a nurse-led stepped care protocol reduces fear of falling (FoF) among older adults after hip fracture surgery. DESIGN: A prospective, single-centre, non-randomized controlled trial protocol. METHODS: A total of 124 older adults will be recruited by convenience sampling and allocated by ward. The intervention group will receive routine care plus a response-adaptive stepped care intervention, whereas the control group will receive routine care alone. Intervention intensity will be adjusted according to Short Falls Efficacy Scale-International (Short FES-I) scores and activity limitation. The primary outcome will be the Short FES-I score at 1 month. Secondary outcomes will include activity limitation, activities of daily living, hip function, anxiety, and depression. Short FES-I and activity limitation will also be reassessed during the inpatient stages to guide progression, while formal outcome assessments will occur at baseline and at 1 and 3 months. Statisticians will remain blinded to group allocation where feasible. Recruitment has commenced. RESULTS: Literature synthesis, expert consultation, and pilot testing were completed before the main trial and used to refine the protocol. Recruitment is underway, and no trial outcome analysis has yet been performed. CONCLUSION: The protocol integrates response-guided psychological support, rehabilitation, family involvement, and post-discharge follow-up within a nurse-led stepped care pathway. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: The pathway gives orthopaedic nurses a structured role in FoF screening, first-line intervention, reassessment, escalation decisions, multidisciplinary coordination, and post-discharge follow-up. IMPACT: This study addresses the lack of a nurse-coordinated, response-adaptive pathway for postoperative FoF and may inform staged care across inpatient and home-based rehabilitation. REPORTING METHOD: Reporting was guided by the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) and the Transparent Reporting of Evaluations with Non-randomized Designs (TREND) statements. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: Ten older adults and their family caregivers participated in pilot testing and contributed to refinement of the intervention materials and procedures. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry: ChiCTR2500107946.

titre: Psychological Care in Heart Failure Rehabilitation: A Meta-Analysis
resume: This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy of psychological therapy versus conventional therapy within cardiac rehabilitation programs for individuals with heart failure (HF). The systematic review included 19 randomised controlled trials (RCTs), including 2,196 HF patients, of whom 1,060 were assigned to standard care, and 1,136 underwent psychological interventions. This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250651620). The meta-analysis demonstrated that psychological interventions were not significantly more effective than conventional care in improving Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) scores (standardised mean difference [SMD] = 0.57, 95% CI: -0.61 to 1.75). Similarly, minimal differential effects were observed in self-care maintenance [SMD = 0.33, 95% CI: -0.03 to 0.69] and self- care confidence [SMD = 0.13, 95% CI: -0.08 to 0.35] among patients with HF. Psychological interventions demonstrated significant reductions in anxiety among HF patients versus routine care [SMD = -0.81, 95% CI: -1.52 to -0.09]. Notably, improvements were also observed in phy- sical capacity metrics (6-minute walking test: SMD = 0.35, 95% CI: 0.01-0.69) and clinical outcomes (readmission rate: OR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.14-0.56). These findings collectively indicate that patient-centred psychotherapy significantly enhances both psychological well-being and physiological recovery in HF populations. However, the timing and population of intervention are still worth discussing; for example, group or partner nursing methods may be more suitable. Key Words: Psychotherapy nursing, Heart failure, Quality of life, Physical state.
revue: Journal of the College of Physicians and Surgeons--Pakistan : JCPSP

titre: Effect of a Virtual Reality Cognitive Psychological Intervention on Depression, Sleep, and Cognition in Adolescent Patients With Depression: A Randomized Controlled Trial
resume: BACKGROUND: Depression is one of the most common mental health issues among adolescents, and its prevalence has been continuously increasing in recent years. Treatment with antidepressants imposes certain limitations. Thus, there is currently an urgent need to explore nonpharmacological therapies for depression among adolescents. OBJECTIVE: The goal of this study was to explore the effects of a virtual reality (VR) cognitive psychological intervention (CPI) on reducing levels of depression and improving sleep and cognitive function in adolescents with depression. METHODS: A randomized controlled trial design was used to select 132 adolescent patients with depression (12 to 18 years of age) hospitalized in a child mental health center at a tertiary hospital in Chengdu, Sichuan Province, China, from March 2024 to July 2024. They were randomly divided into an experimental and a control group with 66 patients per group. The experimental group received usual care (UC) combined with VR-CPI for 7 days, whereas the control group only received UC. Assessments were conducted before and after the intervention using the Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Independent samples t tests were performed to analyze differences in SDS, ISI, and MoCA scores between the 2 groups before and after the intervention. RESULTS: A total of 112 patients completed the trial (experimental group: 53, control group: 59). After the intervention, the experimental group exhibited improvements in SDS (57.42±13.299), ISI (9.08±6.354), and MoCA (28.25±1.980) scores compared with the control group (SDS: 66.93±15.209, ISI: 12.20±7.418, MoCA: 26.34±3.497); all differences were statistically significant (P<0.05). For depression, the experimental group displayed significant improvements compared with the control group in emotional (experimental group: 12.19±4.292, control group: 14.71±5.401, P=0.008), somatic (experimental group: 11.57±3.320, control group: 14.08±4.178, P<0.001), and depressive psychological symptoms (experimental group: 16.55±4.709, control group: 19.12±4.047, P=0.002). For cognition, the experimental group performed significantly better than did the control group in delayed recall (experimental group: 4.79±0.532, control group: 4.15±1.142, P<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: VR-CPI combined with UC exerted a significant improvement effect on levels of depression, sleep quality, and cognitive ability of adolescent patients with depression.This study was registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500097234).

titre: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for Children, Adolescents, and Young Adults With Cancer and Their Parents and for Children, Adolescents, and Young Adults Affected by Parental Cancer: A Population-Stratified Systematic Review
resume: OBJECTIVE: Cancer profoundly affects the entire family system; evidence for acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) remains fragmented within three distinct cohorts: (1) children, adolescents, and young adults (CAYAs) with cancer or cancer survivors, (2) CAYAs impacted by parental cancer, and (3) parents of CAYAs with cancer. This population-stratified systematic review evaluated ACT's acceptability, feasibility, and efficacy. METHODS: Adhering to Preferred Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, 12 databases (including MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Embase) and gray literature were searched from inception to October 2025. Quantitative studies evaluating ACT-based interventions were included. Two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using JBI tools and the Risk of Bias in N-of-1 Trials (RoBiNT) Scale. Data were synthesized narratively by outcome within population strata following synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM), with effectiveness appraised for certainty of evidence using GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation). RESULTS: Nine studies (N = 573) were included (one RCT, one single case experimental design [SCED], four quasi-experimental trials, and three single-group pilot/feasibility studies). No studies targeted children. For AYA populations (both with cancer or cancer survivors and affected by parental cancer), evidence was of very low certainty; psychological flexibility emerged as a plausible mediator of quality-of-life improvements in a single mixed sample study of distressed AYAs affected by their own or a family member's cancer. Moderate-certainty evidence for parents of CAYAs with cancer showed reductions in distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms (d = 0.61-0.83), and increased psychological flexibility (d = 0.63). CONCLUSIONS: ACT shows promise for improving mental health outcomes in parents of CAYAs with cancer. Evidence for both AYAs populations remains limited by methodological heterogeneity, highlighting a need for developmentally tailored, rigorous trials.

titre: The Effectiveness of Non-surgical Interventions for Managing Chronic Low Back Pain
resume: INTRODUCTION: Chronic low back pain (CLBP) is a widespread condition with a substantial effect on quality of life and work capacity. Non-drug, non-surgical options - physical therapy (PT), cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), and acupuncture - appear promising, yet stronger empirical evidence is still needed to confirm their value. OBJECTIVES: This study set out to compare PT, CBT, and acupuncture against standard care for the management of CLBP. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Two hundred participants with a diagnosis of CLBP took part in a randomized controlled trial and were allocated to one of four arms - PT, CBT, acupuncture, or standard-care control. Pain intensity, functional disability, quality of life, and psychological well-being were recorded at baseline and again at 6 and 12 weeks, using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), 36-item short form survey (SF-36), and beck depression inventory (BDI), respectively; outcomes were compared using analysis of variance with post hoc testing. RESULTS: All three active arms outperformed the control. Both PT and acupuncture produced marked reductions in pain (VAS) and disability (ODI) scores (P < 0.01), whereas CBT produced its largest gains in psychological well-being (BDI) (P < 0.01) alongside more modest gains in pain and disability. SF-36 scores rose across every domain in the treatment arms, with PT and acupuncture producing the strongest gains in the physical-functioning and pain domains (P < 0.01). CONCLUSION: PT, CBT, and acupuncture each represent a viable non-surgical option for CLBP, delivering meaningful gains in pain, function, and psychological well-being. Incorporating them into routine care could support a more holistic model of CLBP management, improving outcomes while lowering dependence on drug-based treatment.

titre: Effectiveness of a mindfulness-based cognitive behavioral program on glycemic control and quality of life among adults with diabetes in Damascus, Syria: a randomized controlled trial
resume: AIMS: Depression and diabetes distress worsen glycemic control and quality of life (QoL). This randomized controlled trial evaluated a 14-week mindfulness-based cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) program on Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) and QoL among adults with diabetes in Damascus, Syria. METHODS: Adults with diabetes and mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms were randomized to mindfulness-based CBT or routine care. Per-protocol analysis included 40 completers (n = 20/group). Post-intervention HbA1c was evaluated using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) adjusting for baseline levels. Secondary QoL was assessed across four WHOQOL-BREF domains. RESULTS: Intervention participants achieved significant reduction in HbA1c levels (9.0 ± 1.7% to 7.2 ± 1.4%, p = 0.021), while controls experienced an increase in HbA1c levels (9.1 ± 1.8% to 9.9 ± 1.7%, p < 0.001). ANCOVA demonstrated a significant intervention effect (F (1,37) = 13.53, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.268). Adjusted post-intervention HbA1c was lower in the intervention group (7.48% vs. 9.34%; adjusted mean difference: -1.86%, 95% CI: -2.89 to -0.84, p < 0.001). All WHOQOL-BREF domains improved significantly within the intervention arm (all p ≤ 0.001), with consistent glycemic benefits across subgroups. CONCLUSIONS: Mindfulness-based CBT produced clinically meaningful glycemic and QoL improvements, supporting psychosocial care integration into routine diabetes management in crisis-affected settings. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT07779044.

titre: Hidden Disease Burden of Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Clinical Value of Adaptive Eating Behaviors, Psychological Comorbidities and Quality of Life
resume: Summary of disease burden contributors in eosinophilic esophagitis that are not routinely captured by conventional endpoints and the proposed algorithm and instruments to assess them. ABSTRACT Background Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic type 2-mediated inflammatory disease of the esophagus with growing incidence and prevalence. Current therapeutic targets rely on histology, endoscopy and patient-reported symptoms, but these domains frequently show only modest agreement, and conventional endpoints do not fully capture the burden of disease. Purpose This review summarizes current evidence on disease burden contributors in EoE that are not routinely captured by conventional endpoints, and on the instruments available to assess them. Adaptive eating behaviors, such as drinking liquids to facilitate bolus transit, prolonged chewing, and food modification, represent a standalone domain in EoE and can now be assessed with the Pisa Eosinophilic Esophagitis Adaptation Questionnaire. Esophageal hypervigilance and symptom-specific anxiety, measured with the Esophageal Hypervigilance and Anxiety Scale, influence symptom reporting and health-related quality of life, while anxiety, depression, stigma, and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder add to the psychological burden. Quality of life is better captured by disease-specific than by generic instruments and may improve with effective medical therapy. Quality of life assessments may better detect the negative effects of dietary restrictions on emotional and social well-being. In the present review, we also propose a practical stepwise approach to patients with persistent symptoms despite endoscopic and histological remission. A multidimensional assessment integrating objective disease activity with symptoms, adaptive behaviors, psychological factors, and quality of life may provide a more comprehensive representation of the burden of EoE and of the response to treatment.

titre: Factor Structure of the Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale-II Self Report Symptom Checklist Among Trauma Survivors
resume: The Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale-II Self Report Symptom Checklist (Y-BOCS-II-SR-SC) offers a structured assessment of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) symptoms. A previous evaluation of the Y-BOCS-II-SR-SC suggested the existence of 4 factors: Symmetry/Order, Contamination/Washing, Hoarding, and Sexual/Religious/Aggression symptoms. However, existing factor analytic work has not considered the influence of trauma exposure despite its established impact on the presence, presentation, and function of obsessions and compulsions. Trauma-exposed individuals with OCD (N=258) were recruited to complete the Y-BOCS-II-SR-SC, which was subsequently subjected to descriptive and factor analyses. Contrary to previous research, the present study found strong support for a 3-factor model comprising Saving, Exactness/Prevention, and Cleaning symptoms, evidencing adequate-to-strong internal consistency. Exactness/Prevention symptoms were endorsed by nearly the entire sample (91%), followed by Cleaning (65%) and, lastly, Saving symptoms (36%). Factor analysis in a trauma-exposed sample can provide insight into the clustering, presentation, and underlying function of OCD symptoms that may be related to trauma. Although continued research is needed, findings contribute to a small but growing body of literature supporting the connection between symmetry/exactness and harm prevention symptoms among trauma survivors with OCD.

titre: Reduced Coupling Between Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent Signal and Cerebrospinal Fluid Flow in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
resume: AIMS: Mounting evidence implicates inflammation in the pathogenesis of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Given the interaction between inflammation and the glymphatic system, we aimed to investigate whether altered glymphatic function is present in patients with OCD. METHODS: We assessed glymphatic-related CSF dynamics using resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) in 53 patients with OCD and 74 healthy controls. We measured global coupling between cortical blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal and ventricular cerebrospinal fluid flow, along with the time lags. Given that the goal-directed and habitual learning framework has become a dominant neurobiological model for understanding the development and maintenance of obsessive-compulsive symptoms, we also examined regional couplings and lags within the goal-directed and habitual learning networks. RESULTS: Patients with OCD exhibited weaker BOLD-CSF coupling and negative derivative BOLD-CSF coupling strength than HC, both globally and regionally within the goal-directed and habitual systems. OCD patients also showed a longer time lag of global BOLD-CSF coupling. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that altered glymphatic-associated CSF dynamics are present in OCD, offering critical new insights into the underlying mechanisms of the disorder.

titre: [More than anorexia: The spectrum of eating disorders in primary care]
Developmental subgroups and co-occurring conditions among 5817 minimally speaking autistic youth: a latent class analysis of the SPARK cohort
resume: BACKGROUND: Approximately 30% of autistic children remain minimally speaking beyond kindergarten, using few or no spoken words. Although often studied as a single group, these children show a wide range of social, motor, and nonverbal cognitive abilities. Few studies have systematically examined this heterogeneity. Characterizing minimally speaking autistic subgroups is an important first step toward understanding the genetic and neurobiological mechanisms underlying different spoken language outcomes in autism. METHODS: To fill this gap, we conducted a cross-sectional study of 5817 minimally speaking autistic youth aged 5-17 years (76.8% male) who participated in the Simons Powering Autism Research for Knowledge national study. We estimated latent class models separately for children (5-11 years, n = 4682) and adolescents (12-17 years, n = 1135) using four indicators: everyday spoken language level, social interaction difficulty, number of delayed early motor milestones, and nonverbal cognitive ability. We compared classes on sociodemographic characteristics, co-occurring conditions, and total interventions received using chi-square, Fisher exact, and Welch tests with false discovery rate correction. RESULTS: We identified three child subgroups and two adolescent subgroups, ranging from lower to higher skills across all four domains. Strengths in one domain generally accompanied strengths in others. Within subgroups, early motor development was a relative strength in lower-skill groups and social interaction in higher-skill groups. Among children, lower-skill subgroups had a higher prevalence of atypical head growth, seizures or epilepsy, obsessive-compulsive disorder, sleep disorders, and feeding or eating disorders (sleep disorder, higher- vs intermediate-skill child subgroup: odds ratio 0.54, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.46-0.63) and also received more interventions (lower- vs higher-skill child subgroup: 1.9 more, 95% CI 1.7-2.2). LIMITATIONS: All latent class indicators were derived from caregiver-report questionnaires, which may be subject to recall bias. Although our results show high split-half agreement of class assignments, they still need to be replicated in an independent cohort of autistic children. CONCLUSIONS: Minimally speaking autistic youth show clinically meaningful heterogeneity in their developmental characteristics, co-occurring conditions, and service use. Future studies should examine the extent to which underlying genetic etiologies contribute to these subgroup differences.

titre: Brain Connectivity and Clinical Heterogeneity in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
revue: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging

titre: Cognitive Cerebellum Structure and Functional Connectivity in Relation to Executive Functions in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
resume: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) has been primarily linked to abnormalities within the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit; however, recent evidence suggests that the posterior cerebellum may contribute to the executive dysfunction observed in the disorder. In 56 adults (28 OCD, 28 controls), we assessed executive functions using the BANFE-2 battery and integrated structural MRI (T1) and resting-state fMRI. Although the Global Executive Index did not differ significantly between groups, patients with OCD showed significantly lower scores in the inhibitory control/decision-making domain relative to controls. We quantified cortical thickness and volume (% intracranial volume) in Crus I/II and lobule VI using CERES and examined resting-state functional connectivity (seed-to-voxel) in CONN, adjusting for age, sex, medication, and depression. Compared with controls, patients with OCD showed reduced bilateral cortical thickness in Crus I/II and lobule VI (false discovery rate-corrected q < 0.05; β_OCD - Control = -0.27 to -0.59; ηp2 = 0.34-0.55), with no significant volumetric differences after correction for multiple comparisons. Functional connectivity results revealed a mixed pattern, including focal hyperconnectivity (e.g., left Crus I with primary auditory cortex; left Crus II with occipital cortex) and widespread intracerebellar hypoconnectivity. In addition, significant Group × executive-function interactions (p-family-wise error < 0.05) emerged mainly for bilateral Crus I (Global Executive Index and working memory/flexibility) and left lobule VI (inhibition/decision-making), indicating that the relationship between cerebellar connectivity and executive performance differs in OCD relative to controls. These findings support an expanded model of executive circuits in OCD that incorporates the posterior cerebellum as a relevant node.

titre: Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction in Juvenile Fibromyalgia Syndrome: Prevalence, Clinical Characteristics, and Management in a Single-Center Cohort Study
resume: Objective Patients with juvenile fibromyalgia syndrome (JFS) often report gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms. Disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI) are common in adult fibromyalgia, but data in JFS are limited. We evaluated the prevalence and clinical impact of DGBI in JFS and explored their association with disease severity. Methods This observational study included patients with JFS followed at the Gaslini Institute between March 2024 and October 2025. At each visit, the Widespread Pain Index (WPI) and JFS-related symptoms (fatigue, headache, morning tiredness, and neuropsychiatric features) were assessed using self-reported measures. Patients completed a questionnaire for GI symptoms at each visit, and DGBI diagnoses were established by a pediatric gastroenterologist according to the Rome IV criteria. Results Sixty-three patients (55 female, 87%; mean age at enrollment 16.9 [SD 2.6] years) were included, and 219 questionnaires were collected. Forty-eight patients (76%) had ≥ 1 DGBI, which included functional dyspepsia (63%), irritable bowel syndrome (38%), and functional constipation (15%). Thirty-eight percent of patients with JFS reported limitations in daily activities due to GI symptoms. BMI (kg/m 2 ) was significantly lower in patients with DGBI (BMI Z -score 0.0 [IQR -0.6 to 1.8] vs 2.1 [IQR 0.7 to 3.3]; P = 0.01). In multivariate analysis, a higher WPI was independently associated with DGBI (odds ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.03-1.37; P = 0.02). Conclusion DGBI are very common in JFS and may significantly affect patients' functional capacity. Their presence is associated with more severe and widespread musculoskeletal pain, underscoring the importance of a multidisciplinary approach in the management of JFS.

titre: Validation of Rome V for irritable bowel syndrome
Validation of Rome V for irritable bowel syndrome - Authors' reply
Endocannabinoid system modulators for abdominal pain in irritable bowel syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease: A systematic review of efficacy and safety
resume: Aim: To systematically review the benefits and harms of cannabis, cannabinoids, cannabis-based medicines, and other pharmacological endocannabinoid system (ECS) modulators for visceral abdominal pain in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) or irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Methods: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ECS modulators with placebo or other interventions in IBD or IBS. We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE, WHO ICTRP and ClinicalTrials.gov (29/07/2025). Primary outcomes: proportions of participants with ≥30% and ≥50% reductions in pain intensity. Secondary outcomes: change in pain, physical or emotional functioning, quality of life, gastrointestinal health, and adverse events. We assessed risk of bias using Cochrane RoB-2 and certainty using GRADE. We synthesised findings narratively; due to insufficiently comparable data, meta-analysis was not possible. (PROSPERO: CRD42025616728). Results: We included 14 studies (796 participants). One study reported our primary outcome while all reported at least one secondary outcome. Palmitoylethanolamide + polydatin improved pain, symptom severity (moderate certainty) and emotional and physical functioning (low certainty) in IBS. THC and CBD showed benefits across pain, quality of life, emotional and physical functioning, and disease activity in IBD (low to very low certainty). Adverse events were predominantly mild-to-moderate; severe neurologic events were reported for CBD-dominant botanical extract. Risk of bias ranged from low to high. Conclusion: Evidence for ECS modulators in IBS or IBD visceral abdominal pain is heterogeneous with very low to moderate certainty, limiting conclusions regarding efficacy and safety. Larger, well-designed RCTs using clinically relevant pain outcomes are needed to inform therapeutic development.

titre: Twenty-Four Month Clinical and Laboratory Follow-Up of Children Infected During a Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli Outbreak
resume: Background Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) infections can cause significant long-term renal sequelae. Intermediate-term outcomes for patients who do not develop hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) remain unclear. We evaluated clinical and laboratory outcomes in children with laboratory-confirmed STEC O157 infection in a large childcare outbreak. Methods This prospective longitudinal cohort study enrolled children aged 9 months to Results Of 932 eligible children, 145 (16%) participated: 72 cases (4 asymptomatic, 59 mild-moderate infection, 9 HUS) and 73 controls. Median age was 3.3 (IQR: 2.3, 4.2) years. Functional gastrointestinal disorders occurred at similar rates across groups, except for functional dyspepsia which was more common among STEC-infected children at 6-month follow-up (unadjusted P=0.03). At 24 months, median estimated glomerular filtration rates were similar across groups. After adjustment for multiple comparisons, no laboratory parameters or clinical outcomes differed between groups at any timepoint. One of 9 (11%) children with HUS had proteinuria and hematuria at 24 months. Conclusions Among children with STEC infection without HUS, we did not detect differences in clinical symptoms or laboratory abnormalities during 24-month follow-up compared with controls, providing reassurance regarding intermediate-term outcomes.
revue: Journal of the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society

titre: [Curcumin in children with autism spectrum disorder: systemic inflammation, sensory regulation, and gut-brain interaction disorders. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial (CURATEA)]
resume: Introduction Introduction: low-grade neuroinflammation and gut-brain axis dysfunction are key mechanisms involved in the pathophysiology of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Curcumin, a polyphenol derived from Curcuma longa, exhibits anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and neuroimmunomodulatory properties that may offer therapeutic benefits in this population. Objectives: to evaluate the effects of curcumin supplementation on systemic inflammation, sensory processing regulation, and gut-brain interaction disorders in children with ASD. Methods: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial was conducted in 60 children with ASD over eight weeks. Participants received either curcumin (3,000 mg/day) or placebo. Primary outcomes included high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and fecal calprotectin. Secondary outcomes included the General Index of Sensory Processing Regulation Dysfunction (IGDRPS) and Rome IV criteria for gut-brain interaction disorders. Results: the curcumin group showed significant reductions in hs-CRP (-83.8 %), ESR (-42.3 %), and fecal calprotectin (-73.7 %), along with a 49 % improvement in IGDRPS and complete resolution of gastrointestinal symptoms in 90 % of participants (p < 0.001). No adverse effects were observed. Conclusions: curcumin supplementation reduces systemic and intestinal inflammation, improves sensory regulation, and alleviates functional gastrointestinal disorders in children with ASD, supporting its role as a safe, cost-effective adjunctive intervention within an integrative therapeutic approach.

titre: Fecal Microbiota Transplantation: A Promising Therapeutic Strategy Targeting the Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis in Anorexia Nervosa
resume: Purpose Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a complex psychiatric disorder characterized by self-starvation, body-image disturbance, and serious medical complications. Because current treatments have variable outcomes and relapse is common, the microbiota-gut-brain axis has been investigated as a possible contributor to disease persistence. This review evaluates fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) as an experimental microbiota-directed strategy for AN. Methods PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched for relevant studies published from January 1990 to October 2025. Eligible evidence included human reports, animal studies, and mechanistic studies examining FMT or gut-microbiota alterations in AN and related pathways. Findings Individuals with AN have been reported to show altered microbial diversity and changes in taxa associated with short-chain fatty acid production and inflammation. These findings are heterogeneous and may reflect starvation, diet, medication exposure, or illness-related physiology. Human evidence for FMT in AN is limited to small, uncontrolled studies and case reports, while most mechanistic support comes from animal models or indirect evidence from other conditions. Conclusion Evidence for FMT in AN remains preliminary and is largely based on uncontrolled human observations and preclinical studies. FMT may alter gut microbial composition and gastrointestinal or metabolic measures, but controlled efficacy data are absent and psychiatric benefits remain unconfirmed. Well-designed controlled trials are needed to establish its safety and clinical efficacy.

titre: Retraction of: Unravelling the neuroimmune nexus: insights into epilepsy pathology and the role of S100b protein in brain-gut axis modulation: a literature review
Global research landscape on the brain-gut axis in early life: a bibliometric and visualized study
resume: Introduction Background: the brain-gut axis was recognized as a bidirectional communication system linking the central and enteric nervous systems through neural, hormonal, immune, and metabolic pathways. It played a pivotal role in early-life neurodevelopment, immune programming, and gastrointestinal function. Although the field had grown rapidly, a comprehensive bibliometric evaluation of global research trends, hotspots, and collaborations was lacking. Methods: we conducted a bibliometric and visualized analysis of publications on the brain-gut axis in early life from 2004 to 2024, using the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) database. CiteSpace was used to generate co-authorship, institutional collaboration, keyword co-occurrence, and co-citation networks, as well as burst detection, timeline views, and dual-map overlays. Results: a total of 1,429 publications were analyzed. Research output increased steadily from 2015 and peaked in 2023, reflecting growing global interest. The United States and China were the most productive countries, with strong collaborative ties observed among institutions in North America, Europe, and East Asia. University College Cork, University of California System, and Harvard University were the leading institutions, while J. F. Cryan, T. G. Dinan, and G. Clarke were the most influential authors. Early studies focused on anatomical and developmental aspects, while recent hotspots included autism spectrum disorder, intestinal permeability, fecal microbiota transplantation, and psychological stress. Mechanistic keywords highlighted short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolism, vagus nerve signaling, and microglia-immune interactions. Conclusions: this study provided a comprehensive bibliometric overview of early-life brain-gut axis research over the past two decades. It revealed dynamic thematic evolution, expanding interdisciplinary collaboration, and the emergence of translational opportunities. These findings offer a valuable reference for future research directions in pediatric neurogastroenterology and microbiota-based interventions.

titre: Icariin against neuroinflammation: emerging evidence for gut-brain axis modulation involving short-chain fatty acids, vagal signaling, and extracellular vesicles
resume: Neuroinflammation is a central pathological process in a wide range of central nervous system disorders, yet therapeutic strategies directed solely at single inflammatory targets have shown limited efficacy. Gut-brain axis dysfunction may contribute to neuroinflammatory progression through interconnected metabolic, immune, neural, and vesicle-associated routes. Icariin, a major flavonoid glycoside from Epimedii Folium, has attracted attention because of its anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective, and microbiota-modulating properties. In this review, we summarize current evidence for the anti-neuroinflammatory effects of icariin and explicitly stratify the evidence into three levels: direct icariin-related findings, icariin-related findings without causal gut-brain validation, and mechanisms inferred from broader gut-brain axis biology. Available studies provide relatively stronger support for intestinal barrier protection, microbiota remodeling, peripheral cytokine suppression, and central inflammatory pathway regulation. In contrast, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-associated signaling, vagal neuroimmune communication, and extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated cargo transfer remain plausible but incompletely validated candidate routes. We further compare icariin with its major microbial metabolites, especially icariside II and icaritin, because oral icariin may act partly through metabolite-mediated exposure rather than through robust brain penetration of the parent compound. Major limitations include insufficient causal perturbation, incomplete organ-specific pharmacokinetic data, inter-individual microbiota variability, and uncertain therapeutic time windows. Overall, icariin emerges as a promising multi-target natural product for anti-neuroinflammatory research, but the causal hierarchy and translational relevance of proposed gut-brain pathways require direct validation.

titre: Iron Boride Nanostructures as Oral Acid-Responsive Hydrogen Donors for Alzheimer's Disease Therapy
resume: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative condition with complex causes. Despite extensive research, effective disease-modifying treatment options remain limited. Recent studies have indicated that hydrogen molecule (H2) possesses therapeutic potential for AD, and it is of vital importance to enhance the bioavailability of H2 in the gastrointestinal tract based on the gut-brain axis. In this work, we develop iron boride nanostructures (FBN) as a novel acid-responsive hydrogen-releasing material with a high hydrogen release capacity to enhance the H2 delivery efficacy towards the gastrointestinal tract for AD treatment. In male 5×FAD and 3×Tg-AD mice, oral FBN administration generated H2 under gastric conditions and was associated with AD-like behavioral and pathological improvements, including improved learning and memory and attenuation of neuronal and synaptic damage. FBN treatment was associated with increased synaptophysin (SYP) expression and dendritic spine density. Additionally, FBN treatment was associated with reduced amyloid-beta (Aβ) accumulation and attenuated tau pathology, two key pathological features of AD. FBN treatment was also associated with increased expression of mitochondrial fusion-related proteins and improved mitochondrial morphology. Furthermore, FBN treatment increased antioxidant defense-related proteins and reduced apoptosis-related markers, suggesting a possible enhancement of neuroprotective responses. In addition, FBN treatment induced changes in gut microbiota-related metabolites, suggesting a possible contribution of the gut-brain axis. These findings provide valuable insight into the mechanisms underlying the protective effects of hydrogen against AD and support the development of hydrogen-based therapies for slowing or preventing disease progression.

titre: Morinda Officinalis Oligosaccharides Alleviate Post-Stroke Depression-Like Behaviors Alongside Increased Gut Microbial Diversity and Butyrate Levels and Reduced Hippocampal Pla2g4a Expression
resume: Background and purpose Post-stroke depression (PSD) represents a common and debilitating complication after cerebral ischemia, yet mechanism-based therapies remain an urgent unmet need. The microbiota-gut-brain axis has been implicated in PSD pathophysiology, but the precise molecular pathways are largely elusive. Morinda officinalis oligosaccharides (MOO), a clinically approved antidepressant in China, exhibit poor oral absorption, raising the possibility of a gut-dependent mechanism. Experimental approach Male C57BL/6J mice were subjected to transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) followed by 21 days of chronic restraint stress (CRS) to establish a PSD model. MOO (50 mg/kg/day) was administered via gavage from Day 7 to 27. Depression-like behaviors, 16S rRNA-based gut microbiota profiling, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) quantification, intestinal and blood-brain barrier integrity assessments, and hippocampal proteomics were performed. The transferability of MOO-associated fecal effects was assessed using a donor-controlled fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) design. The butyrate-Pla2g4a relationship was further examined by sodium butyrate supplementation and AAV-mediated hippocampal Pla2g4a overexpression. Key results MOO administration altered gut microbial composition, increased the abundance of probiotics and decreased the abundance of harmful bacteria, and was accompanied by increased fecal butyrate levels. The donor-controlled FMT experiment provided preliminary evidence that fecally transferable factors from MOO-treated PSD donors may contribute to behavioral improvements in PSD recipients. MOO and sodium butyrate treatment were associated with improved indices of intestinal and blood-brain barrier integrity. Hippocampal proteomics identified Pla2g4a, a phospholipase linked to neuroinflammation, as a candidate molecule related to the observed effects. Both MOO and sodium butyrate treatment were associated with reduced hippocampal Pla2g4a expression, and Pla2g4a expression was inversely correlated with butyrate levels. Hippocampal Pla2g4a overexpression attenuated the behavioral improvements associated with sodium butyrate treatment, supporting the functional involvement of Pla2g4a in the response to sodium butyrate. Conclusions and implications MOO treatment was associated with improved depression-like behaviors in PSD mice, accompanied by gut microbial alterations, increased fecal butyrate, improved barrier integrity, and reduced hippocampal Pla2g4a expression. FMT findings provided preliminary evidence that fecally transferable factors from MOO-treated donors may contribute to behavioral improvements, while Pla2g4a overexpression attenuated the behavioral effects of sodium butyrate. These findings highlight a potential association among MOO, gut-derived butyrate, barrier integrity, and hippocampal Pla2g4a in PSD.

titre: C. butyricum Combined With Resmetirom Provides Therapeutic Benefits in MASH Associated With Gut-Liver-Brain Axis Modulation
resume: Background and aims Resmetirom has emerged as a major advance in MASH pharmacotherapy as the first approved liver-targeted THR-β agonist; however, variable therapeutic efficacy and adverse responses may limit its clinical benefits. This study investigated whether C. butyricum could provide additional therapeutic benefits when combined with resmetirom and attenuate nausea/vomiting-like responses in association with changes across the gut-liver-brain axis. Methods In this study, we established a high-fat diet-induced MASH mouse model and administered C. butyricum, resmetirom, or their combination. Comprehensive biochemical, histological, molecular, 16S rRNA sequencing-based microbiome profiling, and gut-brain axis-related analyses were performed to evaluate the effects of combination therapy on hepatic metabolism, inflammation, fibrosis, intestinal barrier integrity, gut microbiota remodelling, microbial metabolites, and resmetirom-associated adverse responses. Results Combined treatment with C. butyricum and resmetirom produced additional therapeutic benefits compared with either monotherapy, markedly improving hepatic steatosis, lipid accumulation, insulin resistance, inflammation, oxidative stress, and fibrosis in MASH mice. At the molecular level, combination treatment was associated with increased hepatic THR-β expression and coordinated changes in AMPK-related lipid metabolism, NRF2/HO-1 antioxidant, and TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB inflammatory markers. Furthermore, combination therapy restored intestinal barrier integrity, alleviated MASH-associated gut microbial dysbiosis, increased beneficial bacterial taxa, and increased faecal butyrate levels. Notably, C. butyricum attenuated resmetirom-induced nausea/vomiting-like responses, accompanied by reduced colonic and cerebral 5-HT/SP signalling, decreased brain Htr3a and Tacr1 mRNA expression, and suppressed neuronal FOS activation. Faecal butyrate levels were inversely associated with hepatic lipid burden and brain 5-HT/SP levels. Conclusions C. butyricum combined with resmetirom provides additional therapeutic benefits and attenuates nausea/vomiting-like responses in MASH, accompanied by coordinated changes across the gut-liver-brain axis. This combination strategy provides a potential microbiota-based adjunctive approach for optimizing the therapeutic benefits of resmetirom in MASH.
revue: Liver international : official journal of the International Association for the Study of the Liver

titre: Pain-Related Outcome Domains and Measures in Randomized Controlled Trials of Treatment for Acute Abdominal Pain: A Systematic Review
resume: Background and objectives Acute abdominal pain frequently presents to emergency departments, yet outcome domains in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) remain poorly characterized. This review identified pain-related domains and outcome measures used in RCTs on acute abdominal pain. Databases and data treatment This PRISMA-guided systematic review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42025630171). PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for RCTs (January 2000-February 2025). Eligible studies included adult and paediatric patients with acute abdominal pain reporting pain assessment. Outcome domains extracted included pain intensity, rescue analgesia, adverse effects, pain interference, quality of life (QoL), and psychological function. Bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB2. Results Of 826 records, 43 RCTs were included; eight included children. In adult trials, pain intensity was assessed using the visual analogue scale (n = 19) or the numeric rating scale (n = 15). Rescue analgesia (44%) and adverse effects (84%) were frequently reported. No study assessed pain interference or psychological function, and QoL was listed as an outcome in one trial. All were conducted in emergency settings, with short-term follow-up within the first hours. Conclusions Pain assessment in acute abdominal pain RCTs is predominantly limited to intensity measures and short-term outcomes. While appropriate for immediate analgesic effects, this approach may be insufficient when broader treatment goals or longer follow-up are relevant. Context-specific outcome selection is needed, aligning domains with clinical purpose and time frame. Significance RCTs on acute abdominal pain assess pain incompletely, focusing predominantly on intensity rather than broader domains such as pain interference and psychological function. None adhered to the INTEGRATE framework for pain assessment. This review provides the first systematic mapping of outcome domains in this area, offering a foundation for context-specific outcome selection aligned with what matters to patients.

titre: Corni Fructus water extract relieves depressive behaviors by reducing oxidative stress and neuroinflammation as well as modulating gut microbiota
resume: Background Depression is a global public health concern with limited therapies. Traditional Chinese medicines are attractive for safety and multi-target actions. Corni Fructus water extract (CFWE) is a candidate, but its mechanisms and the main active ingredients remain unclear. Methods A chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mouse model was established and given CFWE intervention. Depressive-like behaviors were evaluated by sucrose preference test (SPT), tail suspension test (TST), and open field test (OFT). Hippocampal histopathology was examined using H&E staining. Inflammatory and oxidative stress-related factors in the hippocampus and serum were detected using ELISA kits. RT-qPCR and Western blot measured Nrf2/HO-1 and IκBα/NF-κB pathway components. Gut microbiota and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing and GC-MS. LC-MS determined the major chemical constituents of CFWE. Results CFWE significantly alleviated CUMS-induced depressive-like phenotypes, including preserved body weight, reduced immobility time in TST, increased sucrose preference, and greater central distance in OFT (P Conclusion The antidepressant-like effects of CFWE might involve activation of the Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant pathway, suppression of the IκBα/NF-κB inflammatory response, and modulation of gut microbiota composition and SCFA metabolism, while PYY might serve as a candidate mediator in gut-brain communication.

titre: Immunomodulatory Probiotics in Psoriasis: Effects on the Gut-Skin-Immune Crosstalk and Systemic Inflammation: Immunomodulatory Probiotics and Psoriasis Disease
resume: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by dysregulated immune responses and excessive keratinocyte proliferation, with substantial effects on patients' quality of life. Evidence suggests that the gut microbiota and the gut-skin-immune axis may contribute to systemic inflammation and immune dysregulation associated with psoriasis. This narrative review examines the potential immunomodulatory role of probiotics in psoriasis, with particular emphasis on strain-specific biological effects and the mechanisms linking intestinal microbial modulation to psoriasis-related inflammation. Probiotics may influence intestinal microbial composition, epithelial barrier integrity, microbial metabolite production, and immune signaling. Clinical studies have reported potential improvements in psoriasis severity, inflammatory biomarkers, or quality of life following probiotic supplementation; however, the available evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, with substantial variation in probiotic strains, formulations, doses, treatment durations, concomitant therapies, and clinical outcomes. Unlike previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses that primarily summarize clinical outcomes, this review integrates clinical findings with strain-specific mechanistic and experimental evidence to provide a biologically contextualized interpretation of the potential role of probiotics in psoriasis.

titre: Associations between testosterone levels in men at age 31 and quality of life, self-reported health, and morbidity at age 46: the Northern Finland birth cohort 1966
resume: Objective We investigated self-reported health status, comorbidity, and quality of life (QoL) in men at age 46 across testosterone (T) quartiles at age 31 and evaluated whether differences existed between these quartiles. Design and methods The study population was a population-based cohort comprising men born in Northern Finland in 1966. T concentrations were measured at age 31 (n = 2,691) and categorized into quartiles: Q1 Results Men in Q1 were more obese, less likely to smoke, and consumed less alcohol compared with men in Q4 (P Conclusion The overall QoL was excellent across all T quartiles. In this study population, T levels in adulthood seem not to be associated with notable differences in self-reported health, comorbidity, or quality of life in middle age, especially when adjusted for WC. Significance statement This topic is clinically significant because studies have shown that T levels have declined over the past several decades, even among healthy men. Clinicians should, therefore, be aware of the potential impact of low testosterone on men's mental health, sexual function, and overall quality of life.

titre: The Integrative Mechanism of Xiaoyaosan Through Liver-Brain Crosstalk in the Treatment of Depression Combined with MASLD
resume: Depression and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) frequently co-occur, and their bidirectional pathological interactions complicate clinical management. Liver-brain crosstalk provides a systematic framework for understanding these multi-organ connections. Xiaoyaosan (XYS), a classical formula for soothing the liver and relieving depression, has been investigated for its therapeutic potential in both conditions; however, most available evidence remains preclinical. We systematically reviewed 158 original studies graded by evidence level and synthesized the pharmacological mechanisms of XYS. The available evidence suggests that XYS may restore liver-brain communication through vagal, humoral, and gut microbiota pathways. At the vagal pathway level, XYS has been reported to inhibit aberrant afferent transmission of intestinal pro-inflammatory signals to the central nervous system while concurrently enhancing cholinergic anti-inflammatory efferent output, thereby potentially restoring the afferent-efferent balance of autonomic innervation. At the humoral pathway level, XYS may restore the negative feedback function of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, redirect tryptophan metabolic flux away from excessive diversion toward the kynurenine pathway, and alleviate neuroinflammation through upregulation of monoamine neurotransmitters and inhibition of microglial M1 polarization. At the gut microbiota pathway level, XYS may reshape microbial community structure and its metabolic profile, restore the microecological barrier and intestinal mucosal permeability by increasing the abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria and reducing enterogenous endotoxin load. Two integrative nodes, namely the serotonergic redirection of tryptophan flux and the systematic restoration of gut microbiota, are proposed to underlie the dual efficacy. These nodes may form a bidirectional closed loop that links peripheral metabolic signals with central neuroplasticity. Current evidence has notable limitations, including poor clinical relevance of disease models, insufficient causal inference, questionable dose extrapolation, and lack of temporal dynamics. Future studies should prioritize randomized controlled trials in comorbid populations, multi-omics biomarker discovery, and temporal causal network analysis to facilitate clinical translation.

titre: Candida albicans vaccines: from cell wall architecture to protective immunity
resume: Candida albicans is an opportunistic fungal pathogen that colonizes the oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, and vaginal mucosa. Immunosuppression or increased fungal virulence permits extensive mucosal replication and tissue invasion, driving either recurrent superficial infection or life-threatening systemic disease. Vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC) is predominantly caused by. It substantially impairs quality of life in women of reproductive age. Although azoles such as fluconazole are effective, emerging resistance and frequent recurrence limit their long-term utility. These constraints highlight the urgent need for preventive strategies against VVC. This review summarizes the landscape of cell wall antigens and their immunobiology, identifies key translational barriers, and proposes targeted strategies to advance next-generation antifungal vaccines, thereby providing a reference for future vaccine development.

titre: Associations of self-reported and actigraphic sleep with gut microbiome composition and diversity among older adults
resume: Study objectives Poor sleep is linked to adverse health outcomes. Animal studies suggest the gut microbiome may influence sleep, but human findings remain inconsistent. We examined associations of self-reported insomnia symptoms, daytime sleepiness, and actigraphy-measured sleep with gut microbiome diversity and composition in older adults. Materials and methods We studied 869 Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging participants with self-reported sleep and shotgun metagenomic sequencing; 332 also had actigraphy. We tested associations of sleep with alpha diversity, beta diversity, and species composition using regression, PERMANOVA, and ANCOM-BC2, adjusting for age, sex, BMI, physical activity, education, and depressive symptoms. Results Participants had a mean age of 70.7 years; 54.8 per cent were female and 66.9 per cent white. Trouble falling asleep ≥5 times/week was associated with higher Shannon diversity (β = 0.41 SD; 95% CI: 0.09, 0.73) and Pielou's evenness, but not richness metrics. No actigraphy-measured sleep variables were associated with alpha or beta diversity. Beta diversity analyses suggested excessive sleepiness (1-2 or 3-4 times/week) was associated with a different microbial composition, though the variance explained was small. In species-level analyses, frequent insomnia symptoms or excessive sleepiness were associated with depleted or undetected Eubacterium sp. CAG:251. In exploratory actigraphy models, each doubling of sleep efficiency was associated with higher Eubacterium sp. CAG:251 prevalence (PR = 2.15; 95% CI: 1.47, 3.14), while each 30-minute increase in wake after sleep onset was associated with lower prevalence (PR = 0.49; 95% CI: 0.29, 0.81). Conclusions Global diversity findings were limited and inconsistent, whereas subjective and objective sleep disturbances converged on Eubacterium sp. CAG:251. These findings are exploratory and require longitudinal replication.

titre: Development of a Knowledge Map for Managing Symptoms of Graft-Versus-Host Disease in Patients Undergoing Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation
resume: Background Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) remains a critical complication affecting patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), with multifaceted symptoms requiring systematic management. Current clinical practices lack structured tools to guide nurses in addressing GVHD-related symptoms across diverse organ systems. This review aims to synthesize evidence on GVHD symptom management to construct a knowledge graph, enhancing nursing interventions and improving patient outcomes. Methods Relevant authoritative books, guidelines, and expert consensuses such as the "Clinical Nursing Manual for Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation" and the "Chinese Expert Consensus on Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute GVHD After Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (2024 edition)" were referenced. Literature related to GVHD in HSCT was searched, with a time limit from 2014 to 2024. The knowledge graph was constructed using a combination of manual annotation and computer processing. Results A GVHD knowledge graph centered on symptom management for HSCT patients was constructed, encompassing 7 aspects of symptom management, including skin, oral cavity, liver, eyes, gastrointestinal tract, lungs, and bones and joints, as well as health knowledge related to nutrition and psychology. Discussion This knowledge graph provides a structured, evidence-based framework for GVHD symptom management, addressing gaps in standardized nursing protocols. By integrating multidisciplinary recommendations, it supports clinical decision-making, reduces practice variability, and prioritizes patient-centered care. Future studies should validate its impact on complication rates and quality of life in real-world settings. The tool's adaptability allows updates as new evidence emerges, ensuring alignment with evolving guidelines. For nurses, this resource enhances competency in managing complex GVHD presentations, ultimately improving care delivery for HSCT recipients.

titre: Relationship between adverse childhood experiences and alexithymia among Patients with Substance Use Disorders in Egypt: A Cross-Sectional Study
resume: Abstract Background Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) are potentially traumatic events occurring before the age of 18, including abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction. These experiences are strongly associated with emotional dysregulation and increased risk of substance use disorders (SUDs). Alexithymia, defined as difficulty in identifying, describing, and processing emotions with a tendency toward externally oriented thinking, is highly prevalent among individuals with SUDs and may serve as a mediating factor between childhood trauma and addictive behaviors. Objectives This study described childhood adversity and alexithymia and examined their association in Egyptian men receiving addiction treatment. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 105 eligible men aged 18–65 years were recruited consecutively from inpatient and outpatient addiction services at Abbasiya Psychiatric Hospital, Cairo, from 15 February to 15 May 2026. Diagnoses were established using the Arabic Structured Clinical Interview for Axis I Disorders under the fourth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders. Childhood adversity and alexithymia were assessed with the Adverse Childhood Experiences International Questionnaire and the 20-item Toronto Alexithymia Scale. Analyses included Pearson correlation and exploratory multivariable linear regression. Results The mean cumulative adversity score was 6.69 ± 2.74; 87 participants (82.9%) reported four or more adversity domains. The mean alexithymia score was 64.49 ± 8.83. Seventy-two participants were classified as alexithymic (68.6%; 95% confidence interval 59.2–76.7%), 28 as borderline (26.7%), and five as non-alexithymic (4.8%). Cumulative adversity was positively correlated with alexithymia scores ( r = 0.303; 95% confidence interval 0.118 to 0.467; p = 0.002). After adjustment for age, education, marital status, residence, main substance, and route of administration, each additional adversity domain was associated with a 0.93-point higher alexithymia score (95% confidence interval 0.303 to 1.556; p = 0.004). The model explained 21.3% of score variance (adjusted R² = 0.110). Conclusions Greater cumulative childhood adversity was associated with higher alexithymia scores among eligible men receiving addiction treatment at one Egyptian hospital. The findings describe a cross-sectional association and do not establish causality, mediation, or clinical benefit. Independent longitudinal studies incorporating functional and treatment outcomes are needed to assess clinical relevance and applicability to other populations.

titre: Beyond breathing: Lung as a sensory organ
resume: The lung, one the largest branching organs in our body and vital for survival at first breath, is commonly known as the gas exchange organ. Recent novel findings on lung sensing cells, molecules, and lung-brain crosstalk in the emerging discipline of interoception have highlighted the consideration of the lung as a sensory organ. Acknowledging the central importance of lung sensing to human health and disease, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute convened a workshop to synthesize the past, current, and future of lung sensing research, with in-person presentations by approximately 20 interdisciplinary experts and a large virtual audience. Here, we highlight the key topics discussed and summarize a blueprint for the future in this important field.
revue: American journal of respiratory cell and molecular biology

titre: Dissociating Early Heartbeat-Evoked Afferent Gating From Late Associative Failure in Post-Anoxic Coma
resume: Abstract Objective Following cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation, standard clinical EEG often fails to differentiate reversible metabolic depression from structural cortical necrosis. We evaluated whether the Heartbeat-Evoked Response (HER) can dissociate viable subcortical-cortical primary interoceptive afferent gating from non-viable distributed cortico-cortical networks in acute post-anoxic coma. Methods Continuous 19-channel EEG and synchronized Lead-II ECG recordings were analyzed across a harmonized multicenter cohort of 150 comatose post-cardiac arrest patients (discovery cohort: n = 100; independent validation cohort: n = 50; 58 Good Outcome [CPC 1–2] and 92 Poor Outcome [CPC 3–5]). Standardized Low-Resolution Electromagnetic Tomography (sLORETA) and non-linear Hilbert–Huang Transform (HHT) with Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) were applied to evaluate early (150–300 ms) versus late (350–500 ms) post-R-peak windows. Results Favorable recovery was associated with a preserved frontocentral negative deflection peaking at ~ 200 ms (-1.18 µV at electrode Fz), localized via sLORETA strictly to the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC; BA 24/32) and anterior insula. EMD isolated this early component into intermediate intrinsic modes (IMF 2–3; 8–16 Hz), yielding a sharp surge in instantaneous Hilbert energy (Et = 1.85 a.u.) and robust phase alignment (IPLV = 0.95). Non-survivors showed an anomalous positive shift (+ 1.45 µV), energy collapse (Et < 0.40 a.u.), and phase desynchronization (IPLV ≈ 0.18). In the late window (350–500 ms), both groups exhibited diffuse spatial dissipation and loss of discrete cortical generators. Conclusion Preserved early primary interoceptive afferent gating to the ACC/insula—rather than late associative network reverberation—serves as an objective electrophysiological biomarker of viable cortical microcircuitry in post-anoxic coma.

titre: Structural Brain Correlates of Bulimia Nervosa Diagnosis and Symptom Severity: A Coordinated ENIGMA Eating Disorders Working Group Analysis
resume: Importance Bulimia nervosa (BN) ranks second among eating disorders in both prevalence and disease burden, but its neurobiology is poorly understood. Progress has been limited by neuroimaging studies with inconsistent findings across small samples. Objective To identify reliable structural brain correlates of BN diagnosis and severity across multiple cohorts worldwide. Design, setting, and participants This case-control study used 3-dimensional T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and clinical data. Prospective meta-analyses assessed group differences in cortical thickness (CT), surface area (SA), and subcortical volumes (SV) and associations with symptom severity. Data were analyzed between February 1, 2022, and October 1, 2025. Thirteen international sites (17 cohorts) participating in the Enhancing Neuroimaging Genetics through Meta-Analysis (ENIGMA) Eating Disorders Working Group were included, yielding a total of 369 participants with BN and 417 healthy control individuals. Main outcomes and measures Regional CT, SA, and SV extracted from T1-weighted MRI scans (uniformly preprocessed using ENIGMA-standardized pipelines and quality control procedures); binge eating severity; and compensatory behavior severity. Results Participants were all female with a mean (range) age of 23.6 (12.0-53.6) years. Relative to control individuals, the BN group had lower nucleus accumbens volume (Cohen d, -0.20; 95% CI, -0.34 to -0.06) and lower cortical SA of the superior temporal (d, -0.26; 95% CI, -0.41 to -0.12) and transverse temporal cortices (d, -0.24; 95% CI, -0.38 to -0.10). We did not observe significant group differences in CT. Most differences remained significant when controlling for cohort-level variation in body mass index, illness duration, depressive symptoms, psychotropic medication use, and purging as a compensatory behavior. Binge-eating frequency was associated with lower SA of the superior temporal cortex, insula, pars orbitalis, and medial orbitofrontal, rostral middle frontal, and isthmus and posterior cingulate gyri (r value range, -0.20 to -0.14) but not CT or SV. No anatomical characteristics were associated with total compensatory behaviors. Conclusions and relevance This case-control study found that localized brain structural alterations, mostly in SA, were associated with BN and BN symptoms. These findings provide evidence implicating reward, cognitive control, interoceptive, and social cognition circuits in the pathophysiology of BN, advancing neurobiological models of a disorder with a poorly characterized brain basis.

titre: Telehealth Treatment of Anxiety in Patients With Low-Risk Chest Pain in the Emergency Department: The PACER Randomized Clinical Trial
resume: Importance Chest pain is a leading reason for emergency department (ED) visits, with most cases classified as low-risk chest pain (LRCP) after excluding acute coronary syndrome. Many patients with LRCP experience undiagnosed or undertreated anxiety. Objective To determine if 2 types of telehealth-delivered cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) interventions were superior to primary care referral for patients with LRCP and anxiety. Design, setting, and participants The Patient-Centered Treatment of Anxiety After Low-Risk Chest Pain in the Emergency Room (PACER) trial was a randomized, 3-group comparative effectiveness trial conducted across 6 university health systems EDs that enrolled adults with LRCP who were discharged from the ED and had at least moderate anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 [GAD-7] score ≥8 or Patient Health Questionnaire [PHQ] panic screener score ≥2) from April 2021 to July 2024 (12-month follow-up was completed by July 2025). Data analysis began in July 2025 and was completed by January 2026. Interventions All 3 groups received psychoeducation. The 3 interventions compared were (1) recommended primary care follow-up, (2) peer-supported internet-based CBT (iCBT), and (3) therapist-delivered CBT via telehealth. Main outcomes and measures The primary outcome was change over 12 months in the GAD-7 anxiety score. Secondary outcomes included global anxiety improvement, PHQ-8 depression scores, PHQ-14 somatization scores, and Sheehan Disability Scale scores. Outcomes were assessed at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. Results A total of 375 patients were enrolled (265 female individuals [70.7%] and 109 male individuals [29.1%]; 125 Black individuals [33.3%], 28 Hispanic individuals [7.5%], 226 White individuals [60.3%], and 22 individuals [5.9%] of other race; mean [SD] age, 39.9 [13.1] years). Adjusted mean improvement in GAD-7 over 12 months was significant within all arms (4.32, 5.54, and 5.13 points in the primary care referral, peer-supported iCBT, and therapist-delivered CBT groups, respectively, for which the baseline SD pooled over groups that was used to calculate all effect sizes was 4.83). Improvement with peer-supported iCBT was 1.22 points greater (95% CI, 0.01-2.43; effect size = 0.25) than primary care referral, and this effect was strongest (2.8 points) among patients with severe anxiety. Depression, somatization, and disability improved moderately within groups, with no significant between-group differences. Odds of patient-reported global anxiety improvement were 3 times higher in the 2 CBT groups compared with primary care referral. Higher engagement was associated with greater anxiety reduction.
