titre: P073 Double vision and a difficult diagnosis
resume: Abstract Introduction Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is the commonest systemic vasculitis in older adults and is classically characterised by new-onset headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual symptoms. However, atypical presentations and negative cranial investigations can delay diagnosis and treatment. We describe a 63-year-old man presenting with sequential bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsies and headache without classical cranial symptoms. Temporal artery biopsy was negative off steroids. Extensive investigation excluded infective, malignant and autoimmune mimics before PET-CT demonstrated large-vessel vasculitis supporting a diagnosis of atypical GCA. This case highlights the diagnostic value of multimodal imaging and multidisciplinary assessment. Case description A 63-year-old man with hypertension presented with a four-day history of severe left-sided headache associated with nausea, vomiting and peri-orbital pain in November 2024. CT brain was unremarkable and he was initially managed as presumed migraine. He subsequently developed a left sixth cranial nerve palsy causing diplopia prompting neurological assessment. MRI brain and vascular imaging were normal, while inflammatory markers were modestly elevated (ESR 44 mm/hr, CRP 9 mg/L). Given concern for vasculitis, temporal artery biopsy was performed but showed no evidence of giant cell arteritis. Despite negative investigations, empirical treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by 60 mg oral prednisolone was commenced because of high clinical suspicion. Temporal artery ultrasound performed after almost 11-days on steroids was negative. One month later, whilst receiving prednisolone 60 mg daily, he re-presented with worsening headache and developed a contralateral sixth cranial nerve palsy. He denied jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual loss. Repeat inflammatory markers were only mildly elevated and the progression of symptoms despite corticosteroids prompted extensive investigation. Multiple lumbar punctures demonstrated non-specific inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid changes. Comprehensive autoimmune, infective and malignant screening, including haematological and ENT assessment, failed to identify an alternative diagnosis. Repeated attempts to taper corticosteroids resulted in recurrent headaches, constitutional symptoms and marked rises in inflammatory markers (ESR 110, CRP 108). Severe claustrophobia delayed MRI and PET-CT imaging, necessitating hypnotherapy, while corticosteroids were rapidly tapered in the interim. PET-CT performed off steroids, in August 2025 demonstrated faint FDG uptake involving the ascending aorta and aortic arch consistent with aortitis and large-vessel vasculitis. Following multidisciplinary review, a diagnosis of atypical large-vessel giant cell arteritis was made. Tocilizumab was commenced in October 2025, with methotrexate added five months later for ongoing steroid sparing. Diplopia resolved completely, headaches improved substantially and inflammatory markers normalised, allowing gradual corticosteroid reduction. Discussion This case demonstrates the diagnostic challenges posed by atypical giant cell arteritis. Sequential bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsies are an uncommon manifestation of GCA and, combined with the absence of jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and visual loss, initially favoured neurological rather than vasculitic diagnoses. A further challenge was the negative temporal artery biopsy off steroids and ultrasound after 11-days on steroids. Temporal artery biopsy is susceptible to skip lesions and therefore cannot exclude GCA in patients with a convincing clinical presentation. This case reinforces that negative cranial investigations should not provide false reassurance when suspicion remains high. The relapsing clinical course proved equally informative. Symptom recurrence during corticosteroid tapering, accompanied by progressively rising inflammatory markers, suggested ongoing inflammatory disease despite treatment. Extensive investigation excluded infective, malignant and alternative autoimmune disorders, while repeated multidisciplinary discussion ensured the differential diagnosis continued to evolve. PET-CT proved pivotal by demonstrating inflammation within the ascending aorta and aortic arch, supporting a diagnosis of large-vessel GCA that had not been identified by cranial investigations. This highlights the complementary role of whole-body vascular imaging in patients with suspected GCA and inconclusive temporal artery assessment, particularly when large-vessel disease is suspected. The case also illustrates the practical challenges encountered during investigation. Severe claustrophobia delayed MRI and PET-CT, prolonging diagnostic uncertainty and emphasising the importance of adapting investigations to individual patient circumstances. This case reinforces the point that when patients have persistent clinical suspicion for giant cell arteritis despite negative temporal artery ultrasound and biopsy, earlier PET-CT or alternative large-vessel imaging should be incorporated into the diagnostic pathway. Key learning points • This case reinforced that giant cell arteritis should remain an important differential diagnosis in patients over 50 years presenting with new headache and cranial neuropathies, even in the absence of classical cranial symptoms. Sequential bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsies, although rare, may represent an atypical manifestation of GCA. • Negative temporal artery ultrasound and biopsy do not exclude giant cell arteritis. Prior corticosteroid exposure, skip lesions and isolated large-vessel involvement may all reduce the diagnostic yield of cranial investigations. Clinical judgement should therefore remain central when investigations and presentation appear discordant. • A further learning point was the importance of reassessing the diagnosis throughout the disease course. Relapsing symptoms during corticosteroid tapering, rising inflammatory markers and failure to identify an alternative diagnosis all supported ongoing inflammatory disease despite initially inconclusive investigations. • This case also highlighted the value of multidisciplinary collaboration and multimodal imaging. PET-CT ultimately identified large-vessel inflammation and established the diagnosis after extensive neurological, infectious, malignant and autoimmune investigations had proved non-diagnostic. • The principal learning objective from the conference would be to better understand the investigation of suspected large-vessel giant cell arteritis when temporal artery ultrasound and biopsy are negative. In particular, I would welcome discussion regarding the optimal timing of PET-CT, the influence of corticosteroid exposure on imaging sensitivity, and strategies for balancing clinical judgement with negative investigations to minimise diagnostic delay and prevent irreversible complications.

titre: Managing insomnia: An evaluation of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia in clinical and preventive contexts
resume: Insomnia is a highly prevalent and often persistent disorder that remains under-recognized and undertreated in routine care. This thesis examined the relationship between insomnia and mental health symptoms, the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of insomnia interventions, and opportunities to improve access to and optimize insomnia treatment. Although cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment and has been shown to improve sleep and potentially reduce mental health symptoms, access to CBT-I in routine care remains limited, resulting in a substantial treatment gap. In Chapter 2, we examined the relationship between insomnia and symptoms of major depressive disorder (MDD), social anxiety disorder (SAD), panic disorder (PD), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and borderline personality disorder (BPD), using cross-sectional online data. Insomnia was highly prevalent across all symptom domains. Network analyses showed that insomnia severity was directly associated with symptom severity of MDD, GAD, and BPD, whereas associations with SAD, PD, and PTSD were no longer direct when accounting for other comorbid symptoms. In Chapter 3, we presented the study protocol for a series of randomized controlled trials evaluating therapist-guided internet-delivered CBT-I (iCBT-I) in adults with insomnia and co-occurring symptoms of SAD, PD, GAD, PTSD, or BPD. The studies were conducted across three levels of mental healthcare, ranging from individuals not currently receiving or awaiting mental health care to individuals awaiting general or specialized secondary care. In Chapter 4, we evaluated the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of guided iCBT-I among individuals not currently receiving or awaiting mental health care. Guided iCBT-I yielded large and sustained reductions in insomnia severity and improvements in sleep diary outcomes. Small improvements were observed in symptoms of SAD, PD, GAD, and BPD, but were not maintained at six-month follow-up. No effects were found for PTSD symptoms. The economic evaluation showed no differences in societal costs between groups. Although iCBT-I had a high probability of being cost-effective in reducing insomnia severity from a societal perspective, these improvements did not translate into similar improvements in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). In Chapter 5, we conducted a mixed-methods process evaluation of participants' and therapists' experiences with guided iCBT-I across all three levels of care. Overall, the intervention was well accepted, with most participants reporting improvements in sleep and high satisfaction. However, optimizing its impact may require more flexible guidance and adaptable treatment content to better align with individual needs. In Chapter 6, we investigated the long-term preventive effects of CBT-I, circadian rhythm support (CRS), and their combination on depression incidence over four years. Only combined CBT-I and CRS reduced the risk of incident depressive disorders, and this effect was limited to individuals with unspecified insomnia rather than those with the subtype associated with an increased lifetime risk of mental disorders. These findings highlight the potential value of combined or more intensive interventions and treatment approaches tailored to insomnia subtypes. Building on these findings, we identified five key levers for optimizing insomnia treatment: guidance, treatment content, treatment dose, engagement and adherence, and next-step options for individuals who do not respond to initial treatment. Primary care emerged as the central entry point for reducing the treatment gap, while secondary care should focus on integrating insomnia interventions into existing treatment pathways. Future research should inform how insomnia care can be effectively implemented and tailored across settings to improve access and treatment outcomes.

titre: Long-Term Acquisition and Maintenance of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Skills Through a Smartphone-Based Intervention: A Secondary Analysis of the RESiLIENT Trial
resume: Background Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is assumed to confer longer-term benefit partly through the acquisition and maintenance of therapeutic skills, but evidence on these processes after smartphone-based CBT remains limited in subthreshold depression. This exploratory secondary analysis of the RESiLIENT randomized controlled trial examined 50-week changes in five CBT skill domains: behavioral activation (BA), cognitive restructuring (CR), problem solving (PS), assertion training (AT), and behavioral therapy for insomnia (BI). Methods The reported comparisons involved 3,280 participants with baseline PHQ-9 scores of 5 or higher assigned to nine CBT intervention arms or the weekly self-check control arm. Self-reported skill enactment was assessed at baseline and weeks 6, 26, and 50. Standardized mean differences versus self-check were reported for 135 CBT contrasts. P-values and confidence intervals used a Dunnett approximation within each domain and visit. Results Estimated changes in CR skill scores favored several intervention arms over self-check, whereas changes in BA skill scores favored the intervention in some comparisons. Estimated between-group differences in PS, AT, and BI skill scores were generally small. At week 50, standardized mean differences for BA+CR versus self-check were 0.26 (95% CI 0.07–0.46) for BA and 0.27 (0.07–0.47) for CR. The corresponding CR estimate in the CR arm was 0.21 (0.01–0.41). These estimates illustrate exploratory patterns and do not establish superiority of one intervention or skill domain. Conclusions This exploratory study describes varying patterns of change across self-reported CBT skill domains over 50 weeks following a brief smartphone-based intervention. These findings may inform future research on the persistence of CBT skill use and its relationship with longer-term clinical outcomes.

titre: Combination of cognitive behavioral therapy and antidepressant medication versus the monotherapies for obsessive compulsive disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis
resume: Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) and antidepressive medication (ADM) are recommended as first-line treatments for patients with obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) of mild to moderate severity, whereas the Combination of CBT and ADM is recommended for patients with severe OCD. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted of randomized controlled trials with adults or children in which the Combination was compared with the monotherapies, or CBT with ADM. Four databases were systematically searched for studies published until August 2026. Twenty-three studies were included, comprising 1381 participants, 820 adults and 561 children. CBT had a drop-out rate of 14.7%, ADM 18.9%, and the Combination 21.2%, with no significant difference between treatments. There was no significant difference in OCD scores between Combination and CBT ( g = 0.05), but both the Combination and CBT were significantly better than ADM ( g = 0.75 and 0.38, respectively). Average response rate was significantly higher for the Combination (73%) and CBT (64%) compared to ADM (40%). Moderator analyses indicated that pre-treatment OCD severity was not a significant moderator of outcome. The results of the present meta-analysis suggest that current recommendations regarding concurrent Combination treatment may warrant refinement, particularly given the lack of added benefit over CBT alone. Prospero registration id: CRD420261300204.

titre: Reaction-time changes around rule shifts on the Wisconsin card sorting test in obsessive–compulsive disorder and treatment-resistant depression
resume: Conventional Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) indices quantify errors and categorization performance, whereas reaction-time measures may provide complementary information about performance surrounding rule shifts. This study compared conventional WCST performance and rule-shift-related reaction-time patterns among patients with obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), patients with treatment-resistant depression (TRD), and healthy controls (HCs). This retrospective study included 181 participants: 38 with OCD, 67 with TRD, and 76 HCs. Reaction times before and after each of five WCST rule shifts were analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE), adjusting for age, sex, and education. Four conventional WCST indices were compared using Kruskal–Wallis tests, with Holm correction across the four omnibus tests. An additional exploratory analysis examined 19 conventional WCST indices, with Holm correction across these 19 tests. In the full GEE model, planned contrasts averaged equally across the five rule shifts showed a greater pre-to-post change in log-transformed reaction time in OCD than in HCs (β = 0.146, 95% CI 0.064–0.228; Holm-adjusted p = 0.00149) and in TRD than in HCs (β = 0.107, 95% CI 0.037–0.177; Holm-adjusted p = 0.00538). The OCD–TRD contrast was not statistically significant (β = 0.039, 95% CI − 0.046 to 0.123; Holm-adjusted p = 0.370). The group-by-phase-by-shift interaction was not statistically significant. None of the four primary conventional WCST omnibus tests or the 19 exploratory omnibus tests remained statistically significant after their respective Holm corrections. Both clinical-group differences remained significant in full-model sensitivity analyses addressing extreme reaction times, although the OCD–HC estimate was attenuated when very long reaction times were excluded; a contribution of medication to the TRD findings could not be excluded. Patients with OCD and TRD showed greater pre-to-post rule-shift reaction-time changes than HCs when estimates were averaged across five rule shifts. Robust group differences in conventional WCST indices were not established after correction for multiple testing. Reaction-time measures may complement conventional WCST indices, but independent replication is needed before clinical or mechanistic conclusions can be drawn.

titre: Feeding and eating disorders in adults: Systematic review and meta-analysis
resume: Aims Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) in adults is less studied than in younger populations, and prevalence estimates vary across populations and assessment methods. This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the prevalence of positive ARFID screens or study-defined ARFID in adults and examined variation by geographical location, population characteristics, and assessment approach. Food neophobia and food selectivity were secondary narrative outcomes. Methods The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251267471), conducted according to Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, and reported following PRISMA. PubMed, Embase, and the Virtual Health Library were searched without language or date restrictions. Observational studies of adults aged 18–65 years reporting prevalence of ARFID, food neophobia, or food selectivity were eligible. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias was assessed using JBI tools. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted. Results Twenty-three studies (370,230 adults) were included; 20 (368,494 participants) contributed to the ARFID meta-analysis. The exploratory pooled prevalence was 19.5% (95% CI: 7.6%–41.9%; prediction interval: 0.2%–97.2%; I 2 = 99.8%). The pooled point estimate was 24.8% in clinical samples and 4.1% in non-clinical samples, although population type was not a significant moderator ( p = .170). Studies using the Nine Item ARFID Screen (NIAS) yielded 33.7% versus 5.8% for non-NIAS studies, but moderation remained inconclusive. Conclusion Positive ARFID screens and study-defined ARFID are frequently identified in the adult samples studied to date, but the pooled estimate should not be interpreted as general-population prevalence. Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity limits comparability and supports stratified interpretation and diagnostic confirmation.

titre: Michel de Goedt, Éveiller aux choses de Dieu. Théologie de la vie chrétienne,avant-propos du Fr. Marie-Didier Golay (ocd) et présentation de Bruno Charmet, Toulouse, Éditions du Carmel, « Recherches carmélitaines », 2025, 241 p.,
Recurrent Angular and Exfoliative Cheilitis with Mixed Anxiety and Depression Disorder: A Case Report of Psychodermatology
resume: Introduction: Cheilitis is defined as inflammation of the lip area. The factors that affect cheilitis include infection, mechanical factors, poor oral hygiene, factitious activity like lip licking or picking, psychological stress, nutritional deficiencies, and others. Cheilitis is also related to psychiatric disorders, such as anxiety, depression, eating disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and personality disorder. Case: This case report is about a 20-year-old female with recurrent angular and exfoliative cheilitis and a history of mixed anxiety and depression disorders. Psychological stress fluctuation influenced the symptoms. The patient got hydrocortisone topical, urea topical, escitalopram, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and showed clinical improvement. Discussion: Cheilitis could be related to or triggered by psychiatric diseases, psychological conditions, patients’ habits, or self-injurious behavior. Other risk factors such as immune defects and B vitamin deficiencies are also considered to affect that psychodermatological condition. Conclusion: Cheilitis is one of the common cases in clinical practice. It’s important to explore psycho-dermatologic interactions. Physicians must consider patients’ psychological condition in recurrent cheilitis cases and provide proper treatment.

titre: Systems Biology and Machine Learning Reveal Oxidative Stress Hubs and Therapeutic Targets in Diarrhea-Predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome
resume: BACKGROUND: Diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) is a common functional gastrointestinal disorder, and accumulating evidence suggests that oxidative stress is involved in its pathophysiology. This study explored oxidative stress-related mechanisms in IBS-D and screened potential diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets through integrative bioinformatics analysis. METHODS: Transcriptomic datasets from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI)-Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database were analyzed using integrative bioinformatics approaches to identify oxidative stress-related core genes in IBS-D. Eight potential biomarkers were identified and evaluated for diagnostic performance via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Among these, the key gene ACO2 was further investigated using Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG)-based gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) and immune correlation analyses to explore the association between ACO2 expression and disease-related biological processes. In addition, the eight target proteins were used for reverse screening of potentially therapeutic traditional Chinese medicines and their active compounds. RESULTS: In total, 206 oxidative stress-related genes were identified, with predominant enrichment observed in mitochondrial energy metabolism and cellular stress-response pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation and hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1) signaling. The eight potential diagnostic biomarkers demonstrated robust diagnostic performance (area under the ROC curve (AUC) = 0.896) in distinguishing IBS-D patients from healthy controls. Notably, ACO2 emerged as a key hub gene associated with distinct metabolic and immune-related pathway enrichment profiles. In parallel, a competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) regulatory network centered on ACO2 was established, providing additional insight into its potential post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms. Furthermore, reverse screening based on the eight target proteins identified luteolin, phillygenin, quercetin, and wogonin as candidate active compounds from Forsythia suspensa. Molecular docking further indicated favorable binding affinity between these compounds and the biomarker proteins. CONCLUSIONS: This integrative bioinformatics study identifies oxidative stress-related molecular signatures and potential biomarkers in IBS-D. Reverse screening and molecular docking further suggest that luteolin, phillygenin, quercetin, and wogonin from Forsythia suspensa may represent potential candidate compounds targeting these biomarkers. These findings provide a theoretical basis for further experimental validation.

titre: Efficacy of Lactose Reduction in Irritable Bowel Syndrome and Recurrent Abdominal Pain: A Systematic Review
resume: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Lactose intolerance (LI), irritable bowel syndrome in adults (IBS) and recurrent abdominal pain (RAP) in children are frequently diagnosed worldwide. This systematic review aimed to assess the effects of dietary reduction in lactose on symptoms, quality of life and healthcare visits in IBS and children with recurrent abdominal pain. METHODS: PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase and Lilacs were searched for studies on IBS and RAP investigating the effect of a reduction of dietary intake of lactose for at least 4 weeks on abdominal pain, stool characteristics, bloating and distension, and quality of life published up to 15 August 2026. No restriction in language, publication type or data limit was applied. Four reviewers independently screened the abstracts for eligibility, and risk of bias was assessed by two reviewers with ROBINS-2. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or consulting with a senior investigator. Results were summarised in tabular form. The systematic review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024617161). RESULTS: Eighteen studies met eligibility criteria based on the title and abstract. Upon review of full-text articles, three studies in adults and six studies in children were retained for data extraction. Lactose breath tests (LBTs) were performed in all studies. All but one study prospectively compared patient cohorts. IBS was defined by Manning criteria in two studies and Rome II criteria in one study. Only patients with a positive LBT were subjected to dietary intervention in eight of nine studies. No control group was included in one of three and three of six of the studies in adults and children, respectively. None of the studies compared symptomatic evolution based on validated questionnaires. Improvement in pain was reported by two of three and five of six of the studies on IBS and RAP, respectively. The risk of bias was high for all studies. No study assessed quality of life. CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence in support of dietary lactose reduction in patients with IBS and RAP is limited due to a high risk of bias, the use of old criteria, the absence of a valid comparator group and poorly defined outcomes. A positive LBT was associated with improvement in pain after a lactose-free diet. Future studies on the role of lactose restriction in IBS and RAP should recruit patients based on current diagnostic criteria and assess outcome by validated measures, preferentially applying a randomised controlled design.

titre: Family Risk and Resilience Patterns Differentiate Early Childhood Vulnerability to Intergenerational Transmission of Abdominal Pain
resume: Children are at increased risk of developing chronic abdominal pain if a parent has an abdominal pain-related disorder of brain-gut interaction such as irritable bowel syndrome, suggesting family mechanisms of intergenerational pain transmission. However, patterns of family risk and resilience factors that predict children's vulnerability for developing chronic abdominal pain remain unknown. In a sample of parents with an abdominal pain-related disorder of brain-gut interaction and their young child without chronic pain, this cross-sectional study identified subgroups representing different constellations of family risk and resilience factors. It also tested subgroup differences on two vulnerability markers for children's future development of chronic abdominal pain: child emotional functioning and parental protective behavior. Baseline data from 212 parents and their 4-7-year-old child, participating in a randomized controlled trial testing a preventative intervention were included. Latent mixture modeling indicated a 3-group solution: (1) "High Socioeconomic Status, High Functioning" (55%) characterized by lower anxiety and depression and higher family resilience, (2) "Low Socioeconomic Status, High Pain Burden" (13%) characterized by higher pain catastrophizing and gastrointestinal symptoms, and (3) "High Socioeconomic Status, High Distress" (32%) characterized by higher parenting stress. Two of the three groups ("Low Socioeconomic Status, High Pain Burden" and "High Socioeconomic Status, High Distress" groups) showed lower child emotional functioning, and the "Low Socioeconomic Status, High Pain Burden" group also showed higher parental protective behavior, than the "High Socioeconomic Status, High Functioning" group. Results contribute to theoretical models of intergenerational pain transmission and help identify families who could benefit from preventative interventions. PERSPECTIVE: Among families of parents with chronic abdominal pain, low family resilience, low socioeconomic status, high parent pain burden, and high parent psychological distress may make young children more vulnerable to developing chronic abdominal pain in the future. These findings inform targeted interventions to prevent intergenerational transmission of abdominal pain.

titre: Diffuse Uterine and Extrauterine Leiomyomatosis Presenting as a Large Abdominopelvic Mass Mimicking Malignancy
resume: Diffuse uterine and extrauterine leiomyomatosis is an uncommon benign condition that can mimic malignancy on imaging. We report a 48-year-old multiparous woman presenting with abdominal pain and abnormal uterine bleeding. Imaging revealed a large heterogeneous uterine mass with peritoneal involvement. Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. Histopathology confirmed diffuse leiomyomatosis. This rare entity poses diagnostic challenges and may lead to unnecessary aggressive treatment if misdiagnosed. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry are essential for accurate diagnosis. Awareness of this condition is crucial for appropriate management and avoidance of overtreatment.

titre: One-session versus three-session virtual reality exposure therapy for public speaking anxiety: a randomized controlled trial
resume: VR technology has been a useful tool in exposure therapy for working with public speaking anxiety. The common approach to treating public speaking anxiety is a single prolonged VR exposure session, but there is still a lack of consensus on whether dividing the same amount of exposure into several shorter sessions would jeopardize its efficacy. This study aims to compare the efficacy of a single extended session versus the same intervention divided into three shorter sessions of VR-based exposure intervention for public speaking anxiety. Using block randomization, 37 students (mean age 22.4, 70.3% female) were randomized in a two-armed parallel group randomized controlled superiority trial, with 18 participants allocated to the one-session and 19 to the three-session group. No blinding was used in this trial. The intervention involved 9 speaking tasks that were administered in a single session or divided into 3 equal parts. Public Speaking Anxiety Scale, Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale and Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation scale were used as outcome measures pre- and post-exposure. Additionally, convenience, duration, fatigue, adaptability, and intensity of the intervention were evaluated. Results indicate a significant reduction in the level of public speaking anxiety (η 2 p = 0.588) and social anxiety (η 2 p = 0.169) in both groups, but no statistically significant group differences or time-by-group interactions were detected (for public speaking anxiety interaction difference was -3.37; 95% CI [-10.02, 3.29]. Participants reported the single three-hour session to be more tiring and longer compared to the same amount of exposure split into 3 sessions, but did not indicate any difference in terms of convenience, adaptability, or intensity. Across the full program, one participant reported mild negative effects; harms were not systematically assessed. Our study findings provide preliminary evidence supporting the feasibility of different scheduling formats. However, the trial was underpowered and had no untreated control condition, so adequately powered studies in larger and more diverse samples are needed to compare the formats. The trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, No NCT06214039.

titre: A pilot feasibility randomised controlled trial of an online cancer bereavement group
resume: BACKGROUND: Bereavement following the death of a loved one from cancer presents unique challenges related to anticipatory stressors, caregiving demands, and the illness trajectory. Although online bereavement interventions may improve access to support, evidence for therapist-led online groups remains limited. This pilot randomised controlled trial evaluated the feasibility, acceptability and preliminary effectiveness of an online therapeutic group intervention for adults bereaved by cancer. METHODS: In this longitudinal pilot RCT, adults bereaved by cancer were randomised to receive the intervention immediately or following a three-month wait-list period. The intervention comprised eight online group sessions delivered over 12 weeks, integrating trauma-informed cognitive behavioural therapy, compassion-focused therapy and psychoeducation. Primary outcomes were feasibility and acceptability. Secondary outcomes included prolonged grief, depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress, self-compassion, and social disconnection, assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and three-month follow-up. RESULTS: Of 124 randomised participants, 100 (80.6%) commenced the allocated intervention and 97 contributed sufficient data for primary analyses. The study met pre-specified feasibility and acceptability criteria, although patterns of attrition differed according to trial stage. Non-commencement following allocation was higher in the immediate intervention groups (27.0 vs 11.5%) whereas withdrawal after intervention commencement was higher in the waitlist group (24.1% vs 10.9%). Exploratory between-group analyses suggested greater improvements in prolonged grief (d = -1.87), post-traumatic stress (d = -1.55), depression (d = -1.03), anxiety (d = -0.71), and self-compassion (d = 1.15) in the immediate intervention group compared with waitlist controls. No statistically significant between-group difference was observed for social disconnection (d = -0.49). CONCLUSIONS: Therapist-led online bereavement groups appear feasible and acceptable for adults bereaved by cancer and show promise for improving psychological outcomes. A fully powered RCT is warranted to establish efficacy.

titre: Feasibility of acceptance and commitment therapy for repetitive negative thinking versus internet-based CBT: a pilot randomised controlled trial in Swedish primary care among patients with anxiety, depression and stress
resume: BACKGROUND: Repetitive negative thinking (RNT) is a transdiagnostic process relevant to common mental health problems in primary care. RNT-ACT is a brief acceptance and commitment therapy-based protocol targeting RNT in two sessions. This pilot study assessed the feasibility of RNT-ACT compared with therapist-supported internet-based cognitive behavioural therapy (iCBT) in Swedish primary care. METHODS: Thirteen participants were randomised: 7 to RNT-ACT and 6 to iCBT. The primary feasibility outcomes were recruitment rate, intervention non-completion, and patient satisfaction measured with the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ-8). Symptom and process measures were secondary outcomes. Secondary outcomes were assessed at baseline and at 1- and 3-month follow-ups. Analyses were descriptive and exploratory, based on available observations without imputation of missing data. RESULTS: Thirteen of 20 eligible individuals were enrolled (65%), corresponding to 35% of all 37 individuals screened. All participants in the RNT-ACT group completed the intervention, whereas 4 of 6 participants in the iCBT group did not complete the intervention. Mean CSQ-8 scores were 27.8 (SD 3.7; n = 5) in the RNT-ACT group and 23.0 (SD 0.0; n = 2) in the iCBT group. CONCLUSIONS: The small sample size and high iCBT non-completion limit between-group comparisons. Further investigation of recruitment, treatment engagement, and patient and therapist experiences is needed before determining whether and how to proceed to a full-scale RCT. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05946382 registered July 14, 2023.

titre: Depression, Anxiety, and Healthcare Utilization in Adults with Uncontrolled Asthma
resume: INTRODUCTION: Uncontrolled asthma is often associated with recurrent acute exacerbations, progressive and chronic systemic inflammation and decreased lung function, impaired quality of life, and healthcare utilization. A considerable proportion of adult patients with uncontrolled asthma exhibit comorbid elevated symptoms of depression and anxiety. These symptoms are often underrecognized and undertreated in adults with asthma. We examined and synthesized the available literature on the efficacy of pulmonary rehabilitation, cognitive behavioral therapy, and antidepressant drug therapy, and healthcare utilization in adults with uncontrolled asthma with comorbid depression and anxiety. INTERPRETATION AND DISCUSSION: The prevalence of anxiety in adults with uncontrolled asthma ranges from 25 to 54%, and depression ranges from 14 to 50%. To date, the available literature on the efficacy of pulmonary rehabilitation, cognitive behavioral therapy, and antidepressant drug therapy in the treatment of anxiety and depression is limited. Untreated depression and anxiety are associated with recurrent episodes of acute exacerbations, hospitalizations, poorer quality of life, longer hospital stays, and emergency healthcare utilization. Therefore, well-controlled randomized controlled trials are needed to improve the evidence base for optimal care of adults with uncontrolled asthma and ideally to reduce healthcare utilization.

titre: Stuck in thought, stuck in therapy: Does Cognitive inflexibility adversely affect treatment adherence among disorders characterised by obsessive and compulsive symptoms
resume: OBJECTIVE: People with mental disorders characterised by obsessive and compulsive symptoms, e.g. obsessive compulsive and related disorders and eating disorders, show poor adherence to treatment, which represents a clinical challenge. These disorders are characterised by cognitive inflexibility, which can adversely influence clinical outcomes, possibly acting by impairing treatment-adherence. METHODS: A cross-sectional online survey explored cognitive inflexibility and self-reported treatment adherence among 201 participants who reported either obsessive-compulsive related disorder or an eating disorder and had received some form of mental health treatment. Regressions were run to explore the relationships between cognitive inflexibility and treatment-adherence. RESULTS: Cognitive inflexibility was associated with poor psychotherapy adherence. Conversely, psychological wellbeing and male sex were associated with good psychotherapy adherence. No factors were associated with medication adherence. CONCLUSIONS: In a study limited by retrospective assessment of adherence, cognitive inflexibility was found to adversely affect adherence to psychotherapy but not to pharmacotherapy. Cognitive inflexibility may represent a potentially remediable risk factor for poor psychotherapy adherence and serve as a novel-biomarker for personalising care for those with disorders characterised by obsessive and compulsive symptoms. If this relationship is confirmed in prospective studies, clinicians should look for signs of cognitive inflexibility in their patients to aid clinical decision-making.

titre: Cortical traveling wave analysis reveals weaker resting forward theta waves and greater task-related modulation in obsessive compulsive disorder
resume: AIMS: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is associated with abnormalities in large-scale brain network dynamics. Conventional electroencephalography (EEG) captures local oscillatory activity but does not characterize spatiotemporal propagation patterns. This study investigates cortical traveling waves, which index directional information flow across the cortex, to determine whether they provide novel insights into altered neural communication in OCD. METHODS: Resting-state (eyes-closed) and task-based (Go/NoGo, Flanker) EEG were recorded from 25 individuals with OCD and 27 healthy controls (HCs). Traveling waves were quantified along midline electrodes using two-dimensional Fast Fourier Transforms to extract forward (posterior-to-anterior) and backward (anterior-to-posterior) propagation in theta (4-8Hz) and alpha (8-13Hz) bands. Group differences were assessed using Bayesian and frequentist linear mixed-effects models controlling for age and sex. RESULTS: At rest, a significant group-by-direction interaction was observed in the theta band (P = 0.0006), driven by weaker forward traveling wave strength in OCD relative to HC. No group differences were observed for backward waves or in the alpha band. During the Flanker task, the OCD group showed a significantly greater increase in forward theta wave strength from rest than HC (P = 0.022). No associations were found between traveling wave measures and symptom severity. CONCLUSION: OCD is characterized by altered theta-band traveling wave dynamics, specifically reduced forward (bottom-up) signaling at rest, and increased task-related modulation during the Flanker task. These findings suggest disrupted hierarchical cortical communication and inefficient engagement of sensory-driven processes. The absence of symptom correlations suggests a potential trait-like neurophysiological marker or endophenotype of OCD.

titre: Gut-brain coherence: A new therapeutic strategy for stress-related tumor
resume: Chronic psychological stress significantly exacerbates tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis through neuroendocrine dysregulation and tumor-associated immunosuppression. Beyond direct neural pathways, stress is increasingly recognized as a driver of gut microbiota dysbiosis, which triggers systemic or local metabolic reprogramming, and fosters a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment. Understanding the complex interplay between chronic stress and oncogenic processes offers critical insights into the underlying mechanisms of cancer biology. The microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA) has thus emerged as a central pathway connecting stress to tumorigenesis, yet a unifying framework for understanding how its constituent systems interact remains lacking. Here, we propose "gut-brain coherence" as a conceptual framework that captures dynamic functional coordination among the gut microbial ecosystem, neural and neuroendocrine signaling, and immune effector networks. Situated within the broader biology of homeostasis, gut-brain coherence emphasizes the bidirectional communication among these systems during stress-induced dysregulation and recovery. We outline a mechanism-informed approach to assessing gut-brain coherence and a bidirectional intervention strategy integrating microbiota-directed, behavioral, and targeted pharmacological approaches to address both gut-to-brain and brain-to-gut signaling. Together, these perspectives provide a framework for investigating how restoration of microbial-neuroendocrine-immune coordination might mitigate stress-related cancer progression and inform strategies to improve survival and quality of life.

titre: Odd- and branched-chain fatty acids in breast milk and neurodevelopment in early infancy: a prospective cohort study
resume: Purpose Odd-chain and branched-chain fatty acids (OCFAs and BCFAs; OBCFAs) have been linked to human microbiota and may influence neurodevelopment via microbiota-gut-brain axis. However, population-based evidence on OBCFAs and neurodevelopment is sparse. Methods A prospective cohort of 120 healthy mother-infant pairs was studied. Breast milk samples were collected at 42 days and 8 months postpartum, with fatty acid profiles quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Infant neurodevelopment was assessed at 8 months of age using the Bayley Scales of Infant Development Third Edition, including cognitive and motor developmental quotients (DQs). Associations between OBCFAs and infant DQs were examined by linear regression. Results Infants' motor DQs were inversely associated with breast milk OCFAs levels at 42 days postpartum, including C15:0 (β = -4.27, P = 0.003), C17:0 (β = -4.67, P = 0.001), and total OCFAs (β = -5.07, P Conclusions Lower levels of breast milk OBCFAs were associated with better motor development in early infancy. Further research is needed to confirm and clarify the role of OBCFAs in neurodevelopmental programming. Clinical trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR).

titre: Sleep disturbance in inflammatory bowel disease: clinical associations and gaps in care
resume: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Sleep disturbance is highly prevalent in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), affecting up to 70% of patients with active disease and 40% in remission, and is associated with worse clinical and patient-reported outcomes. Understanding of the multifactorial drivers of sleep disturbances in IBD remains limited, and as such, there is an absence of clear guidance for evaluating and managing sleep problems in this population. We aimed to identify factors associated with sleep disturbance and characterize patient beliefs, self-management strategies, and interest in sleep-focused testing and treatments. METHODS: Adults with Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis completed a cross-sectional survey assessing disease activity, sleep quality, stress, chronotype, fatigue, and mood. A study-specific questionnaire evaluated sleep-related beliefs, behaviors, and treatment interest. Descriptive analyses characterized sleep patterns and behaviors, and multivariable regression identified factors associated with poor sleep. RESULTS: Among 204 participants, 76.5% reported poor sleep quality and 55.9% had clinically significant sleep disturbance, which was more common in active disease than remission (80.9% vs 46.0%, P < .001). Active disease (odds ratio [OR], 4.31), higher perceived stress (OR, 1.21), and anxiety (OR, 2.63) were associated with increased odds of clinically significant sleep disturbance, while intermediate (OR, 0.16) and morning chronotypes (OR, 0.07) were associated with lower odds of clinically significant sleep disturbance compared with evening chronotypes. Most participants reported self-management behaviors related to sleep, with widespread use of sleep hygiene and over-the-counter strategies but minimal exposure to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (0.5%). Interest in sleep-focused interventions was high, particularly for wearable monitoring, home-based testing, and behavioral and light-based therapies. CONCLUSION: Sleep disturbance in inflammatory bowel disease is common and reflects interacting inflammatory, psychological, and circadian factors. Use of evidence-based therapies remains extremely limited, highlighting a substantial gap in care.

titre: Associations of depression and apathy with subjective and objective autonomic measures in early Parkinson's disease
resume: Objective Neuropsychiatric symptoms and autonomic dysfunction are critical non-motor features of Parkinson's disease (PD). We aimed to investigate the differential association of depression and apathy with subjective and objective autonomic profiles in patients with early PD. Methods This retrospective study analyzed data from 149 early-to-mid stage PD patients (Hoehn and Yahr stage 1-3) enrolled in the hospital's Parkinsonism Registry between 2022 and 2024. Participants were evaluated using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Apathy Evaluation Scale-Self (AES-S), Scales for Outcomes in PD-Autonomic (SCOPA-AUT) for subjective symptoms, and the Composite Autonomic Severity Score (CASS) for objective physiological deficits. Multivariable regression and ANCOVA were performed using a standardized set of covariates. Results Both depression and apathy were associated with significantly higher total SCOPA-AUT and gastrointestinal scores after adjusting for common covariates. Depression exhibited a broader association, remaining linked to the cardiovascular, thermoregulatory, and pupillomotor domains. In multivariable linear regression, higher BDI scores were independent predictors of total subjective autonomic burden and multiple sub-domains, whereas AES scores did not show independent associations when adjusted for BDI scores. Regarding objective measures, no significant associations were observed for the total CASS scores or any sub-indices after controlling for clinical and medication-related factors. These findings suggest that subjective and objective assessment tools may capture distinct facets of the autonomic clinical profile in early PD. Conclusion Depression and apathy are differently associated with the perception of autonomic dysfunction in early PD, with depression associated with a wider range of subjective distress. Neuropsychiatric status is independently associated with subjective autonomic burden beyond measured physiological deficits, supporting multimodal assessments integrating patient-reported and physiological measures.

titre: A three-hit sequential model of chemo-brain: from peripheral inflammation to central oxidative stress and synaptic dysfunction
resume: Background Chemotherapy-induced central neurotoxicity (CICN), commonly known as "chemo-brain", is a prevalent and debilitating condition in cancer survivors, characterized by persistent cognitive deficits that severely compromise quality of life. Despite extensive research, the pathophysiology of CICN remains fragmented, lacking a unifying model that explains how it progresses from peripheral insult to chronic cognitive consolidation. Aim of review This review proposes a novel Three-Hit sequential model to reconceptualize CICN as a dynamic, staged pathological continuum. Unlike existing multi-hit hypotheses that largely describe cumulative or concurrent CNS risk factors, the Three-Hit model features a therapy-triggered, outside-in cascade with defined temporal checkpoints. The model aims to unify disparate mechanistic findings, explain the enduring nature of cognitive deficits after treatment cessation, and guide stage-specific, mechanism-based precision interventions. Key scientific concepts of review The model delineates three sequential pathological phases. The First Hit (peripheral priming) involves chemotherapy-induced gut dysbiosis and systemic inflammation. The Second Hit (central amplification) entails blood-brain barrier disruption, microglial activation, and oxidative stress-driven synaptic dysfunction. The Third Hit (network consolidation) is defined by epigenetic reprogramming, cellular senescence, and white matter degradation, which collectively solidify chronic cognitive impairment. This staged model may facilitate the design of phase-targeted interventions, including microbiota modulation (First Hit), anti-inflammatory and BBB-stabilizing agents (Second Hit), and senotherapeutics or HDAC6 inhibitors (Third Hit), and may guide neuroprotective strategies toward better-timed application. By linking mechanistic insights to a staged biomarker ecosystem, this review offers a conceptual roadmap for advancing stage-specific therapies for CICN.

titre: Co-constructed Emotion: A Collective Predictive Coding Theory of Interoception and Social Symbol Sharing
resume: Emotion is both a psychological phenomenon rooted in physiological fluctuations and a socially constructed phenomenon shaped by language and culture. However, traditional psychological constructivism has remained confined to individual brain processes, while social constructivism has lacked a bottom-up computational mechanism explaining how language and culture emerge from bodily emotional substrates and dynamically evolve. To bridge this theoretical gap, this paper proposes the Theory of Co-constructed Emotion (TCoE) via Collective Predictive Coding (CPC), a framework coupling physiological regulation with social symbol sharing within a single active inference formulation. We extend the conventional CPC model by explicitly incorporating interoception---which is indispensable for modeling emotion from a physiological perspective---into each agent's generative model, alongside exteroception and internal and external representations. In TCoE, the co-construction of emotion is described as a dual inference process: an internal loop of allostasis regulating individual bodily states, and a social loop of communication sharing emotional concepts with others. These loops mutually minimize prediction errors mediated by shared symbols (emotion words). We argue that this theoretical framework 1) aligns with psychological findings on emotional contagion and concept formation, 2) enables constructive verification in multi-agent robotic systems, and 3) provides a computational redefinition of psychiatric conditions such as alexithymia as a disconnection between interoception and social symbols. Thus, we offer a novel computational foundation for emotion research that unifies individual embodiment and social symbol systems.

titre: Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Suggestion Scale (CHIMSS)
resume: The Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Suggestion Scale (CHIMSS) is a novel set of imaginative suggestions that each demand the utilisation of phenomenological control. This scale consists of three suggestions of each type: motor suggestions for arm levitation, hands coming together, and head nodding; challenge suggestions for hands stuck together, fingers stuck together, and arm immobilisation; imagery involvement suggestions for a beach scene, an animal-identification scene, and a future scene; and hallucination suggestions for a mosquito, two tastes, and hearing a song playing automatically. The scale notably excludes suggestions for amnesia, post-hypnotic behaviour, and visual hallucinations. It also includes three alternative imagery involvement suggestions that can be used in place of the existing ones or in addition: a meadow scene, a woods scene, and a scene involving identification with a celestial being or superhero.The introduction script and suggestions were modified from the Phenomenological Control Scale (Lush et al., 2021). The imagery involvement suggestions were modelled after the Imagery Involvement/Dissociation suggestion in the Elkins Hypnotizability Scale (Elkins, 2013, pp. 99–124).

titre: NICE’s 2026 Consultation Draft Guideline for OCD and BDD (GID-NG10435): A Critical Appraisal with Secondary Analysis of NICE’s Published Data
resume: Background. In September 2026 the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) opened consultation on the first batch of its update to the 2005 guideline for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) (GID-NG10435). The draft replaces stepped care with matched care and reviews first-line treatment.Methods. We appraised the draft and its supporting documents against six questions informed by selected AGREE II domains, analysing NICE’s published effect estimates, sample sizes, sensitivity analyses and economic results descriptively; every value was checked against its source document. Comparison guidelines were identified by a documented search.Results. The adult OCD review included 82 randomised controlled trials and the BDD review 13 studies. The committee cited small samples and wide credible intervals when it did not recommend metacognitive therapy (52 participants) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR; 59 participants). Self-administered cognitive behavioural therapy with therapist support, the second adult option, rests on 61 participants, with a wider credible interval than EMDR’s, and was recommended on other documented grounds. The top-ranked adult option had a probability of 0.17 of being the most cost-effective. The first-listed BDD option ranked fifth of nine in the network meta-analysis. The draft gives no drug-specific dose targets, no consolidated definition of an adequate trial and no primary severity measure for allocation or response. Treatment after non-response to an adequate trial is outside the scope of Batch 1; on the assumptions in NHS England’s 2013 specification, a cascade beginning with 48 million adults in England and Wales yields approximately 48,000 people not responding to a serotonin reuptake inhibitor followed by local graduated exposure. All six selected multimodal OCD comparison guidelines address augmentation; none provides a treatment pathway for BDD.Conclusions. The draft rests on a substantial evidence synthesis. The published rationale does not fully explain why small samples and imprecision precluded recommendations for some treatments but not others; several operational parameters are not specified; and further-line treatment is outside the first batch.

titre: Who with OCD gets referred? A 10-point deprivation gap in English primary care records
resume: BACKGROUND: Psychological treatment and SSRIs are both first-line options for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), but whether people in deprived areas receive the same kind of care is unknown. NICE has published tables from English primary care records (CPRD Aurum) for two possibly overlapping cohorts: 20,253 people diagnosed within three years and 7,271 newly diagnosed.AIMS: To establish whether deprivation is associated with which care is recorded, mental health referral or SSRI prescribing, in adults and children.METHOD: We verified NICE's 1,171 values, rebuilt counts from rounded percentages, repeated every test over all admissible counts with multiplicity, clustering and missing-data sensitivity analyses, and compared findings with national prescribing, NHS Talking Therapies data and 25 published studies.RESULTS: Among newly diagnosed adults, 42% in the most deprived fifth had a mental health referral recorded, against 52% in the least, while SSRI prescribing barely differed (61% against 62%). In the three-year cohort, referral was 41% against 48% and SSRI prescribing higher in the most deprived fifth (54% against 49%). The two outcomes' slope indices differed by 17.0 percentage points (three-year cohort; Holm-adjusted P < 0.001) and 15.5 (newly diagnosed; Holm-adjusted P = 0.041; Bonferroni 0.082). NICE's comorbidity-adjusted estimates were similar. In newly diagnosed children, exploratory analyses showed referral of 46% against 54% (odds ratio 0.70 to 0.75), and lower SSRI prescribing in Asian than White children (0.60 to 0.65). In national NHS Talking Therapies data, OCD formed a smaller share of anxiety referrals in areas whose referrals came more from deprived neighbourhoods (Spearman's rho −0.48), unlike generalised anxiety disorder.CONCLUSIONS: In what are, to our knowledge, England's only national primary care data on OCD and BDD, deprived areas had less recorded mental health referral but no less SSRI prescribing: equal prescribing should not be read as equal care. Child differences need confirmation; linked records could show whether the gap is in treatment received.

titre: Food Intolerance in Irritable Bowel Syndrome: Getting Right Dietary Advice
resume: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is one of the most common GI/neuro disorders. In a 2025 meta-analysis of 96 studies from 52 countries, the pooled prevalence was estimated at 14.1%, with variations in prevalence rates depending on the diagnostic criteria, subtype, and region [1]. Many patients will have the obvious, and about 85-90% of patients will identify specific foods that trigger symptoms [2]. That's why IBS sufferers limit themselves as far as eating is concerned. There is also a link between food intolerance and IBS symptoms and psychological problems and quality of life [3] – taste is not the only thing. The difference between food intolerance and food allergy is that food intolerance does not always indicate food allergy. A non-immunological response which is usually dose-dependent. Small quantities are acceptable; higher quantities will lead to bloating, pain, or alteration in bowel movement [2]. The suspects are fermentable carbohydrates (FODMAPs), lactose, fructose, gluten and histamine, as well as, somewhat speculatively, food additives. It is still under investigation how foods cause symptoms. They are probably related to luminal fermentation, distension, activation of mucosal immunity, activation of mast cells, and gut-brain signaling, among other processes [2, 4]. This complexity also sets up a diagnostic maelstrom. When symptoms suggest lactose intolerance, a breath test is acceptable, and it is a common misdiagnosis of IBS [1]. Non-celiac gluten sensitivity is mainly a diagnosis of exclusion, and symptoms might be related not to gluten, but to the FODMAP content [2]. The low-FODMAP diet is the most evidence-based dietary approach to IBS and should be discontinued if a clinical response is not achieved, according to the American Gastroenterological Association. It asserts that the pros and cons of a gluten-free diet are not yet certain [5]. The low FODMAP diet is also second-line in Italian consensus guidelines, which are also complex and involve nutritional risks [2, 6]. Although it has long been discredited, a recent multicenter, sham-controlled study reported that the food-specific IgG test-guided elimination diet could achieve a primary pain endpoint in 59.6% of patients compared to 42.1% of those on a sham diet, and that the most significant differences were seen in the constipation-predominant and mixed IBS groups [7]. This is an important indicator, but there was less adherence in the active arm, the mechanism has not yet been explained, and there was no endorsement of IgG testing from societies at the time of the 2024 review [2]. While it awaits replication, it should reside in trials and not as routine practice. The job that lies before them is not to pick the correct diet, but to provide any diet in a safe manner. Unsupervised elimination can lead to nutrient deficiencies (e.g., calcium and vitamin D avoidance) and to developing a fear of food and restrictive eating patterns [2]. The AGA and the Italian guidelines emphasize a dietitian-driven individualized approach, structured reintroduction, and a strategy to discontinue what is unhelpful [2, 5]. Future research priorities should focus on developing improved biomarkers to detect intolerances, longer trials examining the relationship of nutritional adequacy and microbiome responses, and research in populations that consume diets different than the Western and Mediterranean diets that have been studied most in the literature. Clinicians need to confirm patients' food-related symptoms rather than confirming all the restrictions, and should not get caught up in the commercialization of the testing that has not been proven.

titre: Talabalarda ta’sirlangan ichak sindromi belgilari va psixoemotsional holat o‘rtasidagi bog‘liqlik
resume: The article examines the relationship between irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and the psycho-emotional state of students. An online survey was conducted as part of the study, in which 56 students took part. Based on the survey results, the relationship between symptoms characteristic of irritable bowel syndrome, stress, anxiety, mood changes and other psycho-emotional factors was analyzed. The results make it possible to assess the interrelation between IBS symptoms and the psycho-emotional state.
revue: Partner conferences of the International Scientific Journal Research Focus

titre: Digital technology use and disorders of gut–brain interaction: a scoping review
resume: This scoping review will map the evidence on associations between digital technology use, including technology-related stress, and disorders of gut–brain interaction (DGBI) such as functional dyspepsia, irritable bowel syndrome, and functional abdominal pain. Following JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR, we will search Scopus and PubMed, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation searching. Two reviewers will independently screen records in Rayyan. We will chart populations, exposures (e.g., technostress, problematic smartphone or social media use, screen time, cyberchondria), DGBI outcomes, study designs, and pathways examined (e.g., sleep, eating behaviour, autonomic function, anxiety). Results will be presented as an evidence map, a narrative synthesis, and an integrative, hypothesis-generating framework. The full protocol is attached.

titre: Perceived Stress and Irritable Bowel Syndrome–Compatible Symptoms Among Turkish Medical Students Without a Prior Diagnosis: A Cross-Sectional Study
resume: Objective: To estimate the frequency of symptoms compatible with the Rome IV criteria for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and examine their association with perceived stress among Turkish medical students without a prior physician-confirmed IBS diagnosis. Methods: This cross-sectional online survey evaluated 1100 Turkish medical students from June to July 2026. Participation was voluntary. Students with a prior physician-confirmed IBS diagnosis were excluded. Data collected anonymously included demographics, lifestyle, Rome IV-based symptoms, and the 10-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10). Results: Out of 362 respondents, 54 with prior IBS and 34 with incomplete surveys were excluded, leaving 274 students in the analytic sample. Forty-two students met the criteria for IBS compatibility (15.3%). No significant differences were identified for sex, smoking, coffee intake, exercise, body mass index, or academic year. Energy drink consumption showed an overall association with symptoms (P = .03). Symptom prevalence varied across perceived stress categories (overall P = .02); however, the crude high- vs low-stress comparison was imprecise (OR, 4.00; 95% CI, 0.80-20.04). In multivariable analysis, each 1-point increase in PSS-10 score was associated with greater adjusted odds of IBS-compatible symptoms (aOR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.03-1.15; P = .003). Energy drink use at least once weekly was also independently associated with higher adjusted odds of symptoms (aOR, 2.41; 95% CI, 1.06-5.48; P = .04). Conclusion: IBS-compatible symptoms were reported by 15.3% of medical students without a prior diagnosis. Higher perceived stress and weekly energy drink use were independently associated with symptom status. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to establish temporality.

titre: OpenGut: An Open-Source Platform for Gut-Computer Interaction Research
resume: Researchers are increasingly exploring the gut as a human-computer interface due to its gut-brain axis, linking physiological states with emotion and cognition. Despite its potential, the gut research space remains highly fragmented and underexplored. This is largely due to the absence of open and accessible hardware and software tools that could enable systematic investigation across disciplines and communities. To address this gap, we conducted semi-structured interviews with six experts to identify pain points in using existing platforms. Based on the themes identified, we formulated a set of requirements, and developed OpenGut, a rapid prototyping platform for gut research. Our open source platform consists of three main components: a wearable hardware platform for data capture and playback, a graphical user interface for visualization and analysis, as well as accompanying documentation for platform setup and customization. We perform technical evaluation of OpenGut for its signal quality, noise suppression, as well as outline potential usage scenarios for gut research.
revue: ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST)

titre: Urinary Microbiota-Derived Metabolites in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of p-Cresol, p-Cresyl Sulfate and Indoxyl Sulfate
resume: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent difficulties in social communication and interaction, along with restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour. Emerging evidence suggests that alterations in the gut microbiota and their metabolic activity may contribute to the pathophysiology of ASD through interactions involving the gut–brain axis. Among the various microbiota-derived metabolites, p-cresol, p-cresyl sulfate, and indoxyl sulfate have attracted increasing attention because of their potential neuroactive properties, associations with intestinal microbial composition, and possible implications for neurodevelopment and behavioural functioning. This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to comprehensively evaluate and quantitatively synthesize the available evidence on urinary concentrations of p-cresol, p-cresyl sulfate, and indoxyl sulfate in children with ASD compared with typically developing children or other relevant control populations. The study will systematically identify, critically appraise, and synthesize observational studies reporting urinary concentrations of these metabolites, with the primary objective of determining whether their levels differ significantly between children with ASD and controls. Secondary objectives include evaluating metabolite-specific differences, exploring potential sources of heterogeneity across studies, and examining associations between metabolite concentrations and clinical or demographic characteristics, including age, sex, ASD severity, gastrointestinal symptoms, and relevant analytical and methodological factors, where data are available. A systematic search will be conducted across relevant electronic databases, and eligible studies will be selected according to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Quantitative synthesis will be performed using appropriate meta-analytic methods, with effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals calculated according to the reported data and measurement characteristics. Heterogeneity will be assessed using statistical measures, and subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, and meta-regression will be considered where sufficient data are available. The methodological quality and certainty of evidence will also be evaluated using appropriate assessment frameworks. The anticipated outcome of this review is to clarify whether urinary microbiota-derived metabolites represent reproducible biochemical differences in children with ASD and to assess their potential relevance as candidate biomarkers. By synthesizing the existing evidence, this study may contribute to a better understanding of microbiota-related metabolic alterations in ASD, identify important research gaps, and inform future investigations into the gut–brain axis, metabolic profiling, and potential diagnostic or therapeutic applications. The findings will be interpreted cautiously, considering the observational nature of the available evidence and the potential influence of confounding factors.

titre: Minimally Invasive Management of Gastrointestinal Malignancies: Current Laparoscopic Practices and Oncological Outcomes
resume: Minimally invasive approaches have increasingly replaced conventional open surgery in the surgical treatment of gastrointestinal (GI) malignancies in recent years. Early concerns regarding oncological safety, including port-site metastasis and peritoneal tumor dissemination, have been largely resolved by robust evidence from large-scale randomized controlled trials (RCTs). These studies demonstrate that laparoscopic and robotic platforms provide oncological outcomes equivalent to those of open surgery. Current minimally invasive procedures strictly adhere to established surgical standards. By successfully integrating the “no-touch” isolation principle, central vascular ligation (CVL), complete mesocolic excision (CME), total mesorectal excision (TME), and D2 lymphadenectomy, these approaches consistently achieve R0 resection margins and favorable long-term survival outcomes. Furthermore, robotic systems overcome the limitations of conventional laparoscopy in confined anatomical spaces, facilitating autonomic nerve preservation and complex intracorporeal reconstructions. By minimizing abdominal wall trauma, minimally invasive surgery significantly reduces intraoperative blood loss, length of hospital stay, and postoperative pain. This accelerated functional recovery limits the systemic immunosuppressive stress response, improves patients’ postoperative quality of life, and most importantly, enables the timely and uninterrupted initiation of adjuvant oncological therapies, which are essential components of curative treatment. This book chapter provides a comprehensive, evidence-based overview of the paradigm shift toward minimally invasive surgical techniques. It critically evaluates their clinical recovery benefits, technological evolution, and oncological safety across a broad spectrum of procedures for esophageal, gastric, colorectal, pancreatic, and hepatic malignancies, underscoring their vital role in contemporary multidisciplinary oncology.

titre: Local practitioners use and share Hypno-Neuro-Imaginative Techniques (HNI) more than a year after training
resume: In conflict-affected South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Association Hypnose Humanitaire (AHH) and Hope Association of Africa implemented a locally led train-the-trainer model using Hypno-Neuro-Imaginative Techniques (HNI). These practices combine hypnosis, imagery and related self-regulation techniques adapted to the local context. This poster examines continued practice, onward sharing and support needs more than a year after training. Eight local professionals completed a four-day training in July 2025. Practitioners retained implementation decisions, with remote supervision from AHH. Informed consent was obtained and AHH conducted an internal ethics review. A descriptive self-report follow-up was completed in August–September 2026 by all seven surviving eligible practitioners, 13–14 months after training. One trainee had died during a field mission. All respondents reported sharing or guiding HNI with others (100%; 7/7), and 86% reported using at least one HNI technique weekly or more (6/7). Seventy-one percent perceived their general wellbeing as improving “a lot” since using HNI (5/7). This was a retrospective perception assessed through an improvement-framed question; deterioration was not directly assessed. Further training and guided practice were requested by 86% (6/7). Continued reported practice and sharing suggest a pathway for strengthening locally led psychosocial support. Interpretation is limited by the small cohort, self-report, possible recall and social-desirability bias, and the absence of a prospective outcome baseline or comparator. Beneficiary outcomes, teaching competence and reduced external dependence remain to be evaluated. Next steps include consolidating locally requested support and prospectively assessing staff wellbeing, beneficiary outcomes, teaching competence and external support requirements. Presented at the Geneva Health Forum 2026. Funding. The South Kivu programme received financial support from Fondation Philanthropique Famille Sandoz, Pully, Switzerland. Project details and collaboration: AHH — Geneva Health Forum 2026. Related publication: Python, A., Ribaux, C., and Hegyaljai Python, M. (2026). Hypno-Neuro-Imagination Techniques for Promoting Mental Health in Humanitarian-Peacebuilding Contexts. Chapter 21 in The Routledge International Handbook of Trauma-Responsive Peacebuilding, edited by Sara Clarke-Habibi and Cordula Reimann (Routledge). Publisher information.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Effect of acceptance and commitment therapy for anxiety disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis
resume: Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) has been increasingly applied in the treatment of anxiety disorders. However, evidence regarding its effectiveness specifically in patients with anxiety disorders has not been comprehensively synthesized. To systematically evaluate the intervention effect of acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) for anxiety disorders. Databases, including Web of Science, Embase, PubMed, the Cochrane Library, APA PsycNET and OVID MEDLINE, were systematically searched from their inception to November 2025. The risk of bias of included RCTs was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Meta-analysis was conducted via RevMan 5.3 software. A total of 8 randomized controlled trials involving 1173 patients were ultimately included. Compared with the WL, ACT was associated with reduced anxiety symptoms ( SMD = −0.67, 95% CI [−0.91, −0.43], p < 0.00001), improved quality of life ( SMD = 0.51, 95% CI [0.20, 0.83], p = 0.001) and improved psychological flexibility ( SMD = 0.63, 95% CI [0.47, 0.79], p < 0.00001) in patients with anxiety disorders. Subgroup analyses found no significant differences according to intervention format ( p = 0.11) or intervention duration ( p = 0.99). Compared with CBT, ACT showed no significant differences in anxiety symptoms ( SMD = 0.19, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.52], p = 0.26), quality of life ( SMD = −0.19, 95% CI [−0.39, 0.00], p = 0.06), or psychological flexibility ( SMD = 0.07, 95% CI [−0.30, 0.43], p = 0.73). The certainty of evidence ranged from low to moderate according to the GRADE assessment. Current evidence suggests that ACT may improve clinical outcomes in individuals with anxiety disorders compared with WL. The current evidence does not indicate a clear difference in treatment effects between ACT and CBT for anxiety disorders. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because the certainty of evidence ranged from low to moderate. Not applicable

titre: A comparative study of cognitive behavioural therapy versus relaxation therapy for fatigue and quality of life among teaching professionals with chronic fatigue syndrome
resume: Background: Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) is a complex and disabling condition characterized by persistent fatigue, cognitive difficulties, impaired functioning, and reduced quality of life. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) and Relaxation Therapy (RT) are non-pharmacological approaches that may support symptom management. This study compared the effectiveness of CBT and RT among teaching professionals with CFS. Methods: A prospective, randomized, comparative interventional study was conducted among 100 teaching professionals diagnosed with CFS. Participants were equally allocated to CBT (n=50) and RT (n=50) groups. Fatigue, psychological distress, functioning, work and social adjustment, and quality of life were assessed using the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI), Short Form-36 (SF-36), Depression Anxiety Stress Scale (DASS), Work and Social Adjustment Scale (WSAS), and WHOQOL. Structured group sessions were conducted for 8 weeks. Pre- and post-intervention outcomes were compared using appropriate statistical tests, with p<0.05 considered significant. Results: Both groups showed significant improvements in fatigue, psychological distress, physical functioning, work and social adjustment, and quality of life (p<0.001). Post-intervention FSS scores were lower in the CBT group than the RT group (3.67±0.52 vs. 4.70±0.51). SF-36 physical functioning (68.84±7.01 vs. 60.78±7.16) and WHOQOL scores (69.76±5.46 vs. 60.56±5.96) were also higher with CBT (p<0.001). Conclusion: Both CBT and RT improved psychological well-being, functioning, and quality of life. CBT may be a useful structured supportive intervention for symptom management in appropriately selected teaching professionals with CFS.
revue: International Journal of Research in Medical Sciences
