titre: Patient-specific subnetwork connectivity predicts deep brain stimulation response in obsessive-compulsive disorder
resume: UNLABELLED: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) can be an effective treatment for severe obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but response is variable, and objective, reliable predictors of who will respond positively are absent. In three individuals with OCD, we implanted intracranial electrodes across the cortico-striato-limbic network before DBS. Prefrontal gamma activity, most prominently in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), distinguished high-from low-symptom OCD states reproducibly across days. Acute stimulation of the ventral capsule/ventral striatum relieved OCD symptoms and, in one patient, significantly shifted this OFC gamma signal. Effective connectivity from therapeutic stimulation sites to these prefrontal regions defined three patient-specific OCD subnetworks; the baseline strength of the nucleus accumbens/ventral pallidum-OFC subnetwork predicted acute and long-term DBS response. Imaging-based modeling of current propagation in stimulation-activated ventral capsule to the OFC tracked acute response, suggesting that this prediction could be approximated from imaging alone. These findings outline a predictive, subnetwork-level framework for personalized DBS in OCD. HIGHLIGHTS: Prefrontal gamma encodes OCD symptom state and persists across recording daysAcute VC/VS stimulation relieves symptoms and can shift the prefrontal gamma signalBaseline subnetwork connectivity predicts acute and long-term DBS responseModeled ALIC-to-OFC tract activation approximates this prediction from imaging. IN BRIEF: Scangos and colleagues mapped three patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder with intracranial electrodes before deep brain stimulation. Prefrontal gamma activity tracked symptom state, and baseline connectivity from stimulation sites to these prefrontal regions predicted acute and long-term stimulation response. Modeled activation of ALIC-to-OFC tracts was associated with response, offering a route to this prediction from imaging alone.
revue: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences

titre: Adhesive small bowel obstruction in a 3-year-old child with history of necrotizing enterocolitis: a case report
resume: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO) is a serious complication following abdominal surgery in children, yet its presenting symptoms often mimic non-surgical conditions such as viral mesenteric adenitis and functional constipation. This diagnostic challenge is particularly acute in young children with a history of neonatal intestinal surgery who cannot reliably communicate their symptoms. This case report describes a former extreme preterm infant with surgical history of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) who presented with acute abdominal pain and was found to have complete mechanical small bowel obstruction due to postoperative adhesions. The objective is to highlight the diagnostic pitfalls in this population and to describe an unusual postoperative course complicated by three concurrent infections. CASE PRESENTATION: A 3-year-7-month-old former preterm girl (23 weeks gestation) with a history of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) requiring jejunal resection and stoma closure presented with one day of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and constipation. Initial ultrasound showed reactive mesenteric lymph nodes and fecal loading, suggesting mesenteric adenitis and constipation. However, given her surgical history, she was admitted for observation. Abdominal x-ray revealed small bowel dilatation with air-fluid levels, and contrast-enhanced CT confirmed complete mechanical small bowel obstruction with pneumatosis intestinalis. She underwent emergent laparotomy, which revealed extensive adhesive bands causing obstruction without volvulus, and adhesiolysis was performed without complication. On postoperative day 17, she developed a one-day fever. Workup revealed three concurrent infections: ESBL-producing Escherichia coli urinary tract infection, adenovirus, and Entamoeba histolytica/dispar. She was treated with intravenous meropenem and metronidazole and recovered fully. CONCLUSION: Children with prior intestinal surgery can present with acute abdominal pain that mimics non-surgical conditions such as mesenteric adenitis and constipation while having a complete adhesive small bowel obstruction requiring emergent surgery. Normal or equivocal ultrasound findings do not exclude this diagnosis, and a low threshold for CT is essential. Postoperative fever in such patients warrants a broad infectious workup, as multiple concurrent pathogens may coexist.

titre: From gut dysbiosis to synaptic dysfunction in insomnia-associated depression: immune mechanisms and nutritional interventions
resume: Insomnia and depression frequently coexist, yet their shared biological mechanisms have not been systematically integrated, limiting the development of targeted preventive and therapeutic strategies. Growing evidence identifies immune dysregulation as a key link between insomnia and depression, with the microbiota-gut-brain axis providing an important mechanistic framework. This review summarizes how insomnia induced gut microbiota alterations disrupt intestinal homeostasis, promote peripheral and central inflammation, and impair synaptic function during depression. It also discusses dietary interventions, food derived bioactive compounds, probiotics, and other microbiota targeted strategies. Targeting microbiota mediated immune pathways may provide new opportunities for the prevention and treatment of insomnia related depression.

titre: Slow power-envelope associations among brain, heart, and gut signals during sleep: an exploratory multivariate transfer entropy study
resume: Sleep and the brain-gut axis both involve the coordinated regulation of the central nervous system (CNS), autonomic nervous system (ANS), and enteric nervous system. Although the role of the brain-gut axis in sleep regulation is increasingly recognized, the dynamic information flow and its directionality among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep remain unclear as statistical associations. In this study, based on overnight sleep data from 24 healthy subjects, we simultaneously collected occipital electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram, and bowel sound signals, constructed a multimodal physiological signal analysis framework, and employed a multivariate transfer entropy method based on non-uniform embedding and k-nearest neighbor estimation to systematically quantify directed statistical associations at the level of slow power envelope co-modulations among the brain, heart, and gut systems within the framework of sleep staging. The results reveal a consistent pattern of directed statistical associations: information transfer from heart to brain, brain to gut, and heart to gut consistently exceeds that in the reverse directions across all sleep stages. Sleep-stage dynamics further dissociate within-system from inter-system information flow: internal information exchange within the brain and gut intensifies with sleep depth and weakens during REM, whereas inter-system pathways show divergent stage-dependent patterns: heart-to-brain flow increases from light to deep sleep, while heart-to-gut and brain-to-gut flow are suppressed during deep sleep. At the frequency-band level, the brain, heart, and gut each exhibit dynamically reorganized source-receiver roles across sleep stages, with specific frequency bands contributing differentially to each inter-system pathway depending on sleep stage. This study identifies exploratory statistical patterns of directional information flow among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep, providing hypothesis-generating observations for future studies on sleep and multi-organ interactions. These directed associations do not establish anatomical pathways, causal regulation, or clinical biomarkers, and should be regarded as exploratory.

titre: Yoga-Based Somatic Avatar Training for Alexithymia: Improving Distress Tolerance in College Students
resume: Introduction The difficulty of identifying and describing feelings (alexithymia) has been associated with problematic coping strategies (e.g. drinking) in college students. Expanding on prior work, the present study explored whether a novel two-week Somatic Avatar (SA) training would improve emotion regulation in college students and if the effect differed between students with varied levels of alexithymia. Method Sixteen college students ( M age = 22.88; 81% non-Hispanic White) completed a two-week protocol that entailed four days of yoga training paired with three days of processing an individualized and animated avatar of their yoga practice. Participants completed demographic questions, the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness scale (MAIA-2), and the Toronto Alexithymia Scale - 20 (TAS - 20) at baseline. They also completed baseline and exit assessments of the Distress Tolerance Scale (DTS). Median split groupings fell naturally in the moderate and high ranges of the TAS-20. Findings After controlling for interoception, a mixed-model analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) showed a significant effect of alexithymia on distress tolerance change scores from pre- to post- SA training, with participants endorsing moderate alexithymia ( p = .006) demonstrating greater improvement in distress tolerance than participants with high alexithymia ( p = .589), F (1, 13) = 6.346, p = .026, partial η2 = .328. Discussion Results suggested that the novel SA training may improve distress tolerance in those who struggle to identify their emotions. Future research should experimentally manipulate the length of training and increase the sample size to assess the effects of training among individuals with high alexithymia.

titre: Job Coaching and Smartphone-Based Cognitive Behavioral Techniques for Returning to Work and Coping With Unemployment (DRIVEN): Randomized Controlled Trial
resume: BACKGROUND: Unemployment has economic consequences and is associated with emotional distress and impairment. Joblessness is often associated with depression, leading to a vicious cycle of reduced drive to seek work, deepening financial stress, and worsening depression. Few scalable interventions exist that integrate job-search strategies with cognitive behavioral techniques. OBJECTIVE: The study aimed to determine the efficacy of a Distress-Informed Return-to-Work Intervention (DRIVEN). The primary hypothesis was that DRIVEN would be more efficacious than the control condition in improving job-search behavior. Secondary analyses examined job attainment, depression, and positive affect. METHODS: A randomized controlled trial was conducted from August 2023 to September 2024. Assessments were at baseline, weeks 1 through 6, and 8 and 16 weeks postintervention. Participants were a nationwide sample of unemployed job seekers aged 18 years or older who had never earned more than US $100,000 in a year. Participants received either (1) DRIVEN, which included 6 weeks of cognitive behavioral exercises in a mobile app combined with three 1-hour coaching sessions over videoconference or (2) emailed articles containing job-search advice. Primary outcome measures were subscales of a modified Job Search Behavior Scale (preparatory and active job search). Secondary outcomes included job attainment and mental health outcomes. RESULTS: Participants were a nationwide sample (N=126; mean age 33.6, SD 6.6 y), including 62 (49.2%) females. During the acute treatment phase, mixed-effects linear models showed that for DRIVEN, preparatory job-search behavior increased by an estimated 0.053 (95% CI 0.031-0.076) units per day from baseline, which was a larger effect than in the control condition (0.011, 95% CI -0.011 to 0.033 units per day; P=.008). Active job-search behavior increased by 0.061 (95% CI 0.038-0.084) units per day from baseline, which was significantly larger than in the control group (point estimate: 0.025, 95% CI 0.001-0.047; P=.03). Depression decreased more in the DRIVEN group vs control (DRIVEN point estimate=-0.214, 95% CI -0.255 to -0.172 vs control group point estimate=-0.122, 95% CI -0.163 to -0.081; P=.002), and participants were more likely to get a job in the DRIVEN group (68.3% vs 50.8%; P=.046). Self-report outcomes did not significantly differ during the follow-up periods. CONCLUSIONS: DRIVEN was superior to emailed job-search advice for the primary outcome (job-search behavior) and secondary outcomes (job attainment, depression, and positive affect). This intervention may be beneficial for distressed unemployed individuals seeking work.

titre: Ceruloplasmin in Disorders of the Nervous System
resume: Ceruloplasmin (Cp) is a multicopper ferroxidase that links copper handling, iron export, and redox homeostasis. Within the nervous system, these functions are critical because disruption of iron and copper balance can amplify oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and neuronal vulnerability. Although Cp has long been studied as a circulating biomarker, most reports characterize it only by protein concentration, leaving its enzymatic and structural status comparatively unexplored. Here, we synthesize human literature on Cp across major neurological disorders, with attention to studies that assess Cp's ferroxidase activity, oxidation, fragmentation, and copper-binding state alongside its circulating levels. The evidence is by far most extensive in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, which together account for the majority of the reviewed literature: reduced ferroxidase activity, increased Cp oxidation, and altered non-Cp-bound copper are repeatedly linked to disease severity, regional iron accumulation, and biomarker-defined patient subgroups; in several studies, these alterations were independent of total Cp concentration. A smaller but growing body of evidence in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, essential tremor, and the cerebellar ataxias points to a related pattern of Cp-linked iron mishandling contributing to neuronal vulnerability. Preliminary findings from a few small studies in schizophrenia and a single study in obsessive-compulsive disorder further suggest that circulating Cp levels track systemic inflammatory and oxidative states in these conditions. From these investigations, a picture emerges where Cp's functional and structural integrity, rather than its abundance alone, is the more informative correlate of disease-relevant metal dyshomeostasis, most clearly demonstrated in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Based on this body of work, we propose that future studies adopt combined assessments of Cp quantity and function to clarify disease-specific Cp signatures and to evaluate whether correcting Cp activity or copper/iron imbalance can improve outcomes.

titre: Selective upregulation of histamine H3 receptor expression in postmortem dorsolateral prefrontal cortex tissue in compulsive disorders: a pilot study
resume: BACKGROUND: Compulsive disorders encompass clinically distinct conditions involving repetitive behaviours and impaired behavioural control, with partially overlapping neurobiological mechanisms. Although prevailing models emphasise cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuitry and monoaminergic signalling, their molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. The brain histamine system, particularly the histamine H3 receptor (H3R), modulates cortical signalling through presynaptic regulation of histamine and other neurotransmitters but remains underexplored in compulsive disorders. METHODS: We conducted a hypothesis-driven transcriptomic analysis of postmortem dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) samples from individuals with compulsive disorders, comprising obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD), and tic/Tourette syndrome, and non-psychiatric controls, using publicly available microarray data. Core histamine pathway genes were examined using regression models adjusted for demographic, postmortem, and technical covariates. HRH3 was designated as the primary gene of interest, with multiple-testing correction applied to secondary pathway genes. RESULTS: HRH3 expression was increased in the DLPFC of individuals with compulsive disorders relative to controls (η² = 0.035, p = 0.033), with anecdotal Bayesian evidence for a group effect (BF₁₀ = 2.96). No other histamine pathway gene differed significantly after multiple-testing correction. HRH4 nevertheless showed an exploratory signal with anecdotal Bayesian evidence (BF₁₀ = 1.20), while Bayesian analyses of the remaining genes favoured the null model. CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide preliminary evidence for increased HRH3 expression in the DLPFC in a diagnostically heterogeneous compulsive-disorders sample, alongside an exploratory HRH4 signal. The functional and causal significance of HRH3 upregulation cannot be determined from bulk-tissue transcriptomic data. Independent replication and cell-type-resolved, receptor-level, and functional studies are required to clarify the role of histaminergic mechanisms in compulsive disorders.

titre: A two year clinical, immunological and gut-brain-axis prospective study to predict treatment response to cladribine tablets in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis
resume: INTRODUCTION: In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) it is challenging to predict which person will benefit from a certain therapy, such as cladribine tablets (CladT). This study aimed to obtain a better understanding of the interaction between the gut-brain axis and CladT to improve treatment response prediction. METHODS: In this multicenter, prospective, observational study, we included 81 people with RRMS starting CladT. We assessed the clinical, immunological and microbiological profiles at baseline and after 3, 12 and 24 months, and compared results between responders and non-responders, classified based on inflammatory disease activity and disability progression (NEDA-3). RESULTS: A total of 35 of 81 (47%) participants were responders. We found no differences in immune cell profiles between responders and non-responders. Network analysis revealed more positive correlations between immune cell clusters within the same parent cluster and a stronger negative correlation between CD8+ T cells and myeloid cells in responders. Microbiological analyses showed that fecal alpha diversity, both overall and for Bacteroidetes, as well as the relative abundance of the species Bacteroides caccae and Prevotella copri in fecal samples, are associated with treatment response to CladT. DISCUSSION: Although we found a trend toward more coordinated immune reorganization in CladT responders, and identified fecal alpha diversity and fecal Bacteroides caccae and Prevotella copri as associated with treatment response, we could not develop a reliable model to predict treatment response before or shortly after the start of CladT. Our results warrant further investigation in larger cohorts.

titre: The gut-brain-vascular axis: converging neuroinflammatory and hypertension-mediated pathways from gut dysbiosis to cognitive decline
resume: Hypertension and cognitive decline are major public health burdens, and both have been associated with gut microbiome dysbiosis. We propose the gut-brain-vascular axis as a testable synthesis in which dysbiosis may contribute to cognitive decline through two converging routes: direct neuroinflammatory signaling and hypertension-mediated cerebrovascular injury. In the proposed direct route, intestinal barrier dysfunction, lipopolysaccharide translocation, altered microbial metabolites, microglial activation, and vagal signaling may promote neuroinflammation. In the indirect route, dysbiosis-associated metabolites, immune activation, autonomic imbalance, and endothelial injury may contribute to hypertension, which is linked to cerebral small vessel disease, impaired cerebral autoregulation, neurovascular uncoupling, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction. The component relationships are supported to different degrees, but the complete temporal pathway and an interaction between the two routes have not been established in humans. This narrative review synthesizes gut-hypertension, gut-cognitive, cerebrovascular, shared-mechanism, and therapeutic evidence and identifies the study designs needed to test the framework. Longitudinal cohorts and trials that measure microbiome, blood pressure, cerebrovascular, and cognitive outcomes together are required to determine whether the proposed routes occur independently, sequentially, or interactively.

titre: The Gut-Brain Homeostatic Continuum in Alzheimer's disease: a systems framework for physiological resilience and disease progression
resume: The gut-brain axis has substantially improved our understanding of Alzheimer's disease (AD) by highlighting the complex bidirectional interactions between the gastrointestinal tract, the microbiota and the central nervous system. Nevertheless, this framework does not fully explain why brain and organismal homeostasis can be maintained for decades despite the continuous and cumulative burden of aging, genetic susceptibility and environmental stressors, or why this resilience ultimately fails in some individuals. In this review, we propose the Gut-Brain Homeostatic Continuum (GBHC), a conceptual framework that extends the classical gut-brain axis into a dynamic, interconnected system of layered homeostatic mechanisms. Rather than viewing gut-brain interactions as parallel signaling routes, the GBHC emphasizes how the preservation of intestinal and blood-brain barrier integrity supports coordinated immune, metabolic and inter-organ regulation, which in turn contributes to systemic proteostasis and the trafficking and clearance of proteins. Through these interconnected processes, peripheral physiological states may influence the capacity of the brain to maintain homeostasis and resilience. Within this framework, AD is viewed as a progressive erosion of organismal resilience rather than the consequence of a single pathological pathway. We discuss how aging, genetic factors and the exposome may progressively challenge interconnected regulatory mechanisms, weakening the capacity to preserve homeostasis and increasing vulnerability to neurodegeneration. This perspective also suggests a complementary approach to biomarker discovery, focusing on multimodal signatures that capture biological trajectories and changes in regulatory capacity. Such signatures could integrate markers of barrier integrity and permeability, immune and metabolic regulation, microbial and host-derived metabolites, extracellular vesicle cargo, and proteostasis-related proteins, including established markers of neurodegeneration such as amyloid-β, phosphorylated tau and neurofilament light chain. Although several aspects of the GBHC remain hypothetical and require experimental validation, this framework provides an integrative model that complements current concepts of AD pathogenesis and opens new perspectives for multidisciplinary research and therapeutic innovation.

titre: Effects of eating behavior patterns and dietary habits on the therapeutic efficacy of Parkinson's disease medications: from phenomena, mechanisms to clinical applications
resume: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common progressive neurodegenerative disorder managed primarily through pharmacological dopamine replacement therapies-including levodopa (L-DOPA), dopamine receptor agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, COMT inhibitors, and novel non-dopaminergic agents like adenosine A2A receptor antagonists. However, long-term pharmacotherapy faces major challenges such as motor fluctuations, levodopa-induced dyskinesias, erratic gastrointestinal absorption, and inter-individual response variability. This review systematically synthesizes how dietary habits, macronutrient compositions, dietary patterns (e.g., Western, Eastern, Japanese, Vegetarian, Mediterranean/MIND, Ketogenic), and eating behaviors (such as restrictive eating, compulsive binge eating, and irregular meal timing) serve as critical extrinsic modulators of drug disposition and clinical performance. Multi-dimensional biological mechanisms underpin these interactions: competitive inhibition at LAT1 transporters by dietary large neutral amino acids (LNAAs), food-induced alterations in gastric emptying and hepatic/intestinal enzyme activity (e.g., CYP3A4, CYP1A2, UGT), neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress modulation via nutrient choices, and microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA) dynamics involving gut barrier integrity, microbial short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, and local bacterial enzymatic degradation of L-DOPA. In real world clinical practice, the absence of precision nutrition frameworks, protein-redistribution diets, targeted chronotherapeutic meal scheduling, and multidisciplinary nutritional support substantially hinders the effective translation of basic pharmacokinetic insights. Consequently, patients frequently encounter formidable clinical challenges, including destabilized pharmacokinetics, recurrent motor complications, and the inability to effectively delay disease progression.

titre: Akkermansia muciniphila improves synaptic remodeling and alleviates sepsis-associated cognitive dysfunction via regulating the gut-brain axis
resume: BACKGROUND: Sepsis-associated cognitive impairment (SACI) is a frequent long-term complication of sepsis characterized by hippocampal neuroinflammation, synaptic loss and gut microbial dysbiosis. Akkermansia muciniphila (AKK) possesses anti-inflammatory and intestinal barrier-protective functions, yet its role and mechanism in SACI remain poorly understood. METHODS: In this study, a CLP-induced septic mouse model was used to explore the protective effect of AKK. Behavioral tests were performed to evaluate anxiety and cognitive function. Hippocampal neuronal injury, microglial activation and synaptic plasticity were assessed by HE staining, immunofluorescence, Western blotting and TEM. Intestinal barrier function, gut microbiota composition and metabolic profiles were analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics, with FMT applied for mechanistic verification. RESULTS: AKK intervention remarkably alleviated anxiety-like behaviors and rescued cognitive deficits in septic mice. AKK inhibited microglial overactivation, activated the BDNF/P-TrkB pathway, and restored the expression of synaptic SYP and PSD95. Meanwhile, AKK preserved intestinal tight junction integrity, reshaped gut microbiota structure, and reversed sepsis-related metabolic disturbances. FMT further provided evidence that AKK-modulated gut microbiota improved survival and cognitive performance. CONCLUSION: In conclusion, AKK ameliorates SACI by suppressing hippocampal neuroinflammation, restoring synaptic plasticity and remodeling the microbiota-gut-brain axis, indicating its potential as a promising candidate for SACI intervention.

titre: Plant-derived nutrition and perimenopausal emotional health: current evidence and research priorities
resume: Perimenopause combines ovarian hormone variability with changes in stress regulation, inflammatory-redox balance, neuroplasticity, and gut-brain metabolism, creating a period of increased vulnerability to depressive symptoms, anxiety, irritability, and sleep disturbance. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on plant-derived foods, bioactives, dietary supplements, and standardized botanical preparations relevant to emotional health during the menopausal transition. Targeted searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Scopus identified literature published through 31 July 2026. Evidence was classified by consumed form and reproductive-stage directness and integrated across three regulatory axes: endocrine-stress regulation, immune-redox-neuroplasticity, and gut-brain-metabolic communication. Human evidence includes small randomized trials of standardized saffron, rhapontic rhubarb, fenugreek, ashwagandha, and shatavari preparations, with product-specific psychological-symptom signals, as well as a null Hypericum-Vitex trial. Evidence for plant-rich dietary patterns and isolated bioactives derives mainly from broader menopausal or adult populations. Across studies, reproductive stage, exposure composition, symptom endpoint, and preparation standardization emerge as key determinants of interpretation. Linking symptom clusters with proposed pathway involvement generates hypotheses for prospective phenotype-stratified nutrition trials. Future studies should combine reproductive staging using the Stages of Reproductive Aging Workshop + 10 (STRAW+10) framework, prespecified emotional outcomes, dietary assessment, standardized product characterization, exposure biomarkers, metabotype profiling, and safety monitoring. This framework positions plant-derived nutrition as a testable component of perimenopausal emotional-health research and functional-food development.

titre: Natural Medicines for Parkinson's Disease: A Bibliometric Analysis of Trends, Challenges, and Future Directions
resume: INTRODUCTION: Parkinson's disease is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder globally. Natural medicines are attracting attention as neuroprotective strategies due to multi-component and multi-target properties, yet a systematic bibliometric overview is lacking. This study reviews research trends and hotspots in natural medicines for Parkinson's disease from 2006 to 2025. METHODS: A systematic search in the Web of Science Core Collection (2006-2025) identified 1,245 relevant articles. Bibliometric tools analyzed collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence, and research frontiers, followed by qualitative synthesis. RESULTS: China and the United States are major contributors. Chinese institutions closely collaborate with partners such as Kyung Hee University in South Korea. Research hotspots have shifted from single-mechanism or single-target studies to multi-target mechanisms, intercellular interactions, and multi-system integration involving the gut-brain axis and neuroimmune modulation. Network pharmacology and microbiome research are emerging as new directions, driving convergence of neuropharmacology, microbiome science, systems biology, and computational biology. DISCUSSION: This paradigm shift supports recognizing Parkinson's disease as a multisystem dynamic network disorder rather than a focal neurodegenerative entity, aligning with multi-target properties of natural medicines. Clinical translation of natural products urgently requires standardized component databases and gut-brain axis-related biomarkers to enable transition from mechanistic research to precision therapy. CONCLUSION: This study provides the first systematic bibliometric overview of natural medicines in Parkinson's disease over the past two decades, revealing a paradigm shift from reductionist single-target approaches to holistic multi-target and multi-system strategies. These findings offer a valuable reference for neuropharmacological research on Parkinson's disease and clinical translation of natural products.

titre: Rhythmic dance interventions and dance/movement therapy for depression and anxiety: a structured narrative review of clinical evidence, candidate mechanisms, and implementation considerations
resume: BACKGROUND: This review synthesized evidence on rhythmic dance interventions (RDI) and dance/movement therapy (DMT) for depression and anxiety, clarified intervention boundaries, and proposed mechanism-informed and implementation-oriented recommendations. METHODS: A structured narrative review was conducted using targeted literature searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from inception to 11 September 2026, supplemented by citation tracing. Sources were selected for relevance to clinical evidence, candidate mechanisms, intervention reporting, safety considerations, and implementation issues. The review was designed as a narrative and translational synthesis rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis. RESULTS: Current evidence suggests that DMT and structured RDI may be associated with improvements in depressive symptoms, anxiety-related distress, stress, quality of life, and psychosocial functioning, although the evidence is heterogeneous and the most direct clinical evidence concerns DMT in adults with depression. Candidate mechanisms include rhythmic entrainment, behavioral activation, reward engagement, emotion regulation, interoceptive and autonomic regulation, social connectedness, and interpersonal co-regulation. However, direct mediation evidence is still insufficient, and key intervention features such as rhythm, synchrony, movement structure, interpersonal configuration, and reflective processing should be treated as reportable and potentially modifiable components rather than validated therapeutic dose parameters. CONCLUSIONS: RDI and DMT may represent promising complementary approaches for depression and anxiety, but they are not interchangeable and should not be regarded as substitutes for psychiatric, psychological, or medical care. Clearer intervention taxonomy, FITT + 3R reporting framework, mechanism-informed outcomes, adverse-event monitoring, and further evaluation of safety and implementation are needed to support responsible translation into healthcare and community settings.

titre: Long-term outcomes of nucleus accumbens/anterior limb of the internal capsule deep brain stimulation in treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder
resume: BACKGROUND: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a therapeutic option for carefully selected patients with severe, treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), but very long-term outcomes remain insufficiently characterized. We evaluated clinical outcomes after DBS targeting the nucleus accumbens/anterior limb of the internal capsule (NAcc/ALIC) over 3-21 years and described the trajectories of early responders, delayed responders, and non-responders. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort included 30 consecutive patients (17 women) who underwent NAcc/ALIC DBS between 2004 and 2022. Outcomes were assessed with the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) at baseline (T0), 1 year after surgery (T1), and the latest follow-up at ≥3 years (T2). Response was defined as a ≥35% reduction from baseline. Repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons was used to assess changes over time. RESULTS: Y-BOCS scores decreased significantly across T0, T1, and T2. At T2, 22 of 30 patients (73.3%) met the response criterion; eight were delayed responders. Of the 15 patients who met the response criterion at T1, 14 retained it at T2 and 1 did not. CONCLUSION: Clinically meaningful improvement was sustained at long-term follow-up, and some patients who had not responded after 1 year met the response criterion later. Once response was achieved, subsequent loss of response appeared uncommon in this cohort. The retrospective design and heterogeneous follow-up duration preclude causal conclusions regarding DBS or the temporal course of improvement.

titre: Ultrasonographic assessment of pelvic parameters associated with mode of delivery in Turkish pregnant women
resume: BACKGROUND: Pelvic morphology plays a crucial role in determining the course and outcome of labor. Ultrasonographic assessment offers a non-invasive and practical approach to evaluating pelvic morphology and pelvic adequacy. The aim of this study was to evaluate the relationship between ultrasonographic measurements of pelvic parameters-specifically the subpubic angle (SPA) and the obstetric conjugate diameter (OCD)- and the likelihood of vaginal delivery versus cesarean delivery due to cephalopelvic disproportion in Turkish nulliparous women. METHODS: This prospective cohort study included 267 nulliparous women with singleton, cephalic pregnancies at ≥ 37 weeks of gestation. Ultrasonographic measurements were performed prior to the onset of labor to assess the SPA and OCD. Maternal, fetal, and pelvic parameters were compared between women who had vaginal delivery and those who underwent cesarean delivery due to cephalopelvic disproportion. Additionally, correlations between pelvic measurements and maternal characteristics were assessed. RESULTS: Of the participants, 219 (82%) had vaginal deliveries, while 48 (18%) underwent cesarean section due to cephalopelvic disproportion. Mean SPA (94.88 ± 7.52° vs. 103.64 ± 7.27°; p < 0.001) and OCD (112.38 ± 8.71 mm vs. 121.29 ± 6.62 mm; p < 0.001) were significantly smaller in the cesarean group. ROC analysis demonstrated that both the SPA and OCD had good discriminatory ability for distinguishing vaginal delivery from cesarean delivery due to cephalopelvic disproportion (AUC: 0.788 and 0.794, respectively). The optimal cut-off values were 100.24° for SPA (81.3% sensitivity, 61.6% specificity) and 116.71 mm for OCD (81.3% sensitivity, 71.2% specificity). Cesarean delivery rates were significantly higher among patients with SPA and OCD values below these cut-off thresholds. A weak positive correlation was found between SPA and OCD (r = 0.269, p = 0.011), while maternal age, BMI, height, and gestational age showed no significant associations with pelvic measurements. CONCLUSION: A narrower subpubic angle and a shorter obstetric conjugate diameter, as measured by ultrasonography, were associated with cesarean delivery. These findings suggest that ultrasonographic pelvic measurements may provide useful, non-invasive information and may complement conventional obstetric assessment.

titre: Efficacy of Electronic Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Alone and Combined With Pharmacotherapy for Depression and Anxiety in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
resume: Electronic cognitive behavioral therapy (e-CBT) is a scalable intervention for anxiety and depressive disorders. While its efficacy against inactive controls is well documented, its comparative effectiveness against first-line pharmacotherapy remains critically underexplored. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO): CRD420261413686) of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing e-CBT with waitlist, active psychotherapy, usual care, or medication in adults with anxiety and depression. Effect sizes were pooled using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) adjustments. Outcomes were assessed using Hedges' g and risk ratios (RR), and evidence certainty was evaluated via the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. Twenty-two RCTs were included in the analysis. Compared to waitlist/attention controls (k, number of independent contrasts = 11), e-CBT demonstrated a large, statistically significant reduction in depression severity (Hedges' g, standardized mean difference = 0.91; 95% CI: 0.63 to 1.18). However, re-expression onto the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) scale yielded an absolute reduction (3.86 points) that fell below the pre-specified minimally important difference (MID) of 5 points. No clear difference was found between e-CBT and active face-to-face or bibliotherapy CBT (k = 3; g = 0.08; 95% CI: -0.59 to 0.75); the wide interval means equivalence could not be established. Adding e-CBT to usual care gave an imprecise, non-significant estimate (k = 3; g = 0.32; 95% CI: -1.41 to 2.05; p = 0.511) that neither confirms nor excludes a benefit. The network geometry revealed zero head-to-head RCTs comparing e-CBT monotherapy directly with antidepressant medication. Nineteen of the 22 trials (86%) were at high overall risk of bias, and funnel-plot asymmetry (Egger's test; p = 0.0056) suggested small-study effects, possibly including publication bias; most GRADE certainty ratings were very low. e-CBT is a scalable option that showed no clear difference from face-to-face CBT in a small number of trials, but its efficacy against inactive controls may be overestimated because of small-study effects and methodological limitations. A critical evidence gap exists regarding its comparative efficacy against pharmacotherapy, necessitating rigorous blinded head-to-head non-inferiority trials.

titre: Infection-related research in Parkinson's disease: an exploratory trends analysis
resume: BACKGROUND: Infection and Parkinson's disease (PD) appear to interact through complex mechanisms. Infection may promote the occurrence and progression of pathological processes related to PD, while PD and its associated dysfunctions may increase the risk of infection. This study depicts the evolution, thematic structure, and emerging directions of infection-related research in PD. METHODS: Publications related to infection and PD from 1999 to June 30, 2026 were retrieved from the WoSCC and Scopus databases. R software packages bibliometrix, CiteSpace, and VOSviewer were used for data analysis. RESULTS: The number of published studies on PD and infection showed a gradual upward trend and increased significantly after 2020. The United States published the largest number of documents (n = 509) and received the most citations (n = 33,628); China and the UK published 218 and 164 papers, respectively. The University of Florida is the most productive institution (n = 23). Dr. Rajesh Pahwa and Dr. Michael S. Okun are among the most productive authors (n = 12). Parkinsonism & Related Disorders (n = 59) and Movement Disorders (n = 46) are the most active journals in this field. The keyword analysis identified five main themes: infection exposure and clinical outcomes; infection-induced neuroinflammation; shared mechanisms of neurodegeneration; virus-related neurological manifestations and PD; and gut microbiota-gut-brain interactions involved in PD pathogenesis and treatment response. CONCLUSION: The research on infection and PD has developed rapidly, especially since the COVID-19 epidemic. This field is going beyond epidemiological association to explore how infection can trigger PD through neuroinflammation, α-synuclein (α-syn) pathology, the gut brain axis, and other factors. Infection management in patients with PD has also become an important clinical concern. This study reviews the development of this field, defines the emerging direction, and provides a reference for future mechanism research and clinical practice.

titre: Delivering online cognitive behavioral therapy to address mental health challenges in correctional workers: a randomized controlled trial
resume: BACKGROUND: Correctional workers (CWs), are frequently exposed to traumatic workplace events, placing them at higher risk of experiencing mental health disorders, including major depressive disorder (MDD), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Despite high prevalence of mental health challenges, CWs underutilize mental health services due to stigma, irregular work schedules, and accessibility issues. While cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is effective, it poses accessibility challenges. Electronic CBT (eCBT) offers a scalable, accessible alternative, but use among CWs remains underexplored. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of diagnosis-specific eCBT programs designed for CWs in reducing symptoms of MDD, GAD, and PTSD compared to treatment as usual (TAU). METHODS: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) was conducted with 84 CWs in Ontario, assigned to either eCBT (n=40) or TAU (n=44). The eCBT program provided diagnosis-specific modules with synchronous personalized feedback from care providers over 12-weeks via the Online Psychotherapy Tool (OPTT). Symptom severity was measured at baseline, week-6, and post-treatment using validated scales for depression, anxiety, PTSD, and quality-of-life. Data analysis included paired samples t-tests, mixed linear models, and effect size calculations (Cohen's d). RESULTS: The eCBT group exhibited significant reductions in symptom severity for depression, anxiety, and PTSD from baseline to post-treatment compared to TAU (p<0.01), with a moderate effect size (Cohen's d=0.68). Symptom severity decreased by 61.37% for eCBT versus 23.29% in TAU. Mixed linear models confirmed a significant treatment-by-time interaction, favoring eCBT (p<0.01). However, no significant differences in quality-of-life improvements were observed between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Diagnosis-specific eCBT programs are effective in reducing symptoms of depression, anxiety, and PTSD for CWs. The asynchronous, accessible format of eCBT addresses current key barriers. Future research should explore strategies to improve adherence and increase the accessibility of services for CWs.

titre: Research on the construction of an adaptive mindfulness-based cognitive therapy system based on large language models and its efficacy in addressing college students' anxiety
resume: To handle the problem of resource scarcity and lack of personalization and adaptability in the traditional approach to mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) in dealing with college students with anxiety disorders, this study proposes the use of the natural language interface and adaptability properties of large language models (LLMs) to come up with an intelligent college-level MBCT intervention system. To begin with, the system functional requirements and the logic of the system intervention were explained in line with the fundamental ideas of MBCT and the cognitive features of students with anxiety. Second, it was created through a four-stage adaptive architecture that includes perception analysis, intervention, and feedback, providing a dynamic process for user status identification, personal generation of intervention plans, and real-time optimization of the intervention process. Finally, there was a randomized controlled trial whose subjects were 120 college students with anxiety who were separated into an experimental group and a control group. The effectiveness of the intervention was assessed using tools such as the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS), and the Automatic Thoughts Questionnaire (ATQ). The findings indicated that the SAS score of the experimental group (38.26 ± 5.12) was significantly less than that of the control group (45.89 ± 6.34), the MAAS score (68.73 ± 7.25) was significantly higher than that of the control group (56.41 ± 8.13); and the ATQ score (42.15 ± 6.08) was significantly less than that of the control group. The study reveals that an adaptive MBCT system using large language models may be effective in reducing anxiety symptoms among college students, improving mindfulness, and enhancing cognitive processes, offering a new, readily available strategy for addressing anxiety in college students.

titre: A clinical laboratory test-wide association scan of polygenic scores identifies biomarkers of psychiatric disorders
resume: BACKGROUND: Psychiatric disorders pose a significant public health burden, and their complex genetic architecture underlies multiple biological pathways, contributing to a lack of diagnostic biomarkers. Laboratory-Wide Association Studies (LabWAS) leverage electronic health record laboratory data as intermediary phenotypes to link genetic risk to physiology. METHODS: Polygenic Scores (PGS) for 25 health-related, psychiatric, and substance use phenotypes were generated for individuals of African (AFR; N=10,473) and European (EUR, N=35,131) ancestry from the Penn Medicine Biobank. Laboratory data was prepared using the LabWAS pipeline, encompassing 78 laboratory tests and 6 vital signs. Linear regression models tested the association of each lab value with PGS adjusting for sex, age, and ten within-ancestry genetic principal components. RESULTS: Four PGS were significantly associated with at least one laboratory value in AFR individuals and 22 PGS in EUR individuals. In EUR individuals, psychiatric PGS partitioned into three physiological profiles: anxiety, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, major depressive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder shared a metabolic/inflammatory signature (higher BMI, glucose, and monocytes; lower high density lipoprotein cholesterol and oxygen saturation); anorexia nervosa, obsessive compulsive disorder, and schizophrenia were characterized by lower BMI; and bipolar disorder demonstrated a more circumscribed profile with lower electrolytes and renal makers. Substance use disorder PGS similarly clustered: tobacco use disorder and externalizing showed metabolic/inflammatory profiles; alcohol-related phenotypes showed lower red blood cell indices; and cannabis use disorder had a more circumscribed profile. CONCLUSIONS: LabWAS reveals physiologic signatures associated with genetic risk for psychiatric disorders, offering new biological insights into their pathology.

titre: Food allergy and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children: evidence and implications for pediatric allergy practice
resume: Families of children with food allergies (FA) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often ask whether the conditions are related and whether dietary changes could improve their children's attention or behavior. This narrative review examines FA-specific evidence and its implications for pediatric allergy practices, drawing on observational studies, reviews, clinical guidance, and contextual mechanistic research. One small FA-specific meta-analysis found no statistically significant association, whereas several individual observational studies reported positive associations. Differences in diagnostic definitions, reporting sources, temporal assessment, and confounder adjustment limited the ability to make comparisons. Studies of broader allergic phenotypes and Mendelian randomization provide no FA-specific causal estimate, and proposed microbiota-immune-brain pathways remain unconfirmed in humans. Restrictive or elimination diets should not be routinely recommended for ADHD because evidence of sustained benefit is limited, and additional restriction may compromise nutrition or worsen feeding difficulties, particularly in children already avoiding allergens. Pediatric allergy care should verify the FA diagnosis, preserve tolerated foods, monitor growth and dietary adequacy, and refer persistent attention or behavioral concerns for appropriate assessment. This review distinguishes direct FA evidence from broader allergy findings and relates these uncertainties to practical decisions about diagnosis, dietary restriction, and coordinated care.

titre: Symptomatic Post-anastomotic Blind Ileal Pouch
resume: Postsurgical blind pouch syndrome is an uncommon late complication of intestinal reconstruction caused by stasis within a poorly emptying bowel segment. Its manifestations range from chronic diarrhea and abdominal discomfort to bleeding, obstruction, inflammation, and perforation, while diagnosis may be difficult when the previous operative anatomy is unknown. We report the case of a 48-year-old man who presented with severe right-sided abdominal pain, distension, and peritoneal irritation three years after emergency bowel resection and an undocumented intestinal anastomosis following a motor vehicle collision. Since the previous operation, he had experienced frequent bowel movements and fecal urgency that substantially impaired his quality of life. Initial computed tomography and diagnostic laparoscopy failed to identify a definitive cause of his symptoms, and extensive adhesions prevented complete characterization of the reconstruction. Persistent severe pain, fever, and marked elevation of inflammatory markers prompted repeat exploration five days later. Laparotomy demonstrated a patent side-to-side ileocecal anastomosis associated with a markedly dilated and thickened blind ileal pouch and a separate atrophic terminal ileal remnant. The blind pouch was resected. Histopathological examination revealed superficial mucosal ulceration, muscular hypertrophy, edema, hemorrhage, focal liquefactive necrosis, and acute-on-chronic transmural inflammation without malignancy. Recovery was uneventful. At three-month follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic and medication-free, with normal bowel function and complete resolution of fecal urgency and abdominal pain. This case highlights that a postsurgical blind ileal pouch may cause severe acute inflammation even without gross perforation and should be considered in patients with unexplained abdominal symptoms after intestinal reconstruction.

titre: From bodily signals to safe action: an interoceptive self-regulation loop for whole-person health
resume: Health systems increasingly measure physiological and behavioral outputs, yet the transition from a bodily signal to a safe, feasible decision remains difficult to specify. We propose the Interoceptive Self-Regulation Loop (ISRL), a provisional framework linking context and exposure, bodily state, interoceptive sampling, appraisal, action, and feedback. Four measurement strata distinguish contextual inputs, functional changes, subjective signals, and clinical indicators. A safety gate operates throughout the loop through condition-specific rules, named clinical responsibility, and documented escalation and follow-up. Its purpose is to support decisions without transferring diagnosis or risk assessment to individuals. The proposed contribution is an explicit, testable account of cross-stratum discordance and evidence-responsive appraisal, rather than the invention of interoception, triage, or behavior-change support. We specify independent candidate measures of appraisal flexibility and action proportionality, illustrate the safety gate using recent-onset chest pain, and compare ISRL with a simpler combination of the common-sense model, COM-B, and identical triage guidance. Six propositions distinguish supporting predictions from the more discriminating tests of discordance, flexibility, and timely care. A bounded initial research program concerns adults in primary care, daily observations, and episode-level decisions, with prospective validation before interventional use. Repeated failure to improve prediction or decisions over the active comparator, despite adequate measurement and precision, would count against retaining ISRL as a distinct framework in that setting. Clinical safety, monitoring burden, cultural adaptation, and unequal access are explicit evaluation outcomes. ISRL remains a theory for investigation, not a validated diagnostic tool or treatment.

titre: A systematic review of qualitative research of eating disorders in autistic adults: convergent and divergent experiences
resume: INTRODUCTION: Autism and eating disorders frequently co-occur, yet relatively little is known about how autistic adults experience eating disorders. METHODS: This systematic review synthesised qualitative evidence to explore the lived experiences of autistic adults with an eating disorder and inform autism-informed clinical practice. A systematic search identified 13 eligible studies, which were appraised using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) Qualitative Checklist and synthesised using thematic synthesis. RESULTS: Findings were organised into three themes: eating disorder experiences cannot be understood independently of autistic ways of processing the world; recovery is enabled through developing self-understanding and integrating autism into personal identity; and recovery is facilitated when support aligns with autistic needs rather than neurotypical assumptions. Autistic characteristics, particularly sensory sensitivities, interoceptive differences, and a preference for predictability, fundamentally shaped the development, maintenance, and recovery of eating disorders. Sensory-driven food restriction was frequently experienced independently of body image concerns, highlighting potential conceptual overlap with Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID). DISCUSSION: Autistic adults described eating disorders as inseparable from their autistic experience, indicating the need for a paradigm shift from conceptualising autism and eating disorders as co-occurring conditions towards a model rooted in lived phenomenological experience. Clinical assessment, formulation, and intervention should adopt autism-informed, individualised approaches that recognise sensory processing and interoceptive differences, while future research should examine these mechanisms across a broader range of eating disorder diagnoses. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420261375735.

titre: School-based mental health support for students with intellectual disability in the Middle East and North Africa: a 26-year scoping review
resume: UNLABELLED: Students with intellectual disability (ID) in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region face significant mental health challenges, yet the extent and nature of school-based support for them remain unclear. This scoping review mapped the English-language evidence on school-based mental health support for this population. Six sources were searched for studies published between January 2000 and May 2026. The initial search identified 255 records, of which 210 were screened, and an update search identified one further study. Six studies were included; two met all eligibility criteria and four met them in part. One study evaluated an intervention, Cognitive-Behavioral Play Therapy, and reported improved self-esteem; it was delivered in residential welfare centers rather than schools. One study reported a strong association between bullying victimization and depressive symptoms among students with mild ID. Four studies surveyed 1,037 practitioners in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates, three of them in mixed disability populations. Practitioners reported moderate and uneven preparedness in behavioral assessment, social skills training, trauma-informed practice, and mental health support, and self-efficacy and perceived school support were associated with teachers' attitudes toward supporting student mental health. No school-delivered intervention was identified, and no included study reported follow-up or a family component. Overall, the English-language evidence identified by this review is small, heterogeneous, and geographically concentrated, and few students with ID took part directly. The findings point to a need for culturally adapted school-based interventions, stronger mental health content in teacher preparation, and explicit inclusion of students with ID in regional education and mental health frameworks. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/HJQMR.

titre: Registered therapeutic trials in adults with functional dyspepsia: a scoping review of design and registration characteristics
resume: BACKGROUND: Functional dyspepsia (FD) affects quality of life and healthcare use. Previous studies have examined individual aspects of FD trial methodology, but a broad account of registered therapeutic trials is still needed. This scoping review mapped their design and registration characteristics to inform future trial design and reporting. METHODS: WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) was searched on 4 September 2026 for registered therapeutic interventional trials in adults with FD. Records referring to the same trial were linked into one trial unit. Two reviewers independently screened trial groups and assessed trial-level eligibility. Corresponding source registries were checked when ICTRP information was missing, incomplete, or inconsistent. Analyses were descriptive. RESULTS: The review included 421 underlying registered trials, of which 191 (45.4%) were first registered during 2021-2026. Randomized allocation was recorded in 315 trials (74.8%), and 324 (77.0%) used parallel-group designs. Registration preceded the recorded study start date in 252 trials (59.9%). An explicit Rome diagnostic version was identified in 278 trials (66.0%). Primary outcomes were specified in 417 trials (99.0%), with FD symptoms represented in 374 (88.8%). A named primary FD symptom instrument was identified in 166 trials (39.4%). A safety or adverse-event outcome was identified in 103 trials (24.5%), intervention duration in 149 (35.4%), and post-intervention follow-up duration in 15 (3.6%). CONCLUSION: Registered FD trials cover a range of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions, but the documentation of eligibility criteria, masking, symptom measures, safety-related outcomes, intervention duration, and post-intervention follow-up varies. Earlier registration and clearer reporting of these elements would help readers interpret trial designs and compare studies.

titre: Bioinspired nanozyme-exoskeletonized yeast-derived polysaccharides for treating comorbid anxiety and depression in inflammatory bowel disease
resume: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic condition frequently accompanied by psychological comorbidities, such as anxiety and depression. Although current treatments may alleviate some of these symptoms, the intricate pathogenesis of these comorbidities highlights an urgent need for therapeutic strategies with combined anti-inflammatory, barrier-reparative, and microbiota-modulating effects. Herein, we develop a series of nanozyme-exoskeletonized yeast-derived polysaccharides (NZEP) by integrating nanozymes with yeast-derived polysaccharides using an insect sclerotization-inspired strategy. Among them, NZEPTA-Ce, with the highest degree of nanozyme-exoskeletonization, is capable of disrupting the inflammatory vicious cycle by inhibiting MAPK and NF-κB-mediated inflammatory signaling pathways. Oral administration of NZEPTA-Ce in mice enables effective retention and accumulation in inflamed colonic regions, reverses the homeostasis imbalance of intestinal inflammation and promotes intestinal barrier repair. Furthermore, NZEPTA-Ce treatment reverses gut microbiota dysbiosis and optimizes the composition of microbial metabolites, thereby alleviating anxiety and depressive symptoms associated with IBD. This study provides a safe and promising therapeutic strategy for the management of IBD patients and their associated psychological comorbidities.

titre: Disrupted microbial queuosine biosynthesis contributes to dysbiosis in human inflammatory bowel disease
resume: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: As a microbiome/diet-derived vitamin, queuine (q) is a micronutrient that eukaryotes acquire from microbiota or diet. Vitamin q, the free base form of queuosine (Q), is used for Q-modification of transfer RNA (tRNA). Although tRNA-Q-modification in regulating eukaryotic cell physiology is recognized, the relationship between Q-tRNA-modification and the human microbiome in health and inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) remains unknown. Which bacteria produce q and how the q-producing bacteria contributing to human health and IBD are not explored. Here, we hypothesize that disrupted microbial Q-biosynthesis contributes to the dysbiosis of human IBD. We performed comprehensive multi-omics integrative analyses using publicly available datasets. Specifically, we re-analyzed publicly available shotgun metagenomic, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), metabolic datasets, and completed meta-analysis. METHODS: To systematically investigate microbial Q-biosynthesis in healthy individuals and IBD patients, we performed a systematic secondary analysis by integrating 9 publicly available metagenomic datasets, 15 scRNA-seq datasets and one metabolic dataset published prior to 2026. We present a novel secondary bioinformatic reanalysis of sequence outputs mapped to the latest microbial taxonomy, functional pathways and microbial Q-related genes. Longitudinal study of shotgun metagenomics across the human lifespan (3146 samples) enabled taxonomic and functional profiling. RESULTS: We first identified key q-producing bacteria (e.g., Bacteroides and Alistipes ) in healthy populations. We then found that patients with IBD had significantly reducation of q-producing bacteria and a coordinated downregulation of the Q-related pathways, including Q, preQ 0 , de novo guanosine ribonucleotide biosynthesis and de novo guanosine deoxyribonucleotide biosynthesis pathways. This functional impairment was primarily driven by reduced contributions from Bacteroides , Alistipes and Akkermansia . The longitudinal stability of the q-producing bacteria community across the human lifespan (1638 samples). We observed a significant negative correlation between host age and the abundance of q-producing bacteria in patients with UC. Moreover, Queuine tRNA-ribosyltransferase 1 (QTRT1) expression in human intestinal epithelial cells was significantly reduced in patients with IBD compared to healthy controls. CONCLUSIONS: Our study used multi-omics datasets to define a novel functional dysbiosis characterized by a reduction of microbial Q-biosynthesis in patients with IBD. Vitamin q and its tRNA modification is lesser-recognized in human IBD. Understanding the cellular and organismal mechanisms of this microbiome-dependent micronutrient will advance the prevention of IBD and improve the quality of life of patients with IBD. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC?: Queuine, vitamin q, is a highly conserved hypermodified nucleoside micronutrition could only be acquired from microbiota or diet. It is used for modification of transfer RNA to protein transitional fidelity, but the specific microbial pathways evolved and the relationship with IBD are unclear. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS: This study identifies a novel functional dysbiosis in IBD patients characterized by the depletion of q-producing gut bacteria (e.g., Bacteroides and Alistipes ) and the downregulated microbial Q biosynthesis pathways, which correlates with host QTRT1 deficiency to potentially drive IBD pathogenesis. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH PRACTICE OR POLICY: 1. Identifies the altered Q-biosynthesis pathway in human IBD. Establishes the "Microbial Q-synthesis-Host tRNA modification" axis as a novel mechanistic link, shifting human IBD microbiome research from taxonomic description to functional epitranscriptomics.Overcomes the inherent biases of traditional meta-analyses through a unified secondary bioinformatic reanalysis, leveraging HMP unified metabolic analysis network 3 (HUMAnN3)-based modeling of 3,000+ samples, to reveal a universal breakdown of the microbial Q-biosynthetic supply chain across all IBD subtypes.Recognize vitamin q as a critical gut-health micronutrient, influencing dietary guidelines and the regulation of functional medical foods for IBD management.
